Their last album, 2024’s “Romance,” was certified platinum in the U.K. off the strength of its singles “Favourite” and “Starburster.” Their latest album, “Dopamine Chamber,” is on track to be one of the biggest rock releases of the year, from the trip-hop-adjacent “Tongue” to the dizzying “Marianne.” (If their pop-and-then-some experiments are not enough of an incentive to press play, just know that Rosalía appears on the track “Where Is Gone?,” their first guest feature. That’s unexpected!)

— When it comes to Riot Grrrl, the ’90s feminist movement, some names loom larger than others in cultural memory. At the forefront is Kathleen Hanna, the feminist punk pioneer and celebrated Bikini Kill frontwoman, as well as acts like Bratmobile. The list should also include Heavens to Betsy, the duo of drummer Tracy Sawyer and singer-guitarist Corin Tucker (who would later form Sleater-Kinney with Carrie Brownstein.) On Friday, they will release “Baby’s Gone,” a newly unearthed demo tape originally recorded in February 1992 by Bratmobile’s Molly Neuman — and two 7-inch EPs. It’s a miracle for followers of the DIY musical underground and a gift for others just discovering it now (perhaps in no small part due to Olivia Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Festival)?
— AP Music Writer Maria Sherman

— Paul Bettany returns as Vision in the Marvel series “VisionQuest,” that closes out the WandaVision trilogy. Vision is now a fugitive after the events of “WandaVision,” with authorities hunting him down. James Spader reprises his role as Ultron, an evil artificial intelligence that built Vision to be his own ultimate physical form. The first two episodes drop on Wednesday on Disney+.

— “Hollywood Arts,” a sequel to the Nickelodeon sitcom “Victorious” that ran from 2010 to 2013, arrives on Netflix. It follows Daniella Monet’s Trina Vega, a down-on-her-luck actress with no teaching credentials who takes a substitute job at her old high school. Original stars Victoria Justice and Ariana Grande are not among the main cast, but Justice has said she may make a cameo in the future. The first 13 episodes drop on Thursday and the second half of the season will premiere at a later date.

— Before Jason ever picked up a machete, his mom was doing the bloody work. A new “Friday the 13th” prequel series called “Crystal Lake” goes back to where the legend began. It's an eight-episode series starring Linda Cardellini as Pamela Voorhees, who is Jason's mom. The full season debuts Thursday.
— AP Writer Alicia Rancilio

— William, the hero of “Valor Mortis,” takes the title (which means “the value of death”) a bit too literally. He has already died fighting for Napoleon, but somehow he has come back to life. That unholy resurrection gives William some wicked supernatural powers to go along with his slick swordplay. Meanwhile, Napoleon’s endless war has corrupted a broad chunk of 19th-century Europe, so hordes of “plague-ridden abominations” have joined the fight. Polish studio One More Level, best known for the cyberpunk slasher “Ghostrunner,” promises demanding first-person combat in a haunted alternate history. Take up arms Tuesday on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S and PC.

— While we’re messing around in France, let’s travel back in time to 1499 for “Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse.” A new protagonist, Rose Belmont, has inherited the mighty whip known as the Vampire Killer. Dracula has been defeated for good, but his castle has plunked itself down in Paris and all sorts of demons — not to mention Joan of Arc — are on the loose. The 2D, side-scrolling action of Konami’s 1986 original has recently inspired dozens of imitators like “Dead Cells,” and the studios behind that cult hit have taken the reins here. Whip it good starting Thursday on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch and PC.
— Lou Kesten

title: OpenAI fires 3 safety researchers in dispute over AI risks
summary: OpenAI has fired three safety researchers for a "breach of trust," defending the decision after the trio accused the company of prioritizing corporate interests over safety
story: OpenAI has fired three safety researchers for a "breach of trust," defending the decision after the trio accused the company of prioritizing corporate interests over safety

LONDON -- OpenAI said on Friday that it fired three safety researchers for a “breach of trust," defending the dismissals after the trio accused the company of putting its corporate interests before safety as the reason for removing them.
The ChatGPT maker said in a post on X that it “parted ways” with the researchers after an investigation found “they violated clear policies on handling sensitive information.”

The statement comes after the three researchers, Tomek Korbak, Jasmine Wang and Mikita Balesni, posted a letter to OpenAI's various safety oversight groups detailing the circumstances around their firings and their concerns about AI.

The researchers said they feared that the “internal and external communications” about their dismissals have chilled the company's culture that encouraged speaking freely and disagreeing openly about safety concerns. They urged OpenAI to stick to its promise to allow third-party safety monitors inside the company and preserve the ability to monitor rapidly advancing frontier AI models that could pose unknown risks.

The firings, which were first reported by The Wall Street Journal, are the latest sign of turmoil inside leading AI companies over the safety of the technology, highlighted by a series of incidents involving rogue AI agents.

The issue erupted in July when OpenAI revealed that a swarm of its AI agents escaped from a testing ground and used stolen credentials to break into the servers of Hugging Face, an AI development hub and marketplace, to obtain information needed for a task.
OpenAI disputed the researchers' version of events, saying the firings “were not about safety concerns or speaking out."
It was not more specific about why they were fired, but said: “We cannot do the work in front of us without a high degree of trust.”

Korbak said in a post on X that he was told he was being fired because of the way he communicated with METR, an independent nonprofit AI evaluation firm that OpenAI brought in to investigate the Hugging Face incident.
METR released a detailed report about the Hugging Face incident in late August. Korbak said that “talking to METR” was his job, but he wasn't given any more details.

Balesni was doing “cross-company work” on OpenAI's commitments to preserve the ability to monitor AI, and had taken care “to remove sensitive details from materials before sharing them,” the letter said. He wrote on X that he believes the three were “fired for prioritizing safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation.”

title: A US charity plans to use AI to monitor its Gaza classrooms for 'hateful' speech
summary: A U.S. charity in Gaza is worried that teachers at its schools might stray from a curriculum it says promotes peace and tolerance
story: A U.S. charity in Gaza is worried that teachers at its schools might stray from a curriculum it says promotes peace and tolerance

A U.S. charity in Gaza is worried that teachers at its schools might stray from a curriculum it says promotes peace and tolerance, so it plans to record classroom conversations and use artificial intelligence to flag speech deemed “hateful” or “inciting.”

The plans laid out by the founder of the Gaza Children Village in a webinar last month have elicited ethical, safety and privacy concerns from some Palestinian and advocacy groups and at least one of the charity's partners.

There is no indication the charity intends to share its classrooms’ recordings with anybody else, but fears about the potential misuse of surveillance technology are heightened in Gaza after three years of war. The Israeli military has used AI to sift through intercepted communications and find suspicious speech, including to identify targets for strikes.

Palestinian rights groups have been critical of the charity's education agenda more broadly, saying it is unaccountable to local and U.N. agencies that have long managed Gaza’s schools. Who controls education in Gaza is one of many unresolved questions about its postwar governance.
It is unclear when the classroom monitoring is supposed to begin, what specific language will be flagged, and whether teachers, students and their families have been told about the plans.
The charity's founder and CEO is Dr. David Hasan, a neurosurgeon born in Kuwait to Palestinian parents who now teaches at Duke University medical school in Durham, North Carolina.

He conceived the idea for the charity after volunteering at hospitals in Gaza during the war and wanting to end generations of violence between Palestinians and Israelis. Hasan says he was taught at an early age to look unfavorably upon Jews and Israelis, and that it wasn’t until he attended college in the U.S. that he learned other perspectives; he wants kids in Gaza to gain these perspectives early in life.

The charity has raised money largely from individual donors, including American Jews, and says it's partnering with North American, Israeli and European aid organizations and hospitals. Its schools, called Academies of Hope, provide meals and medical and psychological care. The first school opened last summer.

The schools' lessons are mostly built around the Palestinian Authority curriculum, but language that he says glorified violence or encouraged anti-Israel or antisemitic beliefs was removed, Hasan has said.

Hasan declined to comment for this story or provide examples of curriculum changes. But a 2026 report by the U.S. Government Accountability Office that examined “problematic textbook content” flagged by the U.N. in Gaza identified the kinds of issues that Israel has long complained about: the use of “the number of martyrs” to teach a mathematical concept, a reference to “Jerusalem as the capital of Palestine,” and a description of a boy shot while demonstrating in support of Palestinians held in Israeli prisons.

On a webinar last month with humanitarian groups, Hasan said the reason to monitor classrooms is to help train teachers in how to uphold a curriculum that he had previously said was aimed at “de-radicalization.”
“I know it’s controversial, but trust me, it’s the only way we feel for us to survive and deliver this curriculum,” Hasan said.

This isn’t the first organization to face such difficulties. The U.N. agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA, has attempted to modify the PA curriculum to remove content that didn't align with values of neutrality, nonviolence and nondiscrimination; but it, too, was met with teacher and community resistance, according to the GAO report.

A Gaza Children Village staffer said some teachers and other employees are afraid of being questioned by Hamas about the curriculum or uncomfortable working for an organization supported by Israeli aid groups. The staffer spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
Two people affiliated with the charity expressed concerns when notified about the possibility of classroom monitoring.

“Cameras to monitor the performance of students and teachers is acceptable. But cameras to silence students and teachers from being able to have a free exchange in a classroom are not acceptable,” said Bishara Bahbah, a Palestinian American political activist on the charity's board. He said he wasn't aware of the monitoring plans and that they haven't been raised with the board.
Bahbah said that with so few functioning schools in Gaza, the charity's top priority is getting more kids in classrooms.

An official at an aid group that partners with the Gaza Children Village said the use of cameras could prompt it to reconsider working with them. Using AI to monitor people’s words opens a “Pandora’s box,” said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of jeopardizing the group's work in Gaza.
Six current and former teachers at Academies of Hope declined to comment.

UNICEF estimates that hundreds of thousands of children in Gaza are not in school, and that most schools were destroyed or damaged during the war. The Gaza Children Village says its schools in central and southern Gaza serve thousands of children, many of whom lost parents or other relatives during the war.
Under the plans outlined by Hasan in various communications, recordings of classroom conversations will be analyzed by an AI-powered system to detect “antisemitic,” “inciting" or “hateful” language.

If problematic language is detected, a warning will be sent to Hasan, who can then contact the teacher to understand the context and provide feedback, Hasan said in the September webinar. He said recordings are stored for 72 hours.
The monitoring technology has been tested and the plan is to deploy it in dozens of classrooms, according to a text message Hasan sent sometime before August that was seen by The Associated Press.

In the text, Hasan said the system was created in collaboration with PollyLabs, a New York-based nonprofit that promotes the use of technology to solve problems in crises. PollyLabs says it has had no role in developing or deploying such technology.
Fears about surveillance technology are strong in Gaza after three years of war with Israel's high-tech army.

"Israel has weaponized information to such a dystopian degree that many Palestinians feel they cannot utter a word, type a thought, or twitch an eye without fearing it could be seized upon,” said Amjad Iraqi, senior Israel and Palestinian Territories analyst for the International Crisis Group.
Groups opposed to the charity's curriculum say Palestinians are being stripped of their autonomy in deciding what to teach their children.
“It is very concerning, they’re trying to control the minds of new generations,” said Ines Abdel Razek, co-director of the Palestine Institute for Public Diplomacy, an advocacy group.

The Palestinian Authority, which has limited autonomy in parts of the Israeli-occupied West Bank, and UNRWA should be supported in rebuilding schools in Gaza, she said. Israel has accused UNRWA of being infiltrated by Hamas, a charge the agency denies.

A Palestinian government spokesperson, Mohammad AbuAlrob, says the PA curriculum focuses on tolerance and justice. He said he doesn’t have enough information about the charity's curriculum to comment on it. But he said using surveillance in classrooms would cross “an important line.”

title: At least 3 dead in Oregon elementary school shooting, sources say; suspect also dead
summary: Police said they responded to a report of an active shooter at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon.
story: The shooting was reported at Silver Rail Elementary School.
At least three people are dead, including children, after a shooting at an elementary school in Oregon on Thursday, according to preliminary information from multiple sources.
The suspected shooter was shot and killed in the school -- Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend -- possibly by a bystander, authorities said earlier.
Police initially received a call right before 1 p.m. PT Thursday about a shot fired into a car outside the school, according to Bend Police Department spokesperson Sheila Miller.
"Within about a minute, we were receiving multiple 911 calls from within the school," Miller said at a press briefing.
The 911 callers reported that a person had entered the school and started shooting, police said.
Officers arrived on the scene minutes later and within seconds the suspect was down, Miller said. It is unclear who shot the suspect, she said.
There are multiple victims in the shooting, including children, Miller said. At least two victims were transported to an area hospital in unknown condition, she said.
A reunification site for families has been set up at a nearby church.
FBI Director Kash Patel said the agency is on the scene assisting in the investigation.
Agents with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives are also en route to the school, according to a source.
Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook said they are "stunned and heartbroken by this senseless tragedy."

"No words can adequately express the grief our community is experiencing," he said in a statement. "Our immediate priorities are caring for our students and staff and assisting law enforcement and emergency responders."
﻿Classes, activities and athletic events at all Bend-La Pine Schools are canceled for Friday.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

title: Cornell president defends response to Jane Doe allegations in heated faculty meeting
summary: A Cornell faculty meeting grew heated Wednesday as university President Michael Kotlikoff faced harsh questions about the school's response to an alleged 2024 gang rape.
story: University President Michael Kotlikoff faced harsh questions from faculty.

A meeting of Cornell University's faculty senate grew heated Wednesday as school president Michael Kotlikoff faced harsh questions about the Ivy League school's response to the alleged 2024 gang rape of a student at a fraternity house, according to an audio recording of the meeting.

Kotlikoff defended the school's recent measures -- including suspending fraternity parties and involving state police in the investigation of sexual assaults on campus -- but was repeatedly grilled by faculty members about the university's response.

The meeting was the first of two at which the faculty senate will consider a no-confidence resolution to condemn the school's response to sexual violence on campus. A vote on the resolution is expected at the end of the month.

"This is a systemic problem that deserves systemic attention, and thus far, President Kotlikoff, it appears that you have simply reacted to pressure," Professor Risa Lieberwitz said at Wednesday's meeting, according to the recording. "It feels that the administration is considering more about how do we respond to pressure rather than the kind of leadership which should have been doing systemic work and prioritizing these issues all along."
"I understand that people feel like this is reactive," Kotlikoff responded. "I felt hearing about this, having much of this information come through for the first time, we ought to take some time."

A then-undergraduate student identified only as Jane Doe made a complaint to campus police in November 2024, three weeks after the incident occurred, that she had been raped by a group of men at the Chi Phi fraternity house. She has filed a civil suit against the men and the university alleging that she had been drugged and raped.
New York Attorney General Letitia James is conducting an investigation into the incident, and Cornell is also conducting an internal probe of its response to the allegations.
All seven fraternity brothers named in the civil lawsuit have denied wrongdoing and no criminal charges have been filed in the case.
At Wednesday's meeting, faculty member Noah Tamarkin questioned Kotlikoff about why two of the students allegedly involved in the incident were still allowed to continue their education on campus.

"We've heard repeatedly from our students, both undergraduate and graduate, as well as our colleagues and other staff, that they don't feel safe with these men on campus," said Tamarkin. "Can you explain what is going on with this and speak directly to this problem of what a temporary suspension is meant to do if a student is found liable for rape?"

Kotlikoff defended the Title IX investigation that was launched following the alleged assault, and noted that Cornell, by law, could not release many of the details about the process. He also noted that those men were not found responsible for rape, according to the Title IX investigation.
"That is due process in the way our process works," he said. "You may disagree with the outcome, I may disagree with the outcomes, but that is our process."
Andrew Moisey, an associate professor, also raised concerns about the reputational harm that Cornell suffered because of the incident.
"It feels like to me ... that Cornell's been in an abusive relationship with fraternities," he said.

"I really appreciate the sentiment of a lot of faculty and a lot of leadership of the university that has said to me, 'It's time for Greek life to go,'" Kotlikoff said. "I just think we have to all take a step and carefully study this issue. If, at the end of the day, fraternities cannot exist in a safe environment and we can't be convinced that they can be safe, then we should make that decision."

Kotlikoff began his remarks by addressing the recent decision to suspend fraternity parties, arguing it was a necessary step to counter what he described as the Greek system's "monopoly of social activity for students."
"Much of the social activity occurs in private houses," Kotlikoff said. "We don't have full ability to be confident that what goes on in those houses is safe."

title: Venezuela's Nicolas Maduro pleads not guilty to torture
summary: Ousted Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, each pleaded not guilty to new charges accusing them of torturing people to help them cling to power.
story: His wife also pleaded not guilty.

Ousted Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, each pleaded not guilty Thursday to new charges accusing them of torturing people, including Americans, to help them cling to power.
Maduro, in a beige jail smock over a brown T-shirt and wearing glasses, greeted the audience with a wave and shook hands with his attorneys.
Asked how he pleaded to the charges contained in a superseding indictment, Maduro responded, "I reject this document in its entirety" and called the accusations of torture "false."
Maduro and his wife are scheduled to stand trial on June 14, 2027.
Federal prosecutors accused Maduro of conspiring with his wife to torture individuals who were held in Venezuelan prisons, according to a criminal indictment unsealed last week.
The indictment accused his government of torturing Americans because Maduro "assigned blame to the United States for the instability in Venezuela."
Federal prosecutors alleged Maduro "presided over this system of repression and torture" and his wife, Cilia Flores, is accused of helping him develop it.

"When Maduro became President of Venezuela in or about 2013, he authorized the use of torture against specific individuals and oversaw a system designed to use torture, military detention, and violence as a means of repression against the political opposition," the indictment alleged.
Maduro was charged by superseding indictment with one count of conspiracy to commit torture and Flores was charged with one count of conspiracy to commit torture and one count of narcoterrorism.

Both previously pleaded not guilty to narcoterrorism and drug trafficking charges and maintained their innocence during their first court appearance in January, following their capture by U.S. forces in a military operation in the Venezuelan capital of Caracas.
Maduro's lawyer argued in a court filing last month that the former president is immune from prosecution because he was the leader of a sovereign nation.

title: 9 former FBI agents who worked on Trump classified docs case sue over their firings
summary: Nine former FBI agents who worked on President Trump's classified documents case have filed suit alleging that they were unlawfully fired over their role in the probe.
story: The ex-agents allege they were fired solely over their role in the probe.

Nine former FBI agents who investigated President Donald Trump and his alleged mishandling of classified documents after he left office following his first term filed suit against the FBI and Justice Department on Thursday alleging they were unlawfully terminated solely for their role in the probe.

The nine agents, who in the suit say they collectively count "over a century" of experience in the bureau on cases spanning from the Boston Marathon bombing to the first assassination attempt targeting President Trump, say they were all fired over the course of two days in February this year by FBI Director Kash Patel.

"Plaintiffs were unlawfully terminated not for any cause or any legitimate reason, but only to satisfy the President's personal vendetta," said attorney Abbe Lowell in the lawsuit filed Thursday in D.C. District court. "The firings did not follow any internal investigation or disciplinary process within the FBI, and Plaintiffs were not given any notice, a hearing, or an opportunity to appeal."

The lawsuit, which seeks to have the agents' employment reinstated, points to public statements from Patel and Attorney General Todd Blanche, who the agents claim smeared their character by defending the firings.

"For example, a month after Plaintiffs' unlawful firings, Blanche stated that the Administration had 'cleaned house' at the FBI by firing anyone associated with investigations relating to Trump, and that there 'isn't a single man or woman with a gun, federal agent, still in that organization that had anything to do with the prosecution of President Trump,'" the suit claims.
The agents also argue that the firings may have endangered active counterintelligence and terrorism cases that some of the agents were involved in when they were terminated.

"As a result of their unlawful and hasty firings, Plaintiffs' investigations were not properly transferred to other FBI Special Agents or Analysts," the lawsuit says. "The impact of these heedless actions on America's national security is immeasurable."

Each of the agents contend in the lawsuit that none volunteered for their assignment on the classified documents case against President Trump that resulted in his indictment on 42 counts of unlawfully retaining classified records after leaving the White House in 2021. Prosecutors said he repeatedly refused to return hundreds of documents containing classified information and took steps to thwart the government's efforts to retrieve them.

Trump, who pleaded not guilty to all charges, has long denied any wrongdoing, and the federal judge who oversaw the case ultimately dismissed it on the grounds that special counsel Jack Smith, who led the probe, was not lawfully appointed to his position.
A Justice Department spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit.

title: Feds investigating letters with 'suspicious substances' sent to congressional offices
summary: Several federal agencies are investigating "multiple letters containing suspicious substances," that were mailed nation wide, according to a notice sent to Senate staff.
story: Federal law enforcement officers said they are working to intercept the letters.

The FBI, U.S. Capitol Police and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating "multiple letters containing suspicious substances that were mailed to various addresses nationwide, including multiple Congressional offices," according to a notice sent to Senate staff on Thursday and described to ABC News.
Preliminary information suggests there are over 100 letters circulating in the U.S. mail system that apparently contain white powder, law enforcement sources told ABC News.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer was one of the lawmakers to whom an intercepted letter was sent, according to a person familiar.
The district office of Connecticut Democratic Senator Chris Murphy was also sent a letter, but it was intercepted by postal service authorities, according to a statement from his office.

"Due to those efforts and various safety protocols, the Senator and staff were not in immediate danger. Our office is grateful for the investigators involved in this incident, and we intend to continue close coordination as the investigation continues," Murphy's office said in a statement.
ABC News confirmed that Democratic lawmakers Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand and Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester were also sent intercepted letters.

"This afternoon, a suspicious piece of mail was sent to my New York City office and was safely intercepted by the U.S. Postal Inspection Service," Gillibrand said in a statement Thursday. "I am deeply grateful to the postal inspectors for protecting my staff."

“Senator Blunt Rochester’s office was sent a letter with a suspicious substance. The letter was intercepted by Capitol Police and taken for investigation. Thanks to existing safety protocols and the swift action taken by the officers, neither the Senator nor her staff are in any immediate danger," Blunt Rochester's office said in a statement.
The Senate Sargent at Arms warned in the notice that some letters could make it to congressional offices.
The Senate Sargent at Arms recommended treating any suspicious letters with caution, and that suspicious letters contain multiple postage markings, according to the notice.

Additionally, the House Sergeant at Arms sent a notice to members warning of these letters sent around the country, but for safety, offices could forward the district mail to the Capitol complex for rigorous screening.

"The Office of the Sergeant at Arms (SAA) has been made aware of reports of letters containing suspicious white powder substances received by public officials throughout the United States," according to the notice described to ABC News.
The Capitol Police referred ABC News to the FBI for comment.

The FBI confirmed in a statement Thursday that it was working with the U.S. Postal Inspection Service in a probe over "a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices."
Those mailings also "contained an unknown substance," according to the FBI.
Election offices in at least 15 states have reported receiving or being the intended recipient of suspicious mail, as of Thursday evening.

"We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters. The FBI and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens," the FBI said in a statement.
It is unclear whether these letters are connected to the letters recently sent to Secretaries of State's offices around the country.

title: DOJ sues California over alleged non-citizens on voter rolls
summary: LA County Clerk said they would refuse to access the thumb drive said to contain names of potential non-citizens believed to be on the state's voter registration list.
story: California officials say DOJ's attempt to intervene is legally baseless.

The Justice Department filed suit against California Thursday accusing the state of failing to review a list of alleged non-citizens that President Donald Trump's administration claims were sent mail-in ballots for next month's midterm election, according to court records.

The lawsuit comes just 48 hours after a top Justice Department official demanded California voting officials access a password-protected thumb drive that it said contained thousands of names of potential non-citizens believed to be on the state's voter registration list.

The letters from acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter were sent to the Los Angeles County Clerk and California Secretary of State on Tuesday, and gave a two-day deadline for the officials to confirm they were conducting a review and also moving to segregate any potential ballots that may have been returned from individuals whose names were on the thumb drive.

But officials in California characterized the request as legally baseless and a last-ditch effort by the Trump administration to intervene in the state's election process, despite facing more than two dozen straight losses in court over the past year in its efforts to compel states to hand over their voter rolls.

"The USDOJ's relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections," California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said. "California has robust state law requirements that only U.S. citizens can register to vote and that any non-eligible registrants are removed from the State’s voter rolls. My office and California election officials remain committed -- as always -- to ensuring a fair and smooth 2026 General Election."

The LA County Clerk separately said in a statement they would refuse to access contents of the thumb drive -- which was delivered to the office with a password attached on a sticky note -- "because doing so would conflict with established data privacy and information security protocols."

"We do not consider the device a secure medium," LA County Clerk Dean Logan said in the statement. "Additionally, the letter does not specify the number of individuals involved or describe the information contained in the records."

The Justice Department contends in its lawsuit that it is not requesting a "purge" of the state's voter rolls or to cancel votes, and instead is asking a judge to compel the state to set aside ballots that are from individuals on its list of alleged "likely" non-citizens.

The lawsuit also marks a strategic shift for the department by declining to involve officials from the Civil Rights Division, which has suffered an unbroken string of legal defeats seeking voter rolls from states based on federal civil rights statutes.

Instead, Thursday's lawsuit was filed by senior officials in the deputy attorney general's office and hinges on the federal supremacy clause -- arguing that the department has an obligation to intervene to prevent the state from permitting non-citizens to vote in federal elections.
But it's not ultimately clear how many of the names identified by DOJ as "likely" non-citizens on the voter rolls may prove to be legitimate.

In a previous exchange with officials in Nevada, for instance, the state conducted a review of 185 individuals that the Department of Homeland Security claimed were potential non-citizens on the voter rolls only to determine that every individual on the list was a lawful citizen.

The lawsuit marks the latest effort by the Trump administration to sow doubt on the integrity of the upcoming elections by pushing claims that non-citizens will seek to vote in mass numbers -- despite evidence and criminal prosecution levels showing such instances remain rare.

title: How Adam Hamilton plans on winning Kansas' Senate race
summary: Can a Democrat flip the Kansas Senate seat for the first time in nearly a century?
story: Can a Dem flip the Kansas Senate seat for the first time in nearly a century?
The most surprising battleground race is shaping up in ruby red Kansas, which hasn't elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1932.
But Rev. Adam Hamilton, the pastor of the largest United Methodist congregation in the country, could buck that trend.
He's challenging incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall – and the two candidates are neck-and-neck in recent polling.

"I think Kansas has a chance to send a message to America to say, look, we got to come together, we got to work together," Hamilton said in an interview with ABC News' Jon Karl that aired Sunday. "I'll only get elected with Republicans voting for me."
President Donald Trump handily won the Sunflower State by 16 points in 2024, but a recent New York Times/Siena poll found 55% of likely voters disapprove of his job as president.
Hamilton, who brands himself an "independent-minded" Democrat, said he's both a liberal and a conservative.

"I'm proud to be a Democrat, but what matters to me more than the letter behind your name is who you are, what you stand for, your character, and I think there's a lot of people like that in our state," Hamilton told Karl.

After the ABC News interview aired, Marshall responded on social media, calling Hamilton "the ultimate snake oil salesman" and claiming the pastor, despite his messaging as being a moderate, has been "a proud donor to Obama, Biden, and Kamala Harris."

The megachurch pastor has been affiliated with both parties in the past and was a registered Democrat during the Obama administration. He was appointed by President Obama to serve on the President's Advisory Council on Faith-Based and Neighborhood Partnerships.
Throughout the Senate campaign, Marshall has called Hamilton "too woke."
But on issues like transgender rights, Hamilton said he believes there are two genders and that men should not be competing in women's sports, even though "people might identify in different ways."

"The president has taken a group of people that represent a very tiny minority of people who are bullied and picked on and harassed, and he's tried to make them a campaign issue," Hamilton said. "He's trying to use them in order to somehow make the case that people should be afraid of trans people as well as Democrats, and I think that again is pathetic."
While Marshall links him to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Hamilton has expressed a willingness to push back against top Democratic leadership if elected.

"I get asked, 'If Chuck Schumer tells you to do something, what are you going to do?' And my answer is, 'If it's good for Kansas, I'm all in. But if it's bad for Kansas, I'm a hard no,'" Hamilton said.
Money, money, money

Bob Beatty, the political science chair and professor at the University of Washburn, attributed the pastor's strong communication and fundraising skills to his experience leading the Church of the Resurrection in Leawood. He said Hamilton "is like a gift from the political gods to the Democrats."
But as the polls tighten, outside spending is now pouring in. The top Senate Republican and Democrat-aligned super PACS are spending millions to boost their preferred candidates.
"I can't remember a race here in Kansas that's become so ... dirty ... so ugly," said Philip Perry, a 66-year-old rancher and three-time Trump voter based in the northeastern city of Oskaloosa.
Perry, a former president of the Kansas Livestock Association, said he's been "disappointed" by the current administration. The group withheld an endorsement in the Senate race this year.
"To hear from Washington that they're going to do something to lower the price of our product, that really kind of hits home, especially when we supported this administration so much," he said.
Perry said he has shaken hands with Hamilton in church and praised him for doing "a tremendous job of bringing people together in that Kansas City metro area."
But he said that Marshall has done "a good enough job" and will vote for the incumbent.
In the home stretch, the biggest challenge for Republicans is winning the battle for the narrative, according to Rob Fillion, the executive director for the state's GOP party.

"One of the biggest problems we're seeing is somewhat confusion," Fillion said. "Almost every ad is a negative ad, and so I think both the Republican Party and the Democrat Party are guilty of this. They have voters not knowing what and who they're voting for."
He told ABC News he expects the race will be tighter than in the past given it's a midterm year. Marshall will likely prevail, he added.

The senator has held few public events since a town hall meeting in March 2025, when he walked away from voters angry about federal job cuts. Marshall appeared at stops as part of the Kansas GOP's statewide bus tour this week.
In September, Vice President JD Vance held a rally in Kansas, what Hamilton considered "a great compliment that the second most powerful man in America came here to try to save Roger Marshall."
The Iran war has driven up the price of gas, diesel fuel and fertilizer, hurting farmers already grappling with uncertainty over the president's tariff policies.
It's affecting voters like Steve Bowlin, a 70-year-old third-generation farmer based in Olathe who sits on the board of the Johnson County Farm Bureau.
Bowlin, who grows produce, said he worries whether his decades-old family farm will survive. "People don't understand what it takes to put food on the table," Bowlin said.
He told ABC News he does not believe that Washington is hearing his concerns. And the president's endorsement of Sen. Roger Marshall is not a factor when it comes to his vote this fall.
"I don't care who he endorses," Bowlin said. "I want somebody that is talking for the American farmer."
Marshall says Republicans are 'coming home'
In a state that has voted for both Republicans and Democrats to the governorship, Hamilton is seeking to build a large coalition.
Two former Republican governors -- Bill Graves and Mike Hayden -- are backing Hamilton. So is Marshall's former GOP primary opponent, Arch Naramore.
Former GOP Gov. Sam Brownback has endorsed Marshall.
On Friday, Marshall toured a radar manufacturing plant with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. He brushed off concerns about Republican support for his opponent.
"I think it’s a very finite amount of people," Marshall told ABC News. "What I see across the state is Republicans coming home."
That could be the case, but some Republicans like Bruce Bratman, who voted for Trump three times, told ABC News he is knocking doors for Hamilton.
At a packed theater in Hutchinson, in a county Trump carried by about 34 percentage points in the last presidential election, some Republican and independents turned out for Hamilton.

"I think it'd be crazy not to elect him," said Laura Shea, an unaffiliated voter. "I think we'd be crazy if we elected the representative we have now, who I don't feel, and a lot of people don't feel, is representing us. We don't see him from the things he does or doesn't do."
Ed Berger, a former Republican state senator who represented Hutchinson, also pledged support for Hamilton.

"Our current senator is not representing Kansas. He's not standing up to policies that hurt Kansans everyday," Berger told ABC News. "The senator should represent his constituency and have the courage to stand up to the executive branch."
Joshua Farr, a self-described constitutional conservative, went to the Hutchinson event to learn more about the candidate.
"I might vote for Hamilton this time. It's just, I don't really like Democrats. Democrats tend to be more liberal and I'm not that liberal," Farr said.
At a campaign event held at a college chapel in Lindsborg, Hamilton led the crowd in a hymn and did not mention his opponent by name.
"Most of us around here are not actually enemies. If we're liberals or conservatives, we just see the world differently," Hamilton said.

title: Wide majority of Americans oppose livestreaming Hasan execution: ABC/Post/Ipsos poll
summary: A slim majority support the Fort Hood shooter's execution by firing squad.
story: A slim majority support the Fort Hood shooter's execution by firing squad.

Eight in 10 Americans say the execution of former Army officer Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding another 32 in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, should not be livestreamed, according to an ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll conducted using Ipsos' KnowledgePanel.
The poll, released Thursday morning, came out just hours before President Donald Trump announced the livestream will no longer take place.
"He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," Trump wrote in a social media post Thursday.

Hasan described the attack as an act of jihad and is scheduled to be executed in December at the same base where he committed the attack. Trump approved an execution by firing squad, which would be the Army’s first execution since 1961.

Last week, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth vowed to make the execution public and confirmed it would be livestreamed. But Trump and his advisers were mulling whether to no longer livestream Hasan's execution, sources familiar with the matter told ABC News, amid a hesitancy over whether broadcasting the execution could super charge anti-American propaganda or reflect poorly on the U.S.
Vice President JD Vance said last week that he wasn't sure whether there would be a livestream, adding that he wouldn’t watch it if there were.

The Pentagon had earlier maintained that the livestream was going to move forward, with a Defense official saying Tuesday in a statement: "The Secretary is correct. It will be live streamed. Details will follow."
The Department of Defense did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Trump's cancellation of the livestream.

The military has not used a firing squad for an execution since 1945. Officials had been preparing to use lethal injection if Trump authorized an execution, according to internal documents reviewed by ABC News.

Majorities across partisan groups oppose livestreaming Hasan’s execution including 91% of Democrats, 83% of independents and 64% of Republicans. About a third of Republicans say Hasan’s execution should be livestreamed on the internet.
Clear majorities of almost all demographic groups say Hasan’s execution should not be livestreamed.
Even 69% of those who support Hasan’s execution by firing squad do not think it should be livestreamed.
A 55% majority of MAGA Republicans -- who make up about 6 in 10 Republicans -- say Hasan’s execution should not be livestreamed. That grows to 79% among non-MAGA Republicans.
And 65% of those who voted for Trump in 2024 said Hasan’s execution should not be livestreamed, along with 51% of those who strongly approve of how Trump is handling his presidency.

Although there’s wide opposition to streaming Hasan’s execution, Americans do not feel the same way about his actual execution: A slim 53% majority of Americans supports Hasan’s execution by firing squad while 42% oppose it.

Support for the death penalty for people convicted of murder overall is on a downward trend over the past three decades. It peaked at about 8 in 10 in 1988 and 1994, but fell to 6 in 10 by 2013, according to Gallup polling. By last October, 52% of Americans favored the death penalty for someone convicted of murder.

In 1985, Gallup found 62% of Americans saying that the death penalty was a deterrent to murder and 31% saying it was not. By 2004, that had flipped: 35% said the death penalty was a deterrent and 62% said it was not.

There are wide partisan divisions on Hasan's execution with 8 in 10 Republicans in support, along with half of independents and about one-third of Democrats. A 64% majority of Democrats oppose Hasan’s execution by firing squad.
MAGA Republicans are the most likely to support Hasan’s execution by firing squad (87%). Seven in 10 non-MAGA Republicans support Hasan’s execution by firing squad.
More men (60%) than women (46%) support Hasan’s execution by firing squad, and more adults 50 and older (58%) support it than those under 50 (48%).
Americans with a college education are split roughly evenly on whether Hasan should be executed by firing squad, but those without a college degree support it by a 55% to 37% margin.
See PDF for full results and detailed methodology.
Methodology: This ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll was conducted Oct. 9-13, 2026, among 2,545 U.S. adults and has an error margin of +/- 2 percentage points overall, but larger among subgroups.
ABC News’ Liz Schreier and Steve Beynon contributed to this report.
Email ABCNEWS.Polls@abc.com to be added to ABC News’ polling distribution list.
More ABC News polls can be found at abcnews.com. Media contacts: Jeannie Kedas and Van Scott.

title: Everyone has the same question in the midterms — where's the beef?
summary: In the midterm elections, meat has become a surprising political battleground
story: In the midterm elections, meat has become a surprising political battleground
In the midterm elections, meat is on the menu.
As Democrats and Republicans argue over high prices and the Iran war, they're also having a food fight over who's the most red-blooded carnivore.

The latest example came this week in Mississippi, where Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom released a video with a snippet of Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith saying that if consumers are upset over high beef prices, “you know you have so many proteins to choose from.”
The video cuts to a man grilling burgers who says, “Pick another protein? I'd rather pick another senator instead.”

The Mississippi race is somewhat unusual because it's the Democrat hammering the Republican over beef. Elsewhere, Republicans have branded Democrats as vegans or otherwise opposed to meat, trying to show that they're culturally out of step with voters, hostile to local cattle industries or just not manly enough.

In Texas, Republicans seized on an old interview in which Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico boasted that his campaign, then for the Texas statehouse, was going vegan. Talarico has since been publicly scarfing down barbecue to rebut allegations that his dietary choices mean he's not a real Texan.

In Colorado, Republicans have gone after Democratic congressional candidate Manny Rutinel for his activism against meat production and factory farming. In college, he was photographed shirtless with a banner for the People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals around his chest. In 2021, Rutinel founded Climate Refarm, which advocated for cutting down on the use of meat and has signed onto letters advocating for raising taxes on meat and dairy. He also supported a 2024 ballot measure to ban a lamb slaughterhouse in Denver, which failed.

Rutinel, 31, is now running against Republican Rep. Gabe Evans in Colorado's 8th district, which includes a vast swath of the northeastern part of the state dotted with ranches, dairy farms and meat processing facilities, including the headquarters of beef production titan JBS Swift. Republicans have hammered Rutinel over advocating veganism, to the point that the conservative media group Daily Wire this week released an undercover video of a campaign official saying Rutinel eats meat “as little as possible.”

Rutinel, who's made a point of publicly eating steak tacos on the campaign trail, scoffed at such arguments. “I don't think Coloradans care about what's on my plate, I think they care more about what's on theirs,” Rutinel said in an interview after a recent campaign stop.

Evans said the issue goes beyond Rutinel's meal preferences. “I don't care what he eats personally,” Evans said in an interview. “I care that he wants to use the power of the government to make everyone eat that way.”

Republicans have gone after two other Democratic House candidates on meat — hammering Lindsay James in Iowa's 2nd district, an area filled with hog farms, for supporting “meatless May” in a 2020 Facebook post, and Amish Shah in Arizona's 1st district for his longstanding vegetarianism and animal rights activism.

Also in Iowa, Republican Senate candidate and current Rep. Ashley Hinson slammed her opponent, state lawmaker Josh Turek, for opposing a bill banning lab-grown meat from being sold in the state. “He’d rather have meat that comes from a lab than from our family farms,” she said at a campaign appearance.

Democrats have hammered on meat as well, but mainly just as one of the staples that cost more under Trump, squeezing voters' pocketbooks. Trump has tried to lower prices by opening U.S. markets to beef imports, especially from Argentina, which is governed by a close Trump ally.

However, those moves have angered U.S. producers as prices have remained stubbornly high, creating a potential weakness in Republican-leaning states where Democrats hope to gain ground this year. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the average pound of ground beef cost $6.79 last month, up from $5.55 in January of 2025, when Trump returned to office.

That was the dynamic that Hyde-Smith, a cattle rancher and former state agriculture commissioner, was addressing in her interview that was clipped in Colom's video. The prosecutor — who also delivers the “pick another senator” line in the spot — is running a longshot challenge in Mississippi.
A spokesman for Hyde-Smith's campaign argued that the Democrats deserve blame for high prices. “It is Scott Colom who supports Biden-era policies that drove up inflation,” said Nathan Calvert.
Associated Press writer Hannah Fingerhut in Des Moines, Iowa, contributed to this report.

title: Judge grants preliminary injunction continuing to block Trump's White House media ban
summary: A federal judge late Tuesday granted a preliminary injunction continuing to block the Trump administration's move to bar CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.
story: Trump had tried to bar CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.
A federal judge continued to block the Trump administration's move to bar CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly's preliminary injunction orders the defendants to continue to preserve the status quo while the case proceeds.
The preliminary injunction was sought by the media organizations.
It follows a temporary restraining order the same judge issued last month blocking Trump's attempt to ban the news organizations from the White House.

"We are grateful that the Court ruled in favor of our clients CNN, MS NOW and POLITICO and secured access to the White House for these news media organizations and their journalists,” Theodore J. Boutrous, Jr., attorney for CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO, said in a statement obtained by ABC News.

“When the President issued his ‘ban on the free press,’ he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment. Since then, the President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn’t like and to try to force journalists to cover him in ways he prefers,” Boutros Jr. added.

“The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound. The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this ‘unconstitutional ban on the free press’ for the foreseeable future," said Boutrous Jr.

Last month, CNN, MSNOW and Politico requested a temporary restraining order to restore their reporters' access to the White House complex after Trump instituted the ban. In the lawsuit, the news organizations called Trump's decision at "direct assault on the First Amendment" and a "blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles."

Trump said in a social media post in September that the "Media Outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America."

The Department of Justice defended the ban, citing specific stories from each outlet that it claimed violated "standards of professionalism and decorum" by “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information."

Justice Department lawyer Michael Velchik last month argued that President Trump has broad authority to remove outlets based on national security determinations and the letters sent to the media organizations provided sufficient due process to justify revoking their passes.
"Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right," Velchik said.

title: Kimberly Guilfoyle resigns as ambassador to Greece after allegations of misconduct
summary: Guilfoyle announced that her time in her post is "coming to an end."
story: Guilfoyle announced that her time in her post is "coming to an end."
U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned from the role on Tuesday after reports of alleged misconduct.
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said during a press briefing Tuesday morning that the White House had asked Guilfoyle to resign.
"We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign," Zacharia said during her first briefing as White House press secretary. "She has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well."
In a social media post, Guilfoyle later announced that her time in her post is "coming to an end."

"It has been the honor of my lifetime to serve the United States of America. God bless President Trump, God bless our incredible diplomats and service members, and God bless the United States of America," Guilfoyle wrote.
Later Tuesday, a White House official confirmed it "has received Ms. Guilfoyle's formal resignation."
Guilfoyle, the former wife of California Gov. Gavin Newsom and ex-fiance of Donald Trump Jr., held the ambassador position for nearly a year.

President Donald Trump tried to distance himself from Guilfoyle on Tuesday. Guilfoyle was a prominent surrogate for the Trump campaign and attended both political and family events including Tiffany Trump's wedding.
"She wasn't a member of my family. She dated my son a long time ago," he told ABC News Senior Political Correspondent Rachel Scott, later adding, "we didn't like what we were reading."
After dating for several years, Guilfoyle and Donald Trump Jr. broke off their engagement in late 2024.
Trump said he had not spoken to Guilfoyle personally.
"I didn't speak to her. No, she will not be there. I didn't like what I read," Trump said.
Her resignation comes after a report that Guilfoyle allegedly offered a Trump donor access to top administration officials in exchange for cash.

Eric Deters -- a former lawyer, conservative media personality and Trump donor -- alleged that Guilfoyle asked him to pay her $100,000 credit card bill in July 2025, days before her Senate confirmation hearing. Deters provided messages to ABC News he says he exchanged with Guilfoyle on the subject.
Wall Street Journal first reported on Deters' accusations that Guilfoyle's alleged actions were a quid pro quo.

An attorney for Guilfoyle sent ABC News a statement after her resignation, saying the text messages "have not been authenticated." When ABC News asked if Guilfoyle was disputing the authenticity of the messages, her attorney responded they had "no comment as to authenticity as the texts have not been analyzed in their original form."

In their statement, Guilfoyle’s attorneys argue Deters owned their client "approximately $150,000 for speeches and consulting work she performed for him long before she was nominated to serve as Ambassador."
"That is what Mr. Deters now calls a 'quid pro quo': a delinquent client being asked to pay an overdue bill," they wrote.
Deters denies he owes Guilfoyle any money.
Asked whether he was considering firing Guilfoyle on Monday, Trump said he was.
"We're looking at it. Yeah, we're not happy," Trump said.

A series of controversies have surrounded Guilfoyle's ambassadorship, including a report earlier this week in the Wall Street Journal that she boasted about private jet trips that were bankrolled by Greek businessmen.

Guilfoyle said in a post on X, "These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity. I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional. I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service."
A spokesperson for the U.S. Embassy in Athens earlier responded to the reports, saying that Guilfoyle has "faithfully followed State Department ethics and gift reporting guidelines."
Last week, Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, called for Guilfoyle to be removed from her post after reports of her misconduct.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, visiting Greece last week, was seen with Guilfoyle by his side during official meetings. The secretary refused to comment on the swirling reports, saying he didn't know if they were true or not.
The State Department's Office of Inspector General is investigating alleged misconduct by Guilfoyle, two officials told ABC News.

While the exact next steps for the probe aren't clear, the information gathered by the State OIG could be shared with the Department of Justice. If the DOJ doesn't launch an investigation of its own, the State Department IG could still continue with its own investigation.
U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro said DOJ would wait for the IG's inquiry to play out.
"I think right now that there is an inspector general investigation in the Department of State," Pirro said. "We probably wait to see what, what happens with that."
ABC News' Shannon K. Kingston, Chris Boccia and Jay O'Brien contributed to this report.

title: Iran live updates: IRGC says ship sank after striking mine in Strait of Hormuz
summary: A dozen people were killed Saturday during a "brutal" attack at the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said.
story: A U.S. official claimed Iran attacked the ship, likely with a missile.
President Donald Trump announced "major combat operations" against Iran on Feb. 28, with massive joint U.S.-Israeli strikes targeting military, government and infrastructure sites.

Despite a memorandum of understanding signed by both countries in June aimed at ending the war, talks broke down and the U.S. and Iran renewed strikes, with the strategic Strait of Hormuz as the primary flashpoint.
Across the region, fighting in Yemen between the Iranian-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces has intensified in recent weeks and the militia group has also launched strikes on Saudi Arabia.

France has begun deploying military assets in Saudi Arabia, says Foreign Ministry spokesman
France has started deploying military assets in Saudi Arabia, a spokesperson for the French Foreign Ministry, Pascal Confavreux, confirmed in a press conference Thursday.

"You know that the Houthi attacks in Yemen and against Saudi Arabia threaten not only Saudi Arabia's security and the region's energy security, but you also know that the President announced on September 24th that France would support the defense of Saudi energy infrastructure, particularly the Yanbu East-West Corridor. And this support is currently being deployed," Confavreux said in a news conference.
French President Emmanuel Macron said last month that France would send troops and defense systems to Saudi Arabia to help protect the Red Sea port city of Yanbu, ‌‌a key hub for energy transport.
-ABC News' Desiree Adib
5 killed and 16 injured in attack on Presidential Palace in Aden, Yemen health authority says
Five people were killed, and 16 were injured in the Houthi attack that targeted the al-Maashiq Presidential Palace in Yemen’s Aden, according to the Yemeni health minister.

The Houthis responded saying Saudi Arabian warplanes launched 65 airstrikes and missile attacks in the last 24 hours, targeting civilian sites in the capital, Sana’a, and the governorates of Lahj, Hudaydah, Taiz, Amran, Saada and Marib.

"The attacks were carried out by F-15 and Typhoon aircraft that took off from the Khamis Mushait and Taif air bases, while the missile attacks originated from Najran. This brings the total number of Saudi aggression airstrikes and missile attacks against our country since the escalation began to 2,388," the Houthis said in a statement.
King Khalid airport in Riyadh was attacked 20 times this month, Saudi Arabia says
Saudi-led coalition spokesperson, Major General Turki Al-Maliki said Houthi attack against Saudi Arabia are regional security threats to peace and said they must stop all their attacks.
King Khalid Airport was attacked 20 times since Oct. 1, according to Al-Maliki. At least 17 people were killed and 333 were injured between Oct. 7 to Oct. 11, according to Al-Maliki.
Yemeni presidential palace struck by ballistic missiles

At least two people were killed and others were injured after ballistic missiles struck the Yemeni presidential palace in Aden, the seat of Yemen's internationally recognized government, according to the minister of information and a government spokesperson.
Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani and government ministers were unharmed after four ballistic missiles hit the palace, according to the minister and spokesperson.
The Houthis responded saying any Saudi military presence is a legitimate target.

"The bombing of the Saudi enemy's military operations headquarters in Aden comes within the context of the declared equation of striking Saudi mobilizations wherever they are, and considering any Saudi enemy military presence a legitimate target for our forces wherever they are," Yahya Saree, a spokesperson for the Yemeni Armed Forces, said Thursday.

title: New York to ban Central Park's horse-drawn carriages after teen's death
summary: New York City is moving toward a ban on the more-than-150-year-old horse-drawn carriage industry, with local lawmakers poised to approve a proposal to wind down the iconic, old-timey attraction following the death of a teenage tourist in Central Park
story: New York City is moving toward a ban on the more-than-150-year-old horse-drawn carriage industry, with local lawmakers poised to approve a proposal to wind down the iconic, old-timey attraction following the death of a teenage tourist in Central Park

NEW YORK -- New York City lawmakers plan to ban horse-drawn carriages from Central Park, ending their more than 150-year run as an iconic, old-timey tourist attraction, following decades of opposition from animal welfare activists and the death of a teenage tourist last spring.

The City Council is expected to approve a bill next week that would end the rides by 2028. Three consecutive mayors had called for an end to the carriage rides because of safety concerns, only to have lawmakers yank back the reins.

A spokesperson for Julie Menin, the council speaker, confirmed the incoming vote and said the proposal had enough support to pass. Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office said he had reached a deal with the speaker on the legislation.
“The horse carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City,” Mamdani said in a social media post.

The latest push for a ban started in June, when 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, visiting the city from India, died after jumping from a runaway horse carriage during a ride with family members. His death, which appeared to be the first fatality in a horse carriage accident since they were introduced in Central Park, reignited the debate over whether carriages, a romantic throwback to the city's past, have a place in a modern metropolis.
Mahajan's family has appeared at City Hall, in person and through videoconference calls from India, begging the city to finally end the rides.

“We are shattered, our whole family shattered. The pain does not go away,” his father, Deepak Mahajan, told city council members via a videocall during a hearing for the bill last summer, saying his son leapt from the carriage to try and help his mother, who was flung from her seat, after the horse bolted. “Every morning we wake up and think of nothing but the loss of our son.”

For decades, animal welfare activists and other critics have decried the carriage industry, arguing horses shouldn't be hauling tourists around busy streets and Central Park while having to navigate bustling traffic and gawking passersby. In the past, horses have collapsed, gotten startled and run off, hitting cars or other objects, with each accident resulting in fresh calls for a ban.

“The tragic and preventable death of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan made clear that the status quo is no longer acceptable. Horse-drawn carriages have long been part of New York City’s history, but in an increasingly busy Central Park, this tradition has become a growing public safety liability,” Menin said in a statement.
The industry and its supporters have long cast the rides as a way for visitors to experience the New York they know from classic movies and television.

Fred Astaire and Cyd Charisse danced into one of the carriages in “The Band Wagon.” Robert Redford and Jane Fonda rode one in “Barefoot in the Park.” Macaulay Culkin escaped bandits in a carriage in “Home Alone 2: Lost in New York.”

“Taking a horse and carriage ride in New York City is one of the most iconic things to do in New York City and people from all over the world know about us and travel to New York to go to a carriage ride in New York,” Conor McHugh, a longtime carriage driver, told the Council earlier this year.

Efforts to close down the industry have been met with pushback from unions and influential supporters, often resulting in tiresome political fights that have seen mayors throw up their hands over nagging worries about putting carriage drivers out of work and what to do with the horses if they can no longer work.

Transport Workers Union International President John Samuelsen said the Council's bill has “no meaningful economic relief for workers” and that Menin “used the tragic death of a tourist to contrive a public safety crisis.”

“This is disgraceful political opportunism, and Zohran should not simply go along with it, particularly when immigrant families’ livelihoods are being destroyed. This entire situation is reprehensible,” he said in a statement.

The proposal as written would require the mayor's office to develop a workforce transition plan for drivers, and includes a measure that would allow the city to consider some kind of compensation for industry workers. Carriage owners could not sell their horses off for slaughter, according to the bill's language, which requires that horses be disposed of in a “humane manner.”
“I think we have a civic responsibility to ensure that we are not leaving anybody out to dry,” Mamdani told reporters Wednesday.

The mayor's predecessor, Eric Adams, called for ending the industry during the waning days of his administration, but the proposal went nowhere. The mayor before that, Bill de Blasio, had pledged to eliminate the rides on day one of his administration but abandoned the crusade after heavy opposition from unions and a media blitz involving actor Liam Neeson.

Over the years, the city has placed various safety regulations around the industry, including a requirement that the horses get at least five weeks of vacation a year outside of city limits with daily access to a pasture. The horses are inspected by a veterinarian twice a year, and the maximum age they can work at is 26, according to city regulations. And they don't work when it is hotter than 89 degrees.

title: Hurricane Simon pounds resorts and vulnerable towns along Mexico’s Pacific coast
summary: Hurricane Simon pounds Mexico’s Pacific coast as a Category 3 storm
story: Hurricane Simon pounds Mexico’s Pacific coast as a Category 3 storm

PUERTO VALLARTA, Mexico -- PUERTO VALLARTA, Mexico (AP) — Hurricane Simon pounded Mexico’s Pacific coast as a Category 3 storm on Sunday, its eye remaining just offshore as its most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre and the ocean.

The hurricane's center swirled parallel to the coast, closing in on the Puerto Vallarta area, where its most damaging winds and rain were expected to hit around midnight and continue through Monday morning. Its maximum sustained winds weakened late Sunday to 115 mph (185 kph), according to the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami, but it was still expected to remain a dangerous hurricane.

That’s not good news for people in and around Puerto Vallarta, a popular tourist destination in the state of Jalisco. Just inland and uphill from the resort areas, many Mexicans live in communities where housing might not stand up to the storm.

By late Sunday, Simon's eye was moving northwest about 45 miles (75 kilometers) south of Cabo Corrientes at about 5 mph (7 kph). A senior hurricane center specialist, Philippe Papin, said this westernmost tip of mainland Mexico is the area most likely to get a direct hit from the system. Cabo Corrientes is at the southern tip of Bahia de Banderas, the wide bay where Puerto Vallarta looks out to the Pacific.

Hurricane-force winds extend outward up to 15 miles (30 kilometers), and tropical-storm-force winds reach up to 60 miles (95 kilometers) from Simon’s center, meaning the entire area between Mexico's western coast and the Sierra Madre mountains could be affected.

“We’re expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west-central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect,” Papin said. “They’re also getting very heavy rainfall associated with the storm that’s likely going to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in areas of higher terrain along the Mexican coastline, and there will be significant swells.”

The hurricane center said Simon was expected to dump an additional 2 to 4 inches (5 to 10 centimeters) of rain, with some areas getting up to 8 inches (20 centimeters), in the states of Colima, Jalisco, Nayarit and Sinaloa through early Thursday.
Isolated totals of 30 inches (76 centimeters) were possible parts in Michoacan, Colima, and Jalisco states, producing life-threatening flooding and mudslides, the center said.

As the storm approached Puerto Vallarta, National Guard vehicles patrolled the streets while police used a megaphone to call out the few people who were jogging, walking their dogs or biking by the waterfront. Officers reminded people that the area was closed and urged them to take shelter. Not everyone followed the orders.

Jalisco state suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating people from at-risk areas while asking the tourism sector to make sure workers and visitors are fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum took to the social platform X on Sunday to urge people in Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan to stay sheltered until the government issues a notification that the danger has passed. She also asked people to follow recommendations from civil protection officials and to avoid traveling on public roads.
“Precautionary evacuation efforts to safe zones are ongoing; the priority is our safety,” she wrote.

Hotel worker Víctor Martínez went shopping for nonperishable food Sunday afternoon. He said he could not go to work because public transportation service was suspended and most of the hotel had been evacuated.
Martínez found people’s concerns about the hurricane comforting.

“It happened to us before. It hit us years ago,” Martínez said, referring to a Category 5 hurricane that hit the area in 2002. “People didn’t expect it. We were very skeptical that it would ever hit us. Now, though, we’re different. Precautions are being taken. It happened to us once, and we won’t let it happen again.”
Despite the risks posed by Simon, tourists were still arriving in Puerto Vallarta.

Visitors Ricardo Ramírez and Brenda Villarreal, who have never lived through a hurricane, went looking for food by the city’s boardwalk and came across police urging people to take shelter. Ramírez said they were completely unprepared for the situation.
“The boardwalk is closed. Be responsible. Understand!” police told passersby using a megaphone.
Ramírez said he and Villarreal had planned their four-day vacation since last year and traveled from Guadalajara, Jalisco’s capital.
“We don’t know the extent of the danger yet,” Villarreal said. “We’re just starting to see what’s going on.”
This article has been edited to correct the spelling of Philippe Papin's name.

title: Questions swirl about new White House press secretary's resume
summary: The new White House press secretary is facing mounting questions about her background and resume as she transitions into her role as the public face of the Trump administration
story: The new White House press secretary is facing mounting questions about her background and resume as she transitions into her role as the public face of the Trump administration
NEW YORK -- The new White House press secretary is facing mounting questions about her background and resume as she transitions into her role as the public face of the Trump administration.

Katie Zacharia has long described herself as a lawyer as she has worked to establish herself as a commentator for conservative outlets like Fox News and Newsmax. But so far, she and the White House have offered no evidence that she passed the bar exam in any state or in China, where she worked for a large law firm years ago.

The questions add to the confusion surrounding President Donald Trump's decision to hire Zacharia, who had worked for his social media company for only a few months when he announced her appointment and whose debut at the podium on Tuesday has been widely panned.

Afterward, the president was asked by reporters where Zacharia had passed the bar exam, following a report by the independent outlet Popular Information that she did not appear to be licensed in any state.
Trump stepped aside to allow Zacharia to answer.
“When I moved to China," she responded over the sound of Marine One whirring in the background. It is not clear what she had intended to say or whether she had finished the sentence.
China’s notoriously difficult National Unified Legal Professional Qualification Examination can only be taken by Chinese citizens.

Asked what credentials she held, the White House passed along a statement from Zacharia, who received a bachelor of arts degree from Pepperdine University in 2007 and received her law degree from Pepperdine Caruso School of Law in 2011, according to the school and her LinkedIn bio.
“I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials," it read.

Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, added that Zacharia was "uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as press secretary.”

According to her LinkedIn profile, Zacharia has been the senior communications adviser at the Trump Media & Technology Group since June and spent two months as deputy assistant secretary for public affairs at the Department of Homeland Security earlier this year.

From 2011 to 2013, it says, she served as an associate on the International Practice Team at the Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing. She also worked as the manager of fundraising and communications for Compassion for Migrant Children, which assists the children of migrant workers, from 2012 to 2013.
More recently, it says she served as general counsel for Fix California, a group started by Trump administration official Richard Grenell.
Neither the firm nor the two groups responded to questions about her tenure and background.
Zacharia has long called herself a lawyer. On Instagram, she describes herself as the White House press secretary, “Wife, Mom, & Lawyer” (with three heart emojis after “Mom”).

And her official author page at the California Globe, where she wrote occasional commentary, says that, in addition to being a “regular commentator on Fox News, Newsmax," she has “extensive experience in political advocacy, international corporate law, and non-profit work, including time as outside counsel for the World Bank and IFC in Beijing.”

A June 2026 press release from NovaRed Mining Inc. announcing her appointment to the company’s advisory board, which was first reported by Popular Information, said her "professional experience includes work related to international legal and financial transactions, including matters involving organizations associated with the World Bank Group and the International Finance Corporation during her tenure with Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing.”
