title: Justice Department sues California over noncitizens getting ballots
summary: The Justice Department sued California, alleging that the federal government has identified more than 20,000 noncitizens who are unlawfully registered to vote.
story: Washington — The Justice Department sued California on Thursday, alleging that the federal government has identified more than 20,000 noncitizens who are unlawfully registered to vote.

The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, came after Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter sent letters to counties earlier this week, including Los Angeles, ordering them to review a list of names of suspected noncitizens who he alleged received mail-in ballots for the upcoming midterm elections.
"State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement announcing the lawsuit.

"If found responsible in a court of law, the State of California will have seriously undermined confidence in our electoral system and violated laws that protect our nation's representative system of government."

In the letter that McCotter sent to the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk, he enclosed a password-protected thumb drive that he said contained names compiled by the Department of Homeland Security, and imposed a 48-hour deadline for the clerk's office to review the list.

Dean Logan, the registrar-recorder and clerk, said in a statement responding to McCotter's demands that the county would not be reviewing the materials on the thumb drive because doing so would conflict with "established data privacy and information security protocols." He said the device was not considered a "secure medium."

Secretary of State Shirley Weber, meanwhile, said the Justice Department had not provided the list of names and blasted the Trump administration for what it said were "unsubstantiated claims" that California had 190,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls.
In Thursday's lawsuit, the Justice Department accused the state of failing to work with the federal government to correct the alleged problems with its voter rolls.
"The Federal Government asked California to work collaboratively to identify any noncitizens registered to vote in the State. California made no serious effort to do so," the lawsuit said.

"The United States thus seeks commonplace election relief when a ballot is called into question. This Court should enjoin California from presently tabulating vote-by-mail ballots from likely noncitizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter's citizenship status can be determined," it added.

In a statement provided to CBS News, the California Secretary of State's office said, "Due to the pending litigation, we have no further information we can share regarding the matter." It directed CBS News to its news release on the situation and Weber's letter to McCotter.
CBS News has also reached out to the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk for comment.

The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division has filed 31 lawsuits in an effort to force states to hand over unredacted copies of their voter rolls. The division has said it wants to ensure states are keeping clean voter lists, but it has since acknowledged that it also intends to share the data with the Department of Homeland Security so that the lists can be screened for noncitizens.

Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division, sent letters to all 50 states in July threatening to take criminal action if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls.
So far, the Justice Department has lost 26 of those cases, and has not achieved one legal victory to date.
It has resorted to using publicly available voter lists and other investigative means to try to identify noncitizens who may be registered in those states.

title: Kristi Noem no longer serving as Trump envoy to Shield of the Americas
summary: Former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem is no longer serving as the Trump administration's envoy to the Shield of the Americas initiative, a State Department official said. She is still at the department.
story: Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem is no longer serving as the Trump administration's special envoy for the Shield of the Americas initiative, a State Department official said Thursday, though she remains involved in the administration's efforts to coordinate security cooperation across the Western Hemisphere.

"Kristi Noem's envoy status expired last month and she is no longer in the role," a State Department official told CBS News Thursday. "She is now a senior advisor to Deputy Secretary Landau and continues to work on the Shield of the Americas portfolio."

The Shield of the Americas is a coalition made up of the United States and several Caribbean and Latin American countries established by the Trump administration earlier this year to cooperate on economic matters, anti-cartel enforcement and other issues.
Noem's envoy designation expired just before the United Nations General Assembly last month in New York, where she continued participating in diplomatic meetings connected to the initiative.

On Sept. 22, she met with Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa, whose government publicly identified her as the special envoy for the Shield of the Americas. She also attended a gathering of Shield of the Americas leaders hosted by President Trump, where he publicly acknowledged her work.
"I want to thank Kristi Noem for doing a really terrific job," Mr. Trump said during his remarks.

Noem was appointed special envoy for the Shield of the Americas in March, after she was removed as homeland security secretary amid mounting scrutiny of her management of the department and the influence of her adviser, Corey Lewandowski.

Her transition to the envoy role coincided with a five-country tour of Latin America and the Caribbean in March, much of which took place as she completed her tenure as homeland security secretary. Lewandowski appeared in photographs during those visits, though the State Department later clarified he had no formal position at the department.

Her public activities in the envoy role appear to have been limited, and included meeting Noboa in Quito on March 25, holding discussions with Ecuadorian and Colombian diplomats in Washington in September, and participating in meetings with regional leaders on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.
This story published first on CBS News at 5:00 p.m. on Oct. 15, 2026.

title: White House's Katie Zacharia confirms she never passed bar exam
summary: The White House described Katie Zacharia as "uniquely qualified" to be the new press secretary.
story: Washington — White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said Thursday that she never passed the bar, although she's called herself a lawyer and President Trump has referred to her as an attorney.

Zacharia made the comment in an interview with conservative commentator Jack Posobiec after the Wall Street Journal  reported that she failed the bar exam in California in 2011 and did not pass the bar in any other U.S. state in which she's lived. Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine University's law school.

Zacharia told Posobiec she took the bar exam in California but didn't pass, saying she was distracted by her plans to get married and move to China for her husband's work around the same time. She said she "didn't think much" of the results, and said she didn't need to pass the exam to do her work in China.

Zacharia also said she never described herself as an "attorney at law," and said there's a "lot of misinformation around the fact that I labeled myself a lawyer." She said she consulted with multiple experts.
"I was very careful how I executed this. I never came across as someone who was an attorney at law," Zacharia said.

Earlier this week, as President Trump was departing for a trip to Alaska, when reporters asked her where she had passed the bar exam, Zacharia responded, "I went to China," sparking confusion about her law background.

A White House official said Zacharia earned her juris doctor from Pepperdine, which the university confirmed to CBS News. The White House official said Zacharia then moved to China with her husband for his job at an American private equity firm, while she worked on international transaction law.

Zacharia told CBS News in a statement Thursday she "practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials," although it's not clear which credentials she meant. Only Chinese nationals may take the bar exam in China.
On Fox News in April, Zacharia said she "lived in Beijing as a corporate lawyer for three years."

Zacharia's Instagram bio also says that she is a lawyer. On Truth Social, Mr. Trump called her "a distinguished Graduate of Pepperdine University, and the Pepperdine Caruso School of Law, an attorney."

But whether it's true that she can say she's an attorney or lawyer is being disputed — and it's a question Zacharia has considered. She told The New York Times that as she was beginning to appear on cable news, she talked with Pepperdine's president about how she could describe herself. The Times said, "She said she was warned not to use the words 'attorney" or 'esquire,' but that 'lawyer' was OK."
But CNN on Thursday reported that Zacharia shared at least 15 social media posts identifying herself as an "attorney" over the last two years.
The White House said Zacharia is "uniquely qualified" for the White House press secretary role.

"Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team," White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement to CBS News. "She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary."

On Wednesday, the Campaign for Accountability, a liberal nonprofit watchdog, filed a complaint with the State Bar of California, questioning whether she had violated California law in referring to herself as a lawyer without having passed the bar. She had been living in California with her family until she became White House press secretary.

The Campaign for Accountability pointed to California Business and Professions Code Section 6126, which says, "Any person advertising or holding himself or herself out as practicing or entitled to practice law or otherwise practicing law who is not an active licensee of the State Bar, or otherwise authorized pursuant to statute or court rule to practice law in this state at the time of doing so, is guilty of a misdemeanor."

"Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson, yet it seems it was all a lie," Campaign for Accountability executive director Michelle Kuppersmith said in a statement. "In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn't puffery; it's a crime. The State Bar should investigate whether Ms. Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials and hold her accountable if she has."
Cheung blasted the left-leaning ethics group.

"This group that filed the 'complaint' is a radical leftist-organization run by rabid numbskulls suffering from a severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome," Cheung posted to X. "Nobody takes them seriously because they are deranged low lifes."
Nora Freeman Engstron, a law professor at Stanford Law School, said the language in California's law isn't ambiguous or unclear.

"California law is crystal clear: You can't hold yourself out as a lawyer unless you're authorized to practice law," she told CBS News. "And the law doesn't just prohibit the unauthorized practice of law. It also prohibits the unauthorized pretense of being a lawyer."

"California law doesn't just prohibit people from practicing law without a license," she added. "It also prohibits them from pretending they're entitled to practice law. You don't have to set foot in a courtroom or represent a single client to run afoul of the statute."

title: Ousted general warned of missile defense shortage before Iran war
summary: Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George, later ousted by Defense Secretary Hegseth, said the shortage of missile defense munitions would extend into 2030.
story: Washington — In late December, two months before the U.S. war with Iran began, Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George warned that his service was critically short on missile defense munitions and that the shortage would last another five years, according to multiple U.S. officials familiar with the matter. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ousted George in April, as the Iran war was underway.

George's risk analysis appeared in the Pentagon's Global Force Management Allocation Plan, a defense secretary-approved annual order determining where  troops and weapons will be allocated across the globe, according to the U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News.

He warned that the stockpile of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense batteries and Patriot missiles would continue to be strategically low until 2030. His assessment was written for the Defense Department's plan for fiscal year 2027 and before the outbreak of the U.S.-Israel-led war with Iran, now in its seventh month.

U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News under condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly said his assessment stemmed from the transfer of Patriots to Ukraine after Russia's invasion in 2022, the expenditure of munitions to defend Israel, and the reduced capacity of the defense industrial base.

CBS News is withholding the exact percentage figures conveyed by U.S. officials because of security concerns, and George declined to comment. U.S. officials say  that while the U.S. possesses a significant stockpile of some offensive munitions, like the Joint Direct Attack Munition and Small Diameter Bombs, missile defense munitions used in Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, batteries, and Patriot missile systems are at low strategic-risk levels.

The THAAD system is one of the U.S. military's most advanced missile defense systems, designed to intercept and destroy incoming ballistic missiles during the final phase of their flight, either inside or just outside Earth's atmosphere. The Army has eight THAAD batteries. Each battery consists of 90 soldiers who operate six truck-mounted launchers, with each truck possessing eight launchers. A full battery controls 48 interceptors, according to a 2025 report from the nonpartisan Congressional Research Service.

The Patriot air-defense system is designed to protect military installations, troops and other critical infrastructure from incoming ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as hostile aircraft. It can engage a broader range of aerial threats at lower altitudes than a THAAD battery, but when used together, they provide even more effective overlapping layers of defense against missile attacks.

The Patriot munition at a critical low is the Patriot Advanced Capability-3, or PAC-3, a high-velocity surface-to-air interceptor designed to destroy incoming tactical ballistic missiles and cruise missiles by ramming into them. PAC-3s can also bring down enemy aircraft, according to U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News.

"Those are the two Army munitions that would be most heavily used in a conflict with China," said Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel and CSIS Defense and Security senior adviser. "You're not gonna use that many Javelins, for example, because the amount of ground combat is going to be relatively limited, even artillery will be limited, but air defense — missile defense — that will be huge."

An April estimate from the Center for Strategic and International Studies showed that it currently takes defense contractors four years and five months to complete delivery of new THAAD interceptor contracts. Patriot PAC-3 interceptor orders have an average delivery time of three and a half years.

CSIS' estimate said that before the Iran war, the U.S. entered 2026 with roughly 2,300 or so Patriot interceptors and expended between 1,050 and 1,430 during the conflict, potentially consuming as much as 61% of its prewar inventory. Fewer than 500 replenishment munitions were expected to be delivered in fiscal year 2026.

The stockpile for THAAD systems prior to the Iran war sat at around 355 interceptors, with the Iran war using between 190 to 290, or about 82% of its prewar inventory, according to CSIS. There were no expected deliveries for replenishment in fiscal year 2026. In the current fiscal year — 2027 — the U.S. has requested more than 800 THAADs.

Two of the nation's largest defense contractors — Lockheed Martin and RTX, through its Raytheon business — are involved in manufacturing these systems and their key components. They've recently signed agreements aimed at accelerating production.
In January, Lockheed Martin announced a plan to quadruple the production capacity of THAADs from 96 to 400 interceptors per year.

While the war with Iran has caused missile defense munitions to be depleted at a much higher rate, decades of Pentagon spending decisions, a shrinking defense industrial base and successive military operations that consume weapons faster than manufacturers can replace them have contributed to the current shortages.

One U.S. official told CBS News that even if the United States could avoid expending additional THAAD or Patriot munitions in Iran or in other conflicts, it would take until the midterm elections of the next presidential administration — 2030 — to replenish the stockpile to the already-low December 2025 levels.

Contacted by CBS News, Pentagon chief spokesman Sean Parnell said, "Claims of U.S. munitions shortages are false. When the Fake News media irresponsibly amplifies these lies, the real-world consequences is clear: our enemies are emboldened to provide — or attack — American troops."
He added that the U.S. still has  "everything required to strike at the time and place of the President's choosing."
"Across multiple combatant commands," Parnell said, "we have already executed successful operations while maintaining a deep, ready arsenal to defend our people and our interests."
How munitions are used around the world

The U.S. military is divided into 11 unified combatant commands, each responsible for either a region of the world or specialized military mission. For operations against Iran, U.S. Central Command, led by Navy Adm. Brad Cooper, is in charge.

Each combatant command needs a certain number of troops and weapons. The Pentagon uses a framework known as Global Force Management to decide where American troops, their units and some of the military's most sought-after weapons are sent around the world.
The Global Force Management Allocation Plan, or GFMAP, is at the center of the process, laying out which forces will be provided to combatant commanders, for what missions and for how long.

The plan is typically organized around the federal fiscal year. Generally, the Pentagon enters a new fiscal year with an existing plan for many of the forces expected to deploy or remain deployed during the coming 12 to 24 months, rather than deciding from scratch each time a commander asks for troops or weapons.
But the plan is not set in stone. Wars erupt, crises develop, missions end and commanders are faced with unanticipated events to address.

For instance, the commander of U.S. European Command might want more Patriots in Poland at the same time that U.S. Central Command wants those same resources in Kuwait, while U.S. Indo-Pacific Command may also need the systems for contingencies involving China.

There's a constant shuffling of troops and assets from one region to another — in one instance in April 2025, Adm. Samuel Paparo, the commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, told the Senate Armed Services Committee that the Army had transferred a Patriot battalion from his region to U.S. Central Command amid ongoing fighting with the Iranian-back Houthi rebels in Yemen.
What led to the current weapons systems shortage?
After the collapse of the Soviet Union, American military planners abandoned the assumption that the U.S. might need to fight a prolonged war against another superpower, explained Cancian.

"After the Cold War, we planned on fighting short regional conflicts against countries like Iraq or North Korea. And for those countries we didn't need the large inventories that we had needed during the Cold War," Cancian said. "We needed much smaller inventories."

He added: "We shrank the industrial base. There was the famous 'Last Supper' which was literally a dinner that the deputy defense secretary put on for the heads of the defense industry, and he told them there's not enough money to keep you all in business, so you're going to have to consolidate or move out of the business, which they did."
The resulting mergers reduced the number of major aerospace and defense contractors from 51 to five, according to the CSIS analysis.

Also, historically, the Pentagon's procurement decisions have reduced spending on ammunition and missiles to free up money for fighter jets, tanks and warships, even while acknowledging that those weapons are essential to war fighting.
Cancian told CBS News that the consolidation of the defense industrial base shaped an industry that produces efficiently during peacetime but is not designed to surge production.

"We squeezed all the surge out because it was seen as unnecessary. So, that's where we end up when the war in Ukraine begins," said Cancian. "And after six months or so, we realized that we just don't have enough munitions and equipment for a protracted conflict."

Under the Biden administration, there was a renewed interest in building surge capabilities back into the defense industrial base but that would take time. As the war between Russia and Ukraine began in full, the U.S. transferred roughly 600 Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine. However, not all of those weapons came from American military stockpiles; some were manufactured through the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative or provided by European countries.

Additionally, both Biden and Trump administrations used Patriot and THAAD missile interceptors to defend Israel against Iranian strikes. Six months before Gen. George's warning assessment, U.S. forces fired roughly 150 THAAD interceptors and almost 80 Patriot interceptors during the Twelve Day War.

Cancian noted that the five-year timeline to bring Patriot and THAAD stockpiles just to the low pre-Iran war levels is based on the assumption that the production schedule stays on track — and that additional military operations do not further deplete the inventory.

title: Judge finds Musk, Noem targeted ex-FEMA official
summary: A federal magistrate judge said Elon Musk and former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem knowingly spread false information about Mary Comans, the former CFO of FEMA.
story: Washington — A federal judge on Tuesday found that billionaire Elon Musk and former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, as well as other senior Trump administration officials, engaged in a coordinated campaign to spread false information about a former FEMA official and impugn her integrity.

U.S. Magistrate Judge William Fitzpatrick condemned the Trump administration for what he said was "outrageous" conduct targeting Mary Comans, who he said was "professionally targeted and personally attacked by government officials for no legitimate reason."
Comans, a career civil servant, was most recently the chief financial officer at FEMA until she was fired in February 2025 without cause.

While Comans was told that her firing was an exercise of the president's power to remove executive officials, the Department of Homeland Security published a press release that falsely accused her of "circumventing" agency leaders to make "egregious" payments to New York City for luxury hotels for undocumented migrants. The Trump administration also accused her of violating an executive order signed by President Trump on the first day of his second term that directed federal agencies to pause funding to nongovernmental organizations providing services to immigrants in the U.S. illegally.

But the decision to continue payments to state and local governments, including two issued to New York City, was made by senior officials at DHS and FEMA, and was approved by employees with the Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, the cost-cutting task force that was overseen by Musk, according to court records. Because of that approval, Comans was told to continue the payments to the state and local governments.

Still, DHS and senior administration officials, including Noem, Musk and Corey Lewandowski, who served as a top aide to Noem, made a series of statements about Comans that they knew were false, the court found.

"These facts establish that high-ranking government officials, including then Secretary of DHS Kristi Noem and Elon Musk, engaged in a coordinated public relations campaign to impugn the personal and professional integrity of Ms. Comans," Fitzpatrick wrote. "For reasons unfathomable to this Court, officials chose to turn the power of the federal government against a singular employee with an impeccable record of public service."

As part of its campaign targeting Comans, Musk, who served as a special government employee and oversaw DOGE, shared a photo of her on X and falsely accused Comans of engaging in "criminal action" by allegedly funneling millions of dollars to hotels in New York City. The court said Musk knew, or should've known, that his DOGE employees approved the payments. Fitzpatrick also said the social media post with Comans' photo and false characterization of her actions "was clearly intended to make her afraid."
"Posting Ms. Comans' picture served no legitimate governmental interest and was little more than state sanctioned intimidation," Fitzpatrick wrote.

The judge also said that Noem and Lewandowski provided false information to Laura Loomer, a far-right conspiracy theorist, about Comans with the expectation that she would disseminate it to her social media followers.

"Armed only with false statements, high-ranking government officials undertook a premeditated campaign to impugn the personal and professional integrity of Ms. Comans, a nonpartisan, career public servant," Fitzpatrick found. "Their intent was to disseminate false and derogatory information about Ms. Comans as widely as possible."
The decision from Fitzpatrick stemmed from a name-clearing proceeding that was conducted after a federal judge ruled in July that Comans was fired without due process.

Comans had filed a lawsuit in July 2025 that challenged her removal and argued that DHS and FEMA harmed her reputation by falsely accusing her of funneling millions of dollars to New York City for the hotels.

The judge said all of the accusations leveled against Comans by Trump administration officials, including that she engaged in criminal activity, misspent federal funds and laundered "forbidden funding," were not true.

"The attacks against Ms. Comans were based entirely on false information, and many government officials knew the accusations were untrue at the time they were made," Fitzpatrick said. "With no regard for the truth and with no consideration for the personal and professional effect on Ms. Comans, government officials exploited their access to mass media outlets to broadcast false information."
CBS News has reached out to DHS and to attorneys for Musk and Noem for comment.

title: White House prepares plans to use "mother of all bombs" on Iran
summary: The White House and Pentagon have prepared plans to use a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb to hit military sites in Iran if ordered by President Trump, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.
story: The White House and Pentagon have prepared plans to use a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb to hit military sites in Iran if ordered by President Trump, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

A Pentagon official told CBS News: "The Department of War plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment."

A White House spokesperson said: "We do not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist. President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon."
Last week, Mr. Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the midterm elections. He also touted "productive conversations" with Iran, though he did not provide specifics.
CNN first reported Thursday on the plans to use the Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, or MOAB, on Iran.

Mr. Trump set a precedent for using the MOAB, also known as the "mother of all bombs," when it was used in 2017 to attack an Islamic State cave complex in Afghanistan. The bomb is the largest U.S. non-nuclear weapon, weighing upwards of 30,000 pounds at a cost of $170,000 per unit.

Iran and the United States have largely held off on striking each other in recent weeks, after several months of on-and-off U.S. strikes on Iranian targets. But Mr. Trump has suggested the war could ramp back up if he is not able to secure a satisfactory agreement with the Iranian government.
In a speech to the United Nations General Assembly last month, the president said he has a "big decision to make" on whether to strike a deal with Iran or "annihilate the Islamic Republic."

Meanwhile, the U.S. is enforcing a blockade on Iranian ports and seeking to keep oil flowing through the Strait of Hormuz. But Iran has continued to threaten and strike ships in the key waterway, keeping global oil prices high.

Over the summer, many of the U.S. strikes against Iran were concentrated on the country's conventional military capabilities near the Strait of Hormuz, including air defense sites and missile and drone storage, according to U.S. Central Command.
Mr. Trump has also floated strikes on Iranian nuclear sites, including Pickaxe Mountain, a deeply buried site that analysts believe could be part of Iran's nuclear program.

title: Eric Deters files defamation lawsuit against Kimberly Guilfoyle
summary: Eric Deters, a GOP donor who said Kimberly Guilfoyle asked him to wire her $100,000, has sued her and her lawyers.
story: Eric Deters, the Republican donor who accused Kimberly Guilfoyle of asking him to wire her $100,000 to pay her American Express bill in exchange for her help with the Trump administration ahead of her Senate confirmation hearing, has filed a defamation lawsuit against Guilfoyle and her legal team.

Guilfoyle was pushed out of her ambassadorship to Greece earlier this week, announcing her resignation Tuesday. Guilfoyle's team publicly disputed the authenticity of text messages Deters shared with multiple news outlets, including CBS News.
Deters filed the lawsuit in Kentucky state court on Thursday.

Deters said Guilfoyle's legal team issued a statement to the Wall Street Journal claiming Deters owed Guilfoyle money and did not fulfill his obligations. The Journal published part of her attorney's statement, that Guilfoyle "was owed a balance for traveling to and supporting these patriotic events," which Deters denies.
"Kim Guilfoyle and her lawyers claimed my allegations were false and they would defend the allegations vigorously," Deters wrote in a statement accompanying his lawsuit. "Now they can in Kentucky."
CBS News has reached out to the attorneys named in the lawsuit — Jesse Binnall and David M. Schwartz — for comment.

title: 9 fired FBI employees who worked on Trump documents case sue
summary: Nine former FBI employees sued the bureau, saying they were unlawfully terminated for working on the investigation into President Trump's classified documents case.
story: Washington — Nine former FBI employees sued the bureau on Thursday, saying they were unlawfully terminated merely for working on former special counsel Jack Smith's investigation into President Trump's retention of classified records after his first term in the White House.

The former special agents, intelligence analysts and staff operation specialists worked on counterintelligence investigations and were fired over the course of two days in February 2026 — just as the United States and Israel were set to begin military strikes against Iran.

The nine plaintiffs represent the latest in a growing number of former FBI agents and other personnel who have filed lawsuits against the Justice Department and the bureau after they were abruptly terminated. Many of the fired employees worked on matters that displeased Mr. Trump and his allies.
The plaintiffs "were unlawfully terminated not for any cause or any legitimate reason, but only to satisfy the President's personal vendetta," the lawsuit alleged.

"The firings did not follow any internal investigation or disciplinary process within the FBI, and Plaintiffs were not given any notice, a hearing, or an opportunity to appeal. Instead, Patel claimed to rely solely upon 'Article II' to support the firings," the suit said, referring to FBI Director Kash Patel and Article II of the Constitution, which lays out the president's executive powers.

The 70-page lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia and names the FBI, Patel, Attorney General Todd Blanche and the Department of Justice as defendants. CBS News has reached out to the Justice Department and FBI for comment.

FBI agents executed a search warrant at Mar-a-Lago in August 2022 and allegedly recovered more than 100 documents with classified markings. In 2023, Smith's office indicted Mr. Trump on more than three dozen charges related to his alleged retention of the records and efforts to obstruct the government's attempts to get them back. The charges were ultimately dismissed by the federal judge overseeing the case, who said Smith was unlawfully appointed special counsel. The Justice Department formally abandoned its appeal of the ruling after Mr. Trump won the 2024 election.
Thursday's lawsuit cites public comments made by top Justice Department officials and the president directed toward the plaintiffs as evidence the firings were motivated by political animus.

For example, Blanche, who was deputy attorney general when the employees were let go, stated that the administration had "cleaned house" at the FBI by firing employees associated with investigations involving the president.
The lawsuit contains some new details about the circumstances surrounding the firings.

In the case of counterintelligence section chief Jennifer Bacon, she learned she was being let go shortly after an agent named Miles Starr had requested access to the classified investigative files about Plasmic Echo, the codename given to the documents investigation.
Starr, the lawsuit said, was a member of Kash Patel's Director's Advisory Team, a group staffed by agents from around the country who support his policy goals.

He also was the lead case agent who testified in the since-dismissed indictment charging former FBI Director James Comey with lying to Congress. That testimony later was criticized by a federal magistrate judge, who accused the FBI of numerous missteps, including a failure to filter out potentially privileged materials.
On Feb. 23, Starr emailed Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky to tell him that he urgently needed access to the Plasmic Echo case files, the lawsuit said.

"Starr did not explain what he needed, but stated that he was on instructions from Patel to access the case file. Bacon granted him access to all Plasmic Echo files in the FBI's case management system, with the exception of one specific subfile. The files Starr had access to contained the names of all nine Plaintiffs," the lawsuit says.
Less than 48 hours later, Bacon and the others were all fired.

The lawsuit also suggested that the firings may have been an attempt to distract from negative press about Patel, who was spotted on Feb. 22 at the Olympic Games in Milan "chugging a beer and, in a display of wild immaturity and lack of personal control, flinging alcohol around the U.S. men's hockey team's locker room."

A special agent in charge who was assigned to inform former special agent Zach Feldman he was being terminated even surmised that the firing might be "related to the news reports from earlier that day about Director Patel drinking alcohol at the Winter Olympics," the lawsuit said.
The military strikes against Iran began on Feb. 28.

"This scandal proved politically perilous for Patel: he drew widespread criticism for his conduct, with numerous sources suggesting that his status with President Trump and position as Director of the FBI were in jeopardy as a result," the lawsuit said.
On Feb. 25, Patel gave an interview to Reuters in which he disclosed that his phone records and those of White House chief of staff Susie Wiles were subpoenaed as part of Smith's investigations.
Eight of the nine plaintiffs were fired the same day, and the ninth was fired the following day.

"With over a century of experience among them, these former FBI agents and analysts served our country with honor and distinction as they investigated leaks of national security and defense information, thwarted threats and attacks from our enemies, and responded to critical incidents like the Boston Marathon bombing," attorneys Margaret Donovan, Abbe Lowell and Rebecca Tinio said in a joint statement.
"In return for their service, they were fired because they did their jobs, as they always did, to follow the facts and the law without bias or favor."

title: As Jolly runs for Florida gov., he confronts prior ties to alleged fraudster
summary: Shortly after David Jolly launched his campaign for Florida governor, his former boss was indicted for taking over $100 million from a disability nonprofit. Jolly says he wasn't aware of the scheme.
story: Less than two weeks after David Jolly launched his Democratic campaign for Florida governor last year, a Tampa grand jury indicted his former boss for allegedly siphoning over $100 million from a nonprofit set up to manage the assets of people with disabilities.

Jolly has called the alleged actions of businessman Leo Govoni "raw cruelty." He has also distanced himself from Govoni, telling voters in a July video that he "was an employee of Mr. Govoni's at a separate company from which the theft later occurred," and "from public filings, his activities appear to have occurred almost exclusively after we left his employment."

While Jolly didn't work at the nonprofit that was the source of the allegedly stolen money, he did work at a for-profit firm where the money was allegedly sent. Federal prosecutors said Govoni had used the firm to enrich himself. And a forensic accountant found that millions of dollars moved from the nonprofit to the firm during the period when Jolly worked there, according to filings from a related court case reviewed by CBS News.

Nothing in the court documents suggests that Jolly knew about or was involved in the scheme laid out in the indictment, and he has not been accused of any wrongdoing. He told the Tampa Bay Times he was not aware of the transfers described by the indictment.

Jolly campaign senior advisor Mark Riddle said in a statement: "Congressman Jolly has been forthright with the public and the press since he learned of this matter when the rest of the world did last year, upon the arrest and public filings against Leo Govoni. Congressman Jolly was one of over 100 W-2 employees among Govoni's many companies. He never served as an officer or in a position of any fiduciary responsibility, nor did he ever have any visibility into the finances of Mr. Govoni or his companies. Congressman Jolly has never been contacted by investigators in the criminal case against Mr. Govoni nor been a subject of the investigation."

Jolly — a former Republican who left the party early in the Trump era — is vying for the governor's mansion against GOP Rep. Byron Donalds. Florida hasn't elected a Democratic governor in this century, but Jolly thinks discontent with the GOP could give him an opening.

Jolly worked at Govoni's Boston Finance Group from 2012 until early 2014, when Jolly won his first election for a Tampa-area U.S. House seat. In 2013, the future congressman earned $250,000 at the firm, according to House financial disclosures. One 2013 statement from his House campaign describes Jolly as a vice president at Boston Finance Group.

Govoni also donated to Jolly's various political campaigns and served as finance co-chair of Jolly's 2016 Senate run. Jolly's wife worked for another Govoni-run firm while he was a House member, and Govoni's son worked in Jolly's congressional office in 2014.

Riddle told CBS News that Jolly "has done something that no Republican politician has done: returned Mr. Govoni's political contributions to his victims. Congressman Jolly calls on the other beneficiaries of Mr. Govoni's contributions to do the same."

Govoni's alleged scheme left behind a trail of alleged victims. After Colorado resident Chase McMinn was shot at work, over $1 million from legal settlements was placed in a trust managed by Govoni's nonprofit to pay for his 24/7 care, according to his father. Between $200,000 and $360,000 disappeared, his father said, and it's not clear if it will ever be returned.
"What [Govoni] did was just so evil," Chase McMinn's father, Milt, told CBS News.
An attorney for Govoni did not comment, saying he would let the case speak for itself. CBS News has reached out to Govoni's son for comment.
Charges against Govoni mention firm where Jolly worked
The federal criminal charges against Govoni describe a complicated web of companies set up by the Clearwater-based businessman and his associates.

At its center is the Center for Special Needs Trust Administration, or CSNT, a nonprofit co-founded by Govoni in 2000 to help manage and invest the financial assets of people with disabilities. Prosecutors say it eventually became one of the country's largest operations of its kind, managing around $200 million in assets across more than 2,000 trusts as of 2024.
Between 2009 and 2012, prosecutors allege, CSNT agreed to lend up to $100 million to Boston Finance Group, a firm run by Govoni that was in the business of offering loans to other companies.
After CSNT declared bankruptcy in 2024, a federally appointed trustee set out to track down the money and sued Boston Finance Group to claw back the loan.

Court papers filed in that lawsuit show that the loan was set up as a revolving line of credit that allowed Boston Finance Group to borrow chunks of money from CSNT over time. In January 2012, Boston Finance Group was granted a $100 million credit line and was required to pay back the money by 2017, with quarterly interest payments until then.

Boston Finance Group drew money from CSNT almost every quarter for a decade, starting in 2010, according to an analysis by a forensic accountant hired by the bankruptcy trustee who pored through both CSNT and Boston Finance Group's bank records.
From March 2013 to February 2014, during Jolly's tenure at Boston Finance Group, the company drew down more than $10 million from CSNT, the accountant's analysis shows.

Two accounting experts told CBS News the forensic accountant who carried out the analysis appeared to follow the correct procedures: Suresh Govindaraj, a professor at Rutgers Business School, and Francine McKenna, a professor at Montclair State University and independent journalist who covers accounting issues at public and pre-IPO companies.
Court records do not mention Jolly or suggest that he was personally aware of those transfers.

By late 2024, the accountant found, Boston Finance Group had borrowed just shy of $100 million from the nonprofit and only paid back around $19 million. The nonprofit was owed around $120 million net, including interest, the accountant said. A judge later found Boston Finance Group liable for the full sum, brushing off the firm's argument that it owed less.

Federal prosecutors say the "overwhelming majority" of the money that Boston Finance Group borrowed from CSNT wasn't invested in order to help clients, and instead, much of it was "distributed … to other GOVONI-controlled entities for illegitimate, non-investment purposes, including the personal enrichment of the defendants and others."

The indictment said Boston Finance Group "functioned as a slush fund and passthrough entity." It is not clear exactly what happened to the money that was transferred during Jolly's time at the firm, or whether those funds played a role in the alleged scheme. The indictment alleges several 2020 transfers from Boston Finance Group to other Govoni-linked entities constituted wire fraud.

"Govoni used his victims' money to live a lavish life, complete with luxury boxes at Tampa Bay Buccaneers games and the Kentucky Derby, pay off his own home mortgage, enable his use of private planes, and cover the living expenses of his friends and family," the Justice Department alleged in one court document last year. "He even distributed some of his victims' money directly into his own personal bank account."
Federal prosecutors charged Govoni with conspiracy, fraud and other charges. He pleaded not guilty and was ordered detained ahead of a trial set for next year.

Milt McMinn told CBS News his son Chase relied on money held by CSNT after he was shot in the head by a customer at an auto shop in the Denver area. The 2017 shooting left him quadriplegic, nonverbal and in need of 24/7 care.
"His life right now is basically a bed and a wheelchair," Milt McMinn said. He described his son as a "great young man."
Chase McMinn's family was able to recover more than $1 million in legal settlements, and a judge directed the money to be managed by Govoni's nonprofit, his father said.
In 2024, the FBI notified the family that it was investigating issues with the trust.
Milt McMinn said he and his wife have had to pay for many of Chase's needs out of pocket, including a rehab center and expenses for Chase's daughter.
The father said he is "really angry" about Govoni's alleged crimes.
"I just don't understand why he would do that," he said.
Govoni and Jolly's relationship

Over the summer, Jolly told the Tampa Bay Times he met Govoni when they were both members of an elder affairs committee at Stetson University. He said Govoni initially brought him on as a consultant, and later hired him at Boston Finance Group in 2012 to help Govoni recover $30 million from a former business partner.

Financial disclosures show Jolly worked at Boston Finance Group from some point in 2012 until March 11, 2014, when he won a special congressional election to replace his late boss, GOP Rep. Bill Young. Over that period, Jolly reported $468,750 in income from the firm.

Govoni and employees of his companies donated thousands of dollars to Jolly's congressional campaigns, and Govoni served as finance co-chair for his 2016 Senate run. Govoni has donated to other politicians, a point Jolly raised over the summer, saying he "worked hard to surround himself with elected officials across Florida."
After he was elected to Congress, Jolly says his wife also worked for Govoni. House financial disclosures list his wife as an employee of Boston Holding Company in 2015 and 2016.

Meanwhile, Govoni's son worked for Jolly's office, the gubernatorial candidate said over the summer. According to his LinkedIn account, LJ Govoni worked as a senior legislative aide from April 2014 to December 2014. LJ Govoni's profile on the site doesn't mention that he worked for Jolly, but says his job "wasn't a career move — it was a personal ask."

"When a close contact was elected to Congress, he asked me to come to Washington and help build the office: establish process, install leadership infrastructure, and make sure the operation ran the way a serious legislative office should," he wrote. "I came, did the work, and returned to the private sector when the foundation was set."

Caitlin  Yilek and 
                                                  
                                  Fin  Daniel Gómez
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Trump calls off plan to livestream Fort Hood shooter's execution
summary: "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," President Trump wrote on Truth Social.
story: Washington — President Trump said Thursday that the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will not be streamed, a decision that comes after his administration faced significant backlash over the Pentagon's initial plan to allow the American people to watch Hasan's death by firing squad.

"I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social. "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed."
The president said the immediate families of the victims can view the execution in person if they choose to.
"They deserve to witness JUSTICE!" he said.

Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring more than 30 at Fort Hood in 2009, is set to be executed by firing squad at 1 p.m. on Dec. 3 at the Texas Army installation, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said earlier this month.
The plan to allow the public to watch Hasan's execution was revealed by Hegseth last week in an interview with far-right political activist Jack Posobiec.
"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public — because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," he said.
Sean Parnell, the Pentagon's chief spokesman, said Hegseth and Mr. Trump spoke about the decision to cancel the planned livestream before the president announced it on social media.
"The Secretary supports the President's decision, and they are completely aligned," Parnell said in a statement.
But the plan sparked broad outcry from Republicans and Democrats, who warned that livestreaming Hasan's death diminished the United States and could fuel radicalization.

House Speaker Mike Johnson told CBS News national correspondent and chief Washington analyst Robert Costa that "the concern would be that you would create a video that would be a recruiting tool for future terrorists." Vice President JD Vance acknowledged that he would not watch the execution.
CBS News reported Tuesday that Trump administration officials were leaning against streaming the death by firing squad.

If the Trump administration had followed through with its plan, it would have placed the United States in a small group of nations carrying out public executions. Afghanistan and Iran are the only two nations that conducted known public executions last year, according to Amnesty International.

It appears the last public execution in the U.S. took place in 1936. An estimated 20,000 people gathered to watch the hanging of Rainey Bethea, a Black man who confessed to the rape and murder of a 70-year-old White woman, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

The last military execution took place in 1961, when U.S. Army Private John Bennett was hanged. Hasan's death by firing squad would be the military's first using that method since 1945, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

title: Trump invokes executive privilege in Kennedy Center legal fight
summary: President Trump has formally invoked executive privilege to shield certain records from a Democratic congresswoman who sits on the Kennedy Center board.
story: Washington — President Trump has formally invoked executive privilege to shield certain records from Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty of Ohio as part of her ongoing legal challenge to the president's effort to temporarily shutter the Kennedy Center for renovations.

White House deputy counsel Joshua Hoyt informed a federal judge on Wednesday of Mr. Trump's formal assertion of the presidential communications privilege, a form of executive privilege. Hoyt said it covers information, documents or communications between Mr. Trump, his advisers and Kennedy Center employees about the president's duties and "the effective functioning" of the performing arts institution.

Hoyt argued that because the president appoints members of the Kennedy Center's board and a related Advisory Committee on the Arts, he must "familiarize himself" with the institution's management, operations, fundraising efforts and planned activities.

"I believe that, without the protection of the presidential communications privilege over the communications described above, presidential advisors and their staff members would be chilled from gathering relevant information, exploring alternatives, and providing fully informed recommendations regarding the performance of the President's duties," the White House lawyer wrote in a declaration.
In a separate filing, Justice Department lawyers accused Beatty of conducting a "fishing expedition" that raises separation-of-powers concerns.

"Even though the President's statutory duties and the Chairman's trust duties overlap, what matters for the purpose of executive privilege is that Plaintiff seeks information, documents, and communications concerning the President's actions in his official capacity," they argued.
Executive privilege is not absolute and can be overcome by an adequate showing of need for the information at issue.

The Kennedy Center's board of trustees, composed of Trump administration officials and the president's allies, elected Mr. Trump as its chairman last year, making him the first sitting president to hold the role. His effort to invoke executive privilege to shield records relating to the Kennedy Center raises new and untested questions of whether the protection extends to the president's actions as chairman of the performing arts institution, which was created by Congress in 1958 and is funded through a mix of federal dollars, ticket revenue and private donations.

The president asserted executive privilege over a number of records relating to his attempt to close the Kennedy Center for two years to allow for renovations, its financial condition, the effort to add Mr. Trump's name to the building's facade and the possibility that the Kennedy Center could be demolished.

Concerns that the building could be razed emerged after Mr. Trump said last month that the Kennedy Center will close and "end up being ripped down" if he and his administration did not get recognition for raising money and spearheading repairs to the institution.
Mr. Trump was also photographed on Air Force One looking at a placard that appeared to say "Kennedy Center Demolished."

The brewing fight over executive privilege comes as part of a lawsuit Beatty filed in December challenging the board's move to change the center's name to the Donald J. Trump and The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts and shutter the institution for two years for renovations. Beatty is an ex officio member of the Kennedy Center's Board of Trustees.

In May, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper blocked the center's closure and ordered Mr. Trump's name to be removed from the building's facade. Construction crews stripped the president's name from the exterior in June, but the front portico of the building has since been covered by a tarp, concealing most of its name.

Cooper has also allowed Beatty to collect information from the Kennedy Center about the decision to close the main building and any potential demolition, and to take depositions, a process known as discovery.

But Beatty's lawyers said that the Justice Department sought to block her inquiries about any input and instructions Kennedy Center staff received from Mr. Trump in his capacity as the board's chair and refused to turn over any documents related to those communications.
They accused the Justice Department of "improperly asserting a blanket privilege in an unprecedented fashion" and asked Cooper to order the Kennedy Center to turn over the material Beatty is seeking.

In response to Beatty's inquiries, Justice Department lawyers said late last month that "to the extent the discovery requests seek communications involving the President or White House personnel, they are inappropriate because they may have the effect of seeking information protected by the presidential communications privilege."

During a deposition with Matthew Floca, executive director and chief operating officer of the Kennedy Center, last week, a Justice Department lawyer repeatedly instructed Floca not to answer certain questions from one of Beatty's lawyers based on a protective assertion of executive privilege.

title: Talarico announces record-breaking $64 million fundraising haul
summary: The Talarico campaign said that brings his total fundraising to $134 million since he announced his candidacy last year.
story: Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico raised a record-breaking $64 million in three months — more than any Senate candidate ever in the third quarter — his campaign announced Thursday.
The campaign said that brings Talarico's total fundraising to $134 million since he announced his candidacy last year.

His Republican opponent, Attorney General Ken Paxton, said earlier this month that he had raised $18 million in the same period. Talarico broke Jamie Harrison's record of $57 million, raised during the third quarter in his unsuccessful 2020 Senate campaign in South Carolina.

Although a Democrat hasn't won a Senate election in Texas since 1988, Democrats there have been powerhouse fundraisers. In 2018, candidate Beto O'Rourke raised a then-record $38 million in the same three-month period.
Recent polls have shown Talarico with a slight lead over Paxton.

Incumbent GOP Sen. John Cornyn, a prolific fundraiser, lost the primary earlier this year to Paxton, who has long struggled as a fundraiser. Republicans have dumped hundreds of millions into the race to support Paxton, even as there have been leaks of audio clips of Paxton appearing to disparage national involvement in the race.
President Trump, who backed Paxton in the primary against Cornyn and is a longtime ally, has traveled to Texas three times in a month to campaign for Paxton.
CNN hosted a town hall with Talarico on Wednesday night, and said Paxton had been invited but declined to respond. CNN and CBS are both owned by Skydance.

At the town hall, Talarico drove home the economic theme of his campaign, telling voters, "We have an affordability crisis because we have a corruption crisis." He also addressed issues ranging from abortion to his recent absence from the campaign trail, confirming that he had the flu and slamming online conspiracy theories about it.

"That decision to stay home for a week sent my opponent and his conspiracy theorists spiraling. I opened up social media and learned that I had apparently dropped out of the race, flown to a mental health facility in Ohio, that I had died," Talarico said. "This is crazy. I mean, these false claims got millions of views online."
Paxton announced Wednesday that his campaign is kicking off a two-week bus tour this weekend near Fort Worth that will wrap up the night before Election Day at the Alamo.
Early voting starts Monday in Texas.

title: DOJ tells California to review whether noncitizens got mail ballots
summary: The Justice Department has ordered California to review a list of people who the federal government believes may have received mail-in ballots for the upcoming election despite not being U.S. citizens.
story: Washington — The Justice Department has ordered California to review a list of people who the federal government believes may have received mail-in ballots for the upcoming November election despite not being U.S. citizens, according to a letter reviewed by CBS News.

In the Oct. 13 letter, acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter imposed a 48-hour deadline to review the list of names, which were provided on a password-protected thumb drive, to determine the citizenship status of each individual.

"For individuals whom you cannot independently confirm citizenship status, we request that you immediately instruct the appropriate elections official to segregate — not cancel — those individuals' vote-by-mail ballots until their citizenship status can be determined," McCotter wrote.

"If individuals on the list have not yet been sent a vote-by-mail ballot, take all immediate and reasonable steps to not provide a ballot to those individuals until we confirm their citizenship status," he added.

In a statement, California Secretary of State Shirley Weber confirmed that her office received a letter from the Justice Department, but said the federal government "did not provide the list [of alleged noncitizens] to our office."
"The USDOJ's relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections," Weber said.
Dean Logan, the registrar-recorder/county clerk of Los Angeles County, confirmed he had received the letter but said the records were on a USB drive that his office had not yet accessed.

"The letter included a USB drive purportedly containing the referenced records, along with a handwritten note providing a password. We have not accessed the drive because doing so would conflict with established data privacy and information security protocols," Logan said in a statement. "We do not consider the device a secure medium. Additionally, the letter does not specify the number of individuals involved or describe the information contained in the records."

He added: "Federal and state laws are clear on how voter eligibility is established — and any action to remove a voter from eligibility must be based on verifiable information, not assertions of unconfirmed data matching."

Similar letters were also mailed out to other counties in the state, a person with knowledge of the matter said. The move comes after Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in July told California's secretary of state that the government believed there were noncitizens listed on its voter rolls.
Reuters was the first to report on the letter.
McCotter's demands represent the latest effort by the Trump administration to press blue states on whether they have people who are unlawfully registered to vote on their rolls.

The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division filed 31 lawsuits in an effort to force states to hand over unredacted copies of their voter rolls. The division has said it wants to ensure states are keeping clean voter lists, but it has since acknowledged that it also intends to share the data with the Department of Homeland Security so that the lists can be screened for noncitizens.

Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division, sent letters to all 50 states in July threatening to take criminal action if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls.
So far, the Justice Department has lost 26 of those cases, and has not achieved one legal victory to date.
It has resorted to using publicly available voter lists and other investigative means to try to identify noncitizens who may be registered in those states.
Since President Trump took office, the department has criminally charged more than 100 people with voter fraud-related crimes.
The crackdown comes as the president has continued to allege, without evidence, that the 2020 election was stolen due to voter fraud.
Experts have repeatedly found across multiple studies that the incidents of voter fraud are minimal and have not been numerous enough to impact the outcome of an election.

A data analysis published last month by Reuters found that states may have added more than 30,000 self-declared noncitizens to voter rolls since 2000 because of software glitches and clerical errors that came about during the processing of driver's licenses and state IDs.
That figure is small relative to the number of registered voters. In the 2024 election, Census data showed there were about 174 million people registered to vote.

title: Ilhan Omar's relatives subpoenaed as part of immigration probe
summary: The subpoenas were issued on Friday, just days before Omar's home in Washington, D.C., was searched early Monday morning by investigators from ICE's investigative unit.
story: Multiple relatives of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar received grand jury subpoenas, as part of the ongoing criminal investigation into her family's history for evidence of possible fraud and false statements in their immigration paperwork, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.
The subpoenas were issued on Friday, just days before Omar's home in Washington, D.C., was searched early Monday morning by investigators from ICE's investigative unit.
Omar's personal cell phone was taken by Homeland Security Investigations during the search, two sources told CBS News.
The subpoenas were first reported by the New York Times.

The decision by the Justice Department to take those overt investigative steps so close to the midterm elections has sparked criticism. It appears to run contrary to the DOJ's own internal guidelines, which stipulate that federal prosecutors and agents "may never select the timing of any action" for the "purpose of affecting any election, or for the purpose of giving an advantage or disadvantage to any candidate or political party."

Customarily, the Justice Department has operated under an unwritten, so-called "60-day rule" cited in a 2016 DOJ inspector general report. It refers to the general practice of prosecutors to avoid the public disclosure of investigative steps related to electoral matters or the return of indictments against a candidate for office within 60 days of a primary or general election.

Omar, a frequent critic of President Trump's — and a frequent target of Mr. Trump and his allies — has denied any wrongdoing, and she has accused the Trump administration of attempting to "target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement."

Mr. Trump said Monday that he had "nothing to do with" the raid. Sources said Attorney General Todd Blanche, however, was aware of the search. The Public Integrity Section, which handles the nation's most politically sensitive criminal investigations, was consulted, the sources also said.

But that section was largely gutted by the Trump administration last year, with only two attorneys remaining in its ranks. It was not immediately clear what type of guidance the section may have provided to the department before the search was executed at Omar's home.

It was also not immediately clear why the government moved to execute the warrant so close to the election, since some of the documents in question date back to Omar's childhood and were completed by her late father.

The warrant to search Omar's home was only approved by a magistrate judge in Washington after an extended back-and-forth discussion with Justice Department attorneys about how to address concerns stemming from the United States v. Rayburn House Office Building case, sources with knowledge told CBS News. That crucial 2007 D.C. Circuit Court case held that in a criminal investigation of a sitting member of Congress, the executive branch can't review information that is seized in a search without allowing that member to first screen it for legislative privilege under the Constitution's Speech and Debate clause.

Initially, the warrant did not take the Rayburn case into account because the investigators searched the congresswoman's home and not her congressional office, but the magistrate judge ordered them to include protocols that would allow Omar and her counsel to review the materials and assert legislative privilege, one of the sources added. CBS News has not yet been able to determine who Omar's lawyer is in this case.
Homeland Security Investigations, or HSI, the department's criminal investigative arm, is leading the investigation, with the Department of Justice assisting.
This is at least the second active criminal investigation involving Omar and her family.

Two sources familiar with the matter previously told CBS News that the U.S. Attorney's Office in Washington, D.C., is also conducting a criminal investigation into the valuation of several of her husband's businesses — which D.C. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro confirmed during a Fox News interview this week.

The businesses run by her husband Tim Mynett came under scrutiny after financial disclosures she was required to file as a member of Congress showed the value of the businesses had jumped to being worth between $6 million and $30 million.
Omar later blamed the valuation calculations on an accounting error and filed an amended form that listed the couple's joint assets as being valued between $18,004 and $95,000.

title: U.S. banks dropped customers over political views, regulator says
summary: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency said nine of the top U.S. banks "debanked" customers over their political or religious views.
story: Top U.S. banks have "debanked" customers because of their political or religious views, as well as their business activities, according to a report from the Treasury Department's Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

The report, released on Wednesday, examines a practice that President Trump has claimed discriminates against conservatives over their views. Debanking has also been highlighted by some cryptocurrency investors, who claim their accounts have been closed because banks are uncomfortable working with crypto industry clients.

The OCC said the report was in accordance with Mr. Trump's 2025 executive order requiring federal banking regulators to review complaints to identify financial institutions that had declined business with clients because of their views.

Some conservatives have argued that they've been unfairly targeted by financial institutions, although the OCC found that some banks had also refused to do business with Democratic-leaning organizations. Debanking can also occur for legal and regulatory reasons, such as if a bank detects potentially fraudulent activity or an account is overdrawn.

The OCC, which reviewed 100,000 complaints and hundreds of bank decisions between 2020 and September 2025, found that the nine largest national banks it supervises had policies that swayed their decisions based on political, religious or business activities.

"Americans should have access to financial services regardless of their beliefs, affiliations or political views. Fair access to financial services is not a mantra — it is a mandate," said Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan V. Gould in a statement on Wednesday.

The incidents cited in the report include the payment processor WePay, which is now defunct and was acquired by JPMorgan Chase in 2017. WePay closed the accounts of several merchants selling MAGA- or Trump-related items, the OCC said.

"Our policies prohibit discrimination against customers based on political or religious views," a JPMorgan spokesperson said. WePay's processes "did not meet our expectations. We identified it, corrected it, and the business no longer operates."

The OCC also found that some banks turned away customers due to their industries. For instance, businesses involved in oil and gas exploration, coal mining or firearms were restricted from some financial services, the agency concluded.
Other banks cited in the report, including Citibank and Wells Fargo, declined to comment and pointed to a statement from the Bank Policy Institute, a trade group for the banking industry.

"The banking industry supports fair access to banking services and has been working to ensure that government regulations and policies enable banks to serve law-abiding customers," the Bank Policy Institute said in response to the OCC's findings.

The group added, "We support efforts to establish clear and consistent standards that promote access while maintaining sound risk management, including the administration's recent efforts to prioritize supervisory attention on material financial risk and rather than reputational risk."
