Rubin also addressed the dramatic price change during his conversation with Fox News Digital, pointing to the attention Molly has received since Clarkson's visit.
He described the new figure as a matter of "supply and demand," while the store has maintained that the bird is not for sale.
Rubin suggested Molly's sudden notoriety has made her one of the most recognizable mechanical birds in the world.
The new sign offers a striking contrast to the original $15,000 price tag that Clarkson cited in her complaint.

The price change adds another twist to a dispute that began Saturday when Clarkson visited the Brooklyn shop and later accused an employee of treating her as though she couldn't afford its merchandise.
KELLY CLARKSON'S STORE CALLOUT SHOWS THE 'POWER' OF CELEBRITY STATEMENTS: EXPERT
Clarkson initially took to social media to describe what she considered a humiliating shopping experience, comparing her treatment to Julia Roberts' character in the 1990 film "Pretty Woman."

"Just drove all the way to Brooklyn to check out this store I thought looked really rad and had a few things in mind to buy and literally was looked at as if I couldn’t afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me," Clarkson wrote.
"Wow, dude. You’re an idiot and just lost a huge sale."
The singer later doubled down on her account after Art of Play disputed her version of events.
Clarkson maintained that she had pointed to a $15,000 price tag and was told the bird was available for purchase, but that an employee suggested finding her something comparable.
"So you’re not only rude, you’re also a liar. Got it," Clarkson wrote in a follow-up post.
Art of Play has maintained that the encounter was a misunderstanding.
In its public response, the store explained that Molly is a permanent fixture in the shop and that employees had offered Clarkson the opportunity to purchase a similar bird from its creator.
KELLY CLARKSON SAYS 'AMERICAN IDOL' PRODUCERS 'LIED' ABOUT $1M PRIZE
Kelly Clarkson rose to fame after winning the inaugural season of "American Idol" in 2002 and has since built a successful career as a singer and television host. (Art Streiber/NBC via Getty Image)
The business also said another singing bird automaton, priced at approximately $2,000, was available.
For Rubin, however, the controversy has become much more personal than a disagreement over an unusual piece of merchandise.
During his conversation with Fox News Digital, the co-owner revealed that he had recently undergone a medical procedure and was not supposed to be working.
"I'm not even supposed to be here today. I got a cancer removed from my face last week," Rubin said.
"I'm getting the stitches out tonight."
Rubin said his concern about the store's safety was the reason he came in despite recovering from the procedure.
The co-owner also wanted to explain what Art of Play represents beyond the dispute that has suddenly brought it national attention.
"This is a curiosity shop," Rubin told Fox News Digital.
He described a business built around objects intended to inspire curiosity, including spinning tops, kaleidoscopes, puzzles, games and playing cards.
"And the reason this place exists is to make people feel like a kid again," Rubin said.

Kelly Clarkson is returning to "The Voice" as a coach for Season 30. (Trae Patton/NBC via Getty Images)
The business began online before operating a small location in San Diego. Rubin said the Brooklyn shop opened approximately two years ago.
Rubin, who is also a children's book author and magician, has spent years working in the world of illusion and performance.

The Brooklyn store also houses a small theater that hosts close-up magic performances, with Molly serving as the opening act, according to Rubin. Art of Play has previously maintained that the bird is permanently attached to the wall and was not available for purchase.
Despite the public dispute, Rubin said Clarkson would still be welcome back at the shop.
"We messaged her. I don't know if she saw it. I don't know if she cares," Rubin said.

title: Joe Manganiello's secret seven-year health battle that nearly killed him
summary: Joe Manganiello reveals Sofia Vergara made the life-saving call to remove his large intestine while he was unconscious during a secret health crisis.
story: ‘America’s Got Talent’ judge Heidi Klum tells Fox News Digital if she would ever set up Sofia Vergara on a date.
Joe Manganiello is opening up about the secret health battle that nearly "took his life" over seven years.
Manganiello sat down with "CBS Mornings" to discuss his health and his newly released memoir, "Bloodlines."
During his appearance, the actor told Gayle King he was offered the role as the main villain, Deathstroke, in Ben Affleck's canceled "Batman" movie.
He wrote in his memoir that, at the same time as the job offer, he was "dying." Manganiello received the call to appear in the movie in 2016.
Joe Manganiello had to have his entire large intestine removed to save his life in 2016. (Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images)

"I got the call about a month out of the hospital after I collapsed on another set," Manganiello told King. "After about a year of feeling these mystery symptoms, I went into the hospital for two months straight and, at the end of my stay, they wound up having to remove my entire large intestine to save my life.
JOE MANGANIELLO DENIES SOFIA VERGARA’S CLAIM MARRIAGE ENDED BECAUSE HE WANTED A BABY: ‘SIMPLY NOT TRUE’

"They had split me open. My entire large intestine had turned to pus, and it was about to explode," he continued. "They took it out, and the surgery left me with an ostomy bag. And in the wake of that, I lost 60 pounds in two weeks. I couldn't walk. My eye went cross-eyed. I lost my voice. I had five catheters."
"I went into the hospital for two months straight and, at the end of my stay, they wound up having to remove my entire large intestine to save my life."
Manganiello explained that, after he was released from the hospital, he was in the process of trying to gain the weight back when he got the call to meet Affleck and appear in the "Batman" movie.
The actor told King he was still married to Sofia Vergara at the time, and she was the one who ultimately made the decision for the doctors to save his life and remove his large intestine.
Sofia Vergara and Joe Manganiello were married from 2015-2023. (WireImage)

"They had to call her as my next of kin and give her options of what she thought I would want done to me while I was unconscious. She chose the right one, and it bought me time," Manganiello said. "It didn't solve the problem. The doctors still had no idea what was causing this, how to treat it. But it bought me enough time."
"But we do have to credit her for saving your life. For making that decision," King replied.
"Absolutely," Manganiello said.

King went on to cite Manganiello's memoir in which he wrote that his mystery illness put a strain on his marriage to Vergara. The former couple married in 2015 and announced their separation in 2023. Their divorce was finalized in 2024.
Joe Manganiello's "mystery illness" symptoms began shortly after he married Sofía Vergara. (FilmMagic)

"That kind of pain was like a flood in my life. You can't predict how that's going to affect people. It affected me a certain way, it affected her," he said. "It was seven years long. People didn't know about it. I was living in secret with this. Only the closest people around me knew."

Joe Manganiello has released his new memoir. (Michael Simon)

title: Billy Crystal says he no longer trusts God after losing home of 46 years then his longtime friend Rob Reiner
summary: Billy Crystal says he no longer trusts God after losing his Pacific Palisades home in the wildfires and the death of close friend Rob Reiner.
story: Legal expert Donna Rotunno analyzes Nick Reiner's probable cause hearing in the murder case of his parents, Rob and Michele Reiner, and explains the low legal standard required to advance the case to trial. Rotunno also discusses the defense's strategy to dismiss charges against the man accused of fatally mowing down NHL star Johnny Gaudreau and his brother, a complex issue involving blood plasma vs. whole blood testing.
Billy Crystal is opening up about how a devastating year changed his relationship with God.

During an interview with CBS Sunday Morning, the comedian, 78, opened up about how losing his longtime Pacific Palisades home in the January 2025 wildfires and the death of his close friend Rob Reiner greatly impacted his faith.

Crystal was asked whether he had been speaking with God after the painful losses. The actor referenced his previous one-man show, "700 Sundays," in which he described conversations with God, before offering a stark response.
BILLY CRYSTAL DESCRIBES PAIN OF LOSING HOME IN PALISADES FIRE AT FIREAID BENEFIT CONCERT: ‘FELL TO MY KNEES’
Billy Crystal says he no longer trusts God after a year of loss.  (Getty Images for Peabody Awards)
"No, ’cause I don’t trust Him," Crystal said.
"Too many bad things have happened," he added. "The Earth is in bad shape. This is a weird, scary time. So no, not anymore."

Crystal’s longtime home was destroyed in the Palisades fire after he and his wife, Janice, lived there for 46 years. The couple raised their children and grandchildren in the house, which Crystal described as a "magical place."
Speaking at a benefit weeks after the disaster, Crystal recalled visiting the remains of what was once his home.
ERIKA KIRK PENS ESSAY ON GRIEF AS READERS GAIN INSIGHTS INTO WRENCHING PAST YEAR

"When we were finally able to get back to our house in the Palisades, which I lived in for 46 years, like thousands of you, our house now looked like this," Crystal said, before a photo of the aftermath of the Palisades Fire appeared on the screen.
Billy Crystal lost his home of 46 years in the Pacific Palisades fire in 2025.  (Getty Images)

"I stepped onto the grounds and fell to my knees and I wailed. I had not cried like that since I was 15 years old, and I was told that my father had just died. I remember looking in the mirror back then with my whole life ahead of me thinking, ‘What’s my life gonna be like without him?'"
"And now folks, I'm 76-years-old, without a mirror and a lot less life to ponder thinking, ‘What is my life going to be like without our home?’" Crystal asked.

The loss became the inspiration for Crystal’s new Broadway show, "860," which is named after the street address of the home. The production recreates his home office onstage and explores his family, career, memories and grief.
NICK REINER INDICTED IN MURDERS OF PARENTS ROB REINER, MICHELE SINGER REINER AT BRENTWOOD HOME
"860" also reflects on the loss of Reiner, who was killed with his wife, Michele, in December 2025. Crystal said he and Reiner had been together at a holiday party the night before their deaths.
Crystal, pictured with the late Rob Reiner and Meg Ryan, says Reiner's death affected him in more ways than one.  (Gregg DeGuire/FilmMagic)
"We said goodbye," Crystal recalled. "And then … what?!?"
Despite the tragedies, Crystal said humor has helped him move forward.
"That’s what I do," he said when asked how he finds humor during the darkest moments. "It’s a healer."
Crystal said performing "860" has already helped him process the loss of his home and friends.

"I’ve absorbed the biggest pains that people couldn’t go through — the loss of home, dearest of friends," he said. "And I’m OK."

title: 'Moonshiners' stars challenge notorious warning that outlaw liquor can make you go blind
summary: Mark Ramsey and Digger Manes from "Moonshiners" challenge stereotypes about Appalachia's distillers as home distilling battles reach the Supreme Court.
story: Mark Ramsey and Eric "Digger" Manes of "Moonshiners" discuss the history of Appalachian moonshining, its misunderstood reputation and why they believe the tradition will survive.
Moonshine’s reputation is enough to make your eyes water.

For generations, Americans have been warned that the notorious outlaw liquor could leave them blind. But "Moonshiners" stars Mark Ramsey and Eric "Digger" Manes say there's more behind that warning than most people realize.
"There's a huge different thought process behind moonshine than there was, say, in the '40s, '30s, early years," Manes told Fox News Digital.
KENNY LAW, 'MOONSHINERS' STAR, DEAD AT 68

Mark Ramsey and his distilling partner Digger Manes are starring in the new season of Discovery Channel's "Moonshiners." New episodes air Tuesday nights at 8 p.m. on the Discovery Channel. (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)

"There was a lot of propaganda out there. It was said that it could make you go blind, make you die, make you go crazy, make you get the jack leg. The government was the one that was poisoning the industrial alcohol the people were stealing to make bathtub gin."

Historical records support part of Manes' account. During Prohibition, the federal government required industrial alcohol to contain toxic additives to discourage people from drinking it, according to the Smithsonian Channel. Some of that alcohol was diverted into the illegal liquor market and sold for consumption, although it was distinct from traditionally distilled moonshine.
Mark Ramsey learned about producing moonshine as a young man. (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)

The consequences were deadly. According to the Smithsonian Channel, 66 people died in New York City on Christmas Day 1926 after consuming poisoned industrial alcohol. The city's medical examiner, Charles Norris, blamed the federal government's practice of adding toxic substances to industrial alcohol, including those involving methyl alcohol, also known as methanol, which can cause blindness and death.
WATCH: ‘MOONSHINERS’ STARS REVEAL THE TRUTH BEHIND A MISUNDERSTOOD TRADITION
But not every warning about illicit liquor was a scare tactic.
Ramsey acknowledged that moonshine posed genuine health risks in earlier generations, particularly when distillers unknowingly used dangerous materials to build their equipment.
Eric "Digger" Manes (pictured here) and Mark Ramsey have mastered the craft of distillation. (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)

"Back in the day, there were people who had health issues because of moonshine," Ramsey explained. "The solder that they used to build the pots had lead in it back in the day, and they didn't know that it was happening. So once it was discovered that the solder had lead in it, even the old timers here, when they built their stills, they no longer soldered their joints on the inside of the pots. All the solder connections were on the outside where the mash never touched the solder anymore."

A moonshine still recently confiscated by the Internal Revenue Bureau is photographed at the Treasury Department between 1921 and 1932. A man stands next to the still and looks at the contents of a glass. (Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
"So yeah, it caused some issues, but it was strictly an accident," he said. "They just didn’t know any better."

While moonshine does not inherently cause blindness, improperly produced spirits can contain dangerous levels of methanol, a toxic form of alcohol. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warns that methanol poisoning can damage the optic nerve, causing permanent vision loss or death.
According to Discovery.com, "A dozen surviving moonshiners must join forces to fight for their way of life, before it's gone forever." (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)

"Moonshiners," which is now in its 16th season, premiered in 2011. The series follows "a diverse group of people living in Appalachia who carry on a 200-year-old tradition passed down from their forefathers, making moonshine," according to the show's synopsis.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Discovery Channel's "Moonshiners" has been airing since 2011. (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)

Distillers can legally produce and sell spirits marketed as moonshine if they comply with federal, state and local licensing, taxation and other requirements. Federal law generally prohibits producing distilled spirits at home for personal consumption, according to the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau, although recent court rulings have challenged the constitutionality of certain restrictions.
According to The Washington Post, federal appeals courts have issued conflicting rulings on a federal restriction on home distilling dating back to 1868.
Mark Ramsey, Amanda Bryant, Kelly Williamson and Eric "Digger" Manes are seen here during the filming of "Moonshiners." (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)

In April 2026, the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that a federal restriction prohibiting distilled spirits plants from operating in homes and certain other locations was unconstitutional. Days later, the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals reached the opposite conclusion, upholding the restriction as a "necessary and proper means" of collecting liquor taxes, the outlet reported.
Barrels of moonshine age at Casey Jones Distillery in Hopkinsville, Kentucky., on Aug. 16, 2017. (Getty Images)

The Hobby Distillers Association and four individual plaintiffs challenged the restriction in the 5th Circuit case, according to The Washington Post. Supporters of legal home distilling hope overturning the restriction could spark a "craft spirits revolution."

The legal battle has since reached the Supreme Court. In July, John Ream, the plaintiff in the 6th Circuit case, asked the justices to review the ruling. The Justice Department filed a separate petition in August, seeking to overturn the 5th Circuit's decision.
Eric "Digger" Manes and Mark Ramsey are the faces of Sugarlands Distilling Company. (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)
Ramsey also challenged longstanding stereotypes about "moonshiners."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Seth Powers, a production staffer at Maine Craft Distilling, boxes bottles of blueberry moonshine. The company is one of several distilleries and breweries to use Maine farm products. (Portland Press Herald via Getty Images)

"A lot of times, people give it a bad name because they just see it as poison and a bunch of heathens out doing stuff they shouldn’t do," he said. "And moonshiners, as a rule, are very, very good people. They were just simply doing what they had to do to survive back in the day."

"[Moonshine] didn't actually sell in Appalachia," Ramsey said. "It went farther north: Ohio, Detroit, New York, the East Coast. ... One of my friends told me ... he took a load of liquor to Ohio and said, 'Them fellas up there, they get it. And every one of them said, 'God bless them hillbillies.'"
Ole Smoky Tennessee Moonshine is seen here on Dec. 10, 2013, at The Garage by Kenneth Cole in New York City. (Getty Images)

"The liquor business back in the day, the heyday of it, probably wouldn't have flourished here in Appalachia so prominently had it not been for our northern neighbors buying it," Ramsey said. "So we had a reason to make it, and they had a reason to want it."
The launch of Original Moonshine at Morrison Hotel Gallery in New York City is seen here on Sept. 11, 2010. (Patrick McMullan via Getty Images)
"We were broke, but could make liquor," Manes added. "And they had money and could buy it."
Ramsey is also optimistic about the future of moonshine. He said a new generation of distillers is eager to carry on the tradition.
Mark Ramsey and Eric "Digger" Manes told Fox News Digital that moonshine became increasingly popular up north. (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)

"As we saw in previous seasons … we always want to know who's going to fill our shoes, who's going to carry the torch forward," he said. "[And] we have so many good distillers up and coming. I think it's got a future, a very healthy one. Things will change. It's been argued that the best drink of liquor hasn't been made yet, so they've got something to shoot for."

Hall of Fame driver Junior Johnson's legal moonshine, Midnight Moon, was available at the bar during NASCAR's Fan Appreciation Day at the NASCAR Hall of Fame on Jan. 31, 2015, in Charlotte, N.C. (NASCAR via Getty Images)

"That's the most beautiful thing about the lessons you learn from these old timers that taught you how to make liquor," Manes said. "You make do with what you've got, and you don't let the situation you're standing in drag you down. You keep going forward."
For Manes, preserving the tradition comes down to pride in his craft.
Eric "Digger" Manes and Mark Ramsey are hopeful young people will want to learn the craft of producing quality moonshine. (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)

"To me, it's more the pride," he said. "It's no different. I don't know what hobby you may have. It may be painting. You may paint pictures. Well, if you do a beautiful portrait, and you stand back, and you look at it, you think, 'Wow, that really does look good.'"

Ole Smoky Tennessee Moonshine is on display at Meatopia X: The Carnivore's Ball during the Food Network New York City Wine & Food Festival at Esurance Rooftop Pier 92 in New York City on Oct. 19, 2014. (John Parra/Getty Images)
Manes said he gets that same satisfaction from turning simple ingredients into moonshine.
"We take what other people would consider slop — that’s the conglomeration of cornmeal and sugar — and make a crystal-clear product that tastes good," he said. "And we love it."
Mark Ramsey and Eric "Digger" Manes are seen here cleaning the inside of a still. (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)
"Good thing about this business is it [doesn't] really have bad times," Ramsey said.

Moonshine runs from the still at Casey Jones Distillery in Hopkinsville, Kentucky., on Aug. 16, 2017. (Getty Images)
"If you’re down in the dumps, you drink to drown your sorrows," he joked. "If you’re happy, you drink to celebrate. So it’s got a good source of customers all the time."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: White House official defends Teresa Giudice’s visit as critics slam reality star’s ex-husband’s pardon push
summary: Lynne Patton shared her cocaine addiction story and the intervention by Eric Trump and Lara Trump that shaped her belief in second chances for Joe Giudice.
story: The "Real Housewives of New Jersey" star told Fox News Digital that even though she and Joe Giudice are divorced she believes he belongs in the United States. Joe was deported in 2019 after serving 41 months in federal prison for fraud charges.

A senior White House official with longstanding ties to "The Real Housewives of New Jersey" star Teresa Giudice is addressing whether her ex-husband, Joe Giudice, deserves a second chance, while emphasizing that any presidential pardon decision rests solely with President Donald Trump.

Lynne Patton, deputy assistant to the president for coalition policy and engagement, took to Instagram to explain why Teresa Giudice and her daughter, Gia Giudice, were invited to the White House for Columbus Day and Italian American heritage celebrations.
Patton's comments about Joe, who was deported to Italy after serving time for fraud-related offenses, also addressed the family's efforts to secure a presidential pardon.
‘RHONJ’ ALUM JOE GIUDICE SAYS HE SHOULDN’T HAVE BEEN DEPORTED AFTER FRAUD CONVICTION
Teresa Giudice and her then-husband Joe Giudice walk on June 21, 2013, in Fort Lauderdale, Florida. The two finalized their divorce in September 2020. (Larry Marano/Getty Images)
Patton emphasized that she has no authority over presidential pardons but offered a personal message about redemption and second chances.

"For those inquiring @teresagiudice and her daughter, @_giagiudice, were at the White House at the invitation of the President & First Lady in honor of Columbus Day & Italian-American heritage. I have known Teresa and her family, including @joe.giudice, for nearly two decades," Patton began her post.
Lynne Patton, pictured here with President Donald Trump, has longstanding ties to the Giudice family. (My View with Lara Trump/Screengrab)

"I’ve attended family gatherings at their former New Jersey homes where Joe taught me how to roll meatballs & Teresa’s beloved father once showed me how to make his famous homemade wine. I am not in charge of pardons. Nor do I decide who receives them."
She added, "That is the President’s sole decision based upon recommendations from the White House Pardon Czar, @alicemariefree, and White House Counsel."
Teresa and Gia Giudice posing for a mirror selfie with Lynne Patton during the "Real Housewives" stars' visit to the White House. (Lynne Patton/Instagram)
Patton then shared her own experience with addiction and the second chance she said the Trump family gave her.
Patton said she relapsed into cocaine addiction while working at the Trump Organization in 2013, crediting Eric Trump and Lara Trump with staging an intervention that she said saved her life.
Her experience, she said, shaped her belief in second chances.

"In 2013 while working at the Trump Organization, I relapsed with cocaine addiction. @erictrump and his then girlfriend, @laraleatrump, held an emotional intervention for me that I credit with saving my life," Patton wrote on Instagram. (Lynne Patton/Instagram)

"To date, I have been drug-free for 13 years. They could have fired me. But instead, they told me that I was worth saving. Even when I didn’t believe that myself. Instead of sidelining me, they gave me more responsibility. I worked harder. Stayed in the office longer. Arrived earlier. More importantly, I earned back their trust & friendship. In turn, that translated into more self-confidence and earned promotions — including a personal request from their father to join him in D.C. It rebuilt my determination to succeed & help others do the same."
Patton also cited her Christian faith and the importance of a father's presence in his children's lives.
TODD AND JULIE CHRISLEY HOME FOR HOLIDAYS AFTER TRUMP PARDONS END PRISON TIME

"With that said, my faith in God compels me to believe that a father’s place is in the home. Statistics confirm the same. More importantly, so does the Bible. Charlie Kirk often declared that the biblical role of the father to his child is to be their protector, both physically and spiritually. Quality time is everything. And no, it is never too late to be the provider who God intended every father to be," Patton added.

"Do I believe that Joe deserves a second chance? Unfortunately, it is not my place to decide. But what I do know is that one of his beautiful daughters desperately needs him now more than ever. And even God supports that."
Joe was deported to Italy in 2019 after serving 41 months in federal prison for financial crimes. He has been living in the Bahamas, while his four daughters remain in the United States.
Teresa Giudice, Gia Giudice and Joe Giudice in 2014. ( Dave Kotinsky/Getty Images)

Gia has publicly advocated for her father's return to the United States. Joe sought a presidential pardon in June 2025, and Gia said in August 2026 that the family had filed a humanitarian packet as part of its efforts to bring him home.

A presidential pardon would not automatically guarantee Joe's return to the United States. According to the Justice Department, a pardon can eliminate certain grounds for deportation, but its immigration consequences depend on the circumstances of the case.

Members of the Giudice family commented on Patton's post, with Joe writing, "Your [sic] the best ❤️❤️❤️❤️."
Gia wrote, "thank you Lynn♥️🙏🏼," while her sister Milania commented, "thank you so much ❤️."
Teresa wrote, "We go way back ❤️," adding, "Love you ❤️."

"I hope Joe is able to come back! They allow all these illegals here with no consequences, and most of them are repeat offenders and dangerous. Bring @joe.giudice home to his family," wrote another.

Teresa and ex-husband Joe Giudice pleaded guilty to fraud and each served time in prison. (Mike Coppola)

title: Selma Blair accused of kicking nurse hours after JFK plane arrest
summary: Selma Blair allegedly kicked a nurse in the chest at a Queens hospital hours after her arrest for an incident aboard a Delta flight to JFK Airport.
story: Actress Selma Blair appeared in Queens court after being accused of assaulting flight attendants, a police officer and a nurse following a Delta flight from Los Angeles to New York.

Selma Blair's alleged airline assault did not end with the police. She is also accused of kicking a nurse in the chest at a Queens hospital hours after she was arrested following an alleged in-flight incident aboard a Delta flight from Los Angeles to New York.

The criminal court affidavit, filed in Queens Criminal Court, says registered nurse Ashley DeLeo was assisting in transporting Blair for further medical treatment at Jamaica Hospital Medical Center at approximately 2 a.m. ET on Oct. 12 when Blair allegedly kicked her.
"The defendant kicked complainant DeLeo in her chest," the affidavit stated, adding that the alleged conduct caused "substantial pain to her chest."
SELMA BLAIR ARRESTED AFTER IN-FLIGHT INCIDENT

Selma Blair appears in Queens Criminal Court Monday, October, 12, 2026 in Queens, New York. The actress was arrested Sunday after allegedly attacking crew members on board a Delta flight into New York City. (Barry Williams/ New York Daily News via Pool)

Blair, 54, was arraigned Monday on two counts of second-degree assault after Port Authority police responded to a call about a "physically abusive passenger" aboard Delta Flight 938, which had arrived at John F. Kennedy International Airport from Los Angeles, officials said.

The "Cruel Intentions" and "Hellboy" actress was taken into custody at JFK and transported to a hospital for evaluation. Two flight attendants reported injuries, and one was taken to a hospital, according to officials.
FRONTIER PASSENGERS TACKLE MAN WHO ALLEGEDLY CHOKED OFF-DUTY FLIGHT ATTENDANT, TRIED TO OPEN DOOR MID-FLIGHT
The court document also alleges Blair kicked a Port Authority police officer while being moved from JFK Terminal 4 into an ambulance at the airport’s B22 exit ramp.

Police Officer Maria Suarez was helping secure Blair on a stretcher at approximately 11:50 p.m. ET when Blair allegedly "removed her leg from the stretcher straps and kicked Officer Suarez repeatedly about the face, neck and chest," according to the affidavit.
CHAOS ERUPTS ON AMERICAN AIRLINES FLIGHT AS UNRULY PASSENGER ALLEGEDLY BITES FELLOW TRAVELER MIDAIR
The affidavit says Suarez suffered swelling to her jaw and "substantial pain to her face, neck and chest." Suarez was treated at a local Queens-area hospital, according to the filing.
Delta said in a statement Monday that it has "zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first."
UNITED FLIGHT FROM CHICAGO MAKES EMERGENCY LANDING AFTER PASSENGER'S 'MULTIPLE ATTEMPTS' TO BREACH COCKPIT

Selma Blair exits Queens Criminal Court, Monday, October 12, 2026. The actress was arrested Sunday after allegedly attacking crew members on board a Delta flight into New York City. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News)
A representative for Blair said the actress suffered a medical emergency during the flight.
"Selma experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct," Blair’s representative said. "Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is currently in stable condition."
SEVERE TURBULENCE DIVERTS NEW YORK CITY FLIGHT TO MIAMI, 8 INJURED

Selma Blair exits Queens Criminal Court, Monday, October 12, 2026. The actress was arrested Sunday after allegedly attacking crew members on board a Delta flight into New York City. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News)
Blair’s attorney said in court that the incident was not intentional and argued that she had missed doses of a "powerful" medication used to control severe neurological symptoms.
"This was not an intentional assault," attorney Shawn Barnes said.
Barnes also said Blair had been working "extensive hours" before the flight and claimed she fell and hit her head during the trip.
"These factors, coupled with altitude, resulted in a state of severe confusion and disorientation," Barnes said.
SELMA BLAIR SAYS 'NO ONE RETURNED MY CALLS' AFTER ANTI-ISLAM COMMENT LED TO HOLLYWOOD FALLOUT

Selma Blair appears in Queens Criminal Court on Monday, October, 12, 2026, in Queens, New York. The actress was arrested Sunday after allegedly attacking crew members on board a Delta flight into New York City. (Barry Williams/ New York Daily News via Pool)
Blair has spoken publicly about her battle with multiple sclerosis, which she was diagnosed with in 2018. She was later released on bond and is expected back in court in January.

title: Sean 'Diddy' Combs hospitalized with head injury while behind bars: report
summary: Sean "Diddy" Combs was reportedly rushed from FCI Fort Dix to a hospital for a head injury, though his team says they are working to confirm details.
story: Criminal defense attorney Donna Rotunno and former inmate Larry Levine join 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to discuss the sentencing of music mogul Sean 'Diddy' Combs and what to expect from his time in prison.
Sean "Diddy" Combs was allegedly rushed from prison with a medical emergency, TMZ reported.
The outlet indicated Diddy, 56, was transported to a nearby hospital to treat a head injury. It remains unclear how the disgraced music mogul was injured.
Despite the reports circulating, Diddy's team and the Federal Bureau of Prisons could not confirm the alleged injuries.
INSIDE DIDDY'S PRISON LIFE WITH MASSAGES, BOOZE AND NUDE PHOTOS: REPORT
Sean "Diddy" Combs was reportedly hospitalized following a medical emergency. (Getty Images)
"We are aware of the reports concerning Sean Combs and are working to confirm the circumstances," reps confirmed to Fox News Digital.
"Sean’s health and well-being are our immediate concern, and we appreciate everyone who has reached out."
The Federal Bureau of Prisons could not provide a comment on Diddy's health or whereabouts.

"For privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not comment on the conditions of confinement for any incarcerated individual, including quarters assignment or medical status," the bureau said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital.
DIDDY'S FEDERAL PRISON RELEASE DELAYED WEEKS AFTER REPORTED SOLITARY CONFINEMENT STINT
Sources told the outlet that Diddy remained conscious and speaking on his own while recovering from the alleged non-life-threatening injury.
Diddy was arrested and charged with multiple counts in September 2024. (Shareif Ziyadat)
Amid alleged medical woes, Diddy's prison release date has changed multiple times since he began serving his sentence.
According to multiple reports, the disgraced rap mogul was reportedly sent to solitary confinement in July after a prison fight with another inmate.
The incident began after a fellow inmate "made a remark to Combs, which instigated the event" at FCI Fort Dix, ABC News reported at the time.
CASSIE VENTURA FLED THE UNITED STATES AFTER TESTIFYING AGAINST DIDDY IN SEX CRIMES TRIAL: DOCS
Diddy was arrested in September 2024 on federal sex trafficking charges. (John Shearer/Getty Images)

In September 2024, the "Last Night" singer was arrested on federal sex trafficking charges after months of sexual misconduct allegations, lawsuits, investigations and the release of surveillance video that appeared to show the rapper severely beating then-girlfriend Cassie in the hallway of a Los Angeles hotel.
He was sentenced to more than four years behind bars in October after being convicted in July on two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution.

title: Sylvester Stallone calls himself an 'idiot' for doing his own stunts, details nine back surgeries
summary: Sylvester Stallone reveals nine back surgeries and three neck fusions from doing his own stunts, calling himself an "idiot" for the decades of damage.
story: Stallone reflects on the toll of decades in action movies, citing nine back operations, three neck fusions and other injuries. He says performers should leave stunts to the professionals.
Sylvester Stallone admitted that he was an "idiot" for performing his own stunts after extensive medical procedures.
During an interview with Fox News Digital, the "Tulsa King" star opened up about the "millions" of regrets he has after decades of being an action star.

"Millions, millions of regrets. I could literally spend a half hour talking about injuries, the amount, not even like one, I'm talking about 30 hours, 30 minutes of just individual ones, because it becomes compounded. I have been injured many, many times, but after 'Expendables,' I ended up with nine back operations, three neck fusions. Both shoulders ripped out, eye, you know, all kinds of lens put ... it's been brutal," Stallone began.
Sylvester Stallone called himself an "idiot" for performing his own stunts. (2026 NBCUniversal Media, LLC)
Stallone admitted that he's never been "quite the same" since the surgeries.
SYLVESTER STALLONE REVEALS SURPRISING HEALTH STRUGGLE BEHIND HIS FAMOUSLY RIPPED PHYSIQUE
"Now you have to like make peace with the pain as much as you can," he shared.
WATCH: Sylvester Stallone calls himself an 'idiot' for doing his own stunts
The biggest lesson he has now, at 80 after decades of crazy stunt work, is to "let other people do their job."
"I think I'm an idiot for doing that."

"Don't be a stage hawk, or whatever you call it, a showboat. I know a lot of people are thinking about doing stunts ... don't. Don't. Let the pro do it," Stallone said. "Let me explain something, you cannot beat gravity, when you hit the ground, you lose, and it's going to come back."

He continued, "I mean, just ask every football player in the world. So yeah, that and people go, 'Aren't you proud of them?' No. I think I'm an idiot for doing that. I'm proud that I broke myself in pieces. Like, duh, no."
The Stallone-led "Tulsa King" is gearing up to release its fourth season on Oct. 16. The actor told Fox News Digital what still excites him about his character, Dwight Manfredi.

"He still hasn't achieved his goal, just when he thinks he's arrived, another situation, another dramatic episode presents itself, which is exactly what the show needs. We don't want him to be like, 'I can finally exhale.' No, you don't wanna," Stallone said.
Sylvester Stallone and Dolph Lundgren starred in "The Expendables" franchise. (Kiyoshi Ota/Getty Images)
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Stallone said the new season opens with a jolt, putting Dwight under pressure from new enemies and tensions within his own crew.

"Well, it's quite shocking to start off with because certain elements happen that it's ... quite unnerving. And now I'm presented with a new level of, you might say, adversaries, gangsters, criminals that are coming at me technologically, politically, and mafioso-ishly from New York," he said. "So, I'm getting bombarded from all sides. Plus, I have internal struggles with some of my own crew. So it's kind of like having like a cuckoo's nest and trying to reign it all in, you know what I mean?"
"Tulsa King" season 4 comes out on Friday, October 16, 2026, on Paramount+.
Sylvester Stallone and Jennifer Flavin currently live in Florida. (Ethan Miller/Getty Images)
Stallone also discussed a major change in his life outside of Hollywood: moving from California to Florida.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
He told Fox News Digital the move helped him feel "invigorated" after he began growing complacent in California.

"In New York, I was a New York animal, like we all are here, I just said, you have to be. And then I got to California and I thought I was in Nirvana," Stallone began. "I did very well in California. And then California sort of changed. And became more populous and everything else. And I felt myself becoming very complacent and dull."
Stallone and his wife, Jennifer Flavin, moved out of California for Florida permanently in 2024.

"When we went to Florida, I didn't know one person. And now we have a great circle. So it's the best move. And my wife was also ... I think a lot of people would like to get a little peace and quiet. You know, they've been around so many billions of people that actually have water and birds and things like that. There's something that's invigorating and nourishing, and I think goes to our biology that makes us happier," he said.
Sylvester Stallone as Dwight Manfredi in "Tulsa King" Season 4. (Steve Swisher/Paramount+)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Flavin and Stallone share three daughters: Sophia, Sistine and Scarlet. His oldest daughter, Sophia, announced her engagement to boyfriend Michael Sheehan in August.
Stallone told Fox News Digital that Sheehan is making him "look bad."

"I thought I actually did it pretty well because she found a guy that I wish every woman found. So I went, 'Wow, he's making me look bad.' With the flowers and this and the constant, 'Oh, here's breakfast, honey.' I went wow, calm down, guys, you're gonna make it terrible for us," Stallone said. "But he is very nurturing. So I actually wish I was sort of like that when I was younger. I didn't learn those skills from my family. A good morning was good morning, punch in the face. He's wonderful and two more to go."

title: Weight-loss drugs may fight 7 serious health problems before the pounds even come off
summary: GLP-1 medications like semaglutide and tirzepatide may be repairing joints, calming inflammation, and protecting vital organs before any weight loss occurs.
story: Sai Yendamuri, M.D., a thoracic surgeon at Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center in Buffalo, New York, speaks to Fox News Digital about whether weight-loss drugs could reduce cancer risk.
GLP-1 medications may provide health benefits that extend beyond weight loss, according to a growing body of research.
From reducing cardiovascular risks to potentially easing joint pain and inflammation, studies suggest these drugs may affect multiple systems throughout the body.
Here are seven potential benefits beyond shedding pounds.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS STRATEGY SHOWS SURPRISING POTENTIAL FOR CHRONIC PAIN RELIEF
No. 1: Protecting heart health
Research suggests semaglutide — the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy — may provide cardiovascular benefits beyond those associated with weight loss.

A major study published in The Lancet found that semaglutide reduced the risk of heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular death among people with existing cardiovascular disease and overweight or obesity. The benefits were observed across different body weights and were not fully explained by weight loss.
Semaglutide has been shown to reduce cardiovascular risks, with benefits that appear to extend beyond weight loss. (iStock)
No. 2: Reducing joint pain and improving mobility
GLP-1 medications have been linked to reduced joint pain, although researchers are still investigating how much of the benefit comes from weight loss versus other effects.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The STEP 9 clinical trial, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, found that semaglutide significantly reduced knee osteoarthritis pain and improved physical function among adults with obesity.
Research suggests GLP-1 medications may help reduce knee osteoarthritis pain, although their ability to repair damaged cartilage has not been established. (iStock)
No. 3: Promoting kidney health
GLP-1 medications may help protect kidney function through several mechanisms, including improvements in blood sugar, blood pressure and inflammation.
GLP-1 BOOM COULD RESHAPE RESTAURANT BARS AS DINERS CUT BACK ON ALCOHOL

In the landmark FLOW trial, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, semaglutide reduced the risk of major kidney-related complications and cardiovascular death by 24% among patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease.
No. 4: Reducing liver inflammation and scarring
MASH, or metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, is a more severe form of fatty liver disease involving inflammation and liver cell damage.
Research suggests GLP-1 medications may help improve liver health, although the extent to which these benefits occur independently of weight loss remains under investigation.
Clinical trials have found that semaglutide can slow the progression of kidney disease in certain patients. (iStock)

A clinical trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine found that semaglutide improved liver tissue findings among patients with MASH, including reductions in inflammation and liver scarring.
Researchers found that 62.9% of semaglutide recipients experienced resolution of MASH without worsening liver fibrosis, compared with 34.3% receiving placebo.
No. 5: Reducing respiratory flare-ups
Real-world research presented at the European Respiratory Society Congress has linked GLP-1 medications to fewer asthma attacks and COPD flare-ups.
Researchers believe the drugs' potential anti-inflammatory effects may play a role, although additional studies are needed to determine whether the medications directly improve respiratory health.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
No. 6: Supporting mental health and curbing addiction
The brain contains GLP-1 receptors in regions involved in regulating appetite, emotions, motivation and responses to rewards.
Emerging research suggests semaglutide may have potential benefits for mental health and addiction.

An observational study published on the preprint server medRxiv linked semaglutide use to lower rates of substance-related and mood disorders. However, the findings have not been peer-reviewed and do not establish that the medication caused the reductions.
Preliminary research has linked semaglutide use to lower rates of certain substance-related and mood disorders, although further studies are needed. (iStock)
No. 7: Soothing severe skin conditions
GLP-1-based medications are also being investigated for their potential benefits in inflammatory skin conditions, including psoriasis.

A clinical trial published in JAMA Dermatology found that adding tirzepatide to an existing psoriasis treatment improved skin clearance among adults with moderate to severe psoriasis and overweight or obesity.

Researchers are continuing to investigate whether these benefits result from weight loss, reduced inflammation or a combination of factors.
The effects of GLP-1 medications can vary by drug and individual, and patients should consult a healthcare provider about potential risks and benefits.

title: Man claims he went blind after taking Ozempic, shares warning for other users
summary: Todd Engel claims Ozempic caused his total vision loss from NAION and has filed a lawsuit against Novo Nordisk over inadequate drug warnings.
story: Todd Engel, 63, was first prescribed Ozempic in 2023 to help manage his diabetes. Approximately four months later, he was diagnosed with NAION (nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy).
A Maryland man claims that a popular weight-loss drug caused his total vision loss, leaving him legally blind.

Todd Engel, 63, was first prescribed Ozempic in 2023 to help manage his diabetes. The GLP-1 medication, which is approved to treat type 2 diabetes, is also commonly prescribed off-label for weight loss.
Approximately four months after starting the medication, Engel was diagnosed with nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION).
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS FACE NUMEROUS LAWSUITS OVER RARE ‘EYE STROKE’ LINKED TO VISION LOSS
The condition, in which reduced blood flow damages the optic nerve, can cause sudden and permanent vision loss.
A Maryland man, Todd Engel, claims that a popular weight-loss drug caused his total vision loss, leaving him legally blind. (Engel family)

"I first noticed it on New Year's Eve, 2024. I had just gotten out of the shower, was getting ready to go to work. And I said to Shelley, ‘I can't see in my right eye. It's totally black. It's totally dark in my right eye,’" Engel told Fox News Digital during an on-camera interview.
"I was horrified. I was very, very upset that I couldn't see."
DOCTORS REVEAL HIDDEN DANGER FOR SOME OZEMPIC, WEGOVY USERS WITH BRAIN DISORDERS
Engel was referred for further testing, including at Johns Hopkins’ Wilmer Eye Institute. He was told he had suffered an "eye stroke," another term used for NAION.
"The blood work came back in the normal range for me. My blood pressure was fine. They said, ‘You can go back to work,’" he said.
"I didn't go blind — I had my vision taken from me, which was catastrophic to me and to my family."
Engel continued taking Ozempic because, according to the family's account, neither he nor his doctors knew of a possible association between semaglutide and NAION.
About 10 months later, vision loss suddenly occurred in his left eye.
"At that point in time, losing sight in both eyes, there was a tremendous amount of concern," he said.
RAPID WEIGHT LOSS ON POPULAR DRUGS COULD ‘STARVE’ THE BRAIN, EXPERT WARNS
Doctors told Engel there was no medication or surgical procedure that could restore his vision.
Shelley Engel said that medical testing did not identify another common factor beyond Ozempic. Her husband immediately stopped taking the drug after losing vision in his second eye.
At the time of his vision loss, Engel was working for Howard County Highways as a heavy equipment operator and truck driver. (The Engel family)
"I didn't go blind — I had my vision taken from me, which was catastrophic to me and to my family," he said.

Engel has filed a lawsuit against Novo Nordisk, the Denmark-based manufacturer of Ozempic, alleging that the company failed to adequately warn patients and doctors about the potential risk of vision loss.
WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS LINKED TO 'OZEMPIC EARS' AND OTHER COSMETIC COMPLAINTS, SURGEONS SAY
He is among hundreds of patients currently pursuing legal action against makers of GLP-1 medications, including Ozempic and Wegovy, over claims that the drugs caused NAION.

The lawsuits allege that manufacturers failed to provide sufficient warnings about the potential risks, although a causal relationship between the medications and the condition has not been definitively established.
Life after vision loss
At the time of his vision loss, Engel was working for Howard County Highways as a heavy equipment operator and truck driver.
He had worked in the field for about 40 years and held a commercial driver's license for nearly as long.
Beyond losing his career, Engel said even ordinary activities he once took for granted have become difficult. (The Engel family)
"I was extremely mechanically inclined with my hands and in my mind. I can't do that anymore, which is extremely upsetting to me," he said.
"People want to be able to retire on their own accord when they want to, not when a medical catastrophic injury such as this ... takes away your livelihood."
PEOPLE ON WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS REPORT FINGERNAILS FALLING OFF AS RESEARCHERS UNCOVER SURPRISING LINK
Beyond losing his career, Engel said even ordinary activities he once took for granted have become difficult.
An avid reader before his vision loss, Engel said he can no longer read newspapers, magazines or books. Inside his home, he has learned to count steps to help navigate familiar spaces.
7 EVERYDAY MISTAKES COULD BE QUIETLY DAMAGING YOUR VISION, EYE DOCTOR WARNS
"I know that coming in from our parking lot, there are 10 steps ... nine going down into our basement, 13 going up into our bedroom."
Engel said he now uses a white cane to navigate outside his home and relies on his family for help with everyday activities. His four grandchildren often guide him during family gatherings.

Engel is among hundreds of patients currently pursuing legal action against makers of GLP-1 medications, including Ozempic and Wegovy, over claims that the drugs caused NAION. (Michael Siluk/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
"They will take me by my hand and talk to me: ‘Pops, three steps straight. Then we're gonna turn right,’" he said.
"For me personally, it's embarrassing. I'm 64 years old. I shouldn't need ... my grandchildren or my wife to help me get from point A to point B."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
His wife, Shelley Engel, said her husband's vision loss has affected the entire family.
"It has completely changed every aspect of our lives," she said. "There is not one piece of our lives that hasn't changed or been touched by this throughout our whole family."

"It has completely changed every aspect of our lives," Engel's wife said. "There is not one piece of our lives that hasn't changed or been touched by this throughout our whole family." (The Engel family)
For Engel, some of the most painful losses involve the things he can no longer do with the people closest to him.
"I will never be able to see my wife's beautiful face again, be able to see children and grandchildren, be able to play ball with them," he said. "And that is very, very upsetting to me."
"I wake up in the dark, I go to sleep in the darkness."
A warning to others
Engel said that if he had been warned about a possible link between Ozempic and vision loss, he would not have taken the drug.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Had I known, had my doctor had any inkling that this could have happened ... I'm sure he would have asked me and I would have said absolutely not," he said. "I will deal with the diabetes ... I refuse to jeopardize my eyes."

Novo Nordisk has disputed that the medication causes NAION, stating that the available evidence does not establish a causal relationship between semaglutide and the eye condition. (LISELOTTE SABROE/Scanpix Denmark/AFP via Getty Images)
The Engels said they are speaking publicly in hopes of preventing others from experiencing the same outcome.
"Do the research for yourselves to make sure that my catastrophic injuries do not happen to you or anybody else," Engel said. "If we can help one person, then that's a pleasure to Shelley and I."
‘It's about information’
The family's attorney, Jonathan Orent, said the legal team is seeking a warning on the U.S. Ozempic label similar to information provided to patients and doctors in Europe.
Orent is co-lead counsel in nationwide litigation involving GLP-1 drugs, including lawsuits alleging vision loss linked to Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro and Zepbound.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"It's amazing what just a simple warning can do," he told Fox News Digital. "That's really what this case is about. It's about information."
Company response

Novo Nordisk, the Denmark-based company that makes Ozempic, has disputed that the medication causes NAION, stating that the available evidence does not establish a causal relationship between semaglutide and the eye condition.
"Novo believes the personal injury lawsuits filed in the U.S. are without merit and we are defending them in court."

"A causal relationship between GLP-1RAs, including semaglutide, and NAION cannot be confirmed based on the totality of data," Liz Skrbkova, head of U.S. Media and Stakeholder Relations for Novo Nordisk, told Fox News Digital.
The company pointed to an analysis of its randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trials that found very few confirmed cases of NAION and no increased incidence among patients taking semaglutide.

title: 10 health conditions may be linked to Alzheimer's years before diagnosis
summary: Depression, vertigo, headaches and stroke were among conditions linked to early-onset Alzheimer's disease years before diagnosis, a Finnish study suggests.
story: Dr. Jeremy Koppel explains the breakthrough blood test for Alzheimer's disease, detailing how it identifies abnormal protein accumulation. He clarifies the test's current role in diagnosing symptomatic individuals.
Certain medical conditions may signal early-onset Alzheimer’s disease several years before diagnosis, a new Finnish study suggests.
Researchers found that depression, vertigo, headaches and other conditions were more common during the five years preceding diagnosis, potentially offering clues for earlier detection.

The researchers analyzed medical records from 407 people with early-onset Alzheimer’s disease and 4,035 people of similar age and sex without the diagnosis, focusing on the 15 years prior to diagnosis.
SUBTLE CHANGE IN HOW YOU SPEAK COULD BE EARLY SIGN OF DEMENTIA RISK, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS
The average age at diagnosis was 60. Early-onset disease is diagnosed in people under 65.
The findings were published in the journal Alzheimer’s & Dementia.
Certain medical conditions may signal early-onset Alzheimer’s disease several years before diagnosis, a new study suggests. (iStock)
The following conditions were found to be significantly more prevalent among those who were ultimately diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer’s.
Vertigo (5.9% of those with diagnosis, vs. 2.1% of those who were not diagnosed)
Depression (5.7% vs. 2.3%)
Headache (4.9% vs. 1.6%)
Stroke (4.4% vs. 2.0%)
Alcohol-related disorders (3.4% vs. 1.4%)
Brain disorders (2.9% vs. 0.9%)
Thyroid disorders (2.5% vs. 0.8%)
Epilepsy (2.2% vs. 0.7%)
Delirium (1.5% vs. 0.1%)
Ear, nose, and throat disorders (5.2% vs. 2.9%)
Researchers found that depression, vertigo, headaches and other conditions were more common during the five years preceding diagnosis. (iStock)
Differences in medical conditions were most pronounced in the five years before an early-onset Alzheimer's diagnosis, the study showed.
3 THINGS TO AVOID IN MIDDLE AGE COULD MEAN 13 MORE YEARS WITHOUT DEMENTIA, STUDY FINDS

The researchers also found that healthcare visits increased substantially among early-onset Alzheimer’s patients immediately before and during the time of diagnosis, which may indicate emerging symptoms.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"It is well-known that the neuropathological changes associated with Alzheimer’s disease begin at least 15 to 20 years before clinical cognitive symptoms appear," Suvi-Johanna Krüger, M.D., Ph.D., study co-author and clinical lecturer at University of Oulu, said in a press release.
"Most previous studies have focused on late-onset Alzheimer’s disease, and considerably less is known about early-onset Alzheimer’s disease."

The researchers analyzed medical records from 407 people with early-onset Alzheimer’s disease and 4,035 people of similar age and sex without the diagnosis, focusing on the 15 years prior to diagnosis. (AP Photo/Evan Vucci, File)
Study limitations
Because the study was observational, it only establishes associations and cannot demonstrate that these conditions can reliably predict Alzheimer's disease.
"Our study cannot determine whether these conditions cause early-onset Alzheimer’s disease or whether they are consequences of the underlying disease process," Krüger noted.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Some conditions may represent risk factors, while others may reflect early symptoms or changes occurring during the prodromal phase of the disease."
It is also possible that genetics, lifestyle and socioeconomic factors played a role in the patients’ outcomes.
"Early diagnosis is important because more treatment and support options are available in the early stages of the disease."
Also, the researchers could not independently verify all medical diagnoses or assess the severity of the patients’ disease. Additionally, the findings may not apply to populations outside Finland.

Larger studies looking at disease biomarkers, genetics and clinical assessments could help determine whether there is a casual relationship between the medical conditions and Alzheimer’s incidence and whether these medical patterns could be used to improve early detection.

For people experiencing any persistent medical symptoms, including issues with memory or cognition, experts say it’s important to see a healthcare provider.

"Early diagnosis is important because more treatment and support options are available in the early stages of the disease," Krüger advised.
"Early diagnosis also gives individuals and their families more time to plan for the future and access appropriate support services."

title: Selma Blair's lawyer cites missed medication, head injury after in-flight arrest: What doctors say
summary: Selma Blair's attorney claims she missed doses of a powerful MS medication, triggering severe neurological symptoms before her in-flight arrest.
story: Dr. Lee Murray, a board-certified neurologist practicing in Jackson, Tennessee, shared the potential health effects that could occur if a multiple sclerosis patient skips doses of necessary medications.
Selma Blair’s recent in-flight arrest has raised questions about the potential effects when a person with multiple sclerosis misses prescribed medication.

The actress, 54, was arraigned Monday on two counts of second-degree assault after allegedly attacking a police officer and nurse following an altercation with flight attendants aboard a Delta flight into New York City, The Associated Press reported.
In court, Blair’s attorney, Shawn Barnes, said that Blair had missed several doses of Nuedexta, "a powerful medication that controls severe neurological symptoms," according to multiple outlets.
SELMA BLAIR ACCUSED OF KICKING NURSE HOURS AFTER JFK PLANE ARREST

The attorney added that Blair hit her head during the flight, which departed from Los Angeles, and was in "a state of severe confusion and disorientation." He also suggested the altitude may have been a factor.
The incident was the result of a "medical emergency" and not criminal misconduct, he claimed.
Selma Blair’s recent in-flight arrest has raised questions about the potential effects when a person with multiple sclerosis misses prescribed medication. (Getty Images)
Blair was diagnosed with MS in 2018.
Fox News Digital reached out to Blair's representatives requesting comment.
What to know about MS medications
There are three primary treatment approaches for multiple sclerosis, according to Dr. Lee Murray, a board-certified neurologist practicing in Jackson, Tennessee, at West Tennessee Healthcare.
"The first-line treatments we utilize try to prevent recurrent inflammatory attacks," Murray, who has not treated Blair, told Fox News Digital.
'HELICOPTER BRAIN' COULD BE MAKING YOU FEEL SICK: HOW TO SPOT IT AND WHAT TO DO
These medications often involve IV infusions, but they can be in the form of pills or injections the patient gives themselves.
"These are oftentimes medications folks take for several years," Murray said. "The hope of that is to keep the MS suppressed, to keep [the patient] from having MS attacks."

Selma Blair exits Queens Criminal Court on Monday, Oct. 12, 2026. The actress was arrested Sunday after allegedly attacking crew members on board a Delta flight into New York City. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News)
When patients experience an MS relapse, doctors may prescribe high-dose steroids, either orally or intravenously, to reduce inflammation and help speed recovery, according to Cleveland Clinic.
Patients with multiple sclerosis often have other health issues, Murray noted.
"If an MS medication dosage is missed, the patient runs the risk of having an MS relapse."

"For instance, patients with MS may have bladder difficulties, or they’ll develop depression or neuropathic pain," he said. "And so we prescribe medications that don't treat the MS itself, but they deal with the symptoms related to MS."
Dr. Yoshua Quinones, board-certified internist with Medical Offices of Manhattan, reiterated that there are different classes of MS medications.
PARKINSON'S PATIENTS MAY PROTECT MEMORY AND MOVEMENT WITH ONE SIMPLE HABIT
"Disease-modifying therapy reduces relapses, new MRI lesions and long-term disability accumulation," Quinones, who also did not treat Blair, told Fox News Digital.
Other medications are used to treat acute relapses or manage symptoms such as fatigue, walking difficulties, spasticity and bladder problems.
Actress Selma Blair and her son Arthur Saint Bleick attend the 26th annual Race to Erase MS Gala at the Beverly Hilton hotel on May 10, 2019, in Beverly Hills. (Getty Images)
Disease-modifying therapies themselves fall into several categories, according to the doctor.

Immunomodulators help regulate the immune system, while anti-trafficking drugs prevent certain immune cells from reaching the brain and spinal cord. Cell-depleting therapies, which are generally considered highly effective treatments, target and remove specific immune cells.
Risks of skipping doses
It’s essential for patients to be compliant with their MS medications, according to Murray.

"If an MS medication dosage is missed, the patient runs the risk of having an MS relapse, which can result in acute or new changes neurologically," he said. "There's a host of different symptoms that can occur."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Potential effects of a relapse may include balance difficulties, vision loss, dizziness, bowel or bladder dysfunction, or weakness, numbness or tingling on one side.

In Blair's case, Murray said, "If the Nuedexta was being used to treat pseudobulbar palsy secondary to her MS, missed doses could result in uncontrolled crying or laughter and emotional lability (rapid or unpredictable changes in emotion or mood)."
"I have never seen a missed dose of Nuedexta cause physical aggression," he added.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

If a patient with multiple sclerosis has missed doses of medication and begins to develop new neurological deficits, they should seek medical attention to determine whether they are in an active MS flare, the neurologist advised.
"Recognizing that and being able to quickly get on high-dose steroids can reverse some of the symptoms the patient may be experiencing," he said.
It’s essential for patients to be compliant with their MS medications, according to a neurologist. (iStock)
Although steroids can speed recovery from an MS relapse, they have not been shown to improve long-term outcomes, according to the MS Society.
Quinones agreed that skipping medications will reduce disease control.

"Poor compliance will increase the risk of relapse and MS-related hospitalizations," he said. "For example, if you stop any anti-trafficking medication, it carries a high risk of rapid disease reactivation. Abrupt cessation of this class can even trigger a rebound worse than baseline."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Cell-depleting agents can act over months, so a single missed or delayed dose is less immediately impactful, Quinones added.
"A single dose of disease-modifying therapy is not catastrophic — however, if constantly missed, it can raise a relapse risk."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The risks of missing medication depend on the specific drug, how long treatment is interrupted and the patient's individual circumstances, according to doctors.
Fox News’ Tracy Wright contributed reporting.

title: Popular erectile dysfunction pill may deliver additional boost to aging men
summary: Tadalafil boosted muscle precursor cell survival in a lab study, but researchers say the active Cialis ingredient also delayed mature muscle development.
story: Jacob Zemer, a New York-based fitness coach who primarily trains clients ranging from 35 to 55 years old, said there are several reasons adults start losing muscle as they get older.
Researchers in Italy have discovered a potential association between the common erectile dysfunction drug Cialis (tadalafil) and muscle regeneration.
The study, published in the journal Molecular Biology Reports, tested the drug on mouse muscle cells in a laboratory.
Over a seven-day period, the researchers looked at how the drug affected muscle cell growth, survival and development.
VIAGRA COULD DO MORE THAN ADVERTISED AS STUDY REVEALS SURPRISING HEALTH SUPERPOWER
Tadalafil was found to increase the number of muscle precursor cells, which are involved in the early stages of muscle formation, and helped more of them survive.
The drug also showed signs of helping muscles repair themselves by encouraging growth and reducing cell death.
Researchers in Italy have discovered a potential association between the common erectile dysfunction drug Cialis (tadalafil) and muscle regeneration. (iStock)
Despite these positive outcomes, the research found that tadalafil delayed the development of fully mature muscle cells.
This suggests that the drug could create and maintain more cells involved in muscle regeneration but does not indicate an increase in muscle size and function in humans.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Because the study was conducted in mouse models, the results may differ when applied to humans, posing a limitation to the study findings.
The study lasted just seven days, so more research is needed to understand the drug's long-term effects, the researchers acknowledged.
"This research opens up exciting new possibilities for future therapeutic strategies in muscle recovery," a researcher commented. (iStock)

Study co-author Dr. Cristina Antinozzi, a researcher in the Endocrinology Unit at the University of Rome Foro Italico, said these findings represent an "encouraging look at how tadalafil might be repurposed to support muscle tissue repair and regeneration."
"That's a fascinating biological signal, but it's far from proving that Cialis builds muscle or improves recovery in people."

"While more work is needed, this research opens up exciting new possibilities for future therapeutic strategies in muscle recovery, though it also highlights the need to monitor how such mechanisms might be viewed or misused in sports and performance contexts," she told Fox News Digital.
Dr. Kien Vuu, a radiologist and founder of VuuMD Performance and Longevity in Los Angeles, who was not involved in the study, agreed that this is an "intriguing early finding."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"In mouse muscle cells studied in a laboratory, tadalafil — the active ingredient in Cialis — helped muscle precursor cells grow and survive, but also delayed their maturation into muscle fibers," he told Fox News Digital.
"That's a fascinating biological signal, but it's far from proving that Cialis builds muscle or improves recovery in people.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Successful regeneration ultimately requires those cells to mature and form functional muscle tissue. This experiment didn't establish that outcome."
Vuu said this is "worth studying" from a longevity perspective because age-related muscle loss contributes "significantly" to frailty, metabolic dysfunction and loss of independence.
Resistance training, adequate protein and quality sleep remain the "most reliable ways" to protect muscle with age, an expert says. (iStock)

"However, this was a laboratory cell study, not a clinical trial," he said. "We need animal studies and eventually human trials examining actual muscle mass, strength, physical function and safety before drawing conclusions about clinical use."
Lifestyle practices such as resistance training, adequate protein and quality sleep remain the "most reliable ways" to protect muscle with age, Vuu added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The expert noted that tadalafil also carries "meaningful risks," including dangerous blood pressure reductions when combined with nitrates.
"So, people should not take it for muscle-building based on these findings," he said.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Doctors may be getting childhood obesity wrong, new research suggests
summary: A Lancet Commission definition of clinical obesity cuts pediatric rates sharply by requiring evidence of health complications beyond body mass index.
story: Murdoch Children's Research Insitute pediatrician Dr. Danielle Longmore discusses a new global childhood obesity definition from the Murdoch Children's Research Institute that looks beyond BMI. Longmore explains how the new definition considers critical health impacts.
A new global definition of childhood obesity is reframing how doctors evaluate youth health, looking past traditional body mass index (BMI) measurements to focus on actual physiological impacts.

According to research from the Murdoch Children's Research Institute in Australia, just 2.1% to 4.9% of children and adolescents qualify as clinically obese under the revised standard, compared to 7% to 10.8% under standard BMI calculations.
Dr. Danielle Longmore, a pediatrician at the Melbourne institute, outlined the shift during an appearance on "Fox & Friends."
YOUR WAISTLINE COULD REVEAL A HIDDEN HEART RISK YOUR BMI MISSES, MAJOR STUDY FINDS

"There's a push to really understand the impact of body fat on health," Longmore said. "BMI is really just measuring size. So, it doesn't really have a way of capturing whether somebody is well or unwell."
The traditional BMI measurement calculates a person's weight relative to their height.
While clinical obesity rates are substantially lower in youth, they surge with age, peaking at 52% among adults aged 65 to 74 as chronic conditions accumulate. (iStock)

The new definition, developed by an international panel of medical experts convened by the medical journal The Lancet, requires evidence of both excess body fat and related health problems or limitations in daily activities.
WEIGHT GAIN IN CERTAIN DECADE OF LIFE MAY BE MORE DANGEROUS, STUDY SUGGESTS
These indicators can range from elevated blood pressure and abnormal blood sugar to impaired mobility or poor sleep.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Longmore noted that many children defined as obese by BMI metrics are active, sleeping well, attending school and otherwise healthy.
The new diagnostic model formalizes what many pediatricians already practice by assessing blood pressure, blood sugar, sleep and physical mobility alongside size. (iStock)

"I think this definition just really clarifies what people have been doing in actual clinical practice," Longmore said, noting that physicians typically evaluate patients for underlying complications rather than relying strictly on scale weight.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
While clinical obesity appears to be significantly less prevalent in youth under the new model, the trajectory reverses dramatically later in life.
The study, which analyzed nearly 800,000 individuals across their lifespan, found that clinical obesity rates climbed through adulthood.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Among adults ages 65 to 74, the rate of clinical obesity reached 52%, as health problems linked to excess body fat became more common with age.
The findings come at a time when prescription weight loss medications, particularly GLP-1 receptor agonists, are gaining in popularity.
Many children categorized as obese by traditional BMI standards are fit, active and otherwise healthy, without secondary medical complications. (iStock)
However, Longmore cautioned that the study's dataset reflects pre-GLP-1 records, making the long-term impact of these treatments an open area for future study.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"This is really just the start of understanding what this new diagnostic entity means, and we really need more research," Longmore said, emphasizing that while the definition refines clinical diagnoses, early health interventions and lifestyle prevention remain critical for children at risk.
