title: Biggest waste of money in your home gym may surprise you, fitness expert says
summary: Fitness coach Jacob Zemer reveals the three home gym essentials — bands, dumbbells and a bench — that let you train every muscle group on a budget.
story: New York-based fitness coach Jacob Zemer spoke with Fox News Digital about the most worthwhile investments for working out at home — and which equipment may not deliver enough bang for the buck.
Americans are spending more on health and wellness, research shows — and for some home gym enthusiasts, the cost can quickly climb into the thousands.
A YouGov poll conducted in September 2026 found that 31% of Americans are spending more on health and wellness than a year ago, while 20% expect to spend more in the coming year.
Meanwhile, a 2026 poll by Garage Gym Experiment, an online community for home fitness enthusiasts, found that 44% of respondents expected to spend at least $1,000 on their home gyms this year.
FITNESS EXPERT REVEALS 6 THINGS PEOPLE OVER 35 SHOULD DO AFTER WORKOUTS TO STAY STRONG
But building an effective home gym doesn’t have to break the bank, according to New York-based fitness coach Jacob Zemer.
The biggest home gym money-waster may not be a particular piece of equipment, he said, but rather anything that takes up significant space and is difficult to set up or use consistently.
Building an effective home gym doesn’t have to break the bank, according to New York-based fitness coach Jacob Zemer, right. (Jacob Zemer)
Zemer spoke with Fox News Digital about the most worthwhile investments for working out at home — and which equipment may not deliver enough bang for the buck.
The 3 home gym essentials
"A lot of people think building a home gym requires an elaborate setup, and it doesn't," Zemer said.
If someone is building a home gym from scratch, the fitness pro recommends starting with a few affordable pieces and adding equipment over time.
10-MINUTE FITNESS HABIT CAN HELP ADULTS OVER 40 MAINTAIN MUSCLE AND STAY STRONG
"You can accomplish everything for every muscle group with just three items," he said.
Exercise bands are a good first investment, Zemer said, "just because they're so incredibly affordable."
They’re also very effective, he said, especially for those who are new to strength training.
Exercise bands are a good first investment, Zemer said, "just because they're so incredibly affordable." (Jacob Zemer)
"You can do everything you need to with just those pieces of equipment — and you can travel with them, bring them on a plane and to a hotel, which makes them very versatile," Zemer said.
When choosing dumbbells, it’s important to consider how much floor space they’ll take up — especially if the home gym is in a room with multiple purposes, according to Zemer.
"With adjustable dumbbells, you can have a very small floor print — however, they are a little bit more costly, and some of them are slightly fragile, so just be mindful of that," he advised.
4 SIMPLE HABITS CAN HELP SLOW MUSCLE LOSS AS YOU AGE, FITNESS EXPERT SAYS
Beginners should first focus on learning the proper form and choosing a weight that makes the final repetitions challenging, according to Zemer.
Progress doesn’t always mean moving to heavier dumbbells, he noted.
When choosing dumbbells, it’s important to consider how much floor space they’ll take up — especially if the home gym is in a room with multiple purposes, according to Zemer. (Jacob Zemer)
"Pushing yourself doesn’t mean adding 20 pounds — it could mean doing one more rep," Zemer said. "You need to progressively get stronger, because your body will adapt to the stimulus you’re using."
Once it becomes easy to complete a high number of repetitions, it may be time to increase the weight.
With some exercises, it can be limiting if you have to lie on the floor or stand, Zemer said.
"You can get quite an affordable bench online," he said. "I would look for one that both declines and inclines, maybe even perhaps sits completely upright. That will give you a lot of versatility."
For added versatility, Zemer suggests looking for a bench that both declines and inclines, and maybe even sits completely upright. (Jacob Zemer)
The biggest waste: equipment you won’t use
Before buying a piece of home gym equipment, Zemer recommends considering how much space it requires, how many exercises it supports and whether it will be easy to use consistently.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Equipment that is bulky or difficult to move, or requires too much setup, may end up becoming an expensive waste of money.
"The most important thing is that it’s quick and easy to set up, easy to grab and therefore more likely to be used," he said. "The more setup it requires, the less likely you will to be use it."
Before buying a piece of home gym equipment, Zemer recommends considering how much space it requires, how many exercises it supports and whether it will be easy to use consistently. (Jacob Zemer)

Zemer learned that lesson after buying lever arms, attachments that connect to a power rack and move up and down for exercises such as presses, rows and squats. Because the equipment was cumbersome to move, he eventually sold it secondhand.
"The secondhand market of gym equipment is brutal, so if you buy something, and you don't use it, the resale value is next to none," Zemer cautioned.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
He recommends prioritizing items that serve multiple purposes, rather than devices designed to target just one body part.
"I always look for equipment that can do multiple things," he said.
"A lot of people think building a home gym requires an elaborate setup, and it doesn't."
Do you need cardio equipment?
Cardio equipment is not essential for everyone, according to the trainer, especially for those who are mobile.
Many people can also raise their heart rate through activities such as walking, running or strength-training workouts performed at a faster pace, he said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

For those who prefer a cardio machine, Zemer recommends choosing an option that is versatile and less likely to aggravate the knees or back, such as a stationary bike or ski erg (an indoor exercise machine that simulates the motion of cross-country skiing).
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Dementia risk more than quadruples among adults with common disorder
summary: Adults with ADHD had more than four times the risk of dementia or mild cognitive impairment, a University of Pittsburgh study of 187,000 people found.
story: Dr. Elizabeth Landsverk, a geriatric medicine and dementia expert, noted that people with ADHD can have more difficulty with organization, which could be one factor contributing to the higher risk of cognitive impairment.
A common neurodevelopmental disorder could be linked to dementia risk, a new study suggests.

Research led by the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, involving more than 187,000 adults aged 50 and older, found that ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) was associated with a substantially increased risk of dementia or mild cognitive impairment (MCI).
The observational study looked at electronic health records and genetic information of participants who were enrolled in the U.S. National Institutes of Health All of Us Research Program.
7 NEW DEMENTIA RISK FACTORS REVEALED — INCLUDING ONE MILLIONS STRUGGLE WITH
Cognitive impairment was observed in 6.7% of participants with ADHD versus 3.4% without the disorder — nearly twice the rate.
After researchers adjusted for age, gender and other health conditions, those with ADHD had more than four times the risk.
A common neurodevelopmental disorder could be linked to dementia risk, a new study suggests. (iStock)
The findings — which were published Oct. 7 in JAMA Psychiatry — only show an association and cannot determine that ADHD increases dementia risk, the researchers acknowledged.

"This doesn’t prove that ADHD causes dementia, but seeing the same pattern show up independently in medical records and in people’s genes gives us greater confidence that the association is not simply an artifact of how ADHD gets diagnosed," said senior author Tharick A. Pascoal, associate professor of psychiatry and of neurology at Pitt, in a press release.
"Two different kinds of evidence are pointing in the same direction."
3 THINGS TO AVOID IN MIDDLE AGE COULD MEAN 13 MORE YEARS WITHOUT DEMENTIA, STUDY FINDS
Meanwhile, those with the highest genetic susceptibility to ADHD were found to have a 35% greater risk of dementia than those with the lowest susceptibility.

"Analyzing genetic information alongside years of health records allows us to identify patterns that might not be visible in a smaller or more traditional study," said Guilherme Bauer-Negrini, co-first author and postdoctoral associate in biomedical data science at Pitt, in the release.
"It goes back to nature versus nurture — particularly if we're starting at age 50, as opposed to starting at 20."
"With this kind of data, we can start to investigate what may be driving this association and whether any of those factors could be modified to support healthier cognitive aging."
Understanding the link

Dr. Elizabeth Landsverk, a geriatric medicine and dementia expert with over 20 years of experience treating patients with Alzheimer’s and cognitive decline, noted that people with ADHD can have more difficulty with organization, which could contribute to the higher risk of cognitive impairment, although neurological differences may also play a role.

"It might [be] that keeping on top of health issues and getting to the doctor is more difficult for them," Landsverk, a California-based doctor who is not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.
Cognitive impairment was observed in 6.7% of participants with ADHD versus 3.4% without the disorder — nearly twice the rate. (iStock)
The study also found that people with ADHD had a 20% higher incidence of utilizing health resources, she pointed out.

"Having just signed up for Medicare, I know that it's really complicated — if you have trouble with focusing and getting things done, you may not be able to get the resources that you need," Landsverk said. "You may not be able to go to the doctor. You may not get your blood pressure taken care of. So there's probably a correlation."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"It goes back to nature versus nurture — particularly if we're starting at age 50, as opposed to starting at 20."
ADHD vs dementia
It can be challenging to distinguish between ADHD and cognitive decline, as some of the symptoms may overlap, according to Landsverk.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"I imagine it can look similar," she said. "You know, you don't remember why you went into a room. You don't know where your keys are, you don't remember the name of an actress."
It is cause for concern if the individual struggles to take care of day-to-day tasks, the expert noted.
The findings only show an association and cannot determine that ADHD increases dementia risk, the researchers acknowledged. (Getty Images)

"You can't pay your bills, you can't get your medications right, you can't get to your appointments, you tell people that you're going to do stuff and then you don't — that's when you need to get checked."
Changes in judgment, mood or social behavior may be more suggestive of dementia than ADHD, Landsverk noted.
Reducing the risk
Although the study found an association between ADHD and cognitive impairment, Landsverk emphasized that some lifestyle behaviors can help people reduce their overall dementia risk.

She pointed to maintaining a healthy weight, avoiding smoking and excessive alcohol, and staying physically active as important modifiable factors, along with controlling blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes.

"There's a lot we can do," Landsverk said, recommending a largely plant-based diet and at least 30 minutes of daily exercise.
Physical activity can also help improve mood and focus, she added.

Anyone experiencing persistent problems with memory, focus, organization or managing everyday tasks should consider seeing an expert for an evaluation, Landsverk advised.

title: 'Helicopter brain' could be making you feel sick: How to spot it and what to do
summary: Doomscrolling is linked to higher anxiety and psychological distress, but a neurologist says it may also trigger what he calls "helicopter brain."
story: Board-certified neurologist Dr. Steven Resnick discusses how overstimulation can lead to the "helicopter brain" effect, which can manifest as physical symptoms, and shares how to reverse it.

A new analysis of 44 studies has linked "doomscrolling" to higher levels of anxiety and psychological distress — but for some, information overload may also contribute to a phenomenon one neurologist calls "helicopter brain."

The research, published in Frontiers in Psychology, found associations between excessive consumption of negative online content and poorer mental health, although it did not establish a cause-and-effect relationship.

Board-certified neurologist Dr. Steven Resnick uses the term "helicopter brain" to describe a nervous system that remains constantly on high alert, much like a "helicopter parent" who constantly hovers over a child to protect them from harm.
FUNCTIONAL MEDICINE EXPERT WARNS EVERYDAY HABITS MAY ACCELERATE CELLULAR AGING

"Imagine your own helicopter — that is your nervous system," Resnick, chief of the Division of Neurology and medical director of the Comprehensive Stroke Center at Mount Sinai Medical Center in Miami Beach, Florida, told Fox News Digital. "Your nervous system’s job is to protect you from harm."
Information overload may also contribute to a phenomenon one neurologist calls "helicopter brain." (iStock)
Information overload, overstimulation and uncertainty can keep the brain on high alert, activating the autonomic nervous system, the neurologist said.
"The brain is scanning for danger," Resnick said. "When it scans for danger, then you have that autonomic nervous system pushing the accelerator."
NEARLY 3 IN 4 AMERICANS ARE BATTLING THE SAME EXHAUSTING HEALTH PROBLEM, CDC REVEALS

The neurologist, who also hosts "The Healthy Mind" podcast, said he often sees patients experiencing symptoms they struggle to explain, including headaches, gastrointestinal issues, fatigue, sleep problems, tingling and dizziness.
In some cases, patients undergo evaluations by multiple specialists before identifying a potential explanation.
"The brain is scanning for danger," the neurologist said. "When it scans for danger, then you have that autonomic nervous system pushing the accelerator." (iStock)
"They end up going to see a neurologist, who sends them to the gastroenterologist, who sends them to the cardiologist, then the rheumatologist," he said.
"They don't understand what they're feeling is actually authentic, it's real — it's the nervous system that is actually activated."
THINK YOUR CORTISOL IS TOO HIGH? EXPERT REVEALS THE TRUTH BEHIND VIRAL WELLNESS CRAZE
Although constant information overload can contribute to this heightened state of alertness, Resnick said the same patterns can emerge in response to everyday stressors and deeply ingrained habits.
The neurologist outlined the following five strategies for recognizing these patterns, calming the nervous system and developing healthier responses to stress.
No. 1: Recognize what you’re feeling
When seeing patients, Resnick said his first step is to listen to them, to ensure that he understands what they’re feeling.

"I hear patients say, ‘I'm scared, I'm fearful, I'm concerned, I'm worried,’ and then you start to realize what their nervous system is telling you," he told Fox News Digital. "I would never have done that by just fixing the problem right away."
When seeing patients, Resnick said his first step is to listen to them, to ensure that he understands what they’re feeling. (iStock)
The nervous system can begin to calm when patients feel truly heard, safe, secure and connected, the neurologist said.
"The solution can be done later," Resnick said. "And we have to stop using the word ‘fixing,’ because a lot of things cannot be fixed — but over time, you can start feeling better."
No. 2: Name the pattern
Recognizing recurring patterns — in thoughts, behaviors and reactions — is an important first step toward changing them, Resnick said.
"Mindfulness is not just about meditation; it's about noticing," he said.

That could mean recognizing the same conflict happening repeatedly with a co-worker, lying awake each night with racing thoughts, or turning to food or cigarettes during periods of stress, according to Resnick.
THIS ONE QUESTION MAY REVEAL WHETHER YOUR BODY IS GETTING THE REST IT NEEDS, STUDY FINDS
When those behaviors repeat, people can begin operating on "autopilot," he said.

"The brain wants to resort to what is familiar, what is safe and what is known," Resnick said. "It keeps going back to that because the brain understands it, retrieves it and does the same thing over and over again."
Breaking that cycle requires recognizing the pattern and making a conscious effort to respond differently, he added.
No. 3: Catch the trigger
Next, the neurologist said it’s important to "catch the cue," or trigger, that kick-starts the pattern.
"It's a stimulus," he said. "It's something that is very sneaky. It goes under your level of consciousness."
"It could be your boss' face. It could be a telephone. It could be a chair or a couch in a room. It could be a smell or a feeling."
The neurologist said it’s important to "catch the cue," or trigger, that kick-starts the pattern. (iStock)
That cue can trigger an almost automatic behavior, Resnick said, such as procrastinating, eating, reaching for a drink or lashing out.
If the behavior provides pleasure or helps someone avoid an uncomfortable feeling or situation, the brain can become more likely to repeat it.
Even worrying can become part of that cycle. If the feared outcome doesn’t happen, Resnick said, the brain may interpret the worry as protective, reinforcing the habit.
ONE TYPE OF SLEEP LINKED TO DRAMATICALLY LOWER RISK OF DEMENTIA, PARKINSON'S AND 81 OTHER DISEASES
Breaking the pattern starts with identifying the specific cues that set it in motion, according to the neurologist.

Rather than viewing anxiety or overthinking as something that happens "all the time," Resnick encourages patients to pinpoint a specific episode, consider what triggered it and recognize the behavior and potential reward that followed.
No. 4: Reward the new habit
The next step is replacing the unwanted behavior with a healthier habit that provides a noticeable reward, Resnick said.
"Give your new habit a reward you can feel," he advised.
DIETITIAN REVEALS SIMPLE EATING STRATEGY FOR BETTER SLEEP — AND ONE HABIT TO AVOID

That reward does not have to be significant. After an early-morning workout, for example, it might be a sense of accomplishment or an improved mood. A healthy shake after the workout could provide another small reward.
"Give your new habit a reward you can feel."
"Even checkboxing something on a piece of paper feels good," Resnick said.
These immediate, positive reinforcements can help the brain begin associating the healthier behavior with something rewarding.
"Rewards are very important," the neurologist said. "Even the small ones are important."
No. 5: Float instead of fight
Finally, when anxiety or panic strikes, Resnick recommends taking a counterintuitive approach: "Float instead of fight."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
In many cases, he said, people are not only afraid of a particular situation, but of the anxious feelings that may result.
Someone with claustrophobia, for example, may fear getting an MRI because they anticipate the physical sensations of anxiety that could arise inside the machine.
A person with claustrophobia may dread getting an MRI because they expect to experience anxiety-related physical sensations while inside the machine. (iStock)
"Don’t fight it," Resnick advised. "You want to allow it. You want to feel it."
Avoiding a situation can reinforce the brain’s perception that it poses a threat, he said, while safely experiencing it can help create a new association.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"After you have that experience where you felt safe, and you went toward it, then your brain and body … pair it as being safe," Resnick said.
The goal, he added, is "to teach the brain safety through your body and through your brain and mind."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
While these strategies may help people better manage stress and anxiety, Resnick emphasized the importance of recognizing the patterns behind the symptoms.
People experiencing persistent or unexplained physical symptoms should seek medical evaluation to rule out underlying health conditions.

title: New belly fat injection cuts dangerous fat surrounding organs by 12% in early human trial
summary: CBL-514 injection triggers apoptosis only in fat cells to reduce visceral fat by 12% in early trials, with implications for insulin resistance.
story: HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. cautions that the nature of GLP drugs means there might be unknown side effects in a ‘Saturday in America’ town hall.
Early human trials of an experimental injection called CBL-514 have shown the potential for reducing deadly visceral fat.
Visceral fat, which sits deep inside the abdomen wrapped around internal organs, affects metabolism and influences insulin resistance. It can impact the development of type 2 diabetes.
Research published in March by the American Heart Association found that visceral fat had a stronger association with the risk of heart failure than body mass index (BMI).
YOUR WAISTLINE COULD REVEAL A HIDDEN HEART RISK YOUR BMI MISSES, MAJOR STUDY FINDS

The trials tested whether the injection could diminish visceral fat deposits. They were conducted by Dr. W. Timothy Garvey of the University of Alabama at Birmingham and Yu-Fang Ling of Caliway Biopharmaceuticals in New Taipei City, Taiwan.
Previous phase 2 trials had already shown that the drug could reduce subcutaneous fat, the layer of fat directly beneath the skin.
An experimental injection called CBL-514 has been shown to reduce visceral fat in early human trials. (iStock)
MRI scans from two phase 2 trials exhibited a decrease in visceral fat in participants who received the CBL-514 drug, while the visceral fat increased in those who received a placebo drug.
Participants who were given CBL-514 received injections into their lower abdomen every three weeks for up to 12 weeks, with doses of up to 600 milligrams.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
The number of injections given to participants depended on the thickness of their abdominal fat.
As the fat layer decreased in volume, the number of injections also decreased.
The amount of injections that participants received depended upon the thickness of their abdominal fat. (iStock)
The CBL-514 injection selectively sparks apoptosis — a process that causes cells to self-destruct — but only in fat cells, leaving nearby cells unharmed.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Four weeks after the final treatment, the average volume of fat had lowered by 12.01% in the group given CBL-514, while it had increased by 5.68% in the group that received a placebo, SciTechDaily reported.
Participants who were given CBL-514 received injections into their lower abdomen every three weeks for up to 12 weeks — with doses of up to 600 milligrams. (iStock)
The potential cosmetic effects, such as a flatter stomach due to subcutaneous fat loss, are appealing to patients, Garvey acknowledged.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

What’s even more important, he noted, however, is the decrease in body weight, improved blood pressure and cholesterol, and the loss of visceral fat that the injection can cause — as these factors impact overall health.

Liposuction, a common surgical cosmetic procedure, cannot remove visceral fat, and thus cannot reduce the health risks caused by a high amount of visceral fat.

title: Hidden clues could help predict a woman’s breast cancer risk years in advance
summary: An AI tool developed at NYU Langone Health analyzes years of 3D mammograms to predict breast cancer risk up to five years before a diagnosis.
story: AI technology is transforming breast cancer screening by assisting doctors in identifying women at higher risk years before cancer develops. Mount Sinai's Breast Surgery Director and author of 'The Breast Advice' Dr. Elisa Port highlights how AI uncovers hidden tumors and slashes false positive results, especially for women with dense breasts. This advancement aims to increase screening adherence among the 30-40% who currently don't get regular mammograms.
An artificial intelligence (AI) tool could help doctors predict a woman's risk of developing breast cancer years in advance, according to new research.

In a new study, published in the American Journal of Roentgenology, researchers at NYU Langone Health and its Perlmutter Cancer Center tested an AI model designed to estimate a woman's risk of developing breast cancer within five years.
The tool looks at several years of a woman's 3D mammograms to track changes in breast tissue over time, rather than looking only at the latest scan, according to the researchers.
NEW ALZHEIMER'S BLOOD TEST PREDICTS WHO IS LIKELY TO DEVELOP DEMENTIA IN 5 TO 10 YEARS
The model was developed using more than 313,000 mammograms from more than 161,000 women, according to the study.
An artificial intelligence (AI) tool could help doctors predict a woman's risk of developing breast cancer years in advance. (iStock)

Connie Lehman, a Massachusetts-based breast imaging specialist and professor of radiology at Harvard Medical School who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital that AI could help identify women whose increased risk might otherwise go unnoticed.

"For decades, as a doctor and breast imaging specialist, I have cared for women who were shocked by a breast cancer diagnosis," Lehman said. "Again and again, I heard: 'How can this be? No one in my family has had breast cancer.'"
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
Traditional risk assessments can consider factors such as family history and genetic mutations, while AI can look for additional clues within a woman's breast tissue, according to Lehman.
The tool looks at several years of a woman's 3D mammograms to track changes in breast tissue over time. (iStock)
"A mammogram can tell us more than whether cancer is visible today — it can also provide information about a woman's risk of developing cancer in the years ahead," she said.
That information could eventually help doctors tailor breast cancer screening to a woman's individual risk, Lehman said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

Women identified as being at increased risk could discuss additional screening, such as MRI, with their health care providers, while women at average risk may continue with routine mammograms, according to Lehman.
The technology could also analyze mammograms a woman has already had, meaning the added risk information would not require another imaging exam or additional radiation, she noted.
Traditional risk assessments can consider factors such as family history and genetic mutations, while AI can look for additional clues in a woman's breast tissue, experts say. (iStock)
Lehman cautioned that an AI risk score is not a cancer diagnosis and cannot predict with certainty whether a woman will develop the disease.

"A higher score can prompt a conversation with your health care provider about additional screening and risk-reduction options," she said. "A lower score does not eliminate risk or replace regular mammography."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The NYU model remains a research tool and is not FDA-authorized for clinical use, according to Lehman.
The researchers also noted that more testing is needed. The study used mammograms from NYU Langone hospitals and imaging equipment from one manufacturer.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The team plans to test the model using data from other medical centers and different 3D mammography systems, according to NYU Langone.
Fox News Digital reached out to the researchers for comment.

title: Silent inflammation could be damaging your body — and 5 habits may help keep it in check
summary: Jim LaValle reveals how the gut-immune-brain interface drives chronic inflammation, and why stress, blood sugar and environmental toxins play key roles.
story: Clinical pharmacist Jim LaValle breaks down how diet, stress, medications, blood sugar, environmental exposures and even overtraining may contribute to inflammation — and why the gut-brain connection matters.

Inflammation is a natural immune response that helps protect the body from injury and infection, but when it becomes chronic, it can pose a health threat, according to the National Institutes of Health.
Over time, chronic inflammation can contribute to rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, inflammatory bowel disease and cardiovascular disease.
Keeping the condition in check can help protect healthy tissues and support overall health, experts say.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY HELP PROTECT AGAINST A DEADLY DISEASE, DOCTOR SAYS
Jim LaValle, a clinical pharmacist and metabolic medicine expert based in Texas, told Fox News Digital that inflammation can be influenced by a variety of factors beyond injury or infection.
Inflammation is a natural immune response that helps protect the body from injury and infection, but chronic inflammation can damage healthy tissues and contribute to serious diseases. (iStock)

LaValle first pointed to the gut-immune-brain connection — the communication between gut microbes, the immune system and the central nervous system — as one pathway that can influence the body's inflammatory response.
Beyond gut health, he said several everyday lifestyle factors can play a role in preventing chronic inflammation.
DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE
No. 1: Manage stress
Managing stress and anxiety can help support the gut-brain connection and keep inflammation in check, according to LaValle.
He pointed to cortisol, a hormone released in response to stress, which he said can "wreak havoc on your chemistry" when levels remain elevated.
Stress can "wreak havoc on your chemistry," the expert warned. (iStock)
Chronic stress can also affect the intestinal barrier, potentially allowing substances that would normally remain inside the gut to pass through more easily, LaValle said.
This increased intestinal permeability is sometimes called "leaky gut."
ZERO SUGAR, MORE PROBLEMS? STUDY REVEALS SURPRISING GUT HEALTH EFFECTS
"So, it turns out that if I'm stressed out a lot, I can be more prone to irritable bowel," LaValle said, as stress can trigger or worsen digestive symptoms in some people.
No. 2: Watch for food triggers
Diets high in sugar, fat and ultraprocessed foods can also affect gut health.
Paying attention to which foods trigger certain symptoms may help identify potential food sensitivities or intolerances, LaValle noted.
Paying attention to what kinds of food trigger certain reactions or sensitivities may help signal what is causing inflammation in the body. (iStock)
Symptoms such as bloating, rashes or discomfort after eating certain foods may signal a food-related reaction, although they can have other causes.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Certain medications, including antibiotics, may also alter the gut microbiome, but their effects vary depending on the drug and the individual, the expert said.
No. 3: Keep blood sugar in check
Maintaining healthy blood sugar levels is another important factor in managing inflammation, according to LaValle.
Maintaining healthy blood sugar levels is another important factor in managing inflammation. (iStock)
LaValle noted that conditions such as diabetes and insulin resistance are often associated with chronic inflammation.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Research suggests that GLP-1 medications, commonly prescribed for type 2 diabetes and obesity, may have anti-inflammatory effects, while scientists are investigating other potential benefits beyond weight loss and blood sugar control.
No. 4: Be aware of environmental exposures
The "exposome," or the environmental exposures people experience throughout their lives, can influence inflammation and the risk of chronic disease, according to the National Institutes of Health.
Microplastics could trigger inflammation signaling, according to the expert. (iStock)

LaValle pointed to emerging research on how environmental exposures — including "forever chemicals," microplastics, metals and pesticides — may affect weight, blood sugar regulation and other aspects of health.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"A lot of us don't think about that kind of impact on our health and how that could trigger inflammation signaling," he added.
No. 5: Don’t over-train
Regular exercise supports overall health, but intense workouts without adequate recovery time can put additional stress on the body, LaValle cautioned.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"You’re not getting a good enough recovery," he said. "You’re training hard. And, in fact, you might be training hard every day to lower that cortisol, but you're not getting good recovery. And that could lead to silent inflammatory signaling as well."
Anyone who is concerned about chronic inflammation or is experiencing persistent symptoms should consult a doctor to determine the underlying cause and appropriate treatment.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Stomach-turning sexually transmitted infection is on the rise, and standard medicines are failing
summary: Shigella bacteria are becoming harder to treat as drug-resistant strains rise, and doctors warn Americans should be concerned but not panicked.
story: Speaking to Fox News Digital, Lenox Hill Hospital internist Michael Aziz discusses the increase in antibiotic-resistant shigella cases and explains why patients experiencing gastrointestinal symptoms should seek medical attention before taking over-the-counter medications.
A highly contagious gut infection that can spread during sex is becoming harder to treat as antibiotic-resistant strains become more common.

An April report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention tracked nearly 17,000 shigella samples, which causes shigellosis that can bring on diarrhea, fever and abdominal cramps, collected between 2011 and 2023.

In 2023, 8.5% of shigella samples with resistance data were classified as extensively drug-resistant, or XDR — resistant to all five antibiotics in the CDC’s definition — compared with none from 2011 to 2015.
The findings point to a growing resistance problem, not a surge in overall infections, noted Dr. Tyler Evans, a California-based infectious disease physician and CEO of Wellness Equity Alliance.
HIGHLY CONTAGIOUS STOMACH BUG SPREADS FAST, HITTING CERTAIN PATIENTS HARDEST
"The infection is not surging. The bacteria are changing," Evans told Fox News Digital. "Case counts can hold steady while the treatment options quietly disappear."
The percentage of Shigella isolates classified as extensively drug-resistant rose to 8.5% in 2023, according to the CDC. (Leonie Asendorpf/picture alliance via Getty Images)
There is no FDA-approved oral antibiotic for XDR shigella, he said.
Shigella bacteria can spread when tiny amounts of stool reach someone's mouth, including through contaminated food or water, unwashed hands or sexual activity.
DANGEROUS DRUG-RESISTANT FUNGUS SPREADS ACROSS US, REACHING 27 STATES
"Shigella is not considered to be a typical sexually transmitted infection," Dr. Andi Toufexis, a Texas-based family medicine physician who specializes in sexual health, told Fox News Digital.
"However, this gastrointestinal bacteria can be spread through sex when one partner comes into contact with the other's fecal matter."
Most patients with extensively drug-resistant Shigella in the CDC analysis were adult men. (iStock)
Shigella is not new, and sexual transmission has been documented since the 1970s, Toufexis said. What is changing is the growing share of tested samples classified as XDR.
MICHIGAN REPORTS 2 DEATHS IN RARE PARASITE OUTBREAK THAT HAS SICKENED MORE THAN 11,000

The CDC report found that most people with XDR shigella were adult men. Sexual exposure data were not routinely collected, so the report could not establish exactly how each infection was contracted. But previous research has found sexual contact among men who have sex with men as an important transmission route.

Eighty-six percent of XDR patients were men with a median age of 41, and of those with a known HIV status, nearly half were living with HIV, Evans noted. People experiencing homelessness and those with weakened immune systems may also face heightened risks, he said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Children younger than 5 are especially likely to get shigella, according to the CDC, and many outbreaks in the U.S. have been linked to childcare and schools. Earlier U.S. outbreaks primarily affected children and involved strains that were susceptible to antibiotics.
Washing hands before preparing food can help reduce the spread of Shigella.

According to the CDC report, 37.6% of patients with hospitalization data were hospitalized for the antibiotic-resistant infection. The CDC reported no deaths among the XDR cases analyzed and said infections may be undercounted because not all positive specimens were cultured or tested for resistance. Most patients with available travel histories reported no recent international travel, though travel information was missing for many.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Evans said Americans should be "concerned, not panicked" about the infection.
Most shigella infections resolve on their own, Toufexis added, but severe illness may need treatment.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Dr. Michael Aziz, an internist at Lenox Hill Hospital in New York City and author of "The Perfect 10 Diet" and "The Ageless Revolution," urged people who suspect shigella to seek medical advice before taking antidiarrheal medicine such as Imodium.
"You want to flush out the bacteria, you want to get it out of your system," Aziz told Fox News Digital.
Experts advise people with Shigella not to take antidiarrheal medicines such as Imodium, which can slow the gut.

To reduce the chance of infection, doctors recommend washing hands, genitals and the anal area before and after sex, using condoms or dental dams and cleaning sex toys after each use. If you or a partner has diarrhea, avoid sex and wait at least two weeks after symptoms end before resuming, Toufexis said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Feeling better does not always mean that an infection is completely gone," she said.
Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

title: One type of sleep linked to dramatically lower risk of dementia, Parkinson's and 81 other diseases
summary: Greater REM sleep was linked to 80% lower Parkinson's risk and 46% lower dementia risk in a major study of over 95,000 adults tracked for years.
story: Erin Palinski-Wade, a New Jersey-based nutritionist and author of ‘The Sleepdemic Solution,’ confirmed that household surroundings and ambient neighborhood conditions can directly interfere with restfulness.
Not all stages of sleep are equal in terms of benefits for the brain.
Greater amounts of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep were associated with lower risks of 83 diseases, including dementia, Parkinson’s disease and heart failure, new research has shown.
Additionally, greater amounts of deep sleep were associated with lower risks of seven conditions.
THIS ONE QUESTION MAY REVEAL WHETHER YOUR BODY IS GETTING THE REST IT NEEDS, STUDY FINDS

That’s according to a study of 95,559 adults who wore wrist accelerometers continuously for seven consecutive days and nights. Researchers in China used deep-learning algorithms to analyze REM sleep, deep sleep, light sleep, total sleep duration, wakefulness after sleep onset and sleep irregularity.
They then looked at health records to assess associations with more than 1,000 diseases over a nearly nine-year follow-up period.
Greater amounts of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep were associated with lower risks of 83 diseases, including dementia, Parkinson’s disease and heart failure, new research has shown. (iStock)
Greater REM sleep was associated with a significantly lower risk of several diseases, including Parkinson’s (80% lower relative risk), dementia (46% lower risk) and heart failure (26% lower risk).
Greater deep sleep was associated with lower risks of seven conditions, including Type 2 diabetes and major depressive disorder.
MORE NAPS, HIGHER RISK? RESEARCH LINKS DAYTIME SLEEP TO HEALTH WARNINGS IN AGING ADULTS

Sleep duration was also found to be highly linked to disease outcome. Six to eight hours per night was found to be the "sweet spot" associated with the lowest risk for 69 diseases. In contrast, sleeping fewer than five hours per night was linked to an increased risk of 37 health conditions.

The study also found that greater night-to-night sleep irregularity and more wakefulness during the night were associated with higher risks of several conditions, including anxiety and substance use disorders.
The findings were published Sept. 17 in the journal PLOS Medicine.
Disrupted sleep may sometimes be an early warning sign of disease rather than simply a cause, a sleep expert noted. (iStock)

"I think what is important is the total duration of sleep, and the percentage that REM takes up," Oki Ishikawa, M.D., pulmonary, critical care and sleep medicine expert at Northwell’s Northern Westchester Hospital, told Fox News Digital.
"The average percentage of REM sleep in this study population was about 20%, and generally 20-25% is considered normal per sleep cycle."
5-STEP SLEEP RESET COULD PROMOTE HEALTHY WEIGHT LOSS, NUTRITIONIST SAYS
Ishikawa, who was not involved in the study, said he does not believe that a higher amount of REM sleep alone will necessarily lower the risk.

"Normal sleep pattern and duration are associated with aspects like maintenance of good immune function and memory, so I think the important message here is to try and get a sufficient amount of sleep in general," Ishikawa sai.
Researchers used deep-learning algorithms to analyze REM sleep, deep sleep, light sleep, total sleep duration, wakefulness after sleep onset and sleep irregularity. (iStock)
Disrupted sleep may sometimes be an early warning sign of disease rather than simply a cause, according to Dr. Chelsie Rohrscheib, head sleep expert at Wesper, a sleep analysis company in New York.

"Conditions such as Parkinson’s disease, dementia and heart failure can begin affecting sleep years before they are diagnosed," Rohrscheib, who also was not involved in the research, told Fox News Digital.
"At the same time, poor sleep may contribute to disease progression, so the relationship likely works both ways."
DIETITIAN REVEALS SIMPLE EATING STRATEGY FOR BETTER SLEEP — AND ONE HABIT TO AVOID
The researchers noted some limitations of the study. Because it was observational, it could only show an association and could not prove that increasing REM or deep sleep directly prevents disease.
"Sleep was measured for only one week using a wrist device, which is less accurate than a clinical sleep study for identifying sleep stages," Rohrscheib said.
"Poor sleep may contribute to disease progression, so the relationship likely works both ways," an expert said. (iStock)
"Some health information was collected years earlier, medications that can affect sleep were not fully considered and some medical diagnoses may have been missed."

As the participants were all from the UK Biobank, the study population was also less diverse and generally healthier than the overall population, so the findings may not apply equally to everyone, Rohrscheib noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Overall, changes in sleep may provide important clues about underlying health, but this study cannot determine whether poor sleep is a cause, an early symptom or both," she concluded.
Rohrscheib also cautioned that while wrist-worn sleep trackers are generally good at estimating sleep stages, they are not 100% accurate.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Without a formal in-lab sleep study, it's impossible to know how much time the participants spent in REM and other sleep stages," she said.
More research is needed to determine whether increasing REM or deep sleep can help prevent certain diseases, the researchers said.
"If you get about seven to nine hours of uninterrupted sleep, you most likely have the opportunity to cycle through REM in a sufficient way."
Future studies could also explore whether the relationship between sleep stages and disease risk varies by age, sex, overall health and other individual characteristics.

Both experts recommended following general sleep hygiene practices, such as maintaining an optimal environment (dark, cool and quiet), keeping a consistent sleep schedule and avoiding sleep-disrupting substances such as alcohol and caffeine.

"If you have other sleep pathologies like sleep apnea … treating that would be a great way to optimize the amount of REM sleep," Ishikawa advised.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
While it can be difficult to measure REM sleep without a wearable, he said the best gauge is whether one feels refreshed upon waking and doesn’t feel sleepy during the day.
"If you get about seven to nine hours of uninterrupted sleep, you most likely have the opportunity to cycle through REM in a sufficient way."

title: Man loses 15 stubborn pounds after age 50 without giving up pizza or donuts
summary: Carl Daikeler lost 15 pounds by swapping breakfast for a 250-calorie shake and eating a big salad for lunch, then enjoying total dinner freedom.
story: Carl Daikeler, CEO and founder of BODi, shares how a simple breakfast, a hearty lunch, and the freedom to eat what he wants for dinner helped him lose 15 pounds and get into the best shape of his life at 63.
Maintaining weight loss in midlife doesn’t necessarily require strict dietary bans or extreme fasting protocols.
Carl Daikeler, co-founder and CEO of the fitness and nutrition company BODi, says a simple routine earlier in the day has helped him manage his weight while allowing more freedom at dinner.
Los Angeles-based Daikeler, 63, who has led the health brand formerly known as Beachbody for 28 years, openly admits that he doesn't have an affinity for healthy foods.
10-MINUTE FITNESS HABIT CAN HELP ADULTS OVER 40 MAINTAIN MUSCLE AND STAY STRONG
"I eat like a third-grader, okay? Pizza's a food group," Daikeler joked in an interview with Fox News Digital.
"I'm just constantly trying to figure out how can I hack my way without having to overturn my life to become one of those diehard health and fitness people, because I'm never going to become that."
The fitness CEO said he maintains long-term weight loss without strict dieting by eating structured, high-nutrient meals during the day to allow total freedom at dinner. (iStock)

When Daikeler turned 57, he found himself unable to lose 15 pounds he had gained around his waistline. Rather than adopting a strict diet, he adjusted two specific meals during the day while leaving his evening schedule unrestricted, he shared.
For breakfast, Daikeler replaced standard options with a nutrient-dense shake containing protein, fiber, prebiotics, probiotics and greens, totaling roughly 250 calories.
NIGHTLY GLASS OF WINE MAY NOT BE AS HARMLESS AS MANY PEOPLE THINK, STUDY SUGGESTS
"I got rid of breakfast, or I changed my breakfast to this shake that we've got called Shakeology," Daikeler said. "I put some spinach in there and I put a banana in there."
For lunch, Daikeler prepares a large salad loaded with baby spinach, carrots and chicken, mixed with toppings that mask the taste of the greens.
Replacing traditional breakfast with a 250-calorie nutrient shake provides essential greens, fiber and protein without requiring major cooking or dietary overhauls. (iStock)
"I hide it with some cheese, some nuts, some sliced strawberries, and it's delicious, and I put chicken in there ... I don't feel like I'm eating a bowl of vegetables, but I am."
By keeping breakfast and lunch relatively structured, Daikeler gives himself more flexibility at dinner.
BEER, WINE OR LIQUOR? MASSIVE STUDY REVEALS WHICH WAS LINKED TO LOWER DEATH RISK
"Now I've got a 'day pass' for everything else ... I eat whatever I want at dinner."
He does, however, follow a single guideline regarding alcohol intake. "I'm careful not to drink too much," he said.
"Now I've got a 'day pass' for everything else ... I eat whatever I want at dinner."
"Once I did that — Shakeology for breakfast, a big salad for lunch, total freedom for dinner, limited alcohol — the 15 pounds just got wiped out. And it stayed off."
Daikeler warns that overly restrictive nutrition plans are usually difficult to stick with long-term, leading many to abandon their health goals entirely.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"If you're trying to be too restrictive, I don't think that's life," he said. "The whole point is living ... So if it's too restrictive, it's going to break."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Instead of completely banning indulgence foods, Daikeler recommends using portion control and mindfulness to enjoy without overeating.
The expert said he focuses on smaller portions rather than cutting favorite foods like pizza out entirely. (iStock)

"I love pizza. But I've learned that I can enjoy pizza without eating the whole pizza," he said. "I like doughnuts. I've learned that I can have literally a quarter of a doughnut and be like, that was delicious. But I get no additional satisfaction by eating the whole doughnut."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
For Daikeler, that balance is part of a broader focus on "health span" — prioritizing quality of life and the ability to stay active as he ages.

"Health span versus lifespan is all about quality of life," he said. "I'm all for longevity, but it's really about quality of life — a way to live and enjoy life that is balanced with maximizing your time on earth."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
While Daikeler said this approach has worked for him, weight-loss strategies are not one-size-fits-all.

According to the National Institutes of Health, different eating plans can support weight loss, but the most effective approach depends on a person's individual health needs, preferences and ability to maintain the habits long-term. Individuals are generally advised to consult a doctor or registered dietitian for personalized guidance.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Ilhan Omar's husband snaps over rumors she fled US after federal immigration fraud raid
summary: Tim Mynett was spotted at the couple's D.C. home as HSI's fraud investigation into Ilhan Omar's immigration paperwork intensifies with new subpoenas.
story: Rep. Ilhan Omar's, D-Minn., husband, Tim Mynett, responds to rumors that the congresswoman fled the country after HSI raided their Washington, D.C., home as part of a federal criminal investigation. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

While Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has not been seen publicly since federal agents raided her Washington, D.C., residence on Monday, her political consultant husband was once again spotted emerging from their shared rental home this week.

Tim Mynett was seen Wednesday stepping out in the neighborhood to walk their Golden Labrador Retriever dog Teddy, a second time later that same day to take out the trash and a third time to walk out his wife's staffer.
"There are rumors that the congresswoman left the country, is that true?" Mynett was asked while on an evening walk with Teddy.

"You guys are annoying the hell out of all the neighbors around here, man," he told Fox News Digital when approached about the developments this week, including President Donald Trump weighing in on the saga.

One of Omar's congressional staffers was captured the same day bringing into the couple's home two large bags from fast food chain Burger King. Security escorted her to the door and staked out in front of the house after she entered with the meal.
ILHAN OMAR’S EMBATTLED HUSBAND APPEARS AT SCENE OF HSI RAID IN MIDST OF CRIMINAL FRAUD INVESTIGATION
An image of Ilhan Omar overlaid over her neighborhood in DC. (Getty Images)

Rumors swirled that Omar fled from the country following the raid carried out by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) as part of a criminal fraud investigation looking into the Somali-born congresswoman’s immigration paperwork, as first reported by Fox News Digital.
Omar’s cellphone and passport were reportedly seized by federal authorities during the search.

The congresswoman's staff helped to get her birth year adjusted from 1981 to 1982 in the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library, according to reporters. Omar gained citizenship automatically through her father’s naturalization since she was reportedly 17 years old at the time. If Omar was born in 1981, she would have been 18 years old, meaning the validity of her citizenship could be threatened because she was no longer a minor.
The altered birthdate was published during her entire time serving in Minnesota’s House and for months into her time serving in Congress.

When asked about the federal investigation earlier this week, Mynett told Fox News Digital he has "no concerns" about what federal authorities will find on his wife while investigating her immigration pathway.
"My wife came here when she was 12 years old as a child war refugee," Mynett said. "No concerns."

His comments to Fox News Digital come after Omar’s relatives were reportedly issued subpoenas as part of HSI’s investigation into the congresswoman's immigration paperwork. At least two of Omar's relatives were subpoenaed, one of which is reportedly Omar’s sister, Sahra Noor.
ILHAN OMAR’S HUSBAND INSISTS HE HAS ‘NO CONCERNS’ AMID FEDERAL IMMIGRATION INVESTIGATION

Fox News Digital asked Mynett about President Donald Trump publicly questioning Omar’s net worth by alleging on Truth Social that her accountant may have reported fraudulent money when her previous financial disclosure listed the couple's shared net worth as high as $30 million.

"Why did Ilhan Omar report a Net Worth of up to 30 Million Dollars just a short time ago, and then immediately say, "Oh, I made a mistake! It’s really $100,000." Could it be that her highly paid accountant actually reported the money that was stolen from her fraudulent activities in Minnesota? Would something like that be possible? Do you think the accountant actually gave the right number the first time, 30 Million Dollars, and then she was forced to disavow because she never would have been able to report where that much money came from? She must have freaked out when she saw that money!" Trump posted to Truth Social on Tuesday.

"Where did her house come from, where did her cars come from, and what about her lovely place in Washington, D.C.? I didn’t know that Congressmen and women made that kind of money, but I do know her husband, according to information and belief, makes almost nothing, so it couldn’t have come from him. How many people did she illegally bring into our Country from Somalia? America wants answers, and we want them, NOW!"
Mynett is at the center of yet another investigation into Omar — this time looking into her finances.
Following Monday’s HSI raid, U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said Tuesday that her office is also investigating Omar's financial disclosures about reporting of her and Mynett’s shared net worth.
OMAR FACES MOUNTING SCRUTINY AFTER FRAUD RINGLEADER SENTENCED TO 41 YEARS
Rep. Ilhan Omar sits with husband Tim Mynett during the first day of the Democratic National Convention at the United Center on August 19, 2024, in Chicago, Illinois. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

Scrutiny of Omar's finances intensified after her 2024 congressional financial disclosure listed business interests associated with Mynett valued between $6 million and $30 million. Omar's office subsequently said the figures were incorrect and amended the filing.

The largest change in the documents was from Mynett’s assets. His reported ownership interests in both his winery and venture capital advisory firm, which were previously valued in the millions of dollars, are listed with no value now.

In Omar’s 2024 financial disclosure records, Mynett’s share in his winery was valued between $1 million and $5 million, and his share at the venture capital advisory firm was valued between $5 million and $25 million. Now, his equity interests are both listed at $0.

Omar's office previously told Fox News Digital that Mynett has partners in both businesses and said the earlier disclosure mistakenly reflected the businesses' total equity rather than his ownership interest. The office also said the original filing listed assets without accounting for liabilities.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Officials noted that the investigation into Omar's financial disclosures is unrelated to the raid on her home.
Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: Fort Hood survivors praise Trump for scrapping Hasan execution livestream: ‘We’re not barbaric’
summary: Alonzo Lunsford, shot seven times by Nidal Hasan, called Trump's decision to cancel the firing squad livestream a "positive move" for the nation.
story: Fort Hood shooting survivor Alonzo Lunsford called President Trump’s decision to allow victims to witness Nidal Hasan’s execution without livestreaming it to the public a "positive move," arguing the execution should not become a spectacle.

Survivors of the 2009 Fort Hood massacre praised President Donald Trump's decision not to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, after warning that broadcasting his death could turn the execution into a spectacle and hand terrorist groups a propaganda tool.

Hasan is still set to be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3, 2026, and Trump said the immediate families of his victims will be permitted to witness the execution in person. But it will no longer be broadcast to the general public as previously announced by Secretary of War Pete Hegseth.
Alonzo Lunsford, who was shot seven times by Hasan during the attack nearly 17 years ago, told Fox News Digital that Trump's decision is a "positive move."
"It proves that we are a better people, a better nation, and that we're not barbaric," Lunsford said in immediate reaction to the walk-back by Trump on Thursday. "We don't glorify such actions."
VETERAN SHOT 7 TIMES IN FORT HOOD MASSACRE HAS A WARNING FOR AMERICANS PLANNING TO WATCH EXECUTION
Fort Hood victim Alonzo Lunsfords says he plans to attend Nidal Hasan's execution. (Courtesy of Alonzo Lunsford)
Lunsford said he supports Hasan's death sentence and execution by firing squad but drew a line at broadcasting it to the public.

"For it to be made a spectacle for everyone to witness how they're gonna do a tailgate or, 'Hey, we're gonna have a cookout and we're gonna watch this man be put to death.' No, it's not about that," Lunsford said. "It's not a spectacle. It's not a pay-per-view event or a WWE wrestling match or even a boxing match."
He also warned that footage of Hasan's execution could be seized upon by terrorist organizations.
"You don't want that to be used as a tool for ISIS or al-Qaeda to recruit and say, 'Hey, this is what happens to you if you do this against the infidel,'" Lunsford said.
Julia Wilson was a civilian employee at Fort Hood when Hasan went on his rampage. She was nine months pregnant during the attack, which was carried out on her due date.
FORT HOOD SHOOTER SHOULD BE EXECUTED '13 TIMES OVER' — BUT NOT ON LIVE STREAM, SURVIVOR SAYS
She was slammed against a wall amid the chaos of the shooting and has said that it was only by the grace of God that she and her then-unborn son survived.
Wilson was already against the livestreaming of Hasan's execution because she didn't want others to be traumatized like she was during the deadly attack.
"I'm ecstatic about that," she told Fox News Digital, reacting to the news that the plan to livestream the event would not proceed.

U.S. President Barack Obama (R) and first lady Michelle Obama pay their respects to the people killed as they attend a memorial service for the thirteen victims of the shooting rampage allegedly by U.S. Army Major Nidal Malik Hasan on November 10, 2009 in Fort Hood, Texas. Hasan, an army psychiatrist, is accused of killing 13 people and wounded 30 during a shooting at the military base. (Getty Images)

"I'm worried about other people's mental health," she continued. "I don't think the government… really put a lot of thought into how this was going to go down and how it was going to transpire until today."

"I don't think they really thought about how this may affect people," said Wilson. "Seeing something like that affects your mental health. I don't care who you are. I don't care what you've seen. Seeing someone murdered in front of you or killed in front of you affects your mental health, whether they deserve it or not."

Wilson also worried that if the livestream had proceeded, it would exist online forever, and that children might discover it while searching the web. "Once it's on out there, it's out there," she said.

Trump said Wednesday that he believed publicly broadcasting Hasan's death could have served as a deterrent, but ultimately sided with those who opposed making the execution available for anyone to watch.

"I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

"He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," Trump continued. "That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose. They deserve to witness JUSTICE!"

Photographs of victims of the shooting are seen surrounding the podium where the memorial service that U.S. President Barack Obama and first lady Michelle Obama will attend for the thirteen victims of the shooting rampage by U.S. Army Major Nidal Malik Hasan on November 10, 2009, in Fort Hood, Texas. Hasan, an army psychiatrist, killed 13 people and wounded 30 in a shooting at the military base on November 5, 2009. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)
Lunsford pointed to warnings surrounding Hasan before the shooting and criticized the Army's handling of the future attacker before he was transferred from Walter Reed to Fort Hood.

"We knew this guy had issues," Lunsford said. "If you are privy to the ticking time bomb report, you will see what he was talking about. This guy had issues and they just passed the buck and moved him from Walter Reed to Fort Hood."
Lunsford wondered what might have happened had Hasan deployed overseas before carrying out an attack.
"Suppose he would have did the deed once he got in country on a FOB, a forward operating base," he said. "Imagine how many American lives would have been lost then."
For Lunsford, allowing victims to witness Hasan's execution remains important even without a public broadcast.
"It's gonna be a traumatic thing for, at least for the families of the fallen," he said. "They'll be able to close the chapter and hopefully close the book."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Lunsford said survivors will continue to live with reminders of the attack long after Hasan is gone.

"Every day we get up, we come to the VA hospital or we have to take our meds in the morning or we get ready to do something that we normally would have been doing prior to 5 November '09 that we're no longer able to do now, that's a constant reminder," he said.
"I am no longer a victim of his," Lunsford added. "I'm a survivor."

title: Trump links Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed to Muslim Brotherhood: 'He's a con man'
summary: Trump called Abdul El-Sayed "100% Muslim Brotherhood" as posts by the battleground Senate candidate's half-sister come under fresh scrutiny.
story: Fox News congressional correspondent Bill Melugin has the latest on U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed's alleged family ties to the Muslim Brotherhood and his campaign denials on 'Special Report.'
President Donald Trump on Thursday linked Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood amid scrutiny over his alleged family ties to the Islamist organization.

"He's a Muslim Brotherhood guy, 100%," Trump said during a lunch in the White House Rose Garden. "He's a Muslim Brotherhood guy. How about having him be on the Senate Intelligence Committee? How about that? The guy's 100% Muslim Brotherhood."

El-Sayed has come under scrutiny from Republicans over social media posts made by his half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, alleging their mother was an active member of the Muslim Brotherhood in Egypt during the 1970s.
COUNTERTERRORISM EXPERT WARNS ABDUL EL-SAYED SENATE BID RAISES HOMELAND SECURITY CONCERNS
President Donald Trump on Thursday said Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is linked to the Muslim Brotherhood, calling him a "fraud" and "con man." (Getty Images)
He has denied any family connections to the group. During a recent interview with NBC's Meet the Press, El-Sayed rejected the assertions when asked to set the record straight.
"I have no ties; we have no ties," El-Sayed said.
EL-SAYED ASKED IF HE BELIEVES AMERICA IS 'READY FOR A MUSLIM PRESIDENT' AHEAD OF SENATE RACE
He accused political opponents of engaging in anti-Muslim rhetoric rather than addressing his policy positions.

"[Opponent Mike Rogers'] only strategy is to point to me and my name and my faith and to say that we're different, and that you should suspect people simply because they are different than you in how they pray," he said.
EL-SAYED’S LIBERAL AGENDA CLASHES WITH MUSLIM VOTERS WHO BACK HIM ANYWAY: ‘MALE VERSION’ OF ILHAN OMAR

Abdul El-Sayed, US Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan, speaks during the Michigan Democratic Party's 2026 nominating convention in Lansing, Michigan, US, on Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (Sarah Rice/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
However, according to Abdelhadi, their mother was an active member of the Muslim Brotherhood.
"Had an amazing talk with my mom about her activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during the early 70s while she was in college #respect," Abdelhadi wrote in a 2012 post on X.
In another 2012 social media post, she wrote: "My family has long been MB, but I've always felt that it has navigated the political sphere poorly/destructively."
During his remarks, Trump said he looked forward to visiting Michigan to "expose this fraud that's running."
"He's a fraud. He's a con man," Trump said.
