Fox News Digital has reached out to El-Sayed's campaign for comment.
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: America's next war could reach US soil, top Army general warns
summary: The Army's new "How the Army Fights" framework prepares American forces for contested deployments as drones and surveillance reshape the battlefield.
story: Acting Army chief Gen. Christopher LaNeve explains how lessons from Iran, Ukraine and cartel drone operations are reshaping the Army's approach to combat, from new technology to soldiers' basic battlefield skills.
The American military has largely operated on a familiar premise: combat the enemy overseas before the fight reaches home.

But as drones, cyberattacks and long-range weapons pose growing threats to U.S. military installations and critical infrastructure, Army leaders are preparing for a future in which American forces could come under attack before they ever deploy overseas.
"If we're going against a pacing threat, power projection will be contested," Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the Army's acting chief of staff, told Fox News Digital on Wednesday.
He said the military is rethinking assumptions that were held during decades of fighting in Iraq and Afghanistan, when American forces could largely count on secure bases and supply lines at home.
FBI WARNS BATTLEFIELD-STYLE DRONE ATTACKS COULD REACH US: 'ONLY A MATTER OF TIME'
Anti-drone laser system trialed on a Stryker combat military vehicle with a machine gun aimed at the sky in Ukraine during a counteroffensive. (Michelle Ursi/Getty Images)

"During the Global War on Terror, we took a lot of things for granted, because we could," LaNeve said during a small-group roundtable at the Association of the United States Army's annual conference in Washington this week.

In a potential conflict with China, disrupting American military bases, transportation networks and communications could delay U.S. forces from reaching the battlefield. The Pentagon's latest report on China's military capabilities warns that Beijing has positioned cyber capabilities inside U.S. critical infrastructure networks that could be used to disrupt American military mobilization during a conflict.

The concerns come as the Pentagon places renewed emphasis on homeland defense and military installations as they prepare to potentially confront threats closer to home. U.S. officials have previously confirmed drone incursions over installations — including Joint Base Langley-Eustis in Virginia and Picatinny Arsenal in New Jersey. Though those incidents have not been publicly attributed to China.

The warning of a future fight on American soil comes amid the How the Army Fights rollout. The new operational framework places greater emphasis on preparing American forces to deploy, communicate and sustain operations even when military bases, supply lines and communications networks are under attack.
The guidance places greater emphasis on the Army's ability to deploy and sustain forces under threat, including when communications, supply lines and military infrastructure are disrupted.
US MILITARY BASES ARE ‘ILL-EQUIPPED’ TO STOP DRONE SWARMS, TOP COMMANDER REVEALS AFTER RUBIO'S UAP WARNING

Army Vice Chief of Staff General Christopher LaNeve testifies during a Senate Committee on Appropriations, Subcommittee on Department of Defense budget hearing at the Dirksen Senate Office Building in Washington, DC on May 19, 2026. (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)
LaNeve said the Army is using the framework to establish clearer priorities for how its formations train, fight and incorporate new technology.
"It was important to get this document out to provide a direction for our Army, a stake in the ground in where we're moving," LaNeve told Fox News Digital in an interview Wednesday.

The changes are being led by an Army leadership team serving in acting capacities following the departures of former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll and Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George. LaNeve remains the Senate-confirmed vice chief of staff.
LaNeve explained how the Army is preparing to keep fighting even when an adversary disrupts military communications.

"I think what you would see inside this command and control capability is the ability to operate disconnected and then reconnect when you have that capability, but to continue to be able to maneuver," he said.

The Army is also rethinking how it protects military installations at home. LaNeve pointed to Joint Interagency Task Force 401, which is working with federal and local law enforcement to strengthen counter-drone defenses around military bases and critical infrastructure.
CARTELS USE DRONES TO SCOUT BORDER AGENTS AND MAP SMUGGLING ROUTES, EXPERT WARNS
A safe that stores most of the federal government's gold bullion and other valuables. (Getty Images)

Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle pointed to the southern border as an example of how soldiers are already confronting drone threats closer to home. He said soldiers are using the mission to test new counter-drone technology against real-world threats, gaining experience they can bring back to their units as the Army prepares for future conflicts.

The Army is also expanding its preparations for biological threats that could disrupt military operations. Officials announced this week that biological incidents will be incorporated into routine combat training as part of a broader effort to ensure soldiers can continue carrying out their missions through disease outbreaks or deliberate biological attacks.

During a separate panel Wednesday, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink warned that advances in surveillance technology could soon make it increasingly difficult for military forces to operate anywhere without being detected.

"We are rapidly heading to a point in time where, depending on what your signature is, how fast you're moving, the enemy is going to have some sense to where you are no matter where you are on the planet," Meink said.
He suggested that level of surveillance could emerge within five years, potentially sooner, as China and other adversaries expand their ability to track and target military assets.

Meink said the Pentagon is working to make its forces more survivable, including through autonomous systems capable of operating in dangerous environments where commanders might hesitate to send manned platforms.

War Secretary Pete Hegseth, speaking alongside Meink and the other service secretaries, criticized what he described as the Pentagon's failure to keep pace with technological advances under the Biden administration.
"On hypersonics, they took a nap. On space, they took a nap. On weaponization of space, they took a nap. On drones, they took a nap," Hegseth said.
LaNeve emphasized that despite the Army's growing reliance on advanced technology, soldiers must still be able to carry out their missions when those systems are unavailable.
"Soldiers are our number one platform. It is the Army's platform," he told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The technology, he said, is intended to make troops more capable, but soldiers must remain grounded in the fundamental skills needed to fight without it.

title: Trump-appointed justice joins Sotomayor in unlikely alliance to rip DOJ's handling of illegal immigrant case
summary: Supreme Court Justices Neil Gorsuch and Sonia Sotomayor joined forces after prosecutors charged a deported man despite ordering him to stay in Oklahoma after his first conviction.
story: Supreme Court justices will begin hearing oral arguments Monday on a wide range of cases this term involving gun rights, religious freedom, immigration detention and the limits of government power.

Conservative Supreme Court Justice Neil Gorsuch has joined forces with liberal Justice Sonia Sotomayor to question the federal government's prosecution of an illegal immigrant, marking the latest unlikely alliance between the two justices.

Gorsuch, appointed by President Donald Trump, and Sotomayor, appointed by former President Barack Obama, raised concerns about the government's decision to prosecute a Mexican national twice for being found unlawfully in the United States — even after a federal court prohibited him from leaving the Eastern District of Oklahoma following his first conviction.

The unlikely pairing emerged Tuesday when the Supreme Court declined to hear an appeal from Jesus Herrera-Salazar, who argued that his second prosecution violated the Fifth Amendment's protection against double jeopardy. Although the justices agreed the Court should not take up the case, Sotomayor issued a separate statement, joined by Gorsuch, warning of serious constitutional problems with the government's actions.
GORSUCH SAYS IDEOLOGICAL DIVIDES ON SUPREME COURT COME DOWN TO ‘HOW YOU READ LAW,’ NOT POLITICS

Supreme Court Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Neil Gorsuch issued a joint statement this week questioning the federal government's prosecution of an illegal immigrant, marking the latest in a series of unusual constitutional alliances between the two justices. (Getty Images)

"From the moment he was released from custody after serving his first term of imprisonment, Herrera-Salazar was presented with a Hobson's choice," Sotomayor wrote in the statement joined by Gorsuch. "In the Government's eyes, whether Herrera-Salazar remained in the Eastern District of Oklahoma or left the United States, he would be breaking the law."

The two justices questioned how the government could punish someone for remaining in the country after effectively prohibiting him from leaving, with the pair's joint statement describing the situation as a "constitutional absurdity."

Their agreement is particularly noteworthy given their differing judicial philosophies, but it is not the first time the pair has found common ground over constitutional protections against government action.

In November 2024, Sotomayor and Gorsuch jointly questioned whether homeowners should be compensated when police destroy private property while carrying out law enforcement operations. A few months later, they again joined forces to raise concerns about warrantless misdemeanor arrests. In both cases, as in the latest immigration dispute, the Court declined to hear the appeals, but the justices issued statements highlighting constitutional questions they believed deserved attention.
The U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for the Trump administration to continue third-country deportations while the justices consider a legal challenge to the policy. (Getty Images)

The pair's latest expression of joint public concern came after Herrera-Salazar, a Mexican national previously removed from the United States, was indicted in 2020 for being found in the country following deportation, a violation of federal immigration law.
'UNPRECEDENTED': JUDGES REVEAL BEHIND-THE-SCENES COORDINATION ON TRUMP IMMIGRATION CASES

He pleaded guilty and served a prison sentence before being placed on supervised release, during which he was expressly prohibited from leaving the Eastern District of Oklahoma without authorization under the terms of his release.

While still under those restrictions, Herrera-Salazar was stopped by police in Heavener, Oklahoma, and subsequently charged again under the same federal immigration statute prohibiting previously deported individuals from being found unlawfully in the United States. A jury subsequently convicted Herrera-Salazar, resulting in another prison sentence and additional supervised release.

The second prosecution prompted Herrera-Salazar to challenge his conviction on double-jeopardy grounds, arguing that the government had effectively punished him twice for the same continuous period of unlawful presence.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit rejected that argument, concluding that the offense is completed when authorities discover a person's unlawful presence and that a subsequent discovery can support a separate prosecution without requiring another illegal entry.
Federal immigration agents arrest a man in the parking lot of an H-Mart grocery store on October 31, 2025, in Niles, Illinois. (Photo by Jamie Kelter Davis/Getty Images)

Sotomayor and Gorsuch questioned that reasoning, pointing to Supreme Court precedent establishing that prosecutors cannot evade double-jeopardy protections simply by dividing one continuous crime into separate periods. Their concern was not whether Herrera-Salazar had violated immigration law in the first place, but whether the government could repeatedly prosecute him for remaining in the United States without evidence of a separate unlawful reentry.

The justices also highlighted that Herrera-Salazar's supervised-release conditions restricted him from leaving Oklahoma, meaning the government was effectively preventing him from ending the conduct for which it later prosecuted him again. Sotomayor warned that, under the government's interpretation, prosecutors theoretically could have brought separate charges against Herrera-Salazar for each day he remained imprisoned following his first conviction.

The statement was issued despite the justices' agreement with the Court's decision not to review the case. Sotomayor explained that Herrera-Salazar had already been removed from the United States and expressed hope that the unusual circumstances surrounding his prosecution would not arise again.
SUPREME COURT KICKS OFF NEW TERM WITH FRESH QUESTIONS OVER ITS LEGITIMACY AND ITS FUTURE

Rather than dissenting from the Court's refusal to hear the appeal, Sotomayor and Gorsuch used what is formally known as a statement "respecting the denial of certiorari" to publicly identify constitutional concerns and urge lower courts to avoid similar problems in future cases.

Members of the Supreme Court pose for a group photo at the Supreme Court on Oct. 7, 2022. Seated from left: Associate Justice Sonia Sotomayor, Associate Justice Clarence Thomas, Chief Justice of the United States John G. Roberts Jr., Associate Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. and Associate Justice Elena Kagan. Standing behind from left: Associate Justice Amy Coney Barrett, Associate Justice Neil M. Gorsuch, Associate Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh and Associate Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
The unusual collaboration follows two earlier cases in which Sotomayor authored statements joined by Gorsuch after the Supreme Court declined review.

In November 2024, the pair raised concerns in Baker v. City of McKinney, a Texas case involving a homeowner whose property was extensively damaged during a police operation to apprehend an armed fugitive.

Police had used tear gas, explosives and an armored vehicle during the standoff, leaving the home severely damaged. Although the justices acknowledged that officers acted properly to protect public safety, they questioned whether the Constitution permits the government to impose the financial burden of such damage on an individual homeowner without compensation.

Meanwhile, in February 2025, Sotomayor and Gorsuch again joined forces, this time questioning whether the Fourth Amendment permitted police to make warrantless arrests for misdemeanors committed outside an officer's presence that they did not personally witness.

That case involved a Florida man arrested for loitering and prowling after police responding to a report of suspicious activity encountered him walking through a residential neighborhood before dawn. A subsequent search uncovered stolen mail, leading to a federal criminal charge.

title: Bill and Hillary Clinton make eleventh-hour midterm moves as party's old guard faces new reality
summary: Bill Clinton heads to Florida to campaign for David Jolly while Hillary Clinton launches "High Stakes" podcast with Kara Swisher for midterms.
story: Fox News host Greg Gutfeld and the panel discuss claims that the former first lady would have won the presidential race if she were a man.

The Clintons are back on the midterm campaign circuit — with Bill Clinton heading to Florida to stump for Democratic gubernatorial nominee David Jolly and Hillary Clinton taking to the podcast microphone as the party makes its final push toward Election Day.

The former president is scheduled to make his first public campaign appearance of the 2026 election cycle on Oct. 20 for Jolly, a former Republican congressman turned Democrat. Hillary, meanwhile, has teamed up with journalist Kara Swisher for a new midterm-focused podcast series and has been making campaign appearances of her own.

The moves bring two of the Democratic Party's most recognizable figures into the midterm fight as the party grapples with competing visions for its future, raising questions about how much influence the Clintons still wield as progressive candidates challenge the Democratic establishment.
BIDEN CONSPICUOUSLY ABSENT FROM CAMPAIGN TRAIL AS OBAMA, HARRIS STEP UP FOR MIDTERM PUSH
Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and her husband, former U.S. President Bill Clinton. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
While the Clintons remain prominent in Democratic politics, one party strategist says Democrats are more focused on winning elections than revisiting the party's past.

"President Clinton remains one of the most gifted political communicators this country has ever known, particularly when it comes to connecting with working-class voters on the economic issues that matter most," said Democratic strategist Kevin Walling. "But I don’t believe that Democrats are looking for a Clinton restoration — they’re looking for a path back to winning."
Democratic strategist Mally Smith offered a more skeptical assessment of how much reach the Clintons have in the closing weeks of the election.

"Hillary and Bill are still relevant to some voters. However, they will mostly be useful in speaking to the Democratic base and those who are highly engaged in politics," said Smith. "It is a hard media environment to breakthrough and even current elected officials, let alone former office holders, will struggle to get people’s attention."

Clinton's Oct. 20 appearance will take place at an interfaith event in Hollywood, Florida, alongside Jolly, who is facing Republican Rep. Byron Donalds in the race to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis.

Jolly is campaigning on affordability, including lowering property insurance costs through a state-backed catastrophe fund, expanding Medicaid, increasing funding for public schools and protecting abortion rights.
Hillary Clinton, meanwhile, traveled to Omaha, Nebraska, on Saturday to rally support for Democratic candidates Lynne Walz and Denise Powell at a "Pumpkins, Pies, and Politics" fundraiser.
HILLARY CLINTON ISSUES ENDORSEMENT IN US MIDTERM ELECTIONS
Bill and Hillary Clinton, seen during President Donald Trump's January 2025 inauguration, are being targeted by House Republicans. (Melina Mara - Pool/Getty Images)

Asked how she would address Democrats who feel their votes no longer matter, Clinton pointed to a series of national crises that have contributed to voter frustration — including her 2016 election loss.

"And you could kind of understand that, for people who feel like they've had a series of hard times. If you look back on the last 25 years in our country, I was a senator from New York on 9/11. That was a trauma. The terrible financial crisis of 2008 was horrific for people. We had an election in 2016 that, you know, raised a lot of questions that we're still trying to find answers for about what, what kind of really went on, and then we had COVID," she said during the Nebraska event.

Clinton teamed up with journalist and podcast host Kara Swisher for a six-week limited series titled "High Stakes," which debuted Oct. 14 and will air weekly through mid-November, focusing on the 2026 midterm elections, key congressional races and issues.

The first episode, which aired Wednesday, centered on rising costs for gas, groceries and healthcare, Elon Musk's political spending and how Democrats can make affordability a winning message, while also examining key Senate races in Michigan and Maine.
HILLARY CLINTON CONCEDES INFAMOUS 9/11 NEAR-FAINTING EPISODE IN 2016 WAS A 'MISTAKE' ON HER PART
Former president Bill Clinton is pictured alongside his wife, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. (Kenny Holston-Pool/Getty Images)

"If the former president can help Democrats compete in a challenging state like Florida, and Secretary Clinton’s podcast can contribute to a substantive national conversation that motivates my party, that’s certainly a positive," said Walling.

The Clintons' increased visibility comes as Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidates have scored primary victories against incumbent or establishment-backed Democrats in states including Colorado, New York and Michigan.
MEET THE FAR-LEFT INSURGENTS WAGING WAR ON THE DEMOCRATIC ESTABLISHMENT IN 2026 MIDTERMS
"The challenge for Democrats is drawing on the wisdom and experience of the party’s past without overshadowing the next generation of leaders who will define its future," he added.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Clintons and Jolly’s campaign for comment.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Somalis in Minnesota unleash fury on Trump after feds raid Ilhan Omar's DC home
summary: Minneapolis Somali community members say they feel personally attacked after federal agents raided Rep. Ilhan Omar's D.C. home in a citizenship probe.
story: Members of Minneapolis' Somali community, including a city councilman, trashed President Trump and his administration after Monday's early morning raid on Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington, D.C. home. (Credit: Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)

MINNEAPOLIS — Members of Minnesota's growing Somali community, including a city council member, tore into President Donald Trump and his administration when speaking with Fox News Digital after Monday's raid on Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington, D.C., residence.

"Somalis — we all feel attacked by President Trump," Jamal Osman, the Somali-born vice president of the Minneapolis City Council, said of the impact of the raid carried out by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents.
"Our president has broken the law many times. ICE [is] terrorizing our community ... and we're not surprised such action has taken place," Osman continued in reference to the search of Omar's home.
FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION

Minneapolis City Council member Jamal Osman speaks during a press conference to address the media following reports that the Trump administration will be targeting Somali immigrants in the Twin Cities, held at City Hall in Minneapolis, Minn., on Tuesday, Dec. 2, 2025. (Leila Navidi/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images)
"We have seen the threats, the horrific language he uses against my community. It's unacceptable, and we're hoping this could stop," Osman said.

A 37-year-old social worker and Minneapolis resident named Abdi, who declined to give his last name or be interviewed on camera, had even harsher words for the president. He, like Osman, said he was born in Somalia.
"I feel like raiding a congresswoman — it feels like Donald Trump and his regime wanted to use their power to dehumanize and also humiliate someone that is part of the Congress," Abdi said.
He claimed that Trump "hates Somali people because of Ilhan Omar."
Abdi said Trump created "hate" and a "fight" with Somalis in America and claimed that they are being followed and harassed in the streets because of the president.
TRUMP RALLY CROWD CHANTS 'DEPORT' AS PRESIDENT RIPS ILHAN OMAR AFTER FEDERAL RAID
"It's personal," he said. "And Ilhan Omar — he doesn't treat her as a congressmember — he treats her as someone who's below him."

"If they take the citizenship away from her, then I will say, ‘Are we in a dictatorship?’ That's using power to use against an American citizen, then maybe the thinking we have for the United States is completely different."
Homeland Security Investigations police search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on October 12, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Leyden/Getty Images)
Osman said the raid is proof of what the Trump administration is willing to do.

"We live in the United States, which is the land of the laws. I don't expect Trump or anyone in this matter to break the U.S. Constitution," he continued. "There's laws. He can, of course, threaten, but there's a court process, there's due process. He can't say he's gonna deport her, he's gonna deport me, thousands of Somalis."
OMAR RAID OUTRAGE GOES FROM BAD TO WORSE WHEN INTERNET NOTICES HER PAST 6-WORD CLAIM: 'COULDN'T AGREE MORE'
Osman's message to the president was simple: "Stop it."
"We're American citizens like everyone else," he said.
Homeland Security Investigations police search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on October 12, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Leyden/Getty Images)
A third person, a 22-year-old Somali American woman who declined to be named or filmed, told Fox News Digital that she wasn't surprised about the raid on Omar's home.

"I thought it was bound to happen soon enough," she said. "They've been talking about her in a negative manner. The government [has been] constantly questioning her immigration status and her naturalization in the country. So it was bound to happen for them to investigate her soon enough."
When reached about the comments from the Minneapolis Somali community, the White House pointed Fox News Digital to the president's public reaction to the raid on Monday.

"I’ve always found her to be totally crooked, personally, but that has nothing to do with me," Trump brushed off. "I think she’s a terrible person. Just a complainer. She comes from a country that is a non-country, and then she comes over here, and she complains about our Constitution."
"I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ. I have nothing to do with it."

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., attends a field hearing at the Minnesota Senate Building on Jan. 16, 2026, in St. Paul, Minn. The hearing, titled "Kidnapped and Disappeared: Trump's Deadly Assault on Minnesota," featured local citizens and politicians discussing Immigration Operation "Metro Surge." (Jim Vondruska/Getty Images)
ILHAN OMAR’S HUSBAND INSISTS HE HAS ‘NO CONCERNS’ AMID FEDERAL IMMIGRATION INVESTIGATION

HSI, the principal investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), executed a search warrant at Omar's home in the nation's capital early Monday morning, as first reported by Fox News Digital.

Sources confirmed to Fox News Digital that the raid stems from an investigation into whether Omar or her late father, Nur Mohamed, fraudulently filled out her citizenship paperwork decades ago. The investigation, the sources note, could lead to the congresswoman's denaturalization.
The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that Omar's phone, passport and computers were seized in the raid — it is not clear which other items or materials were taken from her residence, if any.
Omar has not been seen since the raid, but offered her reaction to the unfolding investigation on social media Monday afternoon.

"This raid by Trump’s DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies. For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back," she said.

"Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies."
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: FBI probes suspicious white powder letters sent to Schumer, Dem senators as threat spreads nationwide
summary: Senior Capitol Hill staff were warned about suspicious letters containing unknown substances mailed to multiple congressional offices and election offices nationwide.
story: Federal officials investigate '86 47' vandalized on the National Mall grass, a message threatening President Donald Trump.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and two other Senate Democrats were the intended recipients of mail that federal investigators say contained "suspicious substances," Fox News Digital has learned. A source familiar confirmed to Fox News Digital that Schumer's office was the intended target, among other congressional offices, of a mysterious envelope containing an unknown substance.
He wasn't the only Senate Democrat targeted.

Sens. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., and Alex Padilla, D-Calif., were both informed by the FBI that their respective offices were sent a suspicious letter on Thursday, following warnings in both chambers of Congress that federal investigators were "investigating multiple letters containing suspicious substances that were mailed to various addresses nationwide, including multiple Congressional offices."
Josh Sorbe, a spokesperson for Murphy, told Fox News Digital that the senator’s office "was sent a letter with a suspicious substance."
ARMED MAN ARRESTED AT US CAPITOL BARRICADE AS POLICE PROBE WHY HE DROVE ONTO RESTRICTED GROUNDS
A U.S. Capitol Police officer at the Capitol in Washington, D.C. (Valerie Plesch/Bloomberg via Getty Images, File)

"Our office was promptly informed of the letter by FBI, SAA, and Capitol Police, and we continue to work closely with them and federal law enforcement," Sorbe said. "Due to those efforts and various safety protocols, the Senator and staff were not in immediate danger. Our office is grateful for the investigators involved in this incident, and we intend to continue close coordination as the investigation continues."

A spokesperson for Padilla told Fox News Digital, "We received the notification from the FBI that one of our offices was mailed a letter containing a suspicious substance, but it was intercepted by USPS."

The two incidents follow warnings sent out to top-ranking staff on the Hill earlier Thursday by both the Senate and House sergeants at arms that the FBI, U.S. Postal Inspection Service, and U.S. Capitol Police were actively investigating the matter, per notices obtained by Fox News Digital.
DEPROGRAMMED: FORMER DSA INSIDER REVEALS ‘FRIGHTENING’ SOCIALIST AGENDA DROVE HIM FROM ‘EXTREME’ IDEOLOGY

"Law enforcement officials are working to intercept any additional letters before they are delivered, however, it is possible that some letters may reach their destinations," the notice from the Senate Sergeant at Arms read.
The exact nature of the suspicious substances, and just how many congressional offices are intended recipients, remains unclear.

Top staff in the House were warned by the House Sergeant at Arms that the office had "been made aware of reports of letters containing suspicious white powder substances received by public officials throughout the United States."

"Although no House Members have been identified as intended recipients at this time, the SAA continues to monitor the situation and coordinate with law enforcement partners," the notice read. "All offices are reminded to remain vigilant and follow safe mail handling procedures to help protect staff from potentially harmful materials."

An FBI spokesperson declined to confirm specific instances or letters, but said in a statement that, "The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices."

"Some of the letters contained an unknown substance, and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident," the spokesperson said. "We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters. This FBI and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens."
MASSIVE TROVE OF REPUBLICAN VOTER AND DONOR INFO BREACHED IN BIDEN DOJ PROBE: SENATE CHAIRMAN
Signs from the Metro DC Democratic Socialists of America. (Brooke Curto/Fox News Digital)

Included in the Senate Sergeant at Arms' notice was an image of one of the envelopes that included a return address in the top-left corner for the Democratic Socialists of America’s (DSA) headquarters in New York City.

It is unclear whether the DSA had any involvement in sending the letters. Fox News Digital reached out to the DSA for comment but has not heard back.A representative for the organization told the New York Post that the DSA "has not occupied this office address since 2013."
"We are also no longer headquartered at 75 Maiden Lane," the rep said.
The notice warned that "all suspicious letters, packages, or substances should be treated as potentially hazardous."

Suspicious letters were also sent to state elections offices around the country. The National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors said in a joint statement that, "Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties."

"Election officials take these matters seriously and work closely with law enforcement and security partners to protect their personnel and facilities," the organizations said. "We have security measures and contingency plans in place to respond to potential threats and emergencies while maintaining essential election operations."

It comes on the 25-year anniversary after an anthrax-laced letter was opened by a staffer in then-Senate Majority Leader Tom Daschle’s office on Oct. 15, 2001.

Since then, Congress has drastically overhauled how it accepts mail. Packages and mail no longer come directly to the Hill, and instead are processed in facilities where they are screened and irradiated before making their way to a congressional office.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: ‘Big Condiment’ warning gets Warren roasted online over progressive's economic priorities
summary: Elizabeth Warren's warning about the $45 billion McCormick-Unilever merger sparked online mockery, with users joking about "Big Condiment" prices.
story: 'The Big Money Show' panelists analyze this high-profile feud between Treasury Secratry Scott Bessent and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Ma., as they spar over economic policy and his response regarding the senator's letters.

A post made by Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., this week quickly became a punchline online after she warned that a proposed $45 billion deal bringing some of America’s best-known condiment and food brands under one roof could drive up grocery prices even further.

The merger would combine McCormick brands such as Cholula and Frank’s RedHot with Unilever Foods products including Hellmann’s and Knorr. Warren argues the deal could weaken competition and leave shoppers with fewer choices.
Users online joked about Warren cautioning against "Big Condiment."
DSA-BACKED CANDIDATES ARE WINNING PRIMARIES AND THEIR VISION FOR AMERICA IS VERY DIFFERENT
"One company could soon control them all," Warren said of four popular condiments. "I have concerns that McCormick and Unilever's $45 billion merger could increase YOUR grocery prices."
The post drew jokes from users who argued that housing, infrastructure and the national debt are bigger concerns than a potential rise in the prices of condiments.
"Yes, a simultaneous increase in the prices of (checks notes) mayo and (checks notes again) hot sauce could bring the country to its knees," one user on X wrote.
"The only thing raising my grocery prices is federal deficit and the resulting inflation you all seem to be ok with," another added.

Venture capitalist Hank Medina sarcastically posted to his X account with 1.7 million followers, "The United States will crumble if big mayo merges with big hot sauce. SOUND THE ALARM FOLKS!!! We have no other condiment alternatives if this happens."
But the real impact of a food merger is no laughing matter.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., urged federal regulators to scrutinize McCormick’s proposed $45 billion deal with Unilever Foods, warning it could reduce competition and raise grocery prices. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Consumer prices rose 3.7% in September from a year earlier, accelerating from 3.4% in August, according to the latest Bureau of Labor Statistics report. Prices climbed 0.6% in September alone, underscoring the persistent affordability pressures facing American households just weeks before the midterm elections.
Narrowing in on grocery prices, they rose 1.8% from a year ago but dipped 0.1% in September, while overall food prices were up 2.5% annually.
With an affordability crisis plaguing the U.S. heading into the midterms, any threat of further impacts on Americans' pocketbooks is worth noting ahead of Election Day.
Meanwhile, Warren has launched a broader campaign to challenge food-industry consolidation — not just against the recent condiment merger proposal.
ECONOMIST CALLS OUT AMERICA’S SOCIALIST ELITE, SAYS THEY GOT RICH BASHING CAPITALISM
McCormick’s proposed $45 billion deal with Unilever Foods would bring brands including Frank’s RedHot, Cholula, Hellmann’s and Knorr under one company. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)
In an Oct. 6 letter to the Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission, she urged regulators to scrutinize the McCormick–Unilever deal alongside two other proposed food-industry mergers.

The Massachusetts progressive argued the multibillion-dollar deal could reduce competition for shoppers' grocery dollars and retailers’ shelf space across overlapping pantry staples, leaving consumers with fewer choices and higher prices.

If the deal announced in March were approved, it would combine McCormick with Unilever’s foods business in a transaction valued at about $45 billion.
The combined company would bring together brands such as Cholula, Frank’s RedHot, Hellmann’s and Knorr. It is expected to close by mid-2027, subject to regulatory and shareholder approvals.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: FIRST ON FOX: Dems' affordability crusade collides with eye-popping price tag for socialist immigration plans
summary: The White House Council of Economic Advisers estimates each illegal immigrant costs taxpayers $166,716 over their lifetime in a bombshell report.
story: DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin responds to President Donald Trump signing a $70 billion bill to fund ICE and CBP through 2029, calling out Democrats for attempting to defund border protection. Mullin highlights issues with sanctuary cities and the increasing number of arrested illegal immigrants with felony charges. He emphasizes the Trump administration's zero-tolerance approach against those who harbor criminals and assault law enforcement.

FIRST ON FOX: A new White House economic report warns that immigration policies backed by the Democratic Socialists of America could cost American taxpayers hundreds of billions of dollars over the next decade, as the Trump administration sounds the alarm over the potential financial consequences of mass amnesty and expanded federal benefits.

As President Donald Trump touts 16 consecutive months without illegal immigrant releases at the southern border, a Council of Economic Advisers report estimates that mass amnesty and expanded federal benefits under Democratic Socialists of America-backed immigration policies could cost taxpayers between $440 billion and $613 billion over the next decade.
Socialist-aligned candidates have gained ground in 2026, winning key Democratic primaries and expanding their influence within the party.

"President Trump … supercharged ICE to remove criminal illegal aliens from our communities, including murderers, rapists, pedophiles, gang members and terrorists," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital.
'SQUAD' DEMOCRAT FORMALLY INTRODUCES BILL TO ABOLISH ICE, BORDER PATROL AND DISMANTLE DHS

"Meanwhile, radical Democrats want to go back to their extreme open border policies and grant amnesty to the illegal aliens they released into our communities. Not only will these radical policies make America less safe, but they will cost the American taxpayer billions of dollars."

With the midterms approaching and Democrats campaigning heavily on affordability, the White House is casting the DSA's immigration agenda as a potential financial and public safety threat — warning that its policies could compound the very cost-of-living pressures Democrats have used to hammer Republicans.
DEMOCRATS SAY THEY'LL MAKE LIFE AFFORDABLE. YOUR WALLET MAY DISAGREE

The council's findings go beyond the cost of mass amnesty, examining the potential impact of expanded federal benefits and reduced immigration enforcement, policies the White House warns could impose a significant financial burden on American families.

USCIS says the Trump administration’s first year saw a sweeping immigration crackdown, including 14,000 ICE referrals, record removals, and widespread fraud detection. (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images | Photo by Jamie Kelter Davis/Getty Images)

The council estimates that the average illegal immigrant carries a lifetime net fiscal cost of $166,716, with the current illegal immigrant population projected to account for between $1.4 trillion and $1.9 trillion in taxpayer costs under its model — figures the administration is highlighting as the "true costs of extreme open borders [and] mass-amnesty socialist policies."
CALIFORNIA FACES UNLIKELY TAX REVOLT AMID BILLIONS IN ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT HEALTHCARE COSTS

The CEA's estimated $166,716 lifetime taxpayer cost per illegal immigrant exceeds the roughly $124,000 it would cost to put a student through four years at an average in-state public university, including tuition, housing, food and other expenses, according to College Board's 2025–26 figures — putting the figure in perspective as American families also grapple with college affordability.

The Council added that while illegal immigrants are generally prohibited from federal benefit programs, some on the left want to reverse that standard and provide subsidized healthcare and programs like food stamps to those in the country unlawfully.
SHOCKING PERCENTAGE OF DEMOCRATS IDENTIFY AS 'DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' ACCORDING TO NEW POLL: 'TOXIC POLICIES'

Beyond expanded federal benefits, the council estimates that ending Trump-backed immigration enforcement measures would wipe out between $227 billion and $287 billion in projected taxpayer savings, producing a net estimated cost of $79 billion to $139 billion over the next decade after accounting for reduced enforcement spending.

An interactive White House webpage released alongside the report allows Americans to explore the projected costs of "socialism" across several policy areas, with the council estimating that the Democratic Socialists of America's broader agenda could cost $49 trillion over ten years — roughly $355,000 per American household. That sweeping projection extends far beyond immigration, which the council separately estimates could cost between $440 billion and $613 billion over the next decade.
DOJ THREATENS TO CUT BILLIONS IN WELFARE FUNDING FROM STATES FOR FAILING TO REPORT ILLEGAL MIGRANTS

If the immigration policies examined in the report were implemented, the White House estimates that expanded eligibility for SNAP, federal housing assistance and Medicaid would add between $361 billion and $475 billion in federal spending over the next decade.

The report estimated that expanding federal benefits under the proposed immigration policies would add $3.6 billion to $4.7 billion in annual food stamp costs, another $2.3 billion to $3 billion in federal housing assistance, and as much as $40 billion a year in additional Medicaid spending.
US STATE DEPARTMENT HAS YANKED MORE THAN 175K VISAS UNDER TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SO FAR

Along with the report, the White House highlighted a 73% uptick in drug interdictions through August 2026 compared with the same period in fiscal year 2024, while separately pointing to declining fentanyl-related deaths as evidence of its broader border enforcement strategy.

The administration also highlighted another key aspect of the immigration-cost paradigm that it changed — remarking that Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for certain foreign-national groups "returned … to its original purpose: temporary."
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SLASHES TIME REFUGEES HAVE TO CHALLENGE LOSS OF LEGAL STATUS
The administration's efforts to terminate TPS designations for certain countries have faced legal challenges, underscoring the ongoing dispute over the scope of federal immigration authority.

The administration has also moved to end certain Temporary Protected Status designations and revoke more than 250,000 visas as part of its broader immigration crackdown, measures the White House has highlighted alongside its efforts to tighten enforcement and reduce what it says are substantial taxpayer costs.

title: Maryland's lone Republican House member calls woman 'rude' for laughing during debate
summary: Republican House member Rep. Andy Harris called an audience member "rude" after she laughed during his remarks on diesel prices during a debate.
story: Rep. Andy Harris, R-Md., speaks to woman in the audience after he was interrupted during a debate against Democrat challenger Dan Schwartz.
Maryland's only Republican House member was heard telling a woman "you are rude" after she started laughing while he was speaking during a debate.
The clash between Rep. Andy Harris and the audience member unfolded Tuesday in Cambridge as the Republican was talking about rising diesel prices during the U.S.-Iran war.

"Let's get the facts straight, the facts are that diesel is, the facts are that diesel prices have gone up, there is no question about it. Why has it gone up? Because the Democrats have environmental regulations..." Harris said before he was interrupted by a woman laughing in the audience.

"Ma'am, I gotta tell you. This is the problem, you all say you believe there is a First Amendment, but only if you agree with you," Harris told the crowd. "You should let me finish the sentence, ma'am. You are rude. You're rude, OK?"
AMERICA'S TRUCKERS ISSUE DIRE WARNING AS SOARING DIESEL COSTS THREATEN 'DOMINO EFFECT'

Rep. Andy Harris, a Republican from Maryland, arrives for a news conference after a Maryland delegation meeting at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Thursday, June 25, 2026. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Harris then turned to the debate moderator and said, "I'm sorry," adding that if she wasn't going tell the audience they were rude, he had to do it himself.
"Let me finish the sentence why there is a shortage of diesel in the world and in the country," Harris continued, before another audience member started talking.
"You are rude too. So do you believe in the First Amendment? Do you believe in my First Amendment right to express myself? It's my turn to express myself, not yours," Harris said.
PRESS FREEDOM GROUPS THAT BLASTED TRUMP TURN FIRE ON DEMOCRAT GOVERNOR OVER ALLEGED MEDIA RETALIATION

Rep. Chip Roy, right, accompanied by House Freedom Caucus Chair Rep. Andy Harris, left, and Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, speaks during a news conference on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 20, 2025. (Getty Images)
Harris, who has represented Maryland's 1st Congressional District since 2010, is running for re-election against Democrat challenger Dan Schwartz.
The debate moderator then asked both candidates to speak to their supporters and ask them to be "polite and respectful" during the debate.

"That is very important that you guys are able to hear from both of us tonight, so please if you don't mind, let's keep all reactions for later when you get home and let's let the congressman speak," Schwartz said.

Rep. Andy Harris, a Republican from Maryland, speaks to members of the media following a House Republican caucus meeting at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Dec. 10, 2025. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)
