title: Trump rules out livestream for Nidal Hasan firing squad execution
summary: President Donald Trump reversed the Pentagon's plan to livestream Nidal Hasan's firing squad execution, saying the event could deter terrorism, but many Americans would rather not watch.
story: Fox News chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin looks at the history of the firing squad being used in the United States and debates over the plan to stream Nidal Hasan’s execution on ‘Special Report.’

President Donald Trump announced that the planned firing squad execution of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will not be livestreamed, reversing an earlier Pentagon announcement that the public would be able to watch the convicted mass killer's final moments.
Trump said in a Truth Social post that broadcasting the execution could serve as a powerful deterrent to terrorism but acknowledged that many Americans would rather not witness Hasan's death.
"He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," Trump wrote.
AMERICANS DRAW THE LINE AT LIVESTREAMING ‘SPECTACLE’ OF FORT HOOD SHOOTER'S EXECUTION: ‘IT’S AN ABOMINATION'
This April 9, 2010, file photo released by the Bell County Sheriff's Department shows Maj. Nidal Hasan at the Bell County Jail in Belton, Texas. (AP)
Hasan’s execution is scheduled for Dec. 3. Trump said immediate family members of the 13 people killed in Hasan's 2009 rampage will be permitted to attend in person if they choose.
"They deserve to witness JUSTICE!" Trump wrote.

The president's announcement comes after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Wednesday that the execution would be made public, telling Real America's Voice that Americans would be able to watch Hasan's death.
"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said at the time.

Major Nidal Malik Hasan, the U.S. Army doctor identified by authorities as the mass shooter at the U.S. Army post in Fort Hood, Texas, is seen in this undated handout photo from a pdf file of the U.S. Government Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences downloaded on November 6, 2009. (REUTERS/Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences/Handout)
Pentagon officials subsequently confirmed Thursday that the execution would be livestreamed, though additional details had not yet been released.
Trump suggested in his Truth Social post that broadcasting the execution could have sent a message to would-be terrorists.
"I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan," Trump wrote.
This undated photo provided by the Bell County Sheriff's Department shows former Army psychiatrist Maj. Nidal Hasan. (HANDOUT/Reuters)
The president added that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device."
Hasan, a former Army major and psychiatrist, was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others during a shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas, on Nov. 5, 2009.
FORT HOOD SURVIVOR SHOT IN HEAD VOWS TO WATCH TERRORIST FACE HISTORIC FIRING SQUAD

He opened fire inside a medical processing building where soldiers were preparing for deployment, shouting "Allahu akbar" before shooting at service members with a handgun. Hasan was shot by law enforcement during the attack and left paralyzed from the waist down.

U.S. Army soldiers salute their fallen comrades during the III Corps and Fort Hood Memorial Ceremony at Fort Hood, Texas, November 10, 2009. The memorial was held to honor the 13 victims of the shootings which took place on the Fort Hood Army post on November 5. (Reuters/Jessica Rinaldi)
During his 2013 military trial, Hasan acknowledged carrying out the shooting and represented himself after dismissing his attorneys. He was sentenced to death.
The execution would mark the first military execution in more than 65 years. The last U.S. military execution took place in April 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was hanged.
However, Hasan could still seek to delay his execution through a habeas corpus petition in civilian court, a legal challenge that experts say could significantly postpone the proceedings.

Trump also used his Truth Social post to criticize the Obama administration's handling of intelligence involving Hasan, pointing to electronic communications between the former Army officer and radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaki that were intercepted by the FBI before the attack.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The president claimed that investigators' failure to identify the communications as a threat amounted to a major intelligence failure.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Collins insists socialist rival won't beat her as Maine's money machine: 'You'll lose big time'
summary: A Suffolk University poll shows Troy Jackson edging Susan Collins 49%-47% ahead of their final Maine Senate debate in a statistical dead heat.
story: Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine speaks exclusively with Fox News Digital after landing a major law enforcement endorsement as she runs for re-election in a crucial Senate showdown

BANGOR, Maine — Republican Sen. Susan Collins is warning that Maine could lose crucial federal funding if voters replace her with Democrat Troy Jackson, as a new poll shows the candidates statistically tied ahead of their final debate Thursday.

Jackson, a one-time logger and former Maine Senate president, edged Collins 49%-47% in a Suffolk University poll conducted Oct. 8-11 and released on the eve of the final debate. Jackson's two-point edge over Collins among likely voters was well within the survey's margin of error, and the poll was the latest to indicate an extremely close contest.

The face-off between Collins and Jackson in the blue-leaning Northern New England state is a top flip opportunity for the Democrats as they try to win back the Senate majority from the Republicans in the midterm elections.
The Fox News Power Rankings rate the race in Maine as a toss up, as do leading nonpartisan political handicappers the Cook Political Report, Inside Elections, and Sabato's Crystal Ball.
CAN A FORMER NFL SIDELINE REPORTER HELP REPUBLICANS FLIP A SENATE SEAT IN BLUE-LEANING MINNESOTA?
Fox News Power Rankings Senate forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
"Maine voters lose out big time if Troy Jackson were to be elected," Collins said in an exclusive Fox News Digital interview on Wednesday.

Collins, who is running for a sixth six-year term in the Senate, has showcased her nearly three decades of Senate experience and her leadership role as Senate Appropriations Committee chair as integral to her ability "to get so much done for the people of Maine." She warned that if Jackson replaced her, "he'll be 100 in seniority, and all of that essential federal funding targeted for the state of Maine, virtually all of it will go away."

Jackson has argued that Collins has not used her Senate power to protect Maine families from soaring energy, food, and housing costs. "Sen. Collins has told us how powerful she is," Jackson said during their first debate. "But power means nothing if you won't use it when the people may need it."
Jackson and Democrats have also repeatedly aimed to anchor Collins to President Donald Trump, whose approval ratings in Maine and across the country are cratering ahead of the midterms.

"That's the choice on this stage — a senator who helps Donald Trump hurt Maine then tells us how concerned she is, or somebody who will stand up against him before another family in Maine has to pay the price," Jackson said during Tuesday's third debate.
DEMS SEE NEW CHANCES TO FLIP SENATE SEATS BUT GOP'S MASSIVE CASH ADVANTAGE AN OBSTACLE

Troy Jackson speaks as he became the Maine Democratic Party's choice to be their U.S. Senate nominee to replace Graham Platner on the ballot in November on July 25, 2026, in Bangor, Maine. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

Collins is known as a moderate Republican who at times has voted against the president. But Jackson and Democrats are targeting the senator over her comments that she didn't regret her 2018 vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, whose crucial vote four years later helped overturn the landmark Roe v. Wade abortion ruling.
And following the fatal shooting in Maine this summer involving Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, Democrats heavily criticized Collins for her support for ICE funding.
But Collins has broken with Trump numerous times in recent months, criticizing his tariff war with neighboring Canada and voting against Attorney General Todd Blanche's confirmation.
"Troy and Chuck Schumer and their allies run ads saying that I'm somehow a puppet of the president. Believe me, that would come as a huge surprise to President Trump," Collins told Fox News Digital.

Collins noted, "I opposed the deal that he made with Vladimir Putin to get a small amount of diesel, and in return lift the sanctions that we just passed into law, and the president is not following the law. I signed a bipartisan letter that urges the president to reconsider that. I opposed the president's signature legislative accomplishment, the One Big Beautiful Bill, because it contained cuts in Medicaid that... I know would be harmful to Maine."
DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING - HERE ARE THREE FACTORS THAT COULD STOP IT
Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine is endorsed by the state chapter of the Fraternal Order of Police, on Oct. 14, 2026 in Bangor, Maine. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
The senator was interviewed in Bangor after landing the endorsement of the Maine chapter of the Fraternal Order of Police.
"I've secured funding for projects throughout Maine, $46 million to help our police and sheriff's departments upgrade their equipment, facilities, and communications," Collins told Fox News Digital.

And she took aim at Jackson, who won a special nominating convention in late July to fill the party's Senate nomination, which was left vacant after primary winner Graham Platner ended his campaign following an explosive report containing an allegation of rape from a woman he previously dated. Platner denied the report but dropped out.
Jackson, who earlier this year unsuccessfully ran for the Democratic gubernatorial nomination, had campaigned alongside Platner during the primary campaign.

"Troy was Graham Platner's biggest supporter and stayed with him to the very end of Graham's campaign, and Graham repeatedly denigrated law enforcement," Collins said. "I never heard Troy publicly condemn those disrespectful and horrible comments."

Collins added, "During his gubernatorial campaign, Troy was endorsed and welcomed the endorsement of the Democratic Socialists of America. One of the key parts of the DSA platform is to defund the police."

The Jackson campaign, responding, pointed out that "Jackson is not a Democratic Socialist" and has repeatedly said he does not support defunding the police. The campaign added that Jackson called on Platner to drop out and "has been clear he will not accept a Platner endorsement."

"Susan Collins is lying about Troy’s record because she knows that Mainers are ready to retire her after she’s voted with Donald Trump 96% of the time to cut their healthcare, confirmed Brett Kavanaugh who overturned Roe v. Wade, enabled Trump’s war in Iran that’s raising energy costs, and failed to stop his reckless tariffs that are causing costs to skyrocket," the Jackson campaign told Fox News Digital.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Campaign signs for Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson are seen alongside a road in Bangor, Maine, on Oct. 14, 2026. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
But Collins disputed the 96% figure, saying that it came from a study that only covered a third of her Senate votes.

"A study that looked at 90% of the votes showed that I supported the president 72% of the time," she added. "The bottom line is, I support him when I think he's right. I don't when I think he's wrong."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Collins, who is the only GOP senator seeking re-election in a state Trump lost in the 2024 election, has a history of surviving Democratic efforts to unseat her.

Six years ago, she trailed Democratic challenger Sara Gideon, the then-Maine House speaker, but the senator ended up winning re-election by nearly nine points while former President Joe Biden carried the state by a similar margin.
Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

title: Fears of China spying on US military prompt GOP hawks to demand retaliation against the shipping giant
summary: Three House Republicans demand DHS revoke COSCO's Qualship 21 enrollment after the Pentagon designated the Chinese shipping giant a military company.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

FIRST ON FOX: Three top House Republicans are demanding a Chinese shipping giant be stripped of special privileges at American ports over concerns the vessels are allegedly spying on U.S. military communications, according to a letter exclusively obtained by Fox News Digital.

COSCO, a shipping and logistics company owned by the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and based in Shanghai, has received favorable treatment under a Coast Guard program designed to reward trusted commercial operators. But China hawks in Congress want to revoke those privileges following a September report that the vessels are being used to gather intelligence.

In an Oct. 14 letter, three top Republican lawmakers identified that as of July 15, 2026, there were 11 COSCO vessels listed in the Coast Guard's Quality Shipping for the 21st Century program, known as Qualship 21 — despite the Pentagon designating them as a Chinese military company.

House China Committee Chairman John Moolenaar, House Intelligence Committee Chairman Rep. Rick Crawford, R-Ark., and Rep. Carlos Gimenez, chairman of the Homeland Security Subcommittee on Transportation and Maritime Security, are pressing Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to revoke COSCO vessels' enrollment in the Coast Guard's program.

A view of Chang Ping Yuan, a very large gas carrier (VLGC), at a port of COSCO Shipping (Qidong) Offshore Co., Ltd. on September 8, 2026, in Qidong, Jiangsu Province of China. (Xu Congjun/VCG via Getty Images)

It follows a September's reporting that COSCO vessels used sophisticated, concealed equipment to intercept military communications and gather intelligence about encryption technologies off American coastlines.

The Coast Guard program was created to allow vessels with strong safety and compliance records to undergo fewer routine inspections when entering U.S. ports. But the lawmakers argue in their letter that COSCO's alleged espionage activities and ties to China's military raise serious questions about why its ships have qualified for preferential treatment.
CHINA ‘WIRETAPPED RED SEA’ WITH SPY HUB 6 MILES FROM US BASE: EX PENTAGON OFFICIAL WARNS

The allegations, attributed to senior U.S. officials, have fueled concerns that Chinese commercial vessels could serve as intelligence-gathering platforms while operating near sensitive American military facilities.

COSCO has denied the allegations, calling them unfounded and maintaining that its onboard communications and navigation equipment is used exclusively for legitimate commercial purposes. The company has said none of its equipment was used to intercept military communications or gather intelligence.

COSCO is one of the world's largest shipping companies and is owned by the Chinese government. Its sprawling commercial fleet operates along major global trade routes, including routes serving American ports.
A U.S. Coast Guard emblem is displayed on the side of a boat on Sept. 25, 2026 in San Diego, California. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

The Pentagon added COSCO to its Section 1260H list of Chinese military companies in January 2025, citing its ownership by a Chinese state agency, activities allegedly conducted on behalf of the People's Liberation Army and contributions to Beijing's military-civil fusion strategy, which seeks to harness civilian industries and technologies for military purposes.
WALL STREET BANKS HELPED CHINESE MILITARY-LINKED FIRM RAISE BILLIONS DESPITE RED FLAGS, LAWMAKERS FIND

The designation does not automatically bar COSCO vessels from entering American ports. But the lawmakers are questioning why a company identified by the Pentagon as having ties to China's military should continue benefiting from a Coast Guard program that reduces inspection frequency.

The Coast Guard updated Qualship 21 eligibility rules earlier this year, expanding the circumstances under which vessels could be removed from the program, including certain associations with sanctioned entities. The lawmakers are now pressing DHS on whether Pentagon national security designations should also factor into eligibility decisions.

In the letter first obtained by Fox News Digital, the lawmakers urged DHS to revoke COSCO vessels' enrollment, refuse future renewals and increase scrutiny of other shipping companies with ties to the CCP and Chinese military.

They are also demanding to know whether the Coast Guard received intelligence warnings about COSCO's alleged surveillance operations before the allegations became public in September — and whether those warnings were considered when deciding if its vessels should retain their privileged status.

The lawmakers specifically questioned whether the Coast Guard reviewed COSCO's eligibility following its Pentagon designation and whether intelligence officials have identified similar risks involving other Chinese or Hong Kong-based shipping operators.
Their concerns extend to what the Coast Guard is doing to detect potential espionage aboard commercial vessels already operating in American waters.
China Shipping containers are seen at the port of Oakland, as trade tensions continue over U.S. tariffs with China, in Oakland, California, on May 12, 2025. (REUTERS/Carlos Barria)

The letter questions whether authorities have conducted additional boardings of COSCO ships, investigated crew members potentially involved in intelligence collection or examined historical shipping routes for unusual movements that could indicate surveillance activities.

The lawmakers also questioned whether the Coast Guard has sufficient legal authority to counter suspected intelligence operations aboard foreign commercial ships, or whether additional coordination with other federal agencies is necessary.

The inquiry reaches beyond COSCO. The lawmakers raised the possibility of removing Hong Kong from the Coast Guard's list of qualified flag administrations, citing concerns about Beijing's control over the territory.
The letter was copied to the director of national intelligence and the Coast Guard commandant.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital reached out to COSCO, DHS and the Coast Guard for comment but did not hear back at time of publication.

title: Obama's billion-dollar baby: Chicago center's price tag hits monumental milestone, tripling original estimate
summary: The Obama Presidential Center's cost has nearly tripled to $1 billion, nearly triple the original estimate
story: Ohio State accounting professor Brian Mittendorf examines the Obama Foundation's financial health, assets and endowment as construction costs hit $1 billion.

FIRST ON FOX - The price tag for the beleaguered Obama Presidential Center is now projected to top $1 billion, nearly triple its original estimate, the foundation overseeing construction of the Chicago facility told Fox News Digital.

Confirmation of the 10-figure cost marks another chapter in the troubled history of the much-delayed project, which opened five years behind schedule amid controversy over its use of public parkland and claims that subcontractors were stiffed out of millions of dollars. It comes as newly released financial records reviewed by Fox News Digital offer a fresh look at the finances of the Obama Foundation, the former president's private nonprofit that oversaw construction of the billion-dollar project.

The sprawling campus on the Windy City's south side was originally expected to open in 2021, with construction costs estimated at $300 million to $350 million. But years of federal reviews, legal challenges and construction delays preceded its eventual opening in June 2026, by which time projected costs had skyrocketed to approximately $850 million.

Hailed by Democrats and supporters as a historic investment in the community and a tribute to the former president's legacy, the center was promoted as a catalyst for jobs, economic growth and new opportunities for underserved communities.
BUREAUCRATS HIDE TRUE PRICE OF OBAMA PRESIDENTIAL CENTER AS TAXPAYERS HIT WITH INFRASTRUCTURE BILL

Former President Barack Obama and the Obama Presidential Center in Chicago, where construction costs are now projected to reach approximately $1 billion, nearly triple the upper end of the original estimate. (Taylor Hill/Getty Images; Talía Sprague/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"While we continue to reconcile costs and plan ahead for additional capital improvements, we anticipate our total cost for constructing the campus is approximately $1 billion — again, all raised in private contributions," Emily Bittner, the Obama Foundation's vice president of communications, told Fox News Digital. "This includes investments in additional public art, insurance, scope changes in our Home Court, project management and exhibit installation, among other categories."

The campus serves as both a museum dedicated to Obama's presidency and the headquarters of the Obama Foundation. It also features a public library branch and an athletic center, but unlike traditional presidential libraries, it does not house his original presidential records, although digital versions and artifacts are featured in its museum.

The climb toward the $1 billion mark has seemed inevitable in recent years, with approximately $909 million in construction-related costs recorded by the end of 2025, when the project was about 80% complete, according to its newly released audited financial statements.

The Obama Foundation's newly released financial disclosures cover the nonprofit's entire operation, not just the Chicago campus. It also runs leadership, education and community programs across the United States and around the world.

The tax filings show donations and grants fell to approximately $151 million in 2025, down from $195 million in 2024. Fundraising has fluctuated sharply in recent years, falling from $311 million in 2022 to $129 million in 2023 before rebounding in 2024 and declining again last year.
OBAMA PRESIDENTIAL CENTER SUBCONTRACTORS FILE FRESH PAYMENT CLAIMS TOTALING NEARLY $900K
Construction equipment is seen outside the Obama Presidential Center in Chicago ahead of the campus opening. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital)
The Obama Presidential Center overhead drone shot in July 2025. (Fox News Digital)
Total liabilities climbed to approximately $103.5 million in 2025, during the final stages of the center's construction, up from $35 million in 2024 and $20 million in 2022.

The Obama Foundation's outstanding borrowing also rose from $15 million at the end of 2025 to approximately $63.5 million by July 2026, according to its audited financial statements. The nonprofit said it borrowed the money to cover short-term costs during the final stages of construction and that the loans were not secured against its rights to the property.
Its money and investments available to cover everyday expenses also fell from approximately $265 million in 2024 to $101 million in 2025.

Brian Mittendorf, a nonprofit accounting professor at the Ohio State University who reviewed the Obama Foundation's tax filings and audited financial statements, said the nonprofit remains on solid financial footing, with more than $1.1 billion in net assets at the end of 2025.

"In terms of the organization's overall financial health, again, I would say financial health looks quite good," Mittendorf told Fox News Digital. "They have a decent amount of cash, investments, liquidity, and so on. So it's not like they're in financial difficulty by any means."
However, he noted that much of the foundation's wealth is tied up in the Presidential Center, rather than assets that could readily be converted into cash.

"Bottom line to me: I don’t see a short-term financial distress here, but I do see an organization that has tied up a lot of its resources in its buildings, which means more costs to come and the need for more revenues to make this sustainable," he said.

Signs reading "Home For Action" and "Bring Change Home" are displayed outside the Obama Presidential Center in Chicago on June 19, 2026. Critics point to the messaging as evidence the Center functions as more than a traditional presidential library. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital)

The Home Court athletic facility is seen at the Obama Presidential Center in Chicago on June 19, 2026. The facility is designed for youth sports, mentoring programs and community events. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital)
OBAMA CENTER SUBCONTRACTOR SHUTS DOWN AMID $4M FIGHT, LAYS OFF 25
Mittendorf warned that raising money to maintain the sprawling campus could prove more challenging than funding its construction.
"It's much easier to raise money when it's for building a building than it is for doing upkeep or paying for insurance or paying utilities," he said.
Obama Foundation officials said its operating costs are covered by revenue and private donations, although they did not provide a figure for the center's annual operating and maintenance expenses.
The Obama Presidential Center sits on 19.3 acres of historic public parkland in Jackson Park. It secured the site through a 99-year agreement with the city for a one-time payment of just $10.
While the foundation funded construction, the land and buildings are legally owned by the City of Chicago.

Critics have long raised concerns over the foundation's failure to fully fund a proposed $470 million endowment — a financial safety net designed to generate income for the center's upkeep and reduce the risk of taxpayers footing the bill if the project runs into trouble.

A previous Fox News Digital investigation found that just $1 million had been set aside for years. Newly released financial statements show the Foundation's overall endowment grew to approximately $14.2 million by the end of 2025, although it remains unclear how much of that money is specifically reserved for the Presidential Center.

Obama Foundation officials said the agreement with the city of Chicago required them to establish an endowment, not fully fund it, before taking control of the site. They said they prioritized fundraising for construction and leadership programs and that they plan to make significant investments in the fund in the coming years.

Richard Epstein, a New York University law professor who has advised opponents of the project, disputed the Obama Foundation's interpretation, arguing that establishing an endowment without adequately funding it defeats its purpose.

"Otherwise, they provide no protection," Epstein told Fox News Digital, arguing that under the Obama Foundation's interpretation, "they could list the endowment as $1 billion and fund it with ten cents."

Former U.S. President Barack Obama holds up a library card while reading to school children with former first lady Michelle Obama at the Barack Obama Presidential Center in John Lewis Plaza on June 19, 2026, in Chicago, Illinois. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)
A map graphic shows the footprint of the Obama Presidential Center inside Jackson Park on Chicago’s South Side along Lake Michigan. (Fox News)

Despite the foundation's substantial assets, some of the subcontractors who helped build it say they are still fighting to recover millions of dollars in disputed payments. A previous Fox News Digital investigation identified several firms claiming major financial losses, including minority-owned businesses the project was intended to support.

Mike Owen, owner of Chicago-based Adamson Plumbing, said his company suffered nearly $4 million in losses tied to the project, forcing him to suspend operations and lay off 25 union workers. His company subsequently filed a $1.72 million mechanics lien seeking payment for disputed work.
Owen told Fox News Digital this week that he still has not recovered the money he is seeking.

The Obama Foundation previously said Lakeside Alliance, the project's construction manager, was responsible for managing and paying subcontractors and that the foundation had no outstanding disputed charges with the alliance. Lakeside Alliance has said contractual closeout on a project of this scale can continue long after opening and that it remains committed to resolving outstanding matters.

The campus features a museum dedicated to Obama's presidency, housed in a 225-foot-tall, eight-story tower, along with a branch of the Chicago Public Library, a children's playground, an auditorium, conference and meeting spaces, public gardens and more than 20 commissioned art installations.

At the southern end of the campus sits Home Court, a 60,000-square-foot athletic and community center, featuring a regulation-size NBA basketball court, training facilities and multipurpose rooms for meetings and events.

The Obama Foundation, which is headquartered at the center, also runs leadership, education and community programs in the United States and around the world, including initiatives to train emerging leaders, support young people and encourage civic engagement.

Obama's original presidential records are instead stored at the National Archives in College Park, Maryland, rather than at the Chicago campus, which is not part of the federally operated presidential library system.

Critics have long questioned why the city granted control of valuable public parkland for a privately operated museum and foundation headquarters rather than a traditional presidential library, although the plans were approved by the Chicago City Council and the Chicago Plan Commission. The arrangement faced years of legal challenges that ultimately failed to stop construction, although opponents maintained that the courts never ruled on the merits of their central argument that the use of public parkland violated Illinois' public trust doctrine.
The foundation has promoted the center as far more than a museum, describing it as a place to develop future leaders and inspire change around the world.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"We are building more than a campus. We are creating a living institution that will inspire, empower, and connect the next generation of leaders," the foundation stated in its 2024 annual report.
Obama echoed that vision during the center's June opening ceremony, saying it was designed to be more than a monument to his presidency.
"We designed the center not to be some lifeless mausoleum," Obama said.
"While we are non-partisan, we are not value-neutral. We have a point of view."
Michael Dorgan is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business.

title: DOJ gives California 48 hours to review list of possible noncitizens on voter rolls
summary: The Justice Department gave California 48 hours to confirm whether noncitizens were mailed ballots, threatening emergency relief if it fails to act.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
The Justice Department is threatening California with possible legal action after it says the state mailed ballots to noncitizens ahead of the midterm elections.

The DOJ sent a letter on Tuesday to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber informing her that federal officials provided Los Angeles County election officials with a list of names of individuals who authorities believe to be noncitizens.

Acting Deputy U.S. Attorney Trent McCotter warned that the state has 48 hours to confirm whether any of the individuals on the list were mailed ballots for the November 3 election. That deadline will expire later on Thursday.
"If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief," the letter states.
MORE THAN A QUARTER-MILLION NONCITIZENS MAY BE REGISTERED TO VOTE IN 4 KEY STATES, DHS ALLEGES

California Secretary of State Shirley Weber speaks during the General Assembly at the California Democratic Party State Convention at the Moscone Center in San Francisco, Calif., on Saturday, Feb. 21, 2026. (Photo by Christina House/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
Weber released a statement protesting the federal demands on Wednesday, connecting it to earlier efforts by the DOJ to expunge noncitizens from California's voter rolls.
DOJ GIVES NEW JERSEY 5 DAYS TO HAND OVER VOTER DATA AFTER NONCITIZEN REGISTRATION SCANDAL

"In July of this year, President Trump and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin made (still) unsubstantiated claims that California had 190,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls. Given the many high-profile examples of states purging U.S. citizens from their voter rolls based on DHS/SAVE data, SOS immediately requested written information about their methodology and data sources to back up their claims. They refused and provided California with nothing," Weber said in a statement.
A large box of pre-assembled mail-in ballots at the Wake County Board of Elections on Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026, in Raleigh, N.C. (AP Photo/Matt Ramey)
"Now the USDOJ, under threat of 'emergency' litigation, demands that California blindly trust this administration without any evidence or legal authority to justify its request," she continued.
WATCH: TRUMP DOJ VOWS TO PURSUE ‘EVERY SINGLE’ VOTING VIOLATION AFTER NJ ROLL SHOCKER

"The USDOJ’s relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states’ protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections," Weber added. "California has robust state law requirements that only U.S. citizens can register to vote and that any non-eligible registrants are removed from the State’s voter rolls. My office and California election officials remain committed — as always — to ensuring a fair and smooth 2026 General Election."
President Donald Trump's administration has heightened scrutiny on state voter rolls since gaining office, as part of the president's wider interest in election integrity.
TRUMP SCORES SUPREME COURT WIN IN ELECTION INTEGRITY FIGHT AS STATES GAIN NEW VOTER ROLL TOOL

Voters cast their ballot during early voting at a polling location at the Metropolitan MultiService Center and Gymnasium in Houston, Texas, on Friday, Oct. 25, 2024. (F. Carter Smith/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

TRUMP SCORES SUPREME COURT WIN ON MAIL-IN VOTING RESTRICTIONS BEFORE MIDTERMS

The court’s order put on hold a federal judge’s June ruling that had deemed the Republican administration’s recently revamped version of SAVE illegal. U.S. District Court Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan had blocked the use of the tool, saying it violated Americans’ privacy rights and could result in voters being wrongly removed from the rolls.

title: Talarico dismisses past comments about God and gender as 'provocative' while invoking Charlie Kirk
summary: James Talarico faced a Christian voter at a CNN town hall who questioned his faith over past comments calling God "non-binary" and citing the Bible.
story: Texas State Rep. James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, admitted in a Wednesday night CNN town hall that his previous comments referring to God as nonbinary were "provocative" and done "in an annoying way." Credit: CNN

Texas’ Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico dismissed his past comments referring to God as "nonbinary" and using the Bible to justify his pro-choice stance on abortion during a Wednesday night CNN town hall.
Participating in a "Jubilee"-style town hall in which voters confronted him one-on-one, Talarico met with a fellow Christian from Texas who pressed him on his past statements.

"You've said some concerning things in the past kind of related to faith and social issues. Things such as God is nonbinary, questions about how many genders there really are and your justifications using the Bible for abortion," Sarah Gardner, a small business owner, said to Talarico.
TALARICO SAYS HE 'HATES CHRISTIANITY' IN UNEARTHED INTERVIEW WITH TRANSGENDER 'LATINX' THEOLOGIAN

"And so, I think that's led a lot of Christian voters to question the authenticity of your faith. And I wanted to ask you a very direct question. Do you believe that the Bible is the absolute source of truth and God's final authoritative word, even when our culture says otherwise?" she asked.

State Representative James Talarico poses for a portrait at his campaign headquarters after launching his campaign for the seat currently held by Senator John Cornyn in Austin, Texas, on September 9, 2025. (Callaghan O'Hare for The Washington Post via Getty Images)

"Yes," Talarico replied. "And I think it's important to remember that even the early church, the disciples who actually knew Jesus of Nazareth, the early church, we often talk about as a singular body when, in reality, was more like early churches because there was a lot of disagreement, there was a lot of debate."
TED CRUZ, CONSERVATIVES RESPOND AFTER TALARICO CRITICIZES BIBLE-RELATED EDUCATION IN SCHOOLS AS 'PROPAGANDA'
Talarico then went on to explain his past comments as being "provocative," drawing a parallel to his own interpretation of scripture to Charlie Kirk’s.
Democrat candidate for US Senate James Talarico speaks during a rally in San Antonio, Texas, on May 29, 2026. (Photo by RONALDO SCHEMIDT/AFP via Getty Images)
"I actually want to clarify a few of the things that you said, because I know that this has been used in these attack ads all over the state," he began.
UNEARTHED CLIP SHOWS TALARICO CALLING PARENTS 'ABUSIVE' FOR DENYING CHILDREN'S GENDER IDENTITY

"The first comment about God not being defined by gender, when I said that I was being provocative. And I want to admit that and come clean about that. But I think what I was saying is actually not controversial theologically. The idea that we can't define God using human categories, not only did I say that, but the late Charlie Kirk said that, the late Pope Benedict said that. And so, yes, I was doing it, maybe in an annoying way, I can admit that," he said.
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico speaks during a campaign rally at the Cailloux Theater on August 31, 2026 in Kerrville, Texas. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

Talarico, a state senator in Texas, previously said, "God is both masculine and feminine, and everything in between. God is nonbinary. In Genesis 1:26, God speaks of God's self in the plural, saying, 'Let us make man in our image.'"
EXPERT TEARS APART TALARICO'S VIRAL CLAIM HIS AGENDA IS BASED ON JESUS'S TEACHINGS: 'BUTCHERING THE BIBLE'
He also dismissed the notion that the Bible refers to abortion.
"The idea that there is a set Christian orthodoxy on the issue of abortion is just not rooted in Scripture," he said during a 2025 appearance on The Joe Rogan Experience.

title: Trump announces Montana 'super range' at midterm rally for Pentagon to test advanced war technology
summary: President Donald Trump announced at a Kalispell rally that the Pentagon will build a military super range in Montana for hypersonic weapons testing.
story: A new military "super range" is coming to Montana to test advanced weapons and technology, including autonomous systems, space and electronic warfare, and supersonic and hypersonic systems, President Donald Trump announced Wednesday.

President Donald Trump delivered "a little breaking news" to supporters at a midterm campaign rally in Montana on Wednesday, announcing that the Pentagon would establish a new military "super range" in the state to test cutting-edge weapons and warfare technology.

The president said the range would support testing of potential autonomous weapons, space and electronic warfare technology, and supersonic and hypersonic systems, positioning Montana to play a greater role in the development of America's next-generation military capabilities.

"I'm pleased to inform you and announce that right here in Montana, the Department of War is going to establish a new super range for testing advanced weapons and technologies," Trump told supporters gathered at Majestic Valley Arena in Kalispell.
TRUMP PENTAGON LAUNCHES COMPETITION FOR AMERICA'S NEXT GREAT MILITARY BASE
President Donald Trump arrives at a campaign rally at Majestic Valley Arena, Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, in Kalispell, Mont. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)
Trump suggested the project had been highly sought after elsewhere in the country.
"The rest of our country maybe won't be thrilled because a lot of other people wanted it also," Trump said.
The president also credited persistent lobbying from Montana's Republican lawmakers, joking that Sen. Tim Sheehy had repeatedly pressed him to bring the project to the state.
"You're getting it, everybody, will you please leave me alone?" Trump quipped. "Leave me alone, Tim. Tim Sheehy would drive me crazy."
The announcement places Montana at the center of a proposed military testing initiative involving some of the Pentagon's most sophisticated emerging technologies.
President Donald Trump greets U.S. House candidate Aaron Flint at a campaign rally at Majestic Valley Arena, Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, in Kalispell, Mont. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)

Hypersonic weapons, which can travel at least five times the speed of sound, are among the advanced military capabilities under development by the Pentagon, according to the Government Accountability Office. The War Department has also identified autonomous systems and electronic warfare capabilities as areas of strategic importance.
ELON MUSK LANDS NEW TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ROLE IN SHAPING FUTURE OF AMERICAN WARFARE
Trump did not specify where in Montana the new range would be located, how much the project would cost or when testing operations would begin.
"Montana will help ensure the American military always reigned supreme," the president told the crowd.
President Donald Trump shakes hands with Senate candidate Kurt Alme at a campaign rally at Majestic Valley Arena, Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, in Kalispell, Mont. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)
Trump made the announcement during his second campaign rally of the day and third stop on a Western swing aimed at supporting Republican candidates ahead of the midterm elections.

The president appeared in Montana's 1st Congressional District to campaign for House candidate Aaron Flint and Senate candidate Kurt Alme, after holding a rally in Arizona earlier Wednesday. He also campaigned in Alaska on Tuesday.

title: Georgia voters set early-voting record as midterm elections heat up
summary: Brad Raffensperger praised record Georgia early voting turnout as the fiery Jon Ossoff and Mike Collins Senate debate exploded over personal attacks.
story: Sen. Jon Ossoff and Rep. Mike Collins trade accusations over alleged neo-Nazi activity linked to Collins' family and campaign donations from Jeffrey Epstein associate Reid Hoffman.
Over 180,000 Georgians cast their ballots on the first day of early voting on Tuesday, setting a record for midterm elections.
Tuesday's total eclipsed the first day of early voting in 2022 by more than 55,000 votes, state election officials say. Georgia's early voting schedule runs through Oct. 30.

"This record-breaking turnout proves that voters have confidence in the integrity of our elections," Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger said in a statement. "It’s a testament to our strong election system overseen by 159 of the best county election officials in the country."

Georgia's contentious U.S. Senate race erupted into a heated confrontation Tuesday night as Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., accused GOP challenger Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., of allowing the dissemination of "neo-Nazi propaganda" inside his own home, prompting Collins to fire back over Ossoff's financial support from a billionaire with ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
MAP IT: DOJ ILLEGAL VOTING CRACKDOWN SWEEPS 17 STATES AS RAZOR-THIN ELECTIONS FACE SCRUTINY
Voting signs outside Friendship Baptist Church, a polling location in Atlanta, Georgia, during the Georgia Midterm Primary Election in Atlanta, Georgia, U.S. May 19, 2026. (REUTERS/Alyssa Pointer)

The exchange unfolded during the candidates' second and final debate ahead of the Nov. 3 general election, which was hosted by the Atlanta Press Club and broadcast by Georgia Public Broadcasting network.
ANTISEMITISM FIGHT EXPLODES IN FLORIDA AS VOTERS HEAD TO THE POLLS: 'POLITICAL POGROM'

During the debate, Ossoff sought to tie his GOP opponent to White nationalism and repeatedly demanded that Collins commit to stopping the dissemination of hateful rhetoric involving his campaign staff, in particular Collins' son-in-law, which Ossoff alleged had continued despite blowback.
Seen pictured are Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., and Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-G., both of whom are running for the U.S. Senate in Georgia. ( )

"How weak a person do you have to be to be unable to stop someone under your own roof from disseminating neo-Nazi propaganda while you run for the Senate?" Ossoff asked, referencing reporting about his opponent's son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, who was the subject of a CNN investigation about sharing Nazi propaganda imagery, promoting antisemitic conspiracy theories and polling his online followers about whether he should produce a video titled, "Why Gen-Z Doesn't Hate Hitler."
FORMER HOUSE INTEL LEADER POINTS TO DEM RHETORIC 'ENCOURAGING' VIOLENCE; EIGHTH MAN CHARGED IN UFC TERROR PLOT

Billionaire Reid Hoffman, left, a known former associate of Jeffrey Epstein, made contributions to the campaign for Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., right, and to a PAC opposing Ossoff's challenger, Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Ben Hendren/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Meanwhile, Collins accused his Democrat opponent of fueling threats against his family and refusing to return campaign support connected to LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman. He also questioned Ossoff over his support for candidates linked to controversial streamer Hasan Piker.
‘MISLEADING VOTERS’: OSSOFF WARNS DONORS HE’S FALLING BEHIND DESPITE LEADING SENATE FUNDRAISING
"I'm a little tired of this, Jon," Collins said. "There's a crazy person in jail right now because of your rhetoric," he alleged, before saying he had received another threat just the previous day.

Sen. Jon Ossoff, a Democrat from Georgia, speaks during a campaign event at The Tabernacle in Atlanta, Ga., on Sunday, May 31, 2026. Georgia's Senate race is seen as a must-win for Democrats if they are to have any path toward retaking the Senate in November. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"You have not denounced, you've not condemned Reid Hoffman, one of your largest donors out there, one that's been supporting you with over $1 million," Collins shot back. "Why don't you denounce that? Why don't you return that money?"

title: This sparsely populated red state quietly climbed to the top of America's financial rankings
summary: North Dakota tops Truth in Accounting's state finances ranking with a $72,300 taxpayer surplus, while 24 states can't cover all their bills.
story: Tax Foundation Senior Fellow Jared Walczak says Wyoming’s abundant land, affordable energy and high-capacity fiber could give the state an edge as others consider new taxes on booming data centers.
Of the 50 U.S. states, 24 don't have enough money to cover their bills. Meanwhile, one under-the-radar red state stands apart from the rest, according to a new analysis of state finances.

North Dakota ranked No. 1 in Truth in Accounting's 2026 Financial State of the States report, ending fiscal year 2025 with $21 billion more than it needed to pay the state's bills. That financial cushion gave North Dakota the highest "Taxpayer Surplus" in the country at $72,300.

The taxpayer surplus figure does not mean that the state's residents receive that amount of money back in their pockets at the end of the year — rather, it represents each taxpayer's share of the state's surplus under the group's methodology.

The divide between the states with surplus versus those with burden matters, especially when the economy weakens. States with stronger balance sheets have more room to weather downturns, maintain public services and meet retirement obligations, while states carrying large unfunded debts can face tougher choices over taxes, spending and borrowing when revenues fall.
THINK YOUR STATE IS EXPENSIVE? NEW DATA REVEALS WHERE AMERICANS FACE THE HIGHEST COST-OF-LIVING
North Dakota's oil boom transformed the state's economy and now generates billions of dollars in tax revenue each year. (Jim West/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
North Dakota's financial position was bolstered by its Legacy Fund, a state investment fund built with oil tax revenue.
Although oil, gas and coal tax revenues declined amid lower energy prices, strong investment earnings and federal grant revenue helped offset the drop, according to the report.

North Dakota was followed in the rankings by Alaska, Wyoming, Utah and Tennessee. The five states all had taxpayer surpluses ranging from $11,400 in Tennessee to topping out in North Dakota with $72,300. Those handful of states' financial position stands in sharp contrast to nearly half the country.
The report found that 24 states did not have enough available assets to cover their financial obligations.

New Jersey ranked last, with a $162.3 billion shortfall. Truth in Accounting translates that gap into a $45,800 "Taxpayer Burden," the highest in the country. Connecticut ranked 49th, followed by Illinois, Massachusetts and California.
The bottom five states had taxpayer burdens ranging from $16,000 in California to $45,800 in New Jersey.
THE RED STATES CHARGING AHEAD WITH AMERICA'S WEALTH AS RIVALS WATCH BILLIONS SLIP AWAY

North Dakota ranked No. 1 in Truth in Accounting's 2026 analysis of state finances, ending fiscal 2025 with $21 billion more than it needed to cover its bills. (Bryan Bedder/Getty Images/Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library)
Long-term retirement obligations are a major source of pressure on state finances.
Across the country, states had $775 billion in unfunded pension liabilities and $490 billion in unfunded retiree health care obligations in fiscal 2025, according to the report.

Despite those shortfalls, most states improved financially in 2025. Strong investment returns boosted pension assets and helped reduce unfunded pension obligations, though Truth in Accounting cautioned that those gains can reverse when markets fall.

title: Most dramatic moments from Rep Mike Lawler's fiery debate against Dem Cait Conley in battle for House control
summary: Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., clashed with Dem Cait Conley over ICE enforcement, sanctuary cities and bail reform in a fiery debate for New York's swing district.
story: Rep. Mike Lawler and Democrat Cait Conley clashed on multiple fronts during their Pix11 News debate less than three weeks before the midterm elections.
Tensions flared on the debate stage Wednesday night, where Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., faced off against Democrat military veteran Cait Conley to represent their suburban New York district in Congress.
Lawler is vying for a third term representing the Empire State's 17th Congressional District.
One of the few swing seats left in Congress, the race could prove decisive for which party controls the House of Representatives for the latter half of President Donald Trump's term.
Below are some of the most dramatic moments during their one-hour head-to-head on PIX11 News:
HOW ONE NYC SUBURB COULD DECIDE WHICH PARTY CONTROLS THE HOUSE
Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., is running for a third term against Democratic challenger Cait Conley. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images ; Tierney L. Cross/Getty Images)
While the debate was filled with the two political rivals criticizing each other, one tense moment came when Lawler turned his ire on moderator Dan Mannarino.

Mannarino had asked both Conley and Lawler what should be done to rein in Immigration and U.S. Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents who run afoul of their own guidelines, invoking the recent shooting of an illegal immigrant in the Bronx by federal officers while the man's 5-year-old was in the car.

Lawler pointed to the man's rap sheet and accused Democrat state leaders of creating the situation with their sanctuary policies and Gov. Kathy Hochul's recent bail reforms. He also accused Conley of supporting those policies.
The moderator began, "Mr. Lawler, I just want to follow up. The question was, how do you ensure if ICE agents do not follow through objectives, and what's the discipline —"
"I understand the question," Lawler said amid the cross-talk.
PROTESTS ERUPT IN THE BRONX AFTER ICE AGENT SHOOTS MAN DURING IMMIGRATION OPERATION
"But you didn't answer the question," Mannarino said.

"I understand the question. But here's the problem, Danny," Lawler shot back. "You guys want to focus on a gangbanger who has put people in harm's way? I want to make sure that our communities are safe."
ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ACCUSED OF MURDERING COLLEGE STUDENT DIALS INTO HEARING FROM HOSPITAL BED

Protesters near the scene where a man was shot by an ICE officer during an operation in the Bronx borough of New York City on Oct. 8, according to local media and police; the suspect, Oscar Belgal. (Charly Triballeau / AFP via Getty Images; WNYW)

The GOP incumbent notably used the immigration standoff to pivot to the case of Sheridan Gorman, a teen from his district who was shot and killed near her college campus in Chicago earlier this year. The accused is an illegal immigrant who was previously arrested for shoplifting but was never turned over to ICE due to Chicago's sanctuary policies.
Conley called Gorman's death an "atrocious crime," while Lawler repeatedly said over her, "It was preventable."
SHERIDAN GORMAN’S MOM SCORCHES DEM LAWMAKERS SHE SAYS REFUSED TO HEAR FAMILIES OF SLAIN AMERICANS

"Can I finish?" an irate Conley shot back. "It was an atrocious crime committed in Chicago. And that man should have been deported. And I do support federal agents and federal law enforcement, federal immigration enforcement, making sure that we deport violent criminals."

Lawler then pointed out, however, that the man would only have been deported if the sanctuary laws were not in place — laws he has repeatedly accused Conley of supporting along with her fellow Democrats.

"This is important," Lawler began as the moderator tried to regain control. "If you think he should have been deported when he was arrested for shoplifting, he should have been turned over to ICE. Under the new law that you support, he will not be turned over to ICE, and he will be released under cashless bail."
"Mr. Lawler, there's not a cross-examination round, so thank you," the moderator said.
Conley quipped at her GOP rival, "If you wanted to be the moderator, you should have volunteered."
A program handed out to supporters of the Gorman family who attended a Memorial Vigil held in Yorktown, N.Y. (Richard Beetham for Fox News Digital)
At another point, the candidates were asked whether there should be a federal definition or law for consent to help stop sexual assault.

Conley took the moment to attack Lawler for being allied with Rep. Max Miller, R-Ohio, a fellow House Republican who has been accused of domestic violence by his wife. Miller has denied the allegations.

Lawler said their matter was "tragic" and should be dealt with in family court without blaming either side. He then accused Conley of taking money from former New York Gov. Eliot Spitzer, who was revealed to be a client in a 2008 federal probe into a prostitution ring. Spitzer was never criminally prosecuted and resigned from his governorship amid the scandal.

"I'm sorry. I do not need — I do not need you to mansplain to me, domestic abuse and sexual assault against women," Conley snapped. "Don't start. I do not need you to mansplain to me, Mike."

title: Woke megachurch pastor, Dem nominee called for repentance over White privilege in wake of George Floyd, BLM
summary: Adam Hamilton once urged his megachurch to repent for White privilege after George Floyd's death as he now challenges Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas.
story: Adam Hamilton, the Democratic Senate nominee in Kansas — the nation's third-largest beef producer — told his congregation that cattle contribute to climate change. (Credit: YouTube/Church of the Resurrection, Jan. 27, 2020)

A former pastor and candidate running to make history in deep-red Kansas once suggested that people should repent for their White privilege as protests against the death of George Floyd rippled through the country.

During the tumultuous summer of 2020, just days after Floyd’s killing in Minnesota, Adam Hamilton called on his congregation at the Church of the Resurrection to recognize their White privilege and repent.

"Like part of what I know is that, is that I grew up in a way that I'm blind to certain things in our society," Hamilton said during a sermon dubbed "Jesus, Protests and Repentance." "I just am. And I have certain benefits by virtue of being educated, White and male, right?"
KANSAS DEMOCRAT BEGS KAMALA HARRIS NOT TO CAMPAIGN WITH HIM, ‘PLEASE DO NOT COME TO MY STATE’

Senior pastor Adam Hamilton spoke during "Heritage" services at 7:45 a.m. Sept. 16, 2012, in Wesley Covenant Chapel at the Church of the Resurrection in Leawood, Kan. (Tribune News Service via Getty Images)
"And we don't like to hear that, especially White folks don't like to hear that. But there are benefits that come along with that," he continued.

Hamilton is running against Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., in what has become one of the tightest races of this midterm cycle, despite Kansas' near-century-long history of not sending a Democratic candidate to the Senate.

"Roger Marshall wants to talk about anything other than his history of suing and jailing mothers and protecting predators by voting against releasing the Epstein Files," Tyson Brody, a spokesperson for Hamilton's campaign, told Fox News Digital. "Once again, he’s attacking Adam for something Roger said himself. Roger’s own pastor called Adam ‘middle of the road.’ Kansans are tired of high gas and grocery prices and ready for a senator who won’t divide us by race, religion, income, or ability to pay a medical bill at 18% interest."
Republicans acknowledge that they are facing headwinds going into November’s election, but until recently, the contest between Marshall and Hamilton wasn’t of much concern for the GOP.
SCHUMER WARNS OF REPUBLICAN ADVANTAGE THAT COULD CHANGE THE BATTLE FOR SENATE CONTROL

Now, the race has taken a turn and been rated a toss-up by the Cook Political Report as voters fume over the cost of fuel, groceries and other economic pain. In response, national Republicans are beginning to dump more resources into the contest to ensure that they maintain the seat.

Throughout the race, Marshall has largely aligned himself with President Donald Trump, only rarely breaking from the administration on certain decisions — last month he called for more advance notice and cooperation between the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the Kansas government after federal immigration agents descended on the southern part of the state.
Marshall has painted Hamilton as a "woke" megachurch pastor, delivering left-leaning ideals from the pulpit.
'JESUS WAS A RADICAL': PROGRESSIVES INVOKE CHRIST TO SELL LEFT-WING AGENDA ON CAMPAIGN TRAIL
Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., arrives in the U.S. Capitol for the first vote of the week on Sept. 22, 2026. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

So has an outside group based in Massachusetts, the Main Street Fund, which ran an ad in Kansas that spliced portions of two different sermons and charged that Hamilton was "way too woke for Kansas," shortly after Hamilton won his primary, The Kansas City Star reported.

During the sermon from June 2020 amid the Black Lives Matter (BLM) protests, Hamilton pushed back against rioting and looting, and argued that while the BLM movement was the focal point at the time, all lives matters.
"Of course all lives matter," Hamilton said. "Everybody understands white lives matter, blue lives matter."

Hamilton continued in his sermon posted on the church’s YouTube page in June 2020 amid the Black Lives Matter protests, "When I'm stopped by the police, I'm never afraid that they're gonna pull a gun on me."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"But every African American man that I know is worried about what might happen when a police pull him over," Hamilton said at the time. "It's not that all the police are bad, they're gonna do something like that, but there's this fear underneath there. And so the hands go on the steering wheel at 10 and 2. They've been taught that from the time they were children. Right?"

"I wasn't taught that, because I don't have to be afraid of that. Right? And there's a whole host of other things that are just a part of life. You know, I can ... well, you get the idea. There are benefits and privileges to my place in life. I have to recognize that," he continued. "To see that. And then I have to listen. I have to listen and understand, and finally be able to see the brokenness in myself, and my indifference. Before I can do anything to help anyone else, I have to have a conversion. I have to repent."And Marshall, who was running for his first term in the Senate at the time, struck a similar somber tone as Hamilton six years ago.

In various posts to social media and interviews with local outlets, Marshall condemned Floyd's slaying and pushed for reforms that would ensure what happened in Minnesota and to federal Protective Services Officer Patrick Underwood, who was killed in a drive-by shooting just days after Floyd's death.

"Additionally, Republicans called on Congressional Democrats to work across the aisle to make sure that what happened to George Floyd and Patrick Underwood never happens again, and significant bipartisan reform can be passed," Marshall said on Facebook following a House Judiciary hearing on police practices and law enforcement accountability.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Press freedom groups that blasted Trump turn fire on Dem governor over alleged media retaliation
summary: Press freedom groups that have condemned Trump's treatment of journalists are now comparing outspoken Trump critic Wes Moore's media practices to those of the president.
story: President Donald Trump's decision to ban three media organizations from the White House draws scrutiny from Fox News chief political analyst Brit Hume. While Hume acknowledges that some network coverage has been comically unbalanced, he questions whether a ban will be effective in changing media behavior. Hume concludes that the action primarily serves to rally the president's base.

A coalition of prominent press freedom organizations that have blasted President Donald Trump's treatment of journalists is now accusing Democratic Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, a Trump critic himself, of retaliating against news outlets scrutinizing his administration.

The accusations came in an Oct. 13 letter from the Freedom of the Press Foundation and six other journalism and civil liberties organizations. The groups raised concerns about the Moore administration's decision to subject even routine inquiries from reporters at Sinclair-affiliated news outlets and The Baltimore Sun to additional legal review.

The additional review came amid a defamation lawsuit filed against Moore by David Smith, executive chairman of Sinclair Broadcast Group and majority owner of The Baltimore Sun. Maryland agencies have explicitly cited Smith's lawsuit in written responses to reporters, informing journalists at Sinclair-affiliated outlets that their inquiries would be referred to legal counsel before receiving a response.

Moore himself has previously criticized Trump's treatment of journalists. During a Sept. 20 appearance on CNN's "State of the Union," the Maryland governor condemned the president's decision to bar reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, accusing Trump of treating the Constitution "like it is a suggestion box simply because he does not like the coverage."
WHITE HOUSE WON'T BACK DOWN AS ATTORNEY PREDICTS HOW TRUMP'S LATEST PRESS TUSSLE WILL PLAY OUT IN COURT
President Donald Trump and Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images | MANDEL NGAN/AFP via Getty Images)

"It's particularly offensive that Moore seeks to boost his national profile by slamming the Trump administration's unconstitutional attempts to ban disfavored media outlets from the White House when he's engaged in such similar antics himself," Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation, said in a statement accompanying the letter.

The press freedom groups that joined in condemning Moore, including the Committee to Protect Journalists, PEN America, Reporters Without Borders and the Society of Professional Journalists, argued that journalists should not face different treatment from government officials because of a dispute involving their outlets' ownership, drawing a comparison to the Trump administration's restrictions on certain White House reporters.

Moore's office strongly disputed the allegations in a statement to Fox News Digital on Wednesday, insisting that reporters have continued receiving responses from state agencies despite the additional legal scrutiny.
BALTIMORE SUN OWNER THREATENS MD GOV WES MOORE WITH LAWSUIT OVER WHAT HE CALLS A DEFAMATORY EPSTEIN LINK

"The central premise of this letter is completely false. There is no blanket refusal to engage," Ammar Moussa, Moore's senior press secretary and director of media strategy, told Fox News Digital. "In the last week alone, state agencies and the Governor's Office have answered dozens of questions from Sinclair outlets, and we're happy to let them share those responses."

"David Smith chose to sue the Governor. Having our legal team look over inquiries is basic due diligence, not a blackout," Moussa continued. "A litigant doesn't get to dictate how the state protects itself, but that hasn't stopped our agencies from doing their jobs for the people of Maryland."
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore speaks during a press conference at the Maryland State House on August 5, 2025, in Annapolis, Maryland. (Jamie Sabau/Getty Images)

The dispute traces back to a defamation lawsuit Smith filed against the governor in July. Smith accused Moore of making false and damaging statements about him during a television interview, including remarks Smith interpreted as suggesting he had ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Smith, whose media holdings include The Baltimore Sun, has been a frequent target of criticism from Moore, who has accused the newspaper's ownership of advancing a political agenda aligned with Trump. Smith maintains that the governor's remarks crossed the line from political criticism into defamation.

A Baltimore Sun newspaper bin stands with others in Baltimore, Maryland, on March 11, 2021. (JIM WATSON/AFP via Getty Images)
The lawsuit was filed by Smith personally, rather than the news organizations whose reporters have since faced additional legal review of their inquiries.

"We urge you to instruct all Maryland agencies that Smith’s lawsuit against you is a personal matter and not an excuse to send media requests into a legal review black hole, and to cease any other unlawful retaliation against news outlets you personally dislike," the coalition letter stated.

"It is particularly jarring that, while government agencies under your watch stonewall reporters based on flimsy pretexts, you take to the airwaves to condemn the Trump administration’s unconstitutional ban of news outlets the president doesn’t like from the White House," the letter continued. "Yes, Trump frequently turns his personal grudges into censorial government policy, to the detriment of the public. But your own conduct appears not much different."

title: Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt opens up about Trump, motherhood
summary: Karoline Leavitt called President Trump "the best boss" and revealed details about her grueling work weeks before leaving the White House press role to spend more time with her children.
story: Former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt joins Sean Hannity to reveal what it's really like working for Donald Trump, handling the media mob, and why she made the toughest decision of her life to leave.

Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt offered a glimpse into her relationship with President Donald Trump during a candid Instagram Q&A, praising her former boss as "kind and uplifting" while opening up about personal life decisions.
Leavitt, 29, fielded a variety of questions from her Instagram followers while traveling Wednesday, touching on everything from Trump's personality to her career plans and life as a mother of two.
When asked whether Trump was nice or kind, Leavitt offered insight into his personality.
"Yes! He’s the best boss," she said.
LEAVITT PULLS BACK THE CURTAIN ON TRUMP'S 'TENSE,' UNFILTERED PRIVATE TALKS WITH PUTIN, XI, STARMER
Karoline Leavitt, then-White House press secretary, conducts a press briefing on Monday, March 30, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
"People don’t see this side of him because the media doesn’t show it but he has been nothing but kind and uplifting to me, even since departing," she continued. "He’s also hilarious. Love him!"

Leavitt, who served as press secretary from January 2025 until August 2026, also addressed a question about landing another job after her decision to leave the White House to spend more time with her children.

"As Press Sec, I was working in the office 60+ hours a week, traveling the world, and always on call 24/7," she said. "Now, I am home with my kids every day and doing some TV hits. These things are not the same, ma’am."
KAROLINE LEAVITT INVITED AS A GUEST ON ABC'S 'THE VIEW' AFTER LEAVING WHITE HOUSE ROLE
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt speaks with reporters at the White House, Thursday, Oct. 2, 2025, in Washington. (AP Photo/Evan Vucci)
Leavitt also confirmed that she would officially begin working as a Fox News Channel contributor next month.
"I will be officially joining Fox News as a TV Contributor on November 1st, so I will continue making appearances on various shows!" she wrote.
FOX News Media CEO Suzanne Scott announced Leavitt's new role earlier this month, and she is expected to provide commentary across the network's programming.

Leavitt previously worked in Trump’s first administration as a presidential writer and assistant press secretary before running for Congress as a Republican in New Hampshire's 1st Congressional District in 2022. She also served as communications director for then-House Republican Conference Chair Rep. Elise Stefanik.
When asked for career advice for people hoping to succeed in public relations or politics, Leavitt encouraged them to gain practical experience before graduating.
KAROLINE LEAVITT ANNOUNCES BIRTH OF SECOND CHILD, A GIRL

Karoline Leavitt, White House press secretary, during a news conference in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, April 15, 2026. (Mattie Neretin/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"My advice to people who want to get into politics or comms is to get real world experience when you're in college," she said. "You'll be taught a lot of things in the classroom, but work experience is where you're really going to learn the game."
Leavitt said she interned at NBC Sports Boston because she initially considered becoming a sideline sports reporter. She also worked at a local news station before securing a White House internship.

"Just try to apply for internships, say yes to every opportunity that you can and don't spend your summers hanging out, spend your summers working and gaining that real world experience, which will help you later in your career."
Leavitt, who made history as the youngest White House press secretary, was also asked how she spends her free time.
"I don't have free time. As a mom of two littles, I'm lucky if I can take a shower in peace. But it's the season of life I'm in and I wouldn't have it any other way!!!!"

title: Pentagon sends hundreds of Army troops to Latin America for training as drug-trafficking campaign expands
summary: Troops from the 10th Mountain Division are deploying to Panama for jungle training as the Pentagon expands military operations against drug traffickers.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

The U.S. military is deploying several hundred Army soldiers to Latin America for training and joint exercises with regional forces as the Trump administration expands its campaign against drug-trafficking networks, Fox News confirmed.

The deployment involves soldiers from the Army's 10th Mountain Division based at Fort Drum, New York, with the first troops from a roughly 600-soldier battalion expected to deploy to Panama, according to The New York Times, which first reported the deployment.
A senior U.S. official confirmed to Fox News that the troops are being forward-staged under U.S. Southern Command (SOUTHCOM), which will determine where they are ultimately deployed.
According to The Times, the troops will first deploy to a new jungle training facility in Panama before eventually training with local forces in Colombia and Honduras.
EXCLUSIVE: TRUMP’S NEW SECURITY ALLIANCE FACES FIRST REAL-WORLD TEST DEEP IN SOUTH AMERICA AS TROOPS DEPLOY

U.S. Marine Corps Lt. Gen. Francis L. Donovan testifies during a Senate Committee on Armed Services hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 15, 2026. (Brendan SMIALOWSKI / AFP via Getty Images)
The troops could also support U.S. special operations personnel who are advising local militaries conducting raids against suspected drug traffickers, the outlet reported.
Separately, several hundred soldiers from the 10th Mountain Division are expected to help staff a new Western Hemisphere military command based in Miami.
The deployment comes as the Pentagon continues military operations targeting suspected drug traffickers across Latin America and the Caribbean.
US MILITARY STRIKES ALLEGED NARCO-TRAFFICKING VESSEL IN CARIBBEAN, KILLING 4 'NARCO-TERRORISTS'
U.S. SOUTHCOM said it has directed USS Fort Lauderdale (LPD 28) and USS Billings (LCS 15) to Venezuela to support State Department-led U.S. government relief operations in Venezuela. (@Southcom/X)
Since the campaign began more than a year ago, U.S. forces have conducted dozens of strikes, with more than 235 people killed.
Gen. Francis Donovan, commander of SOUTHCOM, previously said the military was considering operations against trafficking networks on land.
"Do I see land strikes as options? Yes. We want all options at the table," Donovan said in an interview with The Wall Street Journal.
"Those actions might be strikes, arrests, or the takedown of a safe house," he continued. "It could even be something as routine as increasing the use of cargo scanners at border checkpoints."
TRUMP ADMIN'S LIST OF US-DESIGNATED 'FOREIGN TERRORIST' GROUPS IN LATIN AMERICA EXPANDS TO 21
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth unveils Operation Southern Spear to dismantle narco-terror networks across Latin America. (Jeon Heon-Kyun - Pool/Getty Images)
Donovan added that the goal was to create "total systemic friction" for the cartels.
The Trump administration has pursued agreements with allied nations that could allow it to expand military operations against trafficking networks onto land in multiple Latin American countries.

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth previously said during a visit to Panama in August that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow the U.S. to carry out joint military operations against criminal groups within their borders, although Guatemala denied reaching such an agreement.

title: Was your identity stolen? What to do in the first 24 hours
summary: Identity theft recovery starts with securing bank accounts, freezing credit and enabling two-factor authentication within the first 24 hours.

Discovering that your identity has been stolen can leave you feeling angry, frightened and unsure where to begin. Maybe someone drained your bank account, opened a credit card in your name or filed a fraudulent tax return using your Social Security number. Whatever happened, your next steps can help limit the damage.

The first 24 hours are especially important because identity thieves may continue using your information until you secure your accounts. Fortunately, you can take several steps right away to protect yourself and begin recovering.

IDENTITY RESTORATION: WHAT TO DO AFTER IDENTITY THEFT
Reviewing your credit reports and documenting suspicious activity are important steps toward recovering from identity theft. (Sara Diggins/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images)
Why the first day is so important

Identity theft can quickly spread beyond the account where you first discovered the problem. Someone who gains access to your email, for example, might use it to reset passwords for your banking, shopping or other accounts. That's why acting quickly can make a difference.

However, you don't have to solve everything in one day. Identity theft recovery can take weeks or even months, depending on the circumstances. Your immediate goal is to stop additional fraud, protect your information and create a record of what happened.
What to do in the first 24 hours after identity theft
The following checklist breaks the process into manageable steps. The time frames are guidelines, so prioritize active fraud and compromised accounts rather than waiting for a particular hour.
Start with the accounts most likely to expose your money or personal information.

Contact your bank or credit card company. If someone accessed your account or made unauthorized transactions, call the number on your card or the institution's official website. Report the fraud and ask whether the account should be locked, frozen or replaced. Also ask about disputing unauthorized transactions.Change compromised passwords. Start with the affected account and your primary email address if it may have been exposed. Use strong, unique passwords and a trusted device.Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA). Protect your email, financial accounts and other important services. Use an authenticator app or passkey when supported.Check for unauthorized account changes. Review recovery email addresses, phone numbers, forwarding rules and active sessions. Sign out of unfamiliar devices.
