AI AGENT HACKS GYM SYSTEM TO MOVE UP WAITLIST

AI agents can handle everyday tasks, from tracking flight prices and organizing emails to managing household reminders, while keeping users in control of important decisions. (Photo by Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
What are ChatGPT Dots, ChatGPT Work, Meta Muse and Gemini Spark?

ChatGPT Work is only one way to try an AI agent. OpenAI also offers Dots, which are more persistent. A Dot has its own cloud computer, can remember ongoing work and can keep making progress between conversations. Dots are currently rolling out to eligible ChatGPT Pro, Business Premium and Enterprise users. OpenAI says Dot usage will temporarily not count against eligible users' plan allowances during the introductory period, with longer-term usage terms still to come.

ChatGPT Work is built into ChatGPT and focuses on longer, multi-step tasks. On web and mobile, OpenAI says Work is available on eligible paid plans, including Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu, although access is still rolling out. Work can research, use connected apps and files, create finished materials and run scheduled or recurring tasks.

There are alternatives too. Meta Muse offers a free tier with usage limits, with a paid subscription available if you need more. Gemini Spark is Google's personal AI agent and is available to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in supported regions. It can manage ongoing tasks, use connected Google services and run scheduled workflows.

You do not need the most powerful or expensive agent to try the ideas in this article. Start with whichever service you already use, give it a low-risk task and see whether having AI continue the job actually saves you time.
How to get started with an AI agent in ChatGPT

If you have never used an AI agent, the first step is simply knowing where to find one. We will use ChatGPT Work as an example. OpenAI is rolling the feature out to eligible accounts, so what you see can vary depending on your plan and device. Before you get started, I recommend checking a few privacy settings so you have more control over what ChatGPT does with your information.
You can stop new ChatGPT conversations from being used to train OpenAI's models. Here's how:

Go to ChatGPT.com and sign in. If you do not have an account yet, choose the option to sign up and create one.Click your profile icon.Select Settings.Click Data Controls.Turn off Improve the model for everyone.
Go to ChatGPT.com and sign in. If you do not have an account yet, choose the option to sign up and create one.
Click your profile icon.
Select Settings.
Click Data Controls.
Turn off Improve the model for everyone.
Your conversations can still appear in your chat history, but new chats will not be used to train OpenAI's models.
Open Settings.Select Personalization.Find Memory.Turn off Enable memory if you do not want ChatGPT using remembered information to personalize future conversations.
Open Settings.
Select Personalization.
Find Memory.
Turn off Enable memory if you do not want ChatGPT using remembered information to personalize future conversations.

You can also use Temporary Chat for conversations you do not want saved in your history or used for model training. OpenAI may still retain these chats for up to 30 days for safety purposes. Finally, review your connected apps under Settings > Plugins. Remove any connections you no longer need. Keep in mind that turning off model training does not prevent ChatGPT from processing information you provide to complete a task.
Once you've reviewed those settings, you're ready to give an AI agent its first task. Here's how to get started:

Look near the top of the screen for Chat and Work .Click Work .Start a new chat .In the message box, describe the task you want the agent to handle.Add any useful files or information the task requires. If the job needs access to a supported app, ChatGPT may give you the option to connect it.Be specific about what the agent can and cannot do. For example, you can tell it to research or draft something without sending, booking or buying anything.Send your request and follow along as the agent works. Review its results before approving anything important.
Look near the top of the screen for Chat and Work .
Click Work .
Start a new chat .

Add any useful files or information the task requires. If the job needs access to a supported app, ChatGPT may give you the option to connect it.

Send your request and follow along as the agent works. Review its results before approving anything important.

You do not need to start by connecting your entire digital life. In fact, I would not. Try a simple task first, such as researching several products within a budget or comparing options for an upcoming trip. That lets you see how the agent works before you give it access to email, calendars or other personal information. Once you are comfortable with the basics, the eight ideas below show where an AI agent can start saving you some real time.
MALICIOUS BROWSER EXTENSIONS CAN HIJACK AI ASSISTANTS
ChatGPT Work, OpenAI Dots, Meta Muse and Google Gemini Spark offer ways to automate time-consuming tasks using artificial intelligence. (Photo by Celine Frohnapfel/picture alliance via Getty Images)
1) Have AI prepare you for the day

I do not need another app demanding my attention first thing in the morning. What I would like is something that looks at the information I already have and tells me what I need to know. An AI agent with access to your calendar and other approved information could review what is coming up, flag a meeting you need to prepare for and surface something time-sensitive you might have missed. The key is asking for a briefing instead of another information dump.

Prompt to try:"Review my calendar and relevant messages for today. Tell me what I need to prepare for, flag anything time-sensitive and point out any scheduling conflicts. Do not send messages or change my calendar without asking me first."
That last sentence would absolutely stay in my prompt. I want AI to tell me that my afternoon looks impossible. I do not want it quietly deciding which meeting gets moved.
2) Stop checking the same price over and over

You find a flight. It costs too much. So you check again tomorrow. Then you check again the next day. I have done this with airfare, hotels and products I was not in a hurry to buy. It gets old fast. This is almost a perfect AI agent task because there is very little value in you personally opening the same page 12 times. Give the agent the item and the price you are hoping to hit. Then let it tell you when something changes.

Prompt to try:"Track the price of [item, flight or hotel]. Let me know if the total price drops below $___ or if you find a comparable option that costs less. Show me the details before taking any action."

You can even use this after a purchase. If the retailer offers price adjustments or you are still inside the return window, have the agent keep watching. I like this type of task because the AI does the watching while I keep control of the wallet.
3) Let AI sort the email you do not want to sort

There are days when opening my inbox feels like volunteering for another job. Some emails need an answer. Others are simply FYIs. Then you have the message you meant to answer two days ago sitting underneath six newsletters and a shipping notification. An AI agent connected to your inbox can help with that first pass. It can summarize what arrived, identify the messages that appear to need attention and prepare a reply for you to review.

Prompt to try:"Review my unread email from the last 24 hours. Show me what needs my attention today and summarize the rest. Draft responses where appropriate. Do not send, delete or archive anything without my approval."

I would absolutely keep that approval requirement in place. Let AI write the first draft. Let AI tell you what looks urgent. But before something goes out under my name, I want to see it. That goes double if the recipient is my boss, my doctor or anybody who might interpret an AI hallucination as something I actually meant to say.
4) Make AI remember all the little deadlines you forget

Life is full of deadlines that are incredibly easy to miss because they do not feel urgent until suddenly they are. A subscription renews Friday. A rebate expires next week. Your insurance paperwork is due. Somewhere in your inbox there is a form you completely forgot existed. That is the kind of mental clutter I would love to hand off. An agent could keep track of deadlines you give it and remind you before something needs your attention.

Prompt to try:"Keep track of the deadlines, renewals and appointments I give you. Tell me what is coming up this week and alert me early when I need to do something. Never renew, cancel or submit anything without my approval."
I would keep the agent in reminder mode when money is involved. Tell me the bill is due. Tell me the trial expires tomorrow. Then get out of the way and let me decide what happens next.
5) Let AI figure out what’s for dinner

I don't know about you, but deciding what to make for dinner every night gets old fast. You open the refrigerator, stare at what's inside and somehow still can't think of anything to eat. Why not hand that job to AI? Tell an AI agent what foods you like, what ingredients you already have and how much time you want to spend cooking. It can put together a weekly dinner plan, suggest simple recipes and even help you use up food before it goes bad.
Prompt to try:

"Every Sunday, prepare a dinner plan for the coming week with five easy meals. Use my food preferences and any ingredients I've told you I have. Keep each meal under 30 minutes. Include simple recipes and a grocery list of anything else I'll need. Don't order groceries without my approval."

You can schedule this as a weekly task so the agent prepares fresh dinner ideas without you having to ask each time. Just update it with what's in your refrigerator and pantry before it creates the next plan. That means fewer nights staring into the refrigerator wondering what to cook.
6) Put somebody else in charge of the household to-do list

Every home seems to have a list that nobody actually wrote down. The air filter needs replacing. The dog is running out of food. There is something in the garage you promised to fix about four months ago. Then, at exactly the wrong moment, somebody remembers it. An AI agent could become the place where all those loose ends go. Every time something pops into your head, give it to the agent and let the agent keep track of what is coming due.

Prompt to try:"Keep a household task list based on the things I give you. Remind me when something needs attention and help me keep track of what is still unfinished. Ask me before adding anything to my calendar, ordering something or contacting anyone."

This is one of those uses that sounds almost too simple for AI. That may be exactly why I like it. If it remembers that I need a new refrigerator filter before the old one stops working, we are making progress.
7) Let AI remember who owes you an answer

This one drives me crazy. You send an email. You request a refund. You call somebody about a bill. They tell you they will get back to you. Then life happens. Two weeks later, you suddenly think, "Wait, did anybody ever answer me?" An AI agent could keep track of those loose ends for you. Tell it what you are waiting on and when you expect a response. If nothing arrives, have it remind you. Better yet, let it prepare the follow-up so you do not have to stare at a blank email trying to remember what happened in the first place.
Prompt to try:"Keep track of the requests I am waiting on. If I have not received a response by the deadline I give you, remind me and draft a polite follow-up. Do not send it without my approval."

That could work for a contractor estimate, a disputed charge or a return you are still waiting to hear about. I like this because the agent becomes responsible for remembering that the conversation never actually ended.
8) Have AI watch for the opening you keep missing

Sometimes the issue is not the price. It is getting your hands on the thing at all. Maybe the restaurant you want is booked Saturday night. Your doctor has no opening for three weeks. The product you want keeps selling out. You could keep checking. Or you could make the AI check.

Prompt to try:"Check [restaurant, appointment, event or product] for availability. Let me know when an opening appears that meets these conditions: ___. Do not book, buy or confirm anything without asking me first."

This will depend on the AI agent you are using and whether the website allows that kind of automated access. But the idea is exactly where agents become useful. I do not want to ask AI whether the table is available right now. I want it to tell me Friday afternoon when somebody cancels and suddenly it is.
CyberGuy pro tip: Make your AI agent earn its permissions

Here is the part I would pay close attention to. An AI agent becomes more useful as you give it more access. That can include your email, calendar and other accounts. More access also means there is more that can go wrong. So I would make the agent earn those permissions.

Start by letting it read something. See what it does with the information. If that goes well, maybe allow it to organize information or prepare drafts. Only then would I consider letting it perform a limited action, and even then I would keep approval turned on whenever something important could happen.
Think about email. Let the agent summarize messages first. Then maybe let it draft replies. Sending those replies is another level entirely.

The same thinking applies to shopping and your calendar. OpenAI says Dots can follow rules that determine which actions they can perform on their own and when they need your input. Meta says Muse asks for approval before certain critical actions, including purchases and sending emails. I would use those controls.

And I would never paste passwords, PINs or two-factor authentication codes into a chat window because an AI agent asks for them. If the service offers a secure way to connect an account, use that instead. Give AI what it needs to complete the task. Do not automatically give it everything it asks for.
Do you actually need an AI agent?
Here is an easy way to figure that out. Ask yourself whether the job ends when AI answers you. If you ask ChatGPT to help plan dinner tonight, you probably do not need an agent.
But suppose you say, "Keep watching the price of this flight and tell me when it drops below $300." Now the useful part of the job happens after you leave.

The same goes for appointments. Asking what appointments you have tomorrow can be a normal AI request. Asking AI to alert you when an earlier doctor's appointment becomes available requires something that keeps checking.
Agents make the most sense when the task has an unfinished part. That is where I see the real appeal.
What I still would not hand over to AI

There are some areas where convenience would not persuade me to give up control. I would not give an AI agent unrestricted access to move money or make major purchases. I also would not let one make medical decisions for me or handle a legal decision without a human involved.

Be careful with connected accounts too. If you connect an agent to your inbox or cloud storage for a particular task, check what it can see. Once you no longer need that connection, consider removing it. AI agents may get much better at taking action on our behalf. That does not mean every action should be theirs to take.
IDENTITY RESTORATION: WHAT TO DO AFTER IDENTITY THEFT

AI agents can monitor prices, check appointment availability and draft email responses without requiring users to repeatedly check for updates. (Photo Illustration by Stanislav Kogiku/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

I think AI agents get a lot more appealing when you forget the hype for a minute and ask one simple question: What am I tired of doing myself? For some people, that could be checking a price every morning. Others may want help remembering follow-ups or keeping track of household chores that always seem to surface at the worst possible time. Those are the kinds of tasks I would hand over first.

I become much more cautious when AI moves from watching and reminding to actually doing something in my name. I am happy to let an agent tell me that a restaurant table opened up. Before it books dinner for me, though, I want to know exactly what it is about to do. That is where I see the sweet spot with AI agents. Let them handle the annoying part while you stay in charge of anything that could cost you money, expose your information or create a mess you have to clean up later.
What is the one annoying task you would happily hand over to an AI agent tomorrow, and what is one thing you would never trust it to do for you? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: 16-year-old allegedly led ransomware gang behind hundreds of attacks
summary: Operation KillSwitch dismantled KillSec's ransomware infrastructure, but investigators say a 16-year-old allegedly ran the entire cybercrime operation.
story: Following the arrest of an alleged leader in the Netherlands, a top FBI cyber official released an unusual public address urging the remaining cybercriminals to turn themselves in "while the choice is still yours."

When you picture the person running an international ransomware operation, a 16-year-old probably does not come to mind. Yet investigators say a teenager was the suspected main operator behind KillSec, a cybercrime group linked to around 1,000 suspected attacks worldwide. About 500 of those attacks have so far been identified as successful.

Now, an international law enforcement operation has taken KillSec's leak site and key servers offline. Authorities also secured at least 110 terabytes of stolen data that could have been exposed or used to pressure victims. The takedown offers a remarkable look at how accessible cybercrime has become. More importantly, it shows how attackers continue to find their way into poorly protected systems and turn stolen files into leverage. What investigators uncovered about KillSec shows how the group operated, how AI reportedly played a role and what you can do to make ransomware attacks harder to pull off.
Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better health care. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist.
See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com.
FBI STRIKES BACK AT HACKING GROUP WITH OVERSEAS ARREST OF ALLEGED LEADER
Guardia Civil, Mossos d’Esquadra and FBI personnel took part in the coordinated international investigation targeting KillSec. (Europol)
Police take down KillSec ransomware operation

The crackdown, known as Operation KillSwitch, took place on Sept. 30. Authorities from the United States and several European countries participated in the investigation. Europol and Eurojust also helped coordinate the effort.

Police carried out eight searches in Greece, Romania, Spain and the United Kingdom. Three suspects were provisionally arrested. Investigators also took control of five central servers connected with KillSec's operation. One of the biggest moves involved KillSec's dark web leak site. The group allegedly used the site to name victims and threaten to publish stolen files unless they paid. Authorities have now taken control of that infrastructure.
A 16-year-old is suspected of running the operation

Perhaps the most startling part of this case involves the age of the suspected operator. Investigators identified a 16-year-old as KillSec's suspected administrator and main operator. Another suspected member, described as a developer, turned 18 in August and was reportedly still a minor when some of the alleged crimes occurred.

Investigators also identified people suspected of serving as a negotiator and an affiliate. Authorities say the investigation remains ongoing. Age aside, the alleged operation was anything but small. KillSec has been active since around 2024. According to Europol, the group exploited software vulnerabilities and poorly secured access points to break into organizations. Attackers then copied sensitive internal files to systems they controlled.
How KillSec allegedly pressured its victims

Once attackers had the files, the pressure began. KillSec allegedly listed organizations on its dark web site and threatened to publish their stolen data if they refused to pay. In some cases, the stolen files were reportedly made available after victims declined to hand over a ransom.

Europol says the group received substantial ransom payments from some attacks. That strategy shows how ransomware has changed over the years. Criminals do not always need to lock every file on a computer to create leverage. Stolen information itself can become the threat. If an attacker gets employee records, customer information or confidential business documents, the victim can face serious consequences even when backups work perfectly.
KillSec reportedly used AI to support its attacks

Investigators also uncovered another detail that caught my attention. Europol says members of KillSec used artificial intelligence to help build and maintain ransomware infrastructure and identify potential victims.

That does not mean AI carried out the entire attack by itself. However, it shows how cybercriminals can use the same technology everyone else is experimenting with to speed up parts of their work. A teenager may no longer need to build every piece of an attack from scratch. Tools, stolen credentials, vulnerable systems and AI assistance can lower some of the barriers that once required deeper technical expertise. That should make all of us pay closer attention to basic security habits.
FBI'S FIRST CYBER FUGITIVE ON TEN MOST WANTED LIST RETURNS TO US AFTER CAPTURE IN VENEZUELA
Operation KillSwitch brought together international law enforcement agencies to seize KillSec’s servers, leak site and stolen data. (Felix Zahn/Photothek via Getty Images)
What happens to KillSec now?
The investigation remains active. Authorities are examining computers, servers and other seized evidence. Investigators are also following cryptocurrency and other alleged criminal proceeds.

That evidence could uncover additional attacks, victims or people connected with the operation. Europol also cautions that the current number of successful attacks may change as investigators continue reviewing what they seized.

For now, KillSec's core infrastructure has taken a significant hit. However, ransomware groups have a long history of disappearing, reorganizing and resurfacing under different names. That makes prevention especially important even after a major takedown.
Why this ransomware takedown should get your attention

KillSec appears to have focused mainly on organizations rather than individual home computer users. Still, the methods behind the attacks offer lessons that apply to everyone. Europol says the group exploited software vulnerabilities and poorly secured access points. Those are the same types of weaknesses security experts have warned about for years.

An old router, forgotten account or unpatched computer can give attackers an opening. A compromised password can do the same. Once criminals gain access, they can steal information before anyone realizes something has gone wrong. So, while you probably cannot stop an international ransomware gang yourself, you can make your devices and accounts harder to break into.
7 ways to reduce your ransomware risk
A few simple security habits can close some of the openings attackers commonly look for.

Do not keep putting off updates on your computer, phone, browser and other connected devices. Security updates often fix vulnerabilities attackers already know how to exploit. CISA recommends regularly patching operating systems and software, especially on devices exposed to the internet. Turn on automatic updates when that option is available.

Using the same password across several accounts gives an attacker more opportunities if one login is exposed. Create a different password for each important account. A password manager can help generate and store strong credentials without forcing you to remember every one. You should also check whether passwords you already use have appeared in known data leaks. Your iPhone or Android phone may already have tools that can flag compromised passwords.
HACKER CLAIMS 7.49M CUSTOMER RECORDS STOLEN FROM AMERICAN UTILITY COMPANY
Law enforcement collected laptops, phones and storage devices as evidence during the Operation KillSwitch takedown. (Europol)

A stolen password becomes much less useful when your account requires another form of verification. Enable two-factor (2FA) or multifactor authentication on your email, financial accounts, cloud storage and other important services. When available, consider phishing-resistant options such as passkeys or security keys instead of relying only on text-message codes.

Ransomware becomes far more painful when your only copy of a photo, document or financial record lives on the compromised device. Back up important files regularly. Consider keeping one copy in the cloud and another on an external drive. If you use an external drive, disconnect it when the backup finishes. Some ransomware can also target drives that remain connected to an infected computer.

A convincing email, fake update warning or malicious attachment can provide an attacker with a way into your computer. Avoid opening files you were not expecting. Instead of clicking an urgent update prompt from a webpage or email, open the app itself and check for updates there. If something feels unusual, stop before entering a password or running a downloaded file.

Strong antivirus software can help detect ransomware, malicious downloads and other threats before they spread. Keep the protection updated and run a full scan if your computer suddenly behaves differently, redirects your browser or shows unfamiliar programs. Security software will never replace safe habits. However, it can provide another opportunity to catch a threat before the damage grows. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com.

If you see a ransom message or suddenly lose access to important files, disconnect the affected device from your network. Avoid plugging backup drives into the compromised computer until you know the device is clean. The FBI says it does not support paying ransomware demands because payment does not guarantee that your information will be restored. The agency also encourages victims to report ransomware incidents. You can file a report with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at IC3.gov or contact your local FBI field office. The FBI specifically directs ransomware victims to use those channels. One more thing: type IC3.gov directly into your browser. The FBI has warned that scammers have created fake IC3 websites, including lookalike pages that may appear in sponsored search results.
Kurt's key takeaways

The age of KillSec's suspected operator is going to grab the headlines, and I understand why. Sixteen is incredibly young to be accused of running an operation connected with this many attacks. What stays with me, though, is how familiar the alleged entry points sound. Vulnerable software and poorly protected access can still give criminals exactly the opening they need. That is why I keep coming back to the basics. Update your devices. Protect important accounts with more than a password. Keep a backup that an attacker cannot easily reach. You may never know which security step stopped an attack. That is far better than discovering which one you skipped after your files are already gone.

If a 16-year-old can allegedly help run a ransomware operation tied to hundreds of successful attacks, do you think powerful hacking tools and AI are making cybercrime too easy to enter at a young age? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: Ex-OpenAI engineer charged with planting recording device had one-way flight booked to Saudi Arabia, DOJ says
summary: Abdulrahman Alfozan had a one-way flight to his native Saudi Arabia booked days before federal custody, according to the Department of Justice.
story: Fox News chief correspondent Jonathan Hunt details the arrest of a Saudi OpenAI employee accused of secretly placing a recording device inside a San Francisco conference room. Hunt discusses the alleged security breach, how the device was discovered and OpenAI’s response to the incident.

The former OpenAI engineer charged with planting a recording device inside a conference room at the AI giant's San Francisco office had a one-way flight booked to Saudi Arabia days before he was taken into federal custody, the Justice Department said.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, had a flight booked for Oct. 12 — days after his arrest — for himself, his wife, and another relative, according to court documents.

Federal prosecutors cited his travel plans when asking a federal judge to seal the criminal complaint and arrest warrant against him, arguing that public knowledge of the case would prompt him to possibly flee the country.
8 EVERYDAY THINGS THAT WOULD QUIT WORKING WITHOUT DATA CENTERS

A man described as Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national formerly employed as an OpenAI engineer, looks behind a television where a recording device had been placed in a conference room in OpenAI offices, in a still image from surveillance video. (Department of Justice/Handout via Reuters)
"Disclosure of the specified documents might jeopardize the defendant's arrest," court documents state.
In an Arabic podcast last month, Alfozan recalled meeting Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman during his 2016 visit to Silicon Valley.

Alfozan said he had been contemplating whether to return to his native country. In response, the prince advised young Saudis living and working in Silicon Valley to refine their skills at premier tech companies before bringing their expertise home, the New York Post reported.
OpenAI offices are seen in San Francisco. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images)
"You learn from the source and then, God willing, bring that experience and knowledge back to the homeland," Alfozan reportedly said on the podcast.
Alfozan was arrested Oct. 9 and charged with using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications, according to the Department of Justice.

OpenAI discovered the encrypted device Sept. 30, plugged into a USB port on the back of a television in a conference room used for "highly confidential" discussions involving proprietary research, product plans and business opportunities, federal prosecutors said.

The OpenAI logo is displayed on a smartphone screen on a reflective surface with Dots promotional artwork projected onto it in Creteil, France, on Oct. 1, 2026, as OpenAI begins rolling out Dots in ChatGPT, its new system of autonomous AI agents. (Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

The device, concealed in toilet paper, had allegedly been installed two days earlier. OpenAI traced the device to Alfozan, and security footage showed him near the conference room multiple times, authorities said.
In addition, a chatbot associated with his wife was allegedly used to field prompts about ways to install and hide audio recording devices.

title: 3 children, 1 adult killed in Oregon elementary school shooting; suspected gunman dead, police say
summary: Bend police responded to Silver Rail Elementary School for an active shooter report, where three children and an adult were killed. The suspected gunman was shot dead, police say.
story: Fox News correspondent Christina Coleman has the latest on a school shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon on 'Special Report.'
Three children and an adult were killed in a shooting at an Oregon elementary school Thursday, and the suspected gunman is also dead, possibly shot by a bystander, according to police.

Federal law enforcement sources confirmed the four victims’ deaths to Fox News, while Bend police said they were investigating whether a bystander killed the shooter inside Silver Rail Elementary School.
Officers were going room by room to evacuate Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend as authorities worked to determine who shot and killed the suspect.
"We don't have confirmation yet who shot the suspect. It may have been a bystander," Sheila Miller, Bend Police Department’s communications manager said during a news briefing.
POLICE MAKE ARREST AFTER GUNFIRE DURING CALIFORNIA HIGH SCHOOL FOOTBALL GAME LEAVES 1 DEAD
The area near Silver Rail Elementary School as Bend police respond to a reported active shooter Thursday. (KTVZ)
Bend Fire medics transported at least two people to St. Charles, but their conditions were not immediately known.
The school serves approximately 400 to 450 students and has more than 40 staff members, officials said. It was not immediately clear how many were on campus during the shooting.
Scene near Silver Rail Elementary School after an Oct. 15, 2026, shooting that killed three children and an adult, according to federal law enforcement sources. ( REUTERS/Rob Kerr)
The department’s communications manager choked up as she described the impact on the community.
"This is the kind of thing we never want to see happen in Bend. It's devastating," Miller said.
REPORTED SHOOTING AT VIRGINIA ELEMENTARY SCHOOL 'CONTAINED,' SHERIFF'S OFFICE SAYS
Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., where police responded to a report of an active shooter Thursday. (Google Maps)

Dispatchers received the first call at approximately 12:59 p.m., reporting a shot fired into a car. An alert went out to officers at 1 p.m., and police arrived at approximately 1:02 p.m., the communications manager said.
Seconds after officers arrived, word came over the radio that the suspect was down. Dispatchers received multiple 911 calls reporting an active shooter at the school during the response.
TRANSGENDER EX-STUDENT IDENTIFIED AS ALLEGED SUSPECT IN DEADLY CANADA SCHOOL MASS SHOOTING
Law enforcement at the scene near Silver Rail Elementary School following a report of an active shooter Thursday. (KTVZ)
Hundreds of law enforcement personnel from agencies across Central Oregon responded, according to police.
The FBI’s Portland field office said agents were at the scene assisting local authorities with the investigation.
"We will make every resource they need available," the office wrote on X.
Families were directed to Journey Church at 61303 S. Highway 97 for reunification, while authorities urged the public to avoid the school area.
Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook said the district was "stunned and heartbroken by this senseless tragedy."
Map locating Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, where police responded to a shooting on Oct. 15, 2026. (Fox News)

"We extend our deepest sympathy to the families and to everyone affected by this violence," Cook said in a statement shared by police. "No words can adequately express the grief our community is experiencing. Our immediate priorities are caring for our students and staff and assisting law enforcement and emergency responders."
Bend police also expressed support for those affected.
"We are thinking of the families and friends of Silver Rail Elementary and everyone in Bend and beyond who are affected by this terrible tragedy," the department said.
Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek said she was closely monitoring the situation.
"I am grateful to the first responders who are on the scene," Kotek wrote on X. "I will share as I learn more."
Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., said he and his team were also closely monitoring reports of an active shooter at the school.
"As details continue to come out, my heart is with the Bend community and all of the students and families affected," Merkley wrote on X. "No one should have to fear violence at school."

Rep. Janelle Bynum, D-Ore., whose district includes Bend, called the shooting "every parent’s worst fear."
"Our babies are supposed to do arts and crafts at school, not use their desks as cover from gunfire," Bynum said in a statement posted on X.
"My heart and my prayers and everything else I got is with the families at Silver Rail Elementary. When will it end?"

title: Horse farm owner gets life in prison for boyfriend's murder after claiming self-defense
summary: Caylen Deller claimed she shot Chad Mullen in self-defense at her Florida horse farm, but the jury rejected her testimony after just one hour.
story: Caylen Deller, 32, was convicted of murder in the September 2024 death of Chad Mullen, her on-again and off-again boyfriend.
The Florida woman accused of killing her boyfriend and burying him in a shallow grave was found guilty of his murder.
Caylen Deller, 32, was charged with first-degree murder in the September 2024 death of Chad Mullen, her on-again and off-again boyfriend.

According to prosecutors, Deller killed Mullen at her San Mateo, Florida, horse farm, then got a friend and her horse to help move the body, which was found in a shallow grave over a month after he went missing.

Deller was found guilty of first-degree murder on Thursday after the jury deliberated for over an hour and was sentenced to life in prison. She was also found guilty of tampering with evidence and failure to report the death of a person.
FLORIDA WOMAN CHARGED WITH MURDER EVADING POLICE AFTER BODY FOUND IN SHALLOW GRAVE: SHERIFF

Chad Mullen was fatally shot by his on-again, off-again girlfriend, Caylen Deller, in September 2024. Prosecutors said Deller used a horse and enlisted a friend to help move his body before it was buried in a shallow grave. (Putnam County Sheriff's Office)

On Wednesday, Deller testified that she killed Mullen in self-defense because he choked her and raised a hammer at her when she confronted him about unproven claims that he had sexually abused her young daughter. Deller said Mullen became angry, pinned her against a truck and grabbed her by the throat, alleging she was unable to breathe at the time.
That's when Deller said she grabbed a gun. Deller said she obtained the gun after Mullen allegedly broke into her apartment Aug. 1, 2024.
"I pulled the trigger of the gun and shot him twice," Deller said. "I was extremely afraid.
"I shot Chad twice in self-defense."
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Caylen Deller, 32, was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life in prison for fatally shooting her on-again, off-again boyfriend, Chad Mullen, at her Florida horse farm in September 2024. (Putnam County Sheriff's Office)
The woman said she didn't intend to kill Mullen and believed she was defending herself.
SEND US A TIP

Prosecutors then questioned Deller about why she chose not to contact police and why she kept in touch with Mullen despite having described him as a violent individual, presenting evidence that she placed 28 calls to him between Sept. 2 and Sept. 9, 2024.
GOT A TIP?
Deller testified that she didn't initially call 911 after shooting Deller because she thought police wouldn't believe her self-defense claim. She didn't tell Mullen's family for that same reason.

Caylen Deller was sentenced to life in prison after a jury convicted her of first-degree murder in the death of her boyfriend, Chad Mullen. Deller testified that she shot Mullen twice in self-defense, claiming he attacked her during an argument. (WFOX)
"It was probably not a good idea," Deller said. "I was more concerned about getting in trouble."

title: Las Vegas investigators say they've identified shooting victim's body found in Lake Mead barrel
summary: A barrel containing human remains surfaced at Lake Mead in 2022, and Las Vegas authorities now say they've identified the suspected murder victim.
story: Las Vegas authorities announced Thursday that they have identified the man found shot dead and stuffed in a barrel that washed ashore in May 2022.
Las Vegas authorities say they've identified a suspected murder victim whose remains were found in a barrel in Lake Mead four years ago.

Clark County Coroner Melanie Rouse said at a news conference on Thursday that the victim was identified as Edward Jackson, who was believed to be in his mid- to late 50s when he died. He had a gunshot wound and is believed to have been killed in the early 1980s.

Las Vegas Police Lt. Robert Price said Jackson was from Arkansas and had traveled to various parts of the country, though he had no known ties to Las Vegas. title: Investigators zero in on possible cause of Wisconsin plane crash that killed 6
summary: Flight data shows the Piper Malibu's airspeed nearly doubled to 340 mph as it plunged at 4,000 feet per minute after the pilot reported wing icing.
story: A small plane carrying five adults and a child crashed into a wooded area in Wisconsin on Tuesday night, killing everyone aboard. (Credit: WITI)

A small plane that crashed in Wisconsin, killing six people, including a child, had plummeted toward the ground at a rate of up to 4,000 feet per minute after its pilot reported ice accumulating on the wings, according to newly released flight data and federal investigators.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said the pilot of the Piper PA-46 Malibu was flying at 24,000 feet on Tuesday night when he alerted air traffic control to ice building up on the aircraft's wings and requested permission to descend.

Air traffic controllers approved the request, but the plane entered a descending right turn that became increasingly sharp before communications and flight tracking data were lost, investigators said.
COAST GUARD SUSPENDS SEARCH FOR BOSTON-BOUND MEDEVAC PLANE OFF NANTUCKET WITH 6 ON BOARD
First responders are seen at the scene of a small plane crash in the Town of Dellona in Sauk County, Wisconsin, on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. (FOX6 Milwaukee WITI)
Data from FlightRadar24 showed the plane's airspeed nearly doubled to 340 mph as it descended at a rate of up to 4,000 feet per minute, according to The Associated Press.

"It has all the earmarks of an icing-related loss of control," aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti, a former investigator for both the NTSB and Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), told the outlet.
Ice accumulation poses a serious threat to aircraft because even a thin layer can disrupt airflow over the wings, reducing lift and making a plane more difficult to control.

The six-seat, single-engine aircraft was traveling from Kenosha to Menomonie when it crashed shortly before 10 p.m. in a wooded area of Sauk County near Mirror Lake State Park, about 10 miles west of Wisconsin Dells, authorities said.
A map shows Dellona, Wisconsin, where six perished in a plane crash on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. (Fox News)
Rain was falling as a thunderstorm moved through Dellona at the time of the crash.
FATAL AIR AMBULANCE CRASH EXPOSES GROWING GPS DANGER FACING US FLIGHTS
All six people aboard were killed. Authorities said no structures were damaged and no one on the ground was injured. The identities of the victims had not been publicly released.
The Piper Malibu model has previously faced federal scrutiny over crashes involving icing conditions.
Investigators are probing the aircraft's final communications with an air traffic control tower prior to the crash, authorities said. (FOX6 Milwaukee WITI)

The NTSB conducted a special safety review of seven icing-related crashes involving Piper Malibu and Mirage aircraft between 1989 and 1991, several of which involved relatively inexperienced pilots unfamiliar with handling the sophisticated planes in icy conditions.

The review prompted recommendations for changes to pilot training, aircraft checklists and operating manuals, as well as the addition of an indicator light for systems designed to prevent ice buildup in pitot tubes, which help provide accurate airspeed readings.

The NTSB is leading the investigation into Tuesday's crash. Investigators have not determined an official cause.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Christa Pike is back behind bars after botched execution, but her ultimate sentence faces a new test
summary: Christa Pike's survival of lethal injection could raise double jeopardy and disability claims that may block Tennessee from executing her again.
story: If surviving attempted lethal injections on Sept. 30 left her mentally impaired, Christa Pike could be spared from the death penalty, according to a leading scholar on capital punishment in the U.S., who also breaks down some other possibilities.

If Christa Pike's recovery from two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital has left her mentally impaired, she could be spared from her death sentence, according to a leading expert on capital punishment in the United States.

"Her attorney stated that she still seems a little confused about things and is not clear on, doesn't have a clear memory of what happened to her," said Fordham Law Professor Deborah Denno, a leading expert on capital punishment. "If that continues, that it could be very difficult for the state to execute her for that reason alone. In other words, you have to understand why you're getting a punishment and also connect that to whatever crime you committed."
She added, "We also don't execute people who have intellectual disabilities."
CHRISTA PIKE'S FIRST WORDS REVEALED AFTER SHE UNEXPECTEDLY WOKE UP WHILE LAWYERS THOUGHT SHE WAS 'BRAIN DEAD'

Pike was scheduled to be put to death on Sept. 30 after the Supreme Court vacated a last-minute stay. She was convicted and sentenced to death for the 1995 torture and murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in Knoxville, a classmate she knew from a vocational school called the Jobs Corps Center.

Pike and her then-boyfriend and accomplice were said to be satanists. They were arrested wearing pentagrams, and the boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, carved the symbols into Slemmer's chest and face. At trial, an expert testified that the murder had "satanic elements."

One option is that Gov. Bill Lee could commute her sentence to life in prison without the possibility of parole. He's already put a moratorium on executions in the state for at least the rest of the year. But even so, Denno said a commutation from the governor is a long shot.

title: San Jose girl, 8, dies after living in cockroach-infested home as mother, stepfather face charges
summary: Aurora Williams lived in a cockroach-infested San Jose home with mold and pet feces before a fatal asthma attack, which prompted felony charges against her mother and stepfather.

An 8-year-old California girl died following a severe asthma attack after allegedly living for years in a filthy home infested with cockroaches, mold and pet feces, prompting felony child neglect charges against her mother and stepfather, prosecutors said.

The Santa Clara County District Attorney's Office said this week that the girl's mother, Gabrielle Hanson, 32, and stepfather, Jacob Randolph, 39, knew about the dangerous conditions inside their San Jose home and had been repeatedly warned by medical professionals and social workers about the risks to their seven children.
Despite the warnings, the couple allegedly waited eight hours before seeking medical help when their daughter, Aurora Williams, began experiencing serious medical distress in May.
"It was too late," prosecutors said in a news release announcing the charges.

Gabrielle Hanson and Jacob Randolph face felony child neglect charges after prosecutors alleged that their 8-year-old daughter died following years of dangerous living conditions and inadequate medical care. (San José Police Department)

In February 2025, more than a year before her death, Aurora was taken to an emergency room by a relative after experiencing asthma symptoms, wheezing and difficulty breathing, according to prosecutors.
A bug fell from her shoe and a cockroach was seen crawling on her, prompting her to tell staff, "Oh yeah, bugs just crawl on me."
Hospital staff also reported that Aurora smelled like cat urine, appeared seriously underweight and pale, and said she was hungry and had not eaten.
On May 13, 2026, San Jose police and firefighters responded to the family's home for a medical emergency involving a child.
CALIFORNIA COUPLE CHARGED WITH ABUSING 14 SURROGATE-BORN CHILDREN INSIDE $10M LOS ANGELES MANSION

Jacob Randolph, 39, was charged with felony child neglect in connection with the death of his 8-year-old stepdaughter, according to the Santa Clara County District Attorney's Office. (San José Police Department)
Six other children, ranging in age from 2 months to 17 years, were taken into protective custody by social workers.
Aurora was declared dead four days later, according to prosecutors.

The medical examiner determined that Aurora died from a lack of oxygen to the brain caused by severe asthma and an acute lung injury associated with a viral infection. Medical neglect was identified as a significant contributing factor, and her death was ruled a homicide.
Investigators determined that Aurora and her siblings had been living in "squalid and dangerous conditions" since at least 2019, according to prosecutors.
Detectives also found that Aurora's asthma equipment had not been properly maintained and that her prescribed inhaler was missing during two searches of the home.
COLORADO MOM ALLEGEDLY BOUGHT ALCOHOL DAILY FOR 16-YEAR-OLD DAUGHTER FOUND DEAD WITH 173 EMPTY BOTTLES
Gabrielle Hanson, 32, faces felony child neglect charges following the death of her 8-year-old daughter, Aurora Williams, in San Jose, California. (San José Police Department)
Investigators later discovered a dirty inhaler spacer missing a rubber seal designed to prevent medication from leaking, along with a respiratory mask containing cockroaches.

"Another child is needlessly dead in this county, and once again our prosecutors will do everything in our legal power to hold the people who did this responsible," District Attorney Jeff Rosen said in a statement.

"Prosecuting people after this kind of tragedy is necessary — and not enough," Rosen continued. "There are serious questions about how this child and her siblings lived in this dangerous squalor for so long. In the name of this lost child and the others, this community deserves honest answers and real changes."
The investigation also led to child sexual abuse charges against Aurora's maternal uncle, Jonathan Hanson, 44, involving another child in the home.

San Jose police and firefighters responded to a home on Lancelot Lane on May 13, 2026, for a medical emergency involving a child who was later declared dead. (Sundry Photography/Getty Images)

Prosecutors charged Jonathan Hanson with two counts of molestation and one count of possessing explicit videos of the alleged victim, who was between 11 and 15 years old at the time of the alleged offenses.
Gabrielle Hanson, the alleged victim's stepmother, was also charged with knowing about the alleged abuse and failing to intervene, prosecutors said.
All three defendants were arraigned Tuesday.
Gabrielle Hanson and Randolph were released under supervised own recognizance over prosecutors' objections, while Jonathan Hanson was ordered held without bail.

title: DOJ unveils nationwide tax fraud crackdown involving 76 defendants, nearly $500M in alleged losses
summary: The Justice Department's first-ever National Tax Enforcement Surge targeted 76 defendants across 35 U.S. attorneys' offices in a six-week crackdown.
story: US Attorney Ryan Raybould announces the results of a nationwide tax enforcement search. Prosecutors in North Texas are targeting tax fraud and financial predators who target Main Street investors.

The Justice Department announced a nationwide tax fraud crackdown Wednesday involving 76 defendants and more than $490 million in estimated intended tax losses, including new charges against 31 individuals accused of schemes targeting American taxpayers.

The first-ever National Tax Enforcement Surge brought together 35 U.S. attorneys' offices and IRS criminal investigators over approximately six weeks. The operation resulted in 23 new charging actions involving more than $350 million in alleged intended tax losses, while another 45 defendants were involved in trials, guilty pleas and sentencings associated with nearly $140 million in estimated intended losses.

"Every dollar stolen through tax fraud is a dollar taken from the American people," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a news release "What we uncovered during this concentrated surge is only the tip of the iceberg. The Department of Justice is committed to expanding our investigations and exposing schemes designed to evade accountability, because there is no safe haven for fraudsters."
AG BLANCHE UNVEILS FEDERAL CHARGES AGAINST 160 DEFENDANTS IN PANDEMIC RELIEF SWEEP

Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald speaks during a Justice Department news conference announcing charges in home daycare fraud schemes in San Diego, California, on Sept. 15, 2026. (K.C. Alfred/The San Diego Union-Tribune via Getty Images)
Speaking at Wednesday's news conference, IRS Criminal Investigation chief Jarod Koopman described the operation as a new enforcement strategy and said similar crackdowns would follow.

"The consolidated actions we are announcing today represent an entirely new approach in our enforcement strategy. Partnering with DOJ to strategically surge resources around a broad range of tax crimes. And although this type of enforcement is the first of its kind, it will not be the last," Koopman said.
APPEALS COURT UPHOLDS ORDER BLOCKING IRS FROM SHARING TAXPAYER DATA WITH ICE
The IRS (Internal Revenue Service) headquarters building in Washington DC (Getty Images)

Among the largest cases highlighted was an alleged fraudulent trust scheme in Texas, where four defendants were charged with promoting tax shelters that prosecutors say concealed more than $1.5 billion in income and caused over $200 million in estimated tax losses.

In Georgia, three Mexican citizens were indicted in connection with an alleged $74 million tax refund scheme involving more than 16,000 U.S. Treasury checks. Prosecutors allege the defendants used Mexican identification documents belonging to other individuals to obtain IRS taxpayer identification numbers and file fraudulent returns.
FBI OPERATION TARGETS SCAM COMPOUNDS IN AFRICA WITH ARRESTS, ACCOUNT TAKEDOWNS
IRS CEO Frank Bisignano speaks during a Columbus Day event at the White House in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 9, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Asked during the news conference how much money taxpayers could expect to recover, Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald acknowledged that fraudulent proceeds are sometimes spent before investigators can retrieve them.

McDonald said the Justice Department is building an asset forfeiture and recovery team to pursue assets allegedly purchased with fraud proceeds, including luxury vehicles and real estate. He did not provide a total recovery figure, noting that some cases remain in their early stages.

The crackdown follows the Justice Department's establishment of its National Fraud Enforcement Division in April. Defendants facing criminal charges are presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

title: Wisconsin plane crash kills 5 adults, child as authorities probe final communications with air traffic control
summary: A Piper PA-46 crashed in a wooded area in Sauk County, Wisconsin Tuesday night, killing all six people aboard including a child. The FAA is investigating.
story: A small plane carrying five adults and a child crashed into a wooded area in Wisconsin on Tuesday night, killing everyone aboard. (Credit: WITI)

A small plane carrying five adults and a child was in contact with air traffic control before crashing into a wooded area in Wisconsin Tuesday night, killing everyone aboard and leaving investigators searching for answers about the aircraft's final moments.
The Piper PA-46 was on a return flight from Kenosha to Menomonie when it went down in the Town of Dellona in Sauk County, according to the Sauk County Sheriff's Office.

Authorities received multiple reports of a downed aircraft around 9:31 p.m. Tuesday and dispatched emergency crews to the area of Park Lane, where first responders discovered the wreckage in a densely wooded area west of Herwig Road.
SMALL PLANE CRASHES INTO SHALLOW WATER NEAR REMOTE ALASKA TOWN, KILLING ALL 4 PEOPLE ABOARD
A map shows Dellona, Wisconsin, where six perished in a plane crash on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. (Fox News)

Rescue crews began searching for survivors while investigators worked to identify the aircraft and determine how many people were aboard.
All six occupants were ultimately found dead at the scene, authorities said. Their identities have not been released.
Rescuers said the bodies of all occupants — five adults and one child — aboard the small plane were recovered. (FOX6 Milwaukee WITI)

Investigators are now working to determine what communications took place between the aircraft and a nearby air traffic control tower before the crash, as well as whether weather conditions in the area may have played a role.

"We know that they had contact with the tower prior to the crash and investigators are looking into that today to find out what that communication was," Sauk County Sheriff Chip Meister told FOX6 Milwaukee.
FATHER, SON KILLED IN PLANE CRASH ON WAY HOME FROM BASEBALL GAME
Meister said it remained unclear who owned the aircraft but confirmed that it was not a commercial plane.
No structures were damaged, and no injuries were reported on the ground, according to the sheriff's office.
Investigators are probing the aircraft's final communications with an air traffic control tower prior to the crash, authorities said. (FOX6 Milwaukee WITI)
The crash site remained secured Wednesday as investigators worked to piece together the circumstances surrounding the deadly flight.

A Georgia man who survived cancer and escaped a "crazy" car fire just a month ago died after falling from a Six Flags roller coaster, leaving his heartbroken sister struggling to comprehend how her brother could survive so much, only to lose his life in a tragic amusement park accident.

Hassan Kariem, 42, died Monday after falling from the 200-foot-tall Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia. "He's an amazing person," Clark told the outlet through tears. "The coolest part about me was him."

"He had other issues, but he's healthy, he was able-bodied. I don't understand it," she said.

Clark also recalled her brother's devotion to his loved ones, telling the Post that he worked hard to provide for his family and helped raise his fiancée's daughter, whom he had known since she was 3 years old.
"He could do it all," she said.

The grieving sister also condemned the circulation of disturbing images showing her brother's final moments as he fell from the roller coaster, urging people to stop sharing them.

The Goliath hypercoaster reaches speeds of up to 70 mph and features a 170-foot initial drop, a second 175-foot drop and a 540-degree spiral, according to the park's website.
Atlanta Public Schools confirmed Tuesday that Kariem worked for the district as an IT manager and extended its condolences to his family.

story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
Three teenage boys were charged after a 15-year-old boy with autism was beaten and robbed near a train station in Australia in a violent attack captured on video as other teenagers watched.

The assault happened Oct. 5 in Stawell, a town in the Australian state of Victoria, after the victim was reportedly lured to the area through a Snapchat meetup arranged with two girls, according to Australian news outlet news.com.au.

Video of the attack shows several teenagers punching and kicking the boy, knocking him to the ground and repeatedly striking him as he attempts to get away. One attacker demands the victim hand over his shoes before the group allows him to leave.

The Stawell railway station in Victoria, Australia, near where a 15-year-old boy was allegedly attacked and robbed by a group of teenagers Oct. 5, 2026. (Google Maps)
Victoria Police announced Tuesday that detectives had charged one 14-year-old boy and two 15-year-old boys after an investigation.
Detectives from the Northern Grampians Crime Investigation Unit executed four search warrants in the region before arresting the teenagers, police said.
All three face charges of affray, robbery, recklessly causing injury and theft. They are expected to appear in a children's court at a later date.

The victim, who also has epilepsy, suffered soft tissue injuries and possible head injuries, according to news.com.au. His mother told the outlet doctors were conducting additional scans to determine whether he had bleeding in his brain.
"I’m just lucky to have him alive. … He’s having nightmares," she said.

title: Houthis emerge as global threat beyond Iran control amid Saudi strikes, former envoy warns
summary: Tim Lenderking warns Houthi rebels are building homegrown weapons capabilities independent of Iran, turning Yemen's conflict into a global threat.
story: Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst reports on claims that Iran-backed Houthis are developing advanced missiles using Chinese parts and examines the potential threat to Saudi Arabia and stability across the Middle East on 'The Story.'

The Houthis are increasingly operating independently of Tehran, posing a "clear and very present danger" on the international stage as the terror group rearms and sharpens its strike capabilities, a former U.S. envoy warned Thursday.
The warning came amid deadly missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent days and growing threats to global shipping routes and critical Middle East infrastructure in the run-up.

Turki al-Maliki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, also confirmed Thursday that Houthi attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh had killed 17 and injured 333 others from Oct. 7-11.
Speaking at a news conference in Riyadh, al-Maliki said the Oct. 10 attack involved 10 drones, missiles and other projectiles.
"King Khalid International Airport has been subjected to 20 attacks since (Oct. 1)," he noted.

Tim Lenderking, who served as U.S. special envoy for Yemen from 2021 to 2025 and was posted to Saudi Arabia from 2013 to 2016, said Saudi officials had warned more than a decade ago that the Houthis would become a major threat, a prediction he says has now materialized.
SAUDI FOREIGN MINISTER WARNS HOUTHI THREAT GOES GLOBAL AS TRUMP HOLDS FIRE

The Houthis are increasingly operating independently of Tehran, posing a "clear and very present danger" on the international stage as the terror group rearms and sharpens its strike capabilities, a former U.S. envoy warned. (Handout from Houthi Media Center via Getty Images)
"The Saudis were very clear to our leaders that they viewed the Houthis as a major threat," Lenderking said of his time in the kingdom a decade ago.

At the time, he said, the group was "quietly building up their capability, burnishing their narrative of why they sought to lead Yemen as a messianic group, as a group from northern Yemen, with an agenda, with a mission."

The Houthis had emerged as a religious and political movement in Yemen in the 1990s, but their ties to Iran developed into a military partnership after 2014, when Tehran expanded its assistance and training during Yemen's civil war.

"The Houthis don't really need the Iranians anymore," Lenderking, a former acting assistant secretary for Near Eastern affairs at the U.S. State Department, continued, adding it was still "a very important relationship that "enabled the Houthis to become the powerful force that they are."

Lenderking, now a distinguished diplomatic fellow at the Middle East Institute (MEI), said, over time, the Houthis had developed their own "homegrown indigenous capability" as they capitalized on any disunity across the Gulf region.

Saturday's missile and drone attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh raised concerns that President Donald Trump could be drawn into a broader regional conflict as Saudi Arabia seeks U.S. assistance.
Asked whether the U.S. would defend Saudi Arabia against further attacks, Trump said, "You'll find out soon."
NEW RISK FOR US CONSUMERS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS THREATEN A SECOND MAJOR OIL CHOKEPOINT
Smoke and flames rise from King Khalid International Airport after Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis said they attacked the airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, Oct. 8, 2026. (Reuters)
Speaking at an MEI briefing, Lenderking said the Houthis' sophisticated weapons and targeting capabilities have transformed the group from a regional insurgency into an international security threat.

"They have the capability to hit around the region, including up into the northern reaches of the Red Sea. So, this is a regional problem, and given the fact that the Houthis control the west coast of Yemen," Lenderking said.
"It's an international problem now."
Lenderking cited the precision of the Riyadh airport attack as evidence of the Houthis' growing capabilities compared with earlier strikes during the Gaza conflict.
"They can hit things better. Now, they are hitting Terminal Four of Riyadh Airport, very specifically. It's a clear and very present danger," he said.

The Houthis reportedly launched multiple drones followed by cruise and ballistic missiles that traveled more than 620 miles to Riyadh, prompting an investigation into possible Saudi air defense failures, according to The Associated Press, citing regional officials.

Saudi forces intercepted two more ballistic missiles targeting Riyadh on Monday. On Tuesday, a Houthi strike caused damage to Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran, sparking a fire that spread across several floors, Reuters reported.
Lenderking said the Houthis have built extensive weapons supply chains, smuggling networks and domestic financing operations that allow them to sustain attacks without relying solely on Tehran.
HOUTHIS ENTER US 'KILL BOX' AFTER SEIZING RED SEA 'CORK,' FORMER PENTAGON OFFICIAL WARNS
Houthi supporters demonstrate in solidarity with Iran, amid a two-week ceasefire between U.S. and Iran, in Sanaa, Yemen, April 10, 2026. (Khaled Abdullah/Reuters)

"They get a lot of supplies off the open market through the internet, through commercial exchanges. They have a very well entrenched smuggling network, from big boats onto small boats, onto tiny boats, on the pack animals, on people's backs.

"They are able to move things undetected through government terrain, even through various borders and with a lot of wide open space there. They are constantly moving, building, resupplying, restocking, innovating."

The group's self-sufficiency also extends to financing. Lenderking said the Houthis generate revenue through black-market oil sales, taxation and extortion while also forcing families to provide recruits, allowing the group to continue fighting even if Iranian assistance is cut off.
"They have had support from Iran over the years, so they have money in the bank from that," Lenderking said.

"They relied on sales of black market oil in the past. They extort Yemeni transport companies, businesses. They tax people in areas that they control. They force many families to offer up a son to fight on the front lines."
The Houthis' expanding arsenal has raised concerns about potential Chinese involvement in their weapons supply networks.
OIL SQUEEZE TIGHTENS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS CRIPPLE HORMUZ ESCAPE ROUTES

Tim Lenderking, who served as U.S. special envoy for Yemen from 2021 to 2025 and was posted to Saudi Arabia from 2013 to 2016, said Saudi officials had warned more than a decade ago that the Houthis would become a major threat, a prediction he says has now materialized. (Houthi Media Center via Getty Images)
Yemen's government has accused the rebels of seeking Chinese components for medium-range ballistic missiles, raising concerns about the group's access to advanced military technology.
"There is a Chinese connection here that's very detrimental," Lenderking warned, adding that front companies have helped the group obtain weapons through commercial channels.
Lenderking warned that the Houthis could also target Saudi energy facilities, pipelines and desalination plants, infrastructure critical to the kingdom's economy and water supply.
"The Houthis have hit pipelines," he said. "They have diesel plants and other energy infrastructure in their sights."
Attacks on such facilities could disrupt global energy markets, maritime commerce and regional stability.
The Houthis also control Yemen's western coastline along the Red Sea, a vital shipping corridor connecting Europe and Asia.
With the rebels now capable of striking targets hundreds of miles away, Lenderking warned that the threat extends far beyond Yemen's borders.
"One blast at Riyadh Airport is a huge statement," the expert said.
