title: Cornell president faces contentious faculty senate meeting over Jane Doe allegations
summary: Cornell University’s president was met with scrutiny and sharp questions from its faculty senate on Wednesday, when the group convened to discuss a no-confidence vote over the university’s handling of an alleged 2024 sexual assault at a fraternity house, according to an audio recording obtained by NBC News.
story: Cornell University’s president was met with scrutiny and sharp questions from its faculty senate on Wednesday, when the group convened to discuss a no-confidence vote over the university’s handling of an alleged 2024 sexual assault at a fraternity house, according to an audio recording obtained by NBC News.
Discussion of a no-confidence vote comes after serious concerns were raised by students and staff over how the university responded to the allegations.
University President Michael Kotlikoff defended himself and Cornell’s administration as he took a series of pointed questions from the school staff.

At the meeting, most speakers were heard identifying themselves before speaking. Risa Lieberwitz, a professor of labor and employment law, said the issue of sexual assault “is a systemic problem. It deserves systemic attention.”
She told Kotlikoff that thus far it appeared he had “simply reacted to pressure.”

“It feels that the administration is considering more about how do we respond to pressure rather than the kind of leadership, which should have been doing systemic work and prioritizing these issues all along,” she said.
Kotlikoff argued that replacing its leadership was not the solution.

“We need to be able to work together to be able to change the culture, educate our students, and try and address this problem,” he said at the meeting. “I want Cornell to be a leader in this area, and we have plans to really invest in this area. But the idea that you can somehow, because an event has occurred, eliminate it immediately — it’s just unrealistic.”
Last month, a former student identified as Jane Doe sued the university and seven current and former students in connection with her allegation of sexual assault.

In 2024, Cornell shut down the Chi Phi fraternity chapter at the university and expelled two students after Doe reported the incident. Others were suspended or faced lesser disciplinary action. The university also said it launched the Presidential Task Force on Campus Sexual Assault shortly after the incident and implemented recommendations to address sexual assault on campus.

No criminal charges were brought at the time, and the investigation has been reopened following Jane Doe’s lawsuit. Four of the men, through their attorneys, have denied coercing Jane Doe with drugs or sexually assaulting her. NBC News was not able to reach the other three men named in the lawsuit.
While the faculty senate does not have the authority to remove the president, the move would greatly increase the pressure on Cornell and its administration.

Darlene Evans, a senior lecturer emerita, asked Kotlikoff why he was only taking steps now “towards serious systemic change” when he had been in leadership roles at the university for more than a decade.

Evans noted that more than 35% of female undergraduates surveyed at Cornell University reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual contact involving physical force, threats of force or incapacitation, according to a Cornell University poll conducted last year, a figure that was up from 23% in 2023.

“It wasn’t until a no-confidence vote was introduced that Cornell’s administration announced any real steps to prevent sexual assault on this campus, or to seriously support survivors,” she said. “So saying what we’re going to do now kind of rings hollow here. Why haven’t you taken these things more seriously until now, when there’s a firestorm of press looking at Cornell?”
Kotlikoff announced on Tuesday that all parties at fraternity houses and events would be banned through the rest of the academic year.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
“We don’t have full ability to be confident that what goes on in those houses is safe and so for the time being we will stop that activity,” he said during the meeting on Wednesday.
He also addressed calls from some over whether Greek life at the university should be banned altogether.

“If at the end of the day, fraternities cannot exist in a safe environment, and we can’t be convinced that they can be safe, then we should make that decision,” he said. “But we should make it based on data and study and expertise, not on emotion.”

After a question-and-answer session, the faculty senate began debating the no-confidence resolution, with another meeting scheduled for later this month. Many spoke in favor of the resolution, while others wanted to delay the vote until the results of an upcoming independent investigation.

Earlier this month, the university announced that Sally Yates, the former deputy U.S. attorney general and acting U.S. attorney general, would lead an independent review on how Cornell University responded to the allegations and, more broadly, how it responds to sexual harassment, assault and misconduct on campus.

New York Attorney General Letitia James is also investigating the allegation. A spokesperson said staff members from the attorney general’s office have “spoken with the Tompkins County District Attorney, Jane Doe’s attorney, and several candidates for outside counsel to support the investigation.”

After the meeting, music professor Ariana Kim said she was “really inspired by everyone who spoke and was brave in favor of the resolution — it takes a lot to stand up in front of the president and ask direct questions of him.”
Kim said she has received some 200 emails from alumni saying they support the no-confidence resolution and want the administration to be held accountable.
The professor said some at the meeting held up signs that read, “I stand with Jane Doe,” “How many more?” and “We demand accountability.”
“Some people broke down and held each other after the meeting,” she said.

Political history professor Richard Bensel said that so far the central administration “has not responded in a way that is going to diminish faculty and students’ despair over the way that the university has treated the issue.”
Bensel said he was unsure if he wanted the president to resign, but said he thought university leadership “will not reform itself without passage of the no-confidence resolution.”

“I can imagine a way the trustees through the president can reconcile their relations with the Cornell community but that requires a real change in governance style and I don’t think that is possible under this administration,” he said. “There are real problems in the way the university is run.”

title: Kevin Warsh speech could offer clues on whether Fed will raise interest rates this month
summary: Two inflation reports this week set the stage for a rate hike potentially sooner than previously expected.
story: When Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh strides onstage in Bangkok on Friday morning, it will be after 11 p.m. on Thursday in New York. But investors, economists and politicians in the United States will be awake and hanging on his every word.

Any speech by a Fed chair is closely scrutinized. This week’s talk has an extra dose of urgency, though, after two government reports showed inflation heating up for consumers and businesses — spurring speculation about how soon the Fed will raise interest rates to handle soaring prices.

Warsh will be speaking at the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, where he will be interviewed by IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva. The Fed chairman has repeatedly said he will not use public speaking engagements to intentionally steer the expectations of investors and markets, but his comments could nevertheless signal whether the central bank will hike rates before, or after, the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

It will also be the last speech from a Fed official before policymakers enter a “blackout” period on Saturday that lasts through their next interest rate meeting, which is scheduled for Oct. 27 and 28.
“Broad based” inflation “strengthens the case for an October hike,” Bank of America analysts wrote on Wednesday. “The data continue to underscore two key sources of inflation pressure: AI and Iran.”
Those two factors aren’t likely to be going anywhere soon, either.
The price of politics
Already hammered by soaring interest rates, rising energy prices and stagnant wage growth, American consumers could get an extra dose of financial strain if the Fed raises rates again this month.

Voters are already dissatisfied with President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy, polls show, so another rate hike could add to Republicans’ headaches as they face potentially losing their congressional majorities in the midterms.

In recent weeks, Trump has tried to pull multiple policy levers to lower gas and diesel prices, which have pushed inflation higher in recent months. But none of them have yet slowed prices meaningfully.

“Starting on day one, we will end inflation and make America affordable again,” Trump said on the campaign trail in 2024. Inflation as measured by the consumer price index declined to as low as 2.3% four months into Trump’s term.
But that same month, Trump unleashed a wave of tariffs across the globe, dramatically changing the economic story.

By September, inflation breached the 3% threshold again. In February, Trump launched the war against Iran, causing one of the worst energy supply shocks in history. Inflation jumped as high as 4.1% in May, and looks to be headed back in that direction again.

Another Fed rate hike would also further undermine Trump’s yearslong pressure campaign to push the central bank to cut rates. Since Warsh took his post in May, the central bank has either held rates steady or increased them.
For Subscribers
Trump hasn’t attacked Warsh after years of hammering former Chair Jerome Powell. But the president has started saying that the other members of the Fed’s board are “very hostile.”

“I’m relying on Kevin,” Trump told reporters in September, “but he’s got, you know, a very tough board. He’s got a board that was put there by a lot of other people, and the interest rates are too high.”
For Subscribers
“They’re very political,” Trump said. Four of the Fed’s seven board members were appointed by Trump.

Asked what the president’s expectations are for Warsh’s appearance, the White House pointed to a Truth Social post from September in which Trump had written, “Interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less.”
Diesel and the damage done

Economists and investors are paying close attention to so-called core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices. Both reports this week showed that even this adjusted measure of price growth is running hotter than hoped for.
“Core CPI was the more significant surprise,” wrote analysts at Bank of America.

The core readings showed that skyrocketing fuel prices, particularly diesel, are trickling down. Farmers, truckers and others who keep commerce humming in the United States have to raise their prices in order to digest higher diesel costs. That, in turn, leads to price increases for consumer goods.

“The cost of diesel gets into just about everything,” KPMG chief economist Diane Swonk told NBC News in an August interview.  “Everything from … running a farm … cost of food, but also everything across the economy that’s shipped gets that extra fee tacked onto it.” At the time, she described the surge in diesel fuel prices as likely “an inflationary problem for the next several months.”

Her warning came to fruition in September, according to the consumer price index and producer price index reports this week. With diesel prices remaining solidly above $6 per gallon so far in October, and with no sign that the Iran war is near an end or that attacks on energy assets in the Ukraine-Russia war will be paused, it could keep fueling overall inflation for months.

Big Tech is also fueling inflation. Trillion-dollar companies are spending, and borrowing, big sums for servers, memory and other components that will be used in data centers. That’s caused price spikes across the economy.
Companies including Apple and Nintendo have raised prices as a result. “We have never seen a component price increase this much, this quickly,” Apple told NBC News in June.

Companies are also tapping the public debt markets in an unprecedented way. Data center companies and associated utility firms, chipmakers and cloud providers are expected to raise between $300 billion and $570 billion from the debt market this year, according to Vanguard. Those firms are also offering highly attractive interest rates, sometimes better than U.S. Treasury bonds.
A consequence of that, Warsh noted recently, is that there’s a “competition for capital” driving up interest rates on government debt, too.

“This is a complicated set of things that are affecting the most important asset anywhere in the world, the 10-year Treasury,” Warsh said. “It’s the risk-free asset upon which every price of virtually every asset in the world is related to.”
Without referencing the Iran war, he also said yields were being driven by “geopolitics” and the strength of the economy.

title: ICE agent driving vehicle that struck and injured Houston man is placed on administrative leave
summary: The Harris County DA has interviewed a key witness who was in the ICE vehicle when it hit Miguel Parra Hernandez.
story: The ICE officer accused of running over an immigrant in Houston on Saturday has been put on administrative leave while the incident is investigated, a senior Department of Homeland Security official told NBC News.

As NBC News has reported, a senior DHS official said that multiple ICE officers on the scene at the time were wearing body cameras and that ICE is reviewing video of the scene as part of an internal investigation.
The DHS official said no decision has been made about sharing the video with the public or with the Harris County District Attorney’s Office, which is conducting its own investigation.

District Attorney Sean Teare told NBC News on Thursday that he has interviewed a key witness who was handcuffed in the back of the ICE vehicle when it hit Miguel Parra Hernández. The witness “had a front-row seat to the incident and everything that led up to it,” Teare said. “We did get a significant amount of relevant details from him.”

The witness was interviewed at the Port Isabel Processing Center, about 35 to 40 miles from the U.S.-Mexico border in South Texas, according to the district attorney’s office. The Port Isabel facility is historically known as the last stop before an immigrant is removed from the U.S.

Teare said his office is compiling all information it has gathered or is still gathering, and “in very short order we’re going to come to a point where we present this to a grand jury.” He said that could happen as soon as next week.
Teare and Cesar Espinosa, co-founder and executive director of FIEL Houston, an immigrant civil rights group, identified the witness as José Presa Cañada.

“It’s very troubling” that Presa is in Port Isabel, Espinosa said Thursday. “We want to know why he’s there and why he hasn’t been released yet and why they are trying to deport him so expeditiously.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Teare declined to comment on what was said during the interview with Presa. Teare also has interviewed Parra.

The auto-pedestrian collision Saturday, which left Parra hospitalized with multiple injuries and needing surgery, triggered the investigation, which could result in charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, according to Teare.

The district attorney’s office said it notified ICE soon after the incident that it wanted to interview Presa. In an email, ICE responded that Teare should get to Port Isabel fast because the agency planned to deport Presa, according to the district attorney’s office.
ICE did not immediately respond to a request for information about its detention of Presa and whether it plans to deport him.
ICE has said Parra was not its arrest target on Monday. An agency spokesperson said Parra ran into the ICE vehicle’s path.

The other potential witness who was handcuffed in the ICE vehicle that hit Parra is Luis Delfín Martínez, who is being held in the Montgomery Processing Center in Conroe, north of Houston, according to advocates and relatives.
The district attorney’s office has issued subpoenas for Parra’s medical records, as well as for records of emergency medical personnel who responded when Parra was struck.

Teare, Parra’s attorney Kim Bruno and advocates have been pressing the Trump administration not to deport Parra and the two men in the vehicle and have asked the district attorney and others to protect them.

Teare said in an interview this week that his office had been in touch with consulates for the countries of origin of all three men to let them know it was ready to assist with their applications for visas for witnesses key to criminal cases, known as U visas.
“We’re working with the powers that be in a really significant effort to keep them here in this country,” he said then.

Teare told NBC News that it’s “pretty obvious” from videos his office has collected, including drone video, that ICE intentionally hit and ran over Parra, an allegation ICE has said is reckless and false.

Security video of the incident obtained by NBC affiliate KPRC of Houston shows a white truck facing the opposite direction of traffic on a busy roadway. Parra and another man exit the white truck and run, the video shows.

At about the same time, the video shows, another vehicle jumps a yellow median and heads in Parra’s direction. The video then shows the vehicle, which is not marked, swerving left toward Parra’s path, in front of a truck stopped in a shopping center.
When the parked truck leaves, a man can be seen lying on the pavement behind the ICE vehicle, the video shows.

Teare sought to download data from the ICE vehicle while it was still at the scene, but an agent drove the car away. Driving the car may have automatically erased critical data, said Teare, who led the district attorney’s office’s vehicular crimes division for several years.

title: Pennsylvania house that was scene of mass shooting was ‘filthy,’ filled with bottles of urine
summary: A homicidal family patriarch had become a dominant, isolated, figure inside his “filthy” Erie, Pennsylvania, home before killing eight people.
story: A family patriarch had become “increasingly controlling” inside his “filthy” northwest Pennsylvania home before opening fire and killing eight people last week, officials said Thursday.

Matthew Stone, 45, died of a self-inflicted gunshot on Friday evening, bringing a tragic end to years of descent inside his Perry Street house in Erie, authorities said. The weapon he used was linked to a previous domestic violence allegation, according to police.
Toilets and sinks did not appear to be working and 2-liter bottles filled with urine were all over the house, Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said.
“Detectives described the home as extremely filthy,” Lorah told reporters.
Loved ones painted a disturbing picture of Stone’s dominant role inside that house, police said.
“According to relatives, he controlled the family’s finances ... and restricted when family members could leave the residence or spend time with relatives,” Lorah said.

The police chief went on to say that family members told detectives that his behavior had been going on for years. They described Matthew becoming increasingly controlling after his wife, Michelle Stone, became pregnant with their first child.
For Subscribers

“Over time, contact with extended family became more limited. Michelle stopped maintaining contact with friends,” Lorah said. “Our department also had a record of prior domestic violence incident at that home.”
In that 2019 case, Stone was arrested for allegedly making threats with a .40-caliber handgun. But the case went away when Michelle Stone declined to help press charges, Lorah said.

“A firearm was involved in that case, the same .40-caliber handgun that was used in Friday’s homicides,” Lorah said. “At the preliminary hearing, Michelle changed her original statement and those charges were withdrawn. There were no more recent domestic violence incidents reported to our department. Outside of that 2019 case, Matthew had no criminal history and was legally permitted to possess that firearm.”
For Subscribers
Chief Lorah and Mayor Daria Devlin pledged to examine city contacts with Stone to find if anyone could have intervened before Friday’s bloodshed.

“Were there opportunities to recognize that this family was struggling?” Devlin said. “Were there places where our systems could have responded differently and how do we make sure that families in this community who are suffering and struggling like this don’t fall through the cracks?”

The victims included the killer’s wife, Michelle Stone, 44; pregnant daughter, Angelina K. Stone, 24; sons Matthew Stone Jr., 21, and Jonathan Stone, 19; sister-in-law Lora Lee Roberts, 37, and her friend Twila A. Tanner, 51.
Two other unidentified children, a 5-year-old boy and a nearly 2-year-old girl who were also related to the shooter, were killed inside the house, officials said.
Roberts and her friend Tanner had come to the house when Angelina Stone, who was due to give birth on Monday, asked for a ride to the hospital.

“Angelina had been sending messages indicating she planned to leave the family home after giving birth,” Lorah said. “When detectives searched the home following the shooting, they found numerous belongings packed into bags and boxes in Angelina’s bedroom.”
Angelina Stone had also filed paperwork to change her last name to distance herself from her eventual killer.

“In that affidavit, she described concerns about her father’s declining mental health,” Lorah said. “She explained that she wanted to pursue a career in medicine and did not want her association with her father to affect those plans.”

title: FBI employees involved in Trump classified documents case sue over ‘unlawful’ firings
summary: Nine former FBI employees involved in the classified documents case against President Donald Trump filed suit Thursday against FBI Director Kash Patel and Attorney General Todd Blanche, alleging their firings were “unlawful.”
story: Nine former FBI employees involved in the classified documents case against President Donald Trump filed suit Thursday against FBI Director Kash Patel and Attorney General Todd Blanche, alleging their firings were “unlawful.”

The group’s suit says they were fired without cause for their work on the case involving Trump, and that the firings appeared to be politically motivated. It noted they were booted while Patel was being criticized by the administration for partying with the U.S. Olympic hockey team.

FBI Special Agent Miles Starr, who was working in a unit called the “Director’s Advisory Team” that was apparently formed to look into Trump’s perceived political enemies, had demanded urgent access to the “Plasmic Echo” case file — the code name for the investigation into the classified documents case — on Feb. 23, the lawsuit says. That was after video of Patel chugging a beer and “flinging alcohol around the U.S. men’s hockey team’s locker room at the Winter Olympics in Milan, Italy, began circulating widely on social media and news sites,” the suit says.
The file had the names of the agents who’d worked on the investigation, and they were summarily fired over the next few days without any of the required due process, the suit says.

“Each Plaintiff was provided with a termination letter signed by Director Patel” that falsely claimed that they had exercised “poor judgment and a lack of impartiality in carrying out their duties, leading to the political weaponization of the government,” the suit says.
Patel later told Congress they were fired for cause and after internal investigations, claims the suit says are not true.
NBC News has reached out to the FBI and the Justice Department for comment.

The filing says the former employees “did not volunteer to participate in Plasmic Echo; they were assigned to the case because they were members of specific FBI Counterintelligence and Intelligence squads” and the nine “performed their duties apolitically.”
Among the other cases members of the group had worked on were the Boston Marathon bombing and the investigation into the attempted assassination of Trump in Butler, Pennsylvania.

The plaintiffs, Jennifer Bacon, Zach Feldman, Gilbert Granados, Catherine Herrera, Harrison Kaufman, Jeremy Linton, Erin Matanic, Danielle Ray and Rachel Vaccaro, have “over a century of experience and service to the FBI” among them and were “involved in numerous high-profile investigations to thwart threats and respond to crises and attacks against the United States,” the suit says, and their abrupt firings affected more than just them.
The nine were “involved in ongoing and sensitive counterintelligence and counterterrorism investigations in connection with threats emanating from countries across the globe,” the filing says.

“As a result of their unlawful and hasty firings, Plaintiffs’ investigations were not properly transferred to other FBI Special Agents or Analysts,” it says. “The impacts of these heedless actions on America’s national security is immeasurable.”

The group’s attorneys, Margaret Donovan, Abbe D. Lowell and Rebecca S. Tinio, said in a joint statement that the suit would prove their clients were unlawfully fired and hold the Trump administration accountable for “this blatant attack on the rule of law.”

The agents were dismissed “because they did their jobs, as they always did, to follow the facts and law without bias or favor. To this administration, this is an offense. To the rest of us, it is heroic,” the lawyers’ statement said.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The agents’ investigation helped lead to the then-former president being charged in June 2023 on allegations that he lied and schemed to mislead federal investigators to retain sensitive materials that he knew were still classified after he left the White House.

The indictment alleged that the documents he took with him “included information regarding defense and weapons capabilities of both the U.S. and foreign countries; United States nuclear programs; potential vulnerabilities of the United States and its allies to military attack; and plans for a possible retaliation in response to a foreign attack.”

Trump was later charged with trying to obstruct the investigation. He pleaded not guilty to all the charges, and the case was ultimately dismissed after U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon, a Trump appointee, found the special counsel who led the investigation, Jack Smith, had been appointed improperly.
A Justice Department appeal of that ruling was dropped after Trump was re-elected in 2024.

The lawsuit says it was clear that employees who’d worked on investigations involving Trump were “doomed” because he and other top government officials “made clear in numerous public statements that they intended to exact revenge against anyone Trump deemed to have wronged him.”

“Before and after Plaintiffs’ firings, President Trump, Defendant Patel, Defendant Blanche, and others in Trump’s orbit publicly impugned Plaintiffs’ integrity, despite their unimpeachable service records; smeared their work as politically motivated, when it was not; and made clear that their fate was sealed by virtue of simply having worked on an investigation into Trump’s wrongdoing,” the complaint reads.

The lawsuit notes Starr, the person who accessed the case file, was also involved in the first indictment of FBI Director James Comey last year, a case that was ultimately dismissed and that Comey’s team has said was politically motivated.
The suit seeks to have the employees reinstated to their jobs and awarded back pay for the time they’ve missed.

A similar lawsuit was filed earlier this year by two former FBI special agents who said they were wrongfully fired for what they described as their minimal roles in “Arctic Frost,” Smith’s investigation into the alleged criminal conspiracy to overturn Trump’s 2020 election loss.

Trump pleaded not guilty to the charges in that case, which were dismissed after his election victory due to long-standing Justice Department policy stating that sitting presidents can’t face federal charges.
The Justice Department has moved to dismiss that lawsuit, which is pending.

title: Experts say this is the best time to clean your gutters
summary: Clean your gutters too early and you’ll have to do it again, wait too long and they could overflow. Experts explain when to clean them and how to do it.
story: With all the content available online these days, it can be hard to figure out what’s real and what’s hype. While we don’t always have the answers, we have a direct line to people who do — which is why we present to you our series The Internet Made Me Ask, where we have experts break down the truth about some of the buzziest trends (and questions) on our timelines, like how often you should wash jeans.

Cleaning your gutters is one of those fall chores where timing is everything. Do it too early, and you’ll likely find yourself back on the ladder a few weeks later once the rest of the leaves come down. If you wait too long, you risk clogged gutters overflowing during a rainstorm, which can lead to water damage around your roof, siding, and foundation.
So when exactly is the sweet spot? I spoke to two experts to find out when you should clean your gutters and how to do it safely and effectively.
When is the right time to clean your gutters?

The best way to tell if it is time to clean your gutters is to look at the trees around your yard. “Ideally, you want to do a major clean right after the majority of the leaves have fallen — usually late autumn,” says Zack Nienaber, owner of Nienaber and Sons Lawn Care in Cincinnati. “If you do it too early before the trees shed, you’ll just end up having to do it all over again once the rest drops.”

That said, the exact timing depends on where you live and what kinds of trees surround your home, which is why you really need to let your yard be your guide rather than the calendar. Once the branches overhead look mostly bare, it’s time to get to work. Just don’t put it off for too long: Gutters packed with leaves can’t drain properly, so the next heavy rain could send water spilling over the sides — and the U.S. has been seeing a lot of rain this season, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
What do you need to clean your gutters?

Cleaning your gutters probably isn’t anyone’s idea of a fun weekend, but it doesn’t have to be miserable, either. I’m sharing expert steps on how to do it below, but first, here are some tools that can make the job faster, safer, and a lot less messy. These are the types of tools the experts I spoke to suggest having on hand before you start.
Louisville Fiberglass Extension Ladder

A good extension ladder will help you reach the gutters, says Nienaber. This fiberglass extension ladder reaches up to 21 feet when fully extended, giving you enough height to get to second-story gutters. It supports up to 300 pounds and has slip-resistant, D-shaped rungs to help you keep your footing while you work. The swivel safety shoes at the base help keep the ladder steady. One helpful tip: “Don’t lean the ladder against the gutters — it can bend or crush them,” says Nienaber. “Instead, rest it against the roof.”
Vivd Works Gutter Scooper

Nienaber says a plastic gutter scooper can help you get debris out while protecting your hands. This one is made from high-impact polypropylene and has a deep, curved scoop that lets you grab big clumps of wet leaves at once. It also has an ergonomic handle and fits most gutters, according to the brand.
Handlady Work Gloves

Gloves protect your hands from sharp twigs, rough gutter edges, and all the wet muck you’ll be scooping out. This pair has padded synthetic leather palms that help you keep a firm grip on your ladder and tools, plus a stretchy, breathable back so your hands stay comfortable. They’re also flexible enough that you can handle a scoop or hose.
Alloyman Cordless, Extendable Leaf Blower

If you’d rather stay off a ladder, this cordless leaf blower comes with a 4.5-foot attachment that lets you clear leaves from your gutters while standing on the ground. It has a brushless motor with two speed settings. The kit also comes with two 40-volt batteries and a charger.
How to clean your gutters

Take time to set up your station: Before you start pulling out leaves, set yourself up to work safely. “Make sure your ladder is on stable, level ground,” says Nienaber, who also suggests wearing thick gloves. “I then like to scoop the debris out by hand into a bucket rather than blasting everything down the downspout (the vertical pipe that goes from gutter to ground) and packing it solid.”

Create a game plan for the process: Where you start matters, too. “Begin at the downspout and proceed to the far end of the gutter — this way, you will clear the downspout opening first and prevent yourself from pushing debris into it,” says Constantine Anest, owner of Ethos Roofing & Restoration in Denver.
Rinse last: After you’ve removed the leaves and twigs, finish with a rinse. “Once the bulk is out, flush the system with a hose to make sure the water flows freely through the spouts,” says Nienaber.
Frequently asked questions

Putting off the job can lead to much bigger and more expensive problems than a few stray leaves. “It gets messy fast — heavy, wet leaves turn into packed sludge that adds a ton of weight, which can pull the gutters right off the fascia boards,” says Nienaber. “Worse, blocked water overflows right against your foundation, which leads to basement leaks, or it freezes up into ice dams when winter hits.” In other words, an hour or two on a ladder this fall could save you from costly repairs down the line.

You can usually tell your gutters are due for a cleaning without ever climbing a ladder. If you see leaves peeking out of the top of your gutters, that is a good sign.  Or, if water spills over the edge during a rainstorm instead of flowing into the downspout, says Anest.  If you spot either one, it’s time to clear your gutters out before the next storm rolls in.
